articles.title: Phision shows off a new SSD design with its own NPU and 64GB of memory — which it says can cut data transfers by 10 to 100 times
articles.text:
Phision shows off a new SSD design with its own NPU and 64GB of memory — which it says can cut data transfers by 10 to 100 times
Phison's new SSD design packs an NPU and 64GB memory
- Phison detailed an unnamed SSD architecture at SC26 with an integrated NPU rated at 36,800 DMIPS and 64GB of memory at 130GB/s
- It claims on-drive filtering could cut data transfers by 10 to 100 times for suitable workloads while also taking load off CPUs
- There is no product name, controller, power figure, price, or date yet; Phison says the design is still in development
Phison wants enterprise SSDs to stop acting purely as warehouses and start doing some of the sorting themselves.
At the recent Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) event, the company detailed a computational storage architecture that places an integrated NPU and 64GB of memory with 130GB/s of bandwidth inside the drive.
This marks a break from the usual modus operandi: Rather than shipping entire datasets across PCIe to a host CPU or GPU, the drive is meant to scan and process data in parallel where it already sits, then send back only the relevant results, an approach that Phison says could potentially reduce data transfers by 10 to 100 times while freeing up host CPU resources.
A large claim, with a large caveat?
Phison says the design supports PyTorch, vLLM, OpenVINO, and llama.cpp, and that developers can build for it without specialized programming tools. As TechSpot put it, the idea is for some of the processing to happen before the data ever leaves the drive.
The idea is novel but comes with an interesting caveat: Phison says the reduction applies only to workloads where the approach fits, and the company has published no methodology, test dataset, or benchmark to back it up.
That caveat matters more than it might seem, because a data reduction ratio is mostly a property of the workload rather than the hardware. Sending ten times less data means the drive returns a tenth of what it scanned; a hundred times less means it returns one percent.
A selective filter run over log files or a database table can hit those ratios on any architecture that pushes the filter down to storage, while a job that needs most of the dataset will not come close. That reading of the arithmetic is mine rather than Phison's, but it explains why the claimed range spans a full order of magnitude.

The metric being measured is also somewhat interesting, to say the least: The only compute figure Phison has offered is 36,800 DMIPS. Dhrystone MIPS is an integer CPU benchmark dating back to the 1980s, not the TOPS rating normally quoted for neural processors.
Tom's Hardware argues the figure most likely describes the general-purpose cores sitting beside the accelerator, probably Arm-based, which would be adequate for running the drive but reveals nothing about AI throughput. The same report notes that Phison's Topaz NPU card at Computex carried eight NPUs rated at up to 40 TOPS each, which makes the absence of a comparable figure here all the more conspicuous. For the record, Phison has not said whether the drive's NPU is related to Topaz.
The memory figure is more revealing. Phison has not disclosed the memory type, but 130GB/s is consistent with a 128-bit LPDDR5X interface: at 8,000 MT/s that works out to 128GB/s, and at 8,533 MT/s to roughly 136GB/s. Phison's Topaz NPU supports LPDDR5/5X at up to 8,533 MT/s, so the numbers line up, but I have not received any official confirmation.
Support for llama.cpp will tempt some to picture an SSD that serves large language models, but the bandwidth points elsewhere: Token generation is usually memory-bound, since each new token requires a pass over the model's weights, so bandwidth divided by model size gives a rough ceiling.
An 8-billion-parameter model quantized to 4 bits, at roughly 4.5 to 5GB, would top out around 25 to 30 tokens per second. A 70-billion-parameter model at the same precision would fit in 64GB but peak at about three tokens per second. This means that while the SSD could host an LLM, anything but the most basic ones will struggle to deliver adequate performance.
This fits Hardware Busters' reading that the design is about data reduction close to the NAND rather than running large models, and that it should not be treated as a GPU replacement. Small models that classify, tag, or embed data before it leaves the drive look like the most plausible approach here.
It is also worth separating the 130GB/s figure from how quickly the drive can read its own flash. Memory bandwidth is not NAND bandwidth, and Phison has not disclosed the controller, channel count, host interface, or capacity for this design. Nor has it said whether the drive uses the PCIe 6.0 X3 controller it promoted at the same show.
A promising idea that has been explored before
The most striking context here comes from Phison itself. In a 2021 interview with TechRadar Pro, Sebastien Jean, then Phison's senior director of systems architecture and now CTO of Phison US, said computational storage "appears to be an easy sell, but it hasn't turned out that way." He argued that an SSD already devotes its full resources and power budget to its primary job.
He sharpened that position in a 2025 essay on Phison's blog, writing that when engineers discuss computational storage, "too often it's a pie-in-the-sky approach," and singling out the idea of running Linux on a drive with bigger processors. His alternative was targeted accelerators applying fixed operations to ranges of logical block addresses, such as filtering, checksum verification, and erasure coding.
Computational storage itself, however, has a patchy record. Samsung first floated its SmartSSD in 2018 and followed up with an AMD Xilinx-powered second generation in 2022, when it declared that "the computational storage market has great potential." As TechRadar Pro has previously reported, the drive then faded from Samsung's lineup, with remaining units sold under the AMD Xilinx brand, and even ScaleFlux, one of the category's loudest champions, dropped the term from its company description.
ScaleFlux has done better by keeping the compute out of sight. Its CSD 5320 compresses data in hardware on the fly, and Tom's Hardware notes that drives present themselves to the host as ordinary NVMe SSDs, so applications need no changes.
Standards have moved on, too. NVM Express released Computational Programs and Subsystem Local Memory command sets in January 2024, giving hosts a standard way to load and run programs on a drive. Phison has not said whether its design uses them, or how a host would submit work to the NPU. Framework support is not the same thing as existing code running unchanged.
The design slots neatly into Phison's wider AI messaging. Michael Wu, GM and president of Phison US, said in the announcement that "the next era of computing won't be defined by processing power alone."
However, until Phison publishes a TOPS figure, a power envelope, a host programming model, and a benchmark showing where the 10- to 100-times reduction comes from, this is best read as a statement of direction rather than a tangible product for the AI masses.

articles.title: 'Whenever Blizzard makes a game, it attracts more people to the genre' — Path of Exile 2 game director says that ARPG competition with Diablo is a good thing
articles.text:
No, Path of Exile 2 isn't worried about Diablo V because 'whenever Blizzard makes a game, it attracts more people to the genre'
Game Director suggests a rising tide of blood and loot will raise all ships
It’s been a long two years since its 0.1 launch into Early Access, but Path of Exile 2 is finally reaching its full launch on December 11.
The major milestone includes the two remaining story acts, two playable classes (the Duelist and the Shadow), and much more, but in the time since its initial launch and now, we’ve had a Diablo 4 expansion that was fantastic, Lord of Hatred, as well as the announcement of Diablo 5.
With Blizzard’s own ARPG still some years away, Path of Exile 2’s Game Director Jonathan Rogers was asked, as part of a group interview, how the team feels about Diablo and other genre contemporaries. In short: Grinding Gear Games fears no man (or rival), and actually thinks it’s good for the genre.
Diablo V is a good thing, according to Path of Exile 2’s Game Director
Confirming Path of Exile 2 has been in development for eight years, and that the team couldn’t possibly have lined up its full release on the back of Diablo’s fifth entry being revealed (albeit for 2029!), Rogers was full of praise for Blizzard.
“The nice thing is, though, and this is the thing that's been amazing for us every time, is that whenever Blizzard makes a game, it attracts more people to the [ARPG] genre.”
“And that means that more of those players will also come and play our game as well. So I've always found that, to be honest, them announcing new products and making new things is honestly the best thing for us.”
“If you’re talking about MMOs, generally people only play one MMO at a time. But in the ARPG space, you know, because we’re seasonal, it means you can play multiple ARPGs. So bringing more people to the genre is always going to be better than having less people,” he explains.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
“Generally, people play a season for two weeks to four weeks, and so that means that there's plenty of time left in the year for people to play other ARPGs. And many of our players do play other ARPGs.”
“There's not really the same competition that you might see in other game types, and that’s part of the reason why Path of Exile 2 makes sense to have as well as Path of Exile 1, because they don't need to compete with each other, because once again it's seasonal; people can play both or just one, regardless of what they want.”
Diablo II players, this one’s for you
Still, there are many who would suggest that Path of Exile (the original) was in many ways a spiritual successor to Diablo 2. So what does Rogers say to Diablo fans who haven’t yet taken a trip to Wraeclast?
“If you were a person who played the more modern Diablo games, then the thing I would say to them is that Path of Exile 2 has pretty excellent combat compared to what we were doing in Path of Exile 1,” Rogers admits, pointing to more action-focused combat in the sequel.
“If you were a Diablo 2 player back in the day, then the thing I would say is that we're one of the few people that are doing the same sort of economy and item system stuff that Diablo 2 was doing.”
“That's not too common these days in a lot of games, so that's something that I think that a Diablo 2 player would really appreciate.”
“And sort of surprisingly, there are a lot of people out there who played Diablo 2 who still haven't played Path of Exile yet. So I think it's still worth talking to those players. Because, yeah, it's quite a big segment of the audience.”
You heard the man — you can jump in for free on December 11 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X and S.

The cheapest 2TB PCIe 5.0 drive we've seen so far during Black Friday sales

Although there are plenty of SSD deals going, as you can see in our roundup of the best Black Friday SSD deals, there aren't a ton of PCIe 5.0 drives marked down. articles.title: These are the best Wi-Fi 7 mesh routers from Asus, TP-Link, Eero, Netgear, and MSI that I found on Black Friday
articles.text:
These are the best Wi-Fi 7 mesh routers from Asus, TP-Link, Eero, Netgear, and MSI that I found on Black Friday
There is an embarrassment of riches if you're looking to upgrade to a Wi-Fi 7 router for Black Friday
Mesh routers are among the hottest-selling types of routers in networking, and leading the charge are products based on the Wi-Fi 7 standard. Mesh routers enable you to fully cover your home or office with wireless coverage that would otherwise be impossible with a single, standalone router.
Fortunately, numerous manufacturers are producing Wi-Fi 7 mesh routers, offering a wide range of options to choose from. If you prefer seamless integration with your Amazon account and Alexa services, consider opting for the Eero Pro 7. If you want endless configuration options and no-cost features, such as extensive Parental Controls, the Asus ZenWiFi BT4 has you covered. If you're looking for a delicate balance of performance and features at a bargain price, consider the TP-Link Deco BE95.
However, one thing to keep in mind when shopping for a network upgrade is that not all Wi-Fi 7 routers are created equal. While there are speed differences between products that depend on several factors (channel width, total number of streams, etc.), the primary differentiator among Wi-Fi 7 routers comes down to the number of supported bands. There are dual- and tri-band routers, with the latter offering the best potential performance. Dual-band routers only support the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, while tri-band routers support the higher-performing and shorter-range 6 GHz band. The maximum performance of the 6 GHz band is what gives tri-band Wi-Fi 7 routers a significant theoretical speed advantage over their Wi-Fi 6E predecessors.
Some manufacturers, such as Asus, also offer quad-band routers that feature either two 5 GHz wireless bands or two 6 GHz bands.

articles.title: Canal+ enchaîne les bugs, et cette fois ce sont ses décodeurs qui ont un souci
articles.text:
Canal+ a confirmé mercredi subir une panne sur ses décodeurs. La lecture des replays avec publicités est perturbée par une erreur EESPT. Le groupe promet de rétablir le service « dans les meilleurs délais ».
Les abonnés Canal+ équipés d'un décodeur ont du mal à regarder leurs replays ces jours-ci. Une fois la lecture de la publicité terminée, une erreur EESPT empêche le programme de démarrer. Canal+ a reconnu l'incident le mercredi 25 novembre, sans en préciser la cause. Mais plusieurs abonnés affirment subir la panne depuis deux à trois jours et la rapprochent aux récentes hausses de tarifs.
Sur les décodeurs Canal+, le replay cale après la publicité
Mercredi, Canal+ a publié un message indiquant qu'« un incident technique perturbe actuellement la lecture des programmes en replay avec pub sur les décodeurs CANAL+ ». Ses équipes sont « mobilisées pour rétablir le service dans les meilleurs délais ». Pas plus d'infos donc, à ce stade, sur les causes ni même sur le calendrier d'une éventuelle résolution.
Pour les abonnés, le souci dure depuis deux à trois jours désormais. Certains décrivent une publicité qui se lance normalement, puis un programme qui refuse de démarrer. L'un a débranché sa télévision, comme Canal+ l'avait recommandé selon lui.
Un autre a éteint puis rallumé son décodeur. Mais rien n'y fait. Ce dernier raconte aussi avoir perdu le direct en fin d'après-midi mercredi, « écran noir », et avoir cru le problème réglé ce soir, avant que l'erreur revienne « au bout de 10 minutes ». Un troisième assure ne capter plus que CNews et Europe 1, sans savoir s'il joue de mauvaise foi ou s'il dit vrai.
Certains abonnés Canal perdent patience
Sur le forum d'assistance de Canal+, la colère monte. « Assurez d'abord un service correct ! », écrit un abonné, en majuscules dans le texte. Un autre réclame un « dédommagement financier », et un troisième multiplie les relances (« Alors Canal ?? ») sans réponse visible dans le fil. Joint par téléphone, le service client aurait promis à un abonné un retour à la normale dans la soirée.
On lui a aussi proposé quelques mois d'accès gratuit à Canal+ en clair. C'est « sympa », reconnaît-il, « mais il faudrait que le service fonctionne ». Les prix, comme souvent, nourrissent aussi la rancœur. Un client abonné depuis 22 ans affirme que la location de ses deux décodeurs est passée de 14 à 18 euros. S'y ajoutent selon lui la hausse de l'abonnement et des chaînes supprimées « à leur guise ».
Pas plus tard que lundi, le groupe a aussi reconnu que la version 6.3.1 de son appli ne se lançait plus sur certains iPad sous iPadOS 17.7.1. Reste à espérer que le correctif arrive vite, et qu'il referme une série de bugs dont Canal+ se passerait bien, tout comme ses abonnés.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Two GeoServer Flaws as Researchers Warn of Unauthenticated RCE Chains
articles.text:
Threat actors are actively exploiting two newly patched security flaws in GeoServer, according to watchTowr.
The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243, details of which are below -
- CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An arbitrary file read vulnerability that could enable an attacker to access local text files readable by the GeoServer process or fetch adversary-selected HTTP or HTTPS URLs by means of a single unauthenticated Web Feature Service (WFS) request.
- CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to invoke OWS operations that are otherwise protected by service security rules.
Advisories for both the flaws were published on November 24, 2026, in the following versions -
- CVE-2026-120705: org.geoserver:gs-wfs-core - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7
- CVE-2026-120705: org.geotools:gt-metadata - 35.2, 34.6, and 33.7
- CVE-2026-129243: org.geoserver:gs-ows - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7
"Attackers sent error-based exploit probes to validate that the server is vulnerable by creating and invoking stored queries," the preemptive exposure management firm said in an X post today.
Eye Security, which discovered and reported CVE-2026-120705, said the flaw can be combined with two other vulnerabilities in the same product to create an unauthenticated remote code execution chain -
- CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use of a hard-coded signing key ("geoserver") vulnerability in the "remember me" functionality that could be exploited to forge administrator authentication. (Fixed in org.geoserver:gs-main versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7)
- CVE-2026-120704 (CVSS score: 7.2) - An improper control of the generation of code vulnerability that could allow an administrator, or anyone with access to an administrator session, to execute arbitrary code as the user running GeoServer. (Fixed in org.geoserver.security:gs-sec-jdbc versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7)
In a hypothetical attack chain, a bad actor can follow the steps below -
- Exploit CVE-2026-120705 to access "users.xml," a file containing GeoServer usernames and password hashes, and obtain the password representation along with the static signing key extracted from the security configuration ("security/config.xml").
- Exploit CVE-2026-129245 to forge a valid administrator authentication cookie by using the predictable signing key and the stored password representation without having to know the administrator password.
- Exploit CVE-2026-120704 to abuse an administrator-controlled JDBC configuration to execute code from an uploaded native library on both Linux and Windows versions of GeoServer.
According to the project maintainers, CVE-2026-129245 is also part of a five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain that involves -
- CVE-2026-129244 (CVSS score: 6.9) - WFS stored query exception discloses data directory path
- CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - Service security rules bypassed with a prefixed service name such as x/WFS
- CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Unauthenticated WFS GetFeatureById XML injection
- CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - Predictable "remember me" key allows administrator session forgery
- CVE-2026-129242 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Deserialization in JDBC user and role services allows administrator code execution
"An attacker who obtains an administrator password digest, through any file disclosure or a copy of the data directory, can log in as that administrator," GeoServer maintainers said. "Changing the key in security/config.xml does not help when the same file disclosure also reveals the key."
Jonah Burgess, a Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7, who goes by the online alias CryptoCat has been acknowledged for independently discovering and reporting the five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain on August 2, 2026.
"Prefixing the Web Feature Service (WFS) name, as in x/WFS, slips past the admin-only rule for stored queries. GeoServer turns escaped text in a saved query into live xi:include elements, which leaks the files holding the remember-me key and the admin password digest," the researcher said.
"Those two values forge an administrator cookie without cracking the password. As admin, the attacker points a JDBC user service at an uploaded HSQLDB database, and the bundled driver deserialises a stored value that runs commands."
In light of active exploitation of two of the flaws, users are advised to update to GeoServer versions 2.27.7, 2.28.6, and 3.0.2 released over the past month as soon as possible.
The development comes a little over three months after another critical flaw in GeoServer (CVE-2026-76904, CVSS score: 9.8) witnessed active exploitation efforts as a zero-day.
(The story has been updated after publication to include more details of the flaws and emphasize that advisories for the issues were released on November 24, 2026. The patches were originally released in October and early November 2026.)

articles.title: Razer China partners up with Durex for a limited-edition kit of mousepad and condoms — Long-Lasting Battle Armor meets Heavy Armored Beetle
articles.text:
Razer China partners up with Durex for a limited-edition kit with a mousepad and condoms — Long-Lasting Battle Armor meets Heavy Armored Beetle
An interesting choice for the target demographic.
Razer, the brand best-known for its gaming peripherals and laptops, has another quirky collaboration. This time around, the Singapore-American company managed to squeeze in a partnership with Durex for a limited-edition pack of a Razer Goliath mousepad with two Razer-branded Durex Performa delay condoms.
Before everyone gets too excited, this partnership is specific to the China region. Prospective gamers hoping for a bit of extra after-match fun can reportedly get their hands on the package in two ways: as post-purchase gifts at the Razer or Durex stores on JD.com, or at Tmall's Durex store via redeeming points or as a special offer during live-stream events. There will also be a giveaway held on Dec. 7, though no further details were provided.
There's a lot of inter-cultural play in this promotion, as the Goliathus mouse pad is named Heavy Armored Beetle in China (重装甲虫), while the specific Durex condom variant is 持久战甲, roughly "long-lasting battle armor," or protection — plus, both contain the armor/shell symbol 甲. The doubles fun continues with "DLS", as it can be read as "take Razer" (Dài Léishé) or the local pronunciation of Durex, Dùlěisī. The partnership's slogan is "for gaming, bring Razer; for romance, bring Durex."
Razer and Durex may stand out as quite the odd couple, but the condom maker has been a sponsor of the Chinese League of Legends Pro League since 2023. Meanwhile, Razer is no stranger to quirky collaborations, as we've seen Razer Gillette razors, Razer-Panerai watches, sneakers, pickleball paddles, Dolce & Gabbana-branded headsets, and even tea. The younger Chinese demographic is reportedly more open to this type of initiative, with unconventional branding pairings having good market uptake.
Online commenters were quick to exercise their proverbial mouths, questioning if the target gamer demographics would have a use for the condoms to begin with, and some suggested the decision to offer only two per pack was probably wise. Some outlets were cracking jokes about RGB lighting on the rubbers, too.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: AI server giants including HPE, Dell and more are reportedly hiking prices by 45% months after contracts have been signed as memory shortage bites
articles.text:
AI server giants including HPE, Dell and more are reportedly hiking prices by 45% months after contracts have been signed as memory shortage bites
Signed an AI server deal last year? That could be costly
- Dell, HPE, Lenovo, and Supermicro are reportedly asking for 25% to 45% more on AI server orders months after signing, citing surging memory costs as a key issue
- GPU servers are reportedly up 20% to 30%, while memory-heavy CPU nodes have tripled or more, with memory prices up over 400% since 2024
- Buyers are mostly paying anyway, while four vendors either declined or did not respond to requests for comment
Buying AI servers used to be simple, if expensive: agree on a price, sign the contract, wait for the racks to arrive.
That dynamic has now changed considerably, with the last step becoming where the real negotiation takes place, reports from the Financial Times have claimed.
The FT reported Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro have been going back to customers months after deals were signed and asking for substantially more money before delivery, with insiders familiar with the developments telling it that increases between signing and delivery have reached 25%, 30% and, on some orders, as much as 45%, with suppliers blaming the cost of memory.
Paying up to avoid empty racks
The buyers named by FT are high-frequency and quantitative trading firms, including Jane Street, Optiver, and Hudson River Trading, all of which are expanding their data center footprints.
Most of those customers appear to be absorbing the increases. One person described "a significant disparity between the price initially agreed months in advance" and what firms end up paying on delivery, according to Seeking Alpha's summary of the FT report. Another, quoted by TechSpot, summed it up plainly: "the compute is valuable to us, and we'll pay for it."
For a trading firm, where idle capacity has a cost of its own, that is a rational calculation. It also tells suppliers exactly how much leverage they hold. The FT asked whether the affected buyers had contract clauses protecting them from post-signing changes, and Tom's Hardware reports that none would confirm or deny it.
HPE and Supermicro also declined to comment on the price adjustments, while Dell and Lenovo did not respond. Optiver and Hudson River Trading also declined to comment, and Jane Street did not respond.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The FT points to memory as the main driver, citing JPMorgan research that puts the rise in memory prices at more than 400% since the start of 2024. The impact varies sharply by machine type. GPU servers have reportedly risen by at least 20% to 30%, while CPU nodes, where memory makes up a much larger share of the bill, have tripled or more.
That split is what you would expect. In a GPU server, the accelerators dominate the cost, so even a dramatic DRAM increase gets diluted across the system. In a conventional CPU node, memory is one of the biggest cost components, so the same increase hits far harder.
Relief is not close, either. Nvidia told some of its largest customers in August 2026 that servers built around its chips would cost more than 15% more on systems shipping from early 2027.
Micron has warned that supply will be much tighter in 2027 and 2028 than it was this year, and SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won has said the shortage could run until 2030. Dell vice chairman and COO Jeff Clarke told analysts on November 24 2026, "We think that crunch continues clearly into 2027," according to Yahoo Finance.
The anonymous figures are hard to test, but one case has now become a courtroom affair: In June 2026, XTX Finland Oy, part of the London-based algorithmic trading group XTX Markets, sued Dell Products Unlimited Company in Ireland's High Court, the Irish Times reported.
According to XTX, it agreed in November 2025 to buy 1,680 servers for a 15,000-square-meter data center at a fixed price of about $549 million, and paid an extra $5 million on top of the quote specifically to avoid exposure to future price increases.
Delivery then slipped by two months, and Dell said higher component costs meant XTX would have to pay a further $62 million to $70 million. Some $70 million has been placed in escrow. In an affidavit, XTX director Cameron Scott Hill said Dell was "embarrassed" by the situation.
Dell disputes XTX's claims: It said it was not willing to lose tens of millions of dollars on the deal, that it could not deliver on the terms it believed applied when the agreement was signed, and that other customers facing increases had gone to rival suppliers before coming back and accepting the adjustments. The case has been admitted to the fast-track Commercial Court and is due back in December.
Repricing has been in the small print for a year
None of this is hidden policy: Last December, internal Dell guidance reviewed by Business Insider warned that "ordering today for future delivery does not lock in current prices," as TechRadar Pro reported, at a time when the major OEMs were already planning server price rises of around 15%.
HPE went further in March: CEO Antonio Neri said the company had amended its quoting terms "with the right to reprice existing orders for commodity cost increases," TechRadar Pro reported, noting that memory and storage make up around half of a traditional server's bill of materials.
In August, HPE partly reversed course, guaranteeing quotes on most compute, storage, and GreenLake Flex deals below $1 million net with no adjustment between order and shipment, and doubling quote validity from 15 to 30 days, according to SDxCentral. That helps smaller buyers, but it does nothing at AI cluster scale. For context, XTX's order alone is more than 500 times that threshold.
Suppliers argue they have no choice, and an OEM that committed to a fixed price a year ago and must now buy DRAM at today's rates can genuinely lose money on a deal. Dell's latest results, published two days after the FT report, cut both ways. Revenue more than doubled to $54.9 billion, the AI server backlog hit a record $132.3 billion, and the operating income rate climbed 490 basis points to 14.2%, a gain CFO David Kennedy said was "driven primarily by scale and pricing discipline," according to Dell.
Gross margin, an arguably better gauge of what Dell charges relative to what it pays for parts, rose just 10 basis points to 21.2%. That suggests Dell is largely passing costs through rather than widening its spread, which supports the vendors' argument. What it doesn't explain is why a customer who paid specifically for price certainty should still carry those costs and the risks they carry.
For now, the answer comes down to leverage. Supply trails demand; buyers would rather pay than leave data halls empty, and suppliers know it. The December hearing in Dublin may be the first real test of whether a price guarantee on an AI server order still means anything. Until memory supply catches up, a signed purchase order looks less like a price and more like an estimate.

articles.title: 1Password confirme une fuite de données chez ses clients
articles.text:
1Password confirme qu'un pirate a téléchargé les noms et les adresses e-mail d'une partie de ses clients, après avoir accédé au compte GitHub professionnel d'un employé. Les coffres-forts où sont rangés vos mots de passe sont intacts, mais l'éditeur met ses clients en garde contre le phishing.
Le pirate s'est servi de ce compte GitHub pour accéder au code source de 1Password, puis pour installer un code malveillant sur ses serveurs internes. Avec ce code, il a téléchargé des données de comptes clients, avec les noms, les adresses e-mail de connexion, les dates de création et de dernière connexion, ou encore des jetons tirés de certains liens envoyés par e-mail. L'éditeur parle seulement d'un « sous-ensemble » de ses clients. Le nombre de personnes concernées est inconnu, relève The Verge, pour qui cette fuite pourrait exposer les clients à des tentatives de phishing.
1Password allonge les codes envoyés par e-mail
Les jetons volés viennent de liens d'invitation, de création et de récupération de compte. Un jeton sert à finaliser l'invitation ou la récupération, mais seul, il ne donne pas accès au compte, assure 1Password. Il faut aussi une connexion SSO ou un code à six chiffres, envoyé à l'adresse e-mail enregistrée.
Pour limiter le risque qu'un pirate devine ce code, 1Password l'a allongé à dix caractères, lettres et chiffres mêlés. Selon l'éditeur, une attaque par force brute, qui consiste à essayer toutes les combinaisons, est ainsi pratiquement impossible. 1Password affirme n'avoir trouvé en interne aucune preuve qu'un compte ait été piraté grâce à ces jetons. Il a prévenu directement un petit nombre d'utilisateurs liés à SCIM Bridge ou à Hosted Provisioning, deux outils qui servent aux entreprises à créer automatiquement les comptes de leurs salariés.
Le pirate a également copié du code source dans des dépôts privés et il a accédé au système CI/CD de 1Password, qui assemble et met en ligne automatiquement le logiciel. Ce système contient des secrets d'infrastructure indispensables au fonctionnement du produit, et 1Password a renouvelé tous les identifiants potentiellement compromis. L'éditeur a désactivé le compte GitHub de l'employé, révoqué le jeton volé et supprimé l'accès créé par le pirate. Mais on ignore encore comment le pirate a eu accès au compte GitHub.
- moodVersion d'essai limitée
- databaseStockage illimité
- browse_activityNotification de fuite
- lockChiffrement AES-GCM-256
1Password ne vous demandera jamais votre clé secrète
Comme n'importe quelle instance légitime, pas question pour 1Password de vous demander votre clé secrète. « Vos secrets sont chiffrés avec des clés que vous seul possédez, nous ne pouvons donc pas y accéder, et un pirate qui parviendrait à s'introduire dans nos serveurs ne le pourrait pas non plus », assure l'éditeur.
1Password vous conseille de vous méfier des e-mails, des SMS et des appels inattendus au sujet de 1Password, d'une invitation ou d'une récupération de compte que vous n'avez pas demandée. Et pour cause, en mars 2025, des clients de 1Password avaient reçu de fausses alertes de sécurité sur l'adresse e-mail liée à leur compte, avec un lien vers un faux site.
« 1Password ne vous contactera jamais pour vous demander votre mot de passe ou votre clé secrète », prévient l'éditeur. Saisissez-les seulement dans l'application officielle, ou sur le site de 1Password après avoir tapé son adresse dans votre navigateur. Votre clé secrète vous est demandée uniquement lors de la première connexion sur un nouvel appareil ou un nouveau navigateur.
Vous n'avez rien à modifier dans votre compte. Si vous remarquez quelque chose de suspect, vous pouvez le signaler à l'adresse support@1password.com.

articles.title: U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Agency Takes Some Systems Offline After Cyber Intrusion
articles.text:
The U.S. Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has been hit by a cybersecurity incident that resulted in "unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems," the bureau said on Tuesday. As a precaution, it has taken some systems offline.
The bureau collects suspicious activity reports and other Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) filings from banks and other financial institutions and analyzes them to fight money laundering and terrorist financing.
The BSA E-Filing website is still up, although some services may be temporarily unavailable. The agency has not named the systems it reached or those it took offline.
To support filers affected by the disruption, the bureau is extending some filing deadlines: covered reports originally due between November 18 and December 29 can now be submitted until December 30.
A relief order issued the same day, FIN-2026-R002, applies to three groups:
- Financial institutions that used Secure Direct Transfer Mode (SDTM), the channel for sending batches of BSA reports directly from their own servers, as of November 18
- Companies required to file a beneficial ownership information report during the covered window
- Individuals required to update a FinCEN Identifier during the same window
All other Bank Secrecy Act obligations stay in force, including the duty to monitor for suspicious transactions. The service alert says urgent suspicious activity information can still reach law enforcement through the Financial Institutions Hotline, 1-866-556-3974, which is not affected by the disruption.
The disclosure followed days of filing trouble. Filing providers reported failures in automated batch submissions beginning November 18, and the bureau posted a notice about the disruption to SDTM late last week, according to a filing outages report by the markets news site The Deep Dive.
The bureau has not said whether the intrusion caused those outages. The order grants the relief because of a "service disruption" and does not mention the cybersecurity incident.
Nor has the agency said when the access began, whether any data was viewed or taken, or who was responsible. No group has publicly claimed the intrusion so far. Those answers matter because of what the bureau holds: reports of suspicious financial activity filed by financial institutions nationwide.
The incident is not Treasury's first in recent years: in December 2024, a China-linked group used a compromised BeyondTrust API key in an earlier Treasury breach that reached department systems and documents. No link between the two incidents has been reported.

articles.title: Hackean a 1Password desde la cuenta de un empleado y exponen datos de usuarios
articles.text:
Una cuenta de GitHub perteneciente a un empleado de 1Password fue comprometida y sirvió como puerta de entrada a los sistemas backend de la empresa, donde los atacantes lograron acceder a información de clientes y a código fuente privado.
El incidente, descubierto el 19 de noviembre de 2026, no afectó las bóvedas de contraseñas ni las claves de cifrado, según confirmó la compañía, aunque sí quedaron expuestos datos como nombres, correos electrónicos e identificadores de cuenta.
Cómo ocurrió el hackeo a 1Password a través de GitHub
El origen de la intrusión fue la cuenta de GitHub de un empleado de 1Password. Desde ese punto de acceso, los atacantes consiguieron avanzar hasta los sistemas backend de la compañía, de acuerdo con el reporte de Darkweb Informer.
El alcance no se limitó a un robo de registros. Los responsables del ataque introdujeron código malicioso en servicios backend y llegaron también a la infraestructura de integración y despliegue continuo, conocida como CI/CD, que las empresas emplean para desarrollar, probar y poner en funcionamiento software.
Que el acceso se extendiera hasta ese entorno explica por qué la respuesta de 1Password incluyó medidas técnicas adicionales, más allá de atender la exposición de datos. La información disponible no detalla, sin embargo, qué componentes específicos de la infraestructura CI/CD resultaron comprometidos.
Un hackeo de este tipo, que parte de una cuenta individual comprometida en una plataforma de desarrollo como GitHub, puede derivar en el acceso a sistemas internos de una empresa cuando esa cuenta tiene permisos sobre código fuente o infraestructura de despliegue, sin que ello implique necesariamente el compromiso de los datos cifrados de los usuarios finales.
Qué datos de los usuarios quedaron expuestos
Entre los registros sustraídos se encuentran nombres de clientes, direcciones de correo electrónico, identificadores de cuenta y marcas de tiempo vinculadas a inicios de sesión. También se vieron afectados tokens asociados a ciertos enlaces de invitación y de recuperación de cuentas.
1Password distingue de forma explícita estos elementos de los secretos guardados dentro de las bóvedas. La compañía sostiene que la exposición de nombres, correos o tokens no equivale a que los atacantes hayan obtenido las contraseñas almacenadas por sus usuarios.
La empresa afirmó, además, que no halló evidencia de tomas de control de cuentas ni indicó que los tokens robados se hayan utilizado para ingresar a perfiles o completar procesos de recuperación. El reporte describe qué tipos de registros estuvieron comprometidos, pero no precisa cuántos clientes resultaron afectados ni confirma un uso posterior de esa información.
Esta distinción resulta central para interpretar el incidente: una filtración puede exponer datos vinculados con una cuenta sin que eso signifique que terceros accedieron al contenido cifrado dentro de ella.
Medidas tomadas por 1Password tras detectar la brecha
Tras identificar la intrusión el 19 de noviembre, 1Password deshabilitó de inmediato la cuenta de GitHub comprometida. La compañía también rotó todas las credenciales que podían haber quedado expuestas a raíz del acceso no autorizado.
Como parte de la respuesta, la empresa reforzó sus controles de seguridad internos y solicitó a expertos externos en ciberseguridad que revisen el manejo del incidente. Esa revisión, según el reporte, continúa en curso.
Entre los cambios técnicos anunciados figura la extensión de los códigos de verificación utilizados en procesos de recuperación de cuenta, que pasaron de seis dígitos numéricos a 10 caracteres alfanuméricos.
1Password no presentó esta modificación como una prueba de que los códigos anteriores hubieran sido utilizados por los atacantes, sino como una medida preventiva adoptada después del hallazgo.
Qué implica el incidente para los usuarios del servicio
1Password sostiene que sus clientes no necesitan restablecer sus contraseñas, dado que no encontró evidencia de que las bóvedas o las claves de cifrado hayan sido vulneradas. Esta indicación se circunscribe a las contraseñas almacenadas dentro del servicio.
Esa afirmación no contradice el hecho de que ciertos datos de cuenta y tokens de enlaces formaron parte de los registros sustraídos durante el ataque. Ambas cosas, señala la compañía, pueden ser ciertas al mismo tiempo sin implicar una filtración de las bóvedas.
El reporte no incluye un llamado general a restablecer contraseñas ni confirma casos de toma de cuentas. Sí deja establecido que nombres, correos electrónicos, identificadores, marcas de tiempo y algunos tokens de invitación o recuperación estuvieron entre los elementos robados, un alcance que la propia empresa pide no confundir con un compromiso del contenido protegido dentro del gestor de contraseñas.

articles.title: I bought a refurbished iPhone 17e, and I'll never go back to buying new
articles.text:
Refurbished iPhone sales are on the rise — here's why buying pre-owned is a great idea (and why I'll never go back to buying new)
If you're thinking about upgrading your phone this November, take my advice: pick up a refurbished unit (and thank me later)
As a journalist who’s been covering the tech world for the better part of a decade, I can honestly say that I’ve never seen a worse time for consumers to buy a brand-new phone.
The race to build AI-fueling data centers (and the vast amounts of RAM they require) has wrought havoc on the cost of smartphones — the fact that Samsung’s entry-level flagship, the Galaxy S26, now has a starting price of $999 / £959 / AU$1,649 (a year-on-year increase of $200 / £160 / AU$100) should tell you everything you need to know.
And if, like me, you’re an iPhone user, then things aren’t much better. After keeping prices fairly steady for several years, Apple finally gave in and increased the cost of every iPhone it had on sale in September. We’re now in a situation where Apple’s cheapest handset, the iPhone 17e, costs an eye-watering $699 / £699 / AU$1,149. Even as a fan of the brand, I’ll tell you right now that you can find much better value by scouting out the best Android phones, particularly if you’re after a mid-range device.
It shouldn’t be too surprising, then, that online retailer MusicMagpie has reported a 53% surge in refurbished iPhone sales, following the release of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. It makes a lot of sense as consumers try to sniff out any bargains on potential upgrades, but I completely get any scepticism that some folks may have about going down the refurbished route, particularly as I was once among you.
I always preferred to buy my phones new, but after taking the plunge last year and writing about my experience of using a refurbished phone for the first time, I honestly don’t see myself ever going back.
Refurbished tech has completely won me over
When I last wrote about this topic, I had a refurbished iPhone 16 to hand, but in the time since, I had to lend that device to my wife following a rather disastrous meeting between her iPhone 15 Pro and the concrete floor of a car park.
After trying to stick it out with Android for a time, I decided that I was too deep into Apple’s ecosystem to truly give it up, so I decided to go in search of another refurbished Apple phone.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
In the end, I settled on a ‘like new’ refurbished iPhone 17e from Giffgaff, coming to the conclusion that what I needed more than anything was access to iOS, a recent chipset with plenty of updates ahead of it, and a compact phone that was easy enough to use one-handed (I almost broke a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra when trying to hold my daughter in one arm and text with the other).
Just like with my time using the iPhone 16, this newer model has proven to me that opting for a refurbished unit is a reliable choice. My iPhone 17e arrived as fresh as if it had just been unboxed for the first time, along with 100% battery health. In the time that I’ve been using it, the phone hasn’t failed me, keeping up with everything from texting on WhatsApp to video editing on Instagram Edits.
For context, the phone was priced at £529 at the time of purchase, which is a massive £170 less than the iPhone 17e's current retail price at the Apple Store. As a family man with bills to pay, that’s not an insignificant amount of money, and it says a lot that, as I’ve been scouring this year's slate of Black Friday phone deals, I’m yet to see an offer on a new iPhone that comes anywhere near offering the same level of value.
It also doesn’t help that, if recent predictions are to be believed, the cost of buying a new big-ticket phone is only set to get worse in 2027.
Refurbished phones will only get more appealing
According to a recent IDC report, the ongoing RAM crisis isn't expected to subside until 2028 at the earliest, and that only means that prices for consumers are likely to keep rising as companies have to pay greater amounts for memory. It’s a vicious cycle, but I think the one silver lining is that it should drive retailers to offer more choice on refurbished tech as interest continues to grow.
Already, there are a good amount of incentives available to tempt users into giving refurbished tech a try. For instance, my iPhone 17e is covered by a free 24-month warranty, which Giffgaff offers for all of its ‘like new’ phones, while Vodafone provides a free battery replacement service for up to three years from the point of purchase with certain contracts. In the US, I'd look at Best Buy and Back Market, while OzMobiles and JB Hi-Fi are popular choices in Australia.
All of this comes on top of the now-accepted standard to provide professionally refurbished tech, which is great for peace of mind.
As more retailers look to hop aboard the refurbished bandwagon, it should hopefully lead to a wider array of incentives on offer to attract business, so my hope is that buying a refurbished phone will only become a more rewarding prospect as time goes on.
For now, however, the very fact that refurbished tech gives Apple fans a way of circumventing the brand’s sky-high prices is already a big win, and if you are thinking about upgrading to a more recent iPhone this Black Friday, I can’t recommend buying pre-owned enough.

articles.title: Intermarché va faire entrer l'IA d'Anthropic dans ses magasins d'ici quelques semaines
articles.text:
Le Groupement Mousquetaires, qui fédère Intermarché, Netto ou Bricomarché, va déployer l'IA d'Anthropic, Claude, à partir du mois de janvier 2027. Avec une première salve de 500 magasins, avec Amazon Web Services en coulisses.
Ce mercredi 25 novembre, le Groupement Mousquetaires a officialisé un partenariat avec Anthropic pour déployer son chatbot Claude dans l'ensemble de ses activités. Une première phrase concernera 500 magasins et 300 collaborateurs des fonctions support à partir de janvier prochain, avant une extension progressive à tout le groupe. L'assistant, fourni via la plateforme du géant Amazon Web Services (AWS) doit devenir un levier de performance pour les enseignes Intermarché, Bricomarché et Netto.
500 magasins et 300 salariés pour commencer, Claude arrive chez les Mousquetaires
Le coup d'envoi a été fixé à janvier 2027, donc quasiment demain. D'abord, ce sont 500 points de vente et 300 collaborateurs des fonctions support qui auront accès à Claude, le temps d'identifier les usages qui tiennent vraiment la route, métier par métier. Un premier cercle encore modeste pour un groupement qui réunit plus de 3 100 chefs d'entreprise indépendants, plus de 4 300 magasins et 160 000 salariés entre la France, la Belgique, la Pologne et le Portugal, certes. De la logistique au juridique, en passant par les achats et l'informatique, aucun métier n'est censé être « épargné », pas même dans les quelque 60 usines agroalimentaires du groupe.
Mais il n'est pas question pour autant de jouer les apprentis sorciers. Stéphane Sinopoli, adhérent Intermarché chargé de la monétisation de la data, réclame des cas d'usage déployés « de manière rapide et ROIste », et glisse au passage une formule qui sonne un peu comme un pique. « Contrairement à d'autres, notre priorité restera la performance de nos points de vente », dit-il. Cette prudence est parfaitement compréhensible. L'an dernier, Anthropic avait confié la gestion d'une petite boutique à Claude, et l'expérience s'était soldée par des pertes, comme le racontions sur Clubic.
Les Mousquetaires veulent être pionniers de l'IA dans la distribution
Pour l'infrastructure, les Mousquetaires s'en remettent à Amazon Bedrock, la plateforme d'AWS qui donne accès aux principaux modèles d'IA générative, dont Claude, dans un environnement sécurisé. Amazon et Anthropic ont d'ailleurs des intérêts bien imbriqués. Après 8 milliards de dollars déjà investis, le groupe de Seattle a promis en avril jusqu'à 25 milliards supplémentaires à l'éditeur de Claude. Chez Anthropic, Thomas Remy, qui dirige notamment la France, plaide pour une IA « fiable, responsable », capable de « renforcer les capacités des équipes ». Il promet de travailler aux côtés de celles des Mousquetaires pour que Claude devienne, au quotidien, « une ressource utile et fiable ».
Ce choix tranche en tout cas avec celui d'autres grands acteurs français et européens, qui privilégient des solutions dites « souveraines ». La Caisse des Dépôts a ainsi retenu Mistral AI pour équiper ses agents, tandis que la branche numérique de Schwarz, maison mère de Lidl, prépare avec le français Bull une offre d'infrastructures d'IA sous contrôle européen.
Chez les Mousquetaires, on revendique plutôt une longueur d'avance. « Avec Anthropic et AWS, nous faisons le choix d'être pionniers dans le déploiement de l'IA à grande échelle dans la distribution française », affirme Jean-Philippe Sassi, adhérent Intermarché et responsable de la DSI du groupe. Reste le volet humain, sans doute le plus délicat. Le groupement s'engage à accompagner ses salariés dans l'évolution de leurs métiers, et c'est aussi sur ce terrain que le projet sera jugé.

articles.title: “Hoy estamos frente a un consumidor que no se deja deslumbrar por descuentos”, Google Colombia
articles.text:
Andrea Monroy, directora del sector retail en Google Colombia, afirmó que “hoy estamos frente a un consumidor que no se deja deslumbrar por descuentos” como los que se encuentran por la temporada de Black Friday.
De hecho, la inteligencia artificial, como el asistente Gemini de Google, es una de las herramientas que más usan los latinoamericanos para analizar precios y hacer compras. “La IA le ha dado el poder de verificar el valor de cada peso invertido”, agrega Monroy.
Según el estudio Ipsos Black Friday Colombia comisionado por Google, la intención de compra supera el promedio de la región de habla hispana en Latinoamérica, pero sin dejarse convencer de la publicidad un 100%.
Por otra parte, Monroy advirtió sobre el desafío para los comercios: “aquellas empresas que integren inventarios en tiempo real, garanticen políticas claras de logística y se posicionen con información confiable lograrán no solo maximizar sus ventas, sino fidelizar a un cliente más informado y leal”.
Google indica que en Colombia, la experiencia de compra integra cada vez más los canales digitales y las tiendas físicas: las ventas en línea ya concentran el 30% de la facturación de Black Friday y el 37% de Cyber Lunes.
Cómo es el consumidor colombiano en Black Friday, según Google
El consumidor colombiano llega más planificado al Black Friday 2026, que se realizará del 27 al 29 de noviembre. Tras las ventas de COP $2,6 billones registradas en 2025, la nueva edición se perfila como una fecha clave para las compras de fin de año.
Según el estudio de Ipsos comisionado por Google en agosto de 2026, el 73% de los colombianos se declaró optimista sobre su situación económica personal y el 72% espera que las promociones superen a las del año anterior. Además, el 61% planea aprovechar Black Friday para adelantar las compras navideñas.
La intención de compra en Colombia supera el promedio de los países hispanohablantes de América Latina. Sin embargo, las decisiones de consumo están atravesadas por una evaluación previa de precios, promociones y necesidades concretas.
Apenas el 8% de los compradores afirma tomar decisiones impulsivas durante esta temporada. En cambio, el 53% llega con una decisión de compra definida, mientras que el 39% monitorea promociones y busca una relación conveniente entre precio y beneficio antes de concretar una adquisición.
Las preferencias cambian según la generación. La Generación Z prioriza la tecnología y las ofertas relámpago; los millennials se inclinan por la moda, los televisores y las compras en cuotas sin intereses. Los baby boomers, por su parte, muestran la mayor intención de compra en viajes y turismo.
La búsqueda de información es otro factor relevante: el 75% de los colombianos utiliza YouTube antes de comprar.
De acuerdo con el informe, los creadores de contenido se consolidan como una fuente de consulta para quienes buscan referencias sobre productos y ofertas.
Estafadores suplantan a Amazon, Apple y Netflix durante Black Friday
Amazon, Apple y Netflix se encuentran entre las marcas más utilizadas por ciberdelincuentes para engañar a compradores durante el Black Friday, según un análisis de Kaspersky sobre amenazas detectadas entre enero y octubre de 2026.
Los atacantes aprovechan el aumento de las compras en línea, los descuentos y la urgencia de las promociones para robar credenciales, datos bancarios y dinero.
Los productos de la compañía de ciberseguridad bloquearon 19.063.077 intentos de acceso a enlaces de phishing dirigidos a usuarios de tiendas digitales, bancos y sistemas de pago durante los primeros diez meses del año.
Esa cifra implicó un aumento del 198,1% frente a los 6.394.854 ataques registrados en el mismo período de 2025.
Del total de casos detectados, el 44,54% apuntó a compradores en línea; el 28,55%, a usuarios bancarios, y el 26,91%, a sistemas de pago.
Kaspersky detectó más de 220.071 mensajes de spam vinculados con ventas durante las primeras dos semanas de noviembre, un alza del 50,2% frente a 2025. Estos correos ofrecen cupones inexistentes, sorteos, tarjetas regalo o descuentos por tiempo limitado.

articles.title: Credential Remediation Is Slow When You Don’t Know What Will Break
articles.text:
TL;DR
- More than 64% still valid after four years: GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 found that most valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, because teams stall on what a revoke will break.
- Validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets: Prioritize by impact instead, weighing what a credential can access and whether it leaked publicly, and update the risk score as new context arrives.
- Revoke last, never first: Issue a replacement, store it in the vault, switch every consumer to the vault call, deploy and monitor, then revoke the original and confirm it no longer authenticates.
Every modern enterprise depends on credentials. This is how humans, systems, and now AI connect securely to data, services, and each other. GitGuardian helps secure that credential layer through three connected capabilities: Detect, Remediate, and Prevent. The journey starts with detection, but credential remediation is where many secret security programs bog down. This is the second of three articles we are releasing to explain how we help address detection, remediation, and prevention.
The first article in this series, “The Credential Layer Is Expanding Faster Than Security Teams Can See It,” covered detection across every surface where credentials live. Just knowing they exist is not enough. Teams need to take action to remediate those findings. To do that, they need context around every credential they find.
Without the right context, it is impossible to know what risks the secret carries. It is also difficult to understand which systems rely on those secrets and the risk levels that revoking the secret brings. Nobody wants to break production, but we also cannot allow attackers to leverage those secrets.
The resulting decision paralysis leaves many teams struggling to rotate immediately. Sometimes it can take years for the secret to be revoked finally. That is actually all too common, as shown by GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 research that found that 64% of valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, a full 4 years later.
It would be great if there were a one-size-fits-all solution for remediating every leak; in reality, each one is tied to a specific integration. What we can do is streamline the processes needed to get to the end, making it much easier for organizations of any size. And it does take the whole organization to properly deal with leaked secrets.
Why credential remediation is so hard for so many teams
A team that discovers an exposed credential rarely has all the authority or knowledge needed to fix it without causing further issues. A security engineer can see it’s valid and dangerous, but that security engineer usually cannot immediately tell which services will fail when it is revoked. Breaking production is considered a much higher risk than the possibility of a stolen and abused secret, so they need to go looking for answers, which is a time-consuming process.
The developers who know where and why a key is used and, hopefully, how to rotate it safely are often busy shipping new features and managing existing requests from the business. An alert in their email that shows only a file path and a secret type asks those busy devs to stop their workflow and launch their own investigation. These requests, all too often, sink into the backlog.
At the same time, the larger the organization, the harder it is to find the right person who knows the answer to “what breaks if this key is revoked?” Application security teams monitor code where keys are used, identity and access management (IAM) teams govern identities that were issued keys, and the Platform Engineering team runs the vaults holding the keys. They all have different perspectives and, in most organizations that are early in their secrets security maturity journey, can only tell part of the story.
Endpoint security teams are also watching what happens at the workstation level. They are beginning to track secrets stored there, as software supply chain attacks have increasingly targeted these plaintext credential stores over the last couple of years. A secret leaked here might even be the triggering event for the rotation in case of compromise from an infostealer. The endpoint team is historically not connected to AppSec or Platform teams.
One credential can touch all these teams while each individual, isolated group sees only its own slice of the credential layer. Now, multiply the communication and coordination issue across hundreds or thousands of potential leaks, and the scale of the remediation problem becomes clearer.
Action before investigation invites downtime
The risk of revoking before fully understanding the fallout is fairly high for the business. This is weighed against potential future abuse. Of course, this math changes during an active breach when the clock is ticking and when exfiltration or lateral movement is already occurring. Those emergencies do not get backlogged. Mature organizations understand that addressing leaks before an emergency arises is the better plan overall, but remediation times are still measured in weeks for most teams. How long a remediation process takes really boils down to how fast and accurately responders can gather and communicate information about the issue. Responders need to know a lot of things, starting with whether the credential works, what it can access, and who owns it before they can even ask questions like “where else does it appear?” and “which systems depend on it?”
For example, envision two valid cloud credentials. One grants read-only access to a single storage bucket, and the second one is a root-level key with administrative control over production. While their privileges and dependent workloads determine the appropriate level of urgency, both require the same level of insight and investigation to triage the remediation process and decide whether the response is a rotation next sprint or a revocation this very second.
The ultimate goal is to remove the leaked key rapidly, but in a way that does not interrupt production or break pipeline builds. Rotating secrets safely simply requires resources and a coordination plan. If this process is always piecemeal and manual, then mistakes are more likely to happen.
A security team that causes an outage once will face resistance the next time it asks to rotate anything.
Prioritize by impact, not just validity
Validity is the first and clearest signal most responders look at. Alone, this is an incomplete signal. GitGuardian research from the State of Secrets report found that validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets such as custom API tokens and SSH keys, because those secrets cannot be verified automatically.
While validity still matters, access to sensitive data or core systems raises urgency. If the leak happened publicly on the internet, that raises the urgency even further. Any risk scoring needs to explain which factors drove it. It also needs to be a living risk score, adjusting for new information as new context arrives. Scoring it once upon discovery is akin to trusting an initial CVSS score in a CVE disclosure. It is a helpful guide but needs to be updated based on what is really going on in your organization. The organization and its risk tolerance will decide what happens next. Having as much information centrally available as possible is key to a rapid response, as responders reach the boundaries of what systems they can actually touch.
Route the work to the right people who can push the change
Remediation requests should let the developer or platform team act immediately, without requiring the team to repeat the investigation that has already taken place.
Any request to replace a key for a production system should include validity and known exposure locations. It should list dependencies too, and where possible show how it connects to business operations. The more the person picking up the request understands about the issue, the sooner they can act. In an ideal world, all remediation requests would be routed to their named owners. In the messy reality of the enterprise, you will likely need to involve the developer who leaked the secret and gather data from commit attribution or source metadata. We need to establish communication because there is a probability that they will need further instructions or guidance.
Requests should not be ‘thrown over the fence’ and then forgotten about. Follow-up and confirmation about remediation progress should be centrally collected and shared so every department knows where the rotation process is at any given moment. This accountability proves resilience efforts when an auditor shows up.
Engineers need to be enabled with a clean way to communicate once they start the work and once their ticket is ready to close. Routing the work through existing ticketing tools keeps it alongside other engineering work, but those tickets also need to integrate with the responder’s security operational tooling.
Rotate, revoke, and vault: the order matters
Safe rotation means following a specific set of steps, in the right order, so you don’t break anything. Remember: “Availability” is one of the legs of the CIA (confidentiality, integrity, availability) security triad.
For mature organizations, this could be as straightforward as rotating the secret in a vault, since the production applications and systems relying on the credential are all already consuming it from the secrets manager. Any plaintext copies are then rendered harmless once the original offending secret is revoked.
For organizations and situations where no existing vaulted copy is in use, this process often starts with issuing a replacement credential. If the responder can do this, they should do so immediately and store it safely in the vault. Then, replace every occurrence of the plaintext secret with that vault call, across every known consumer. The remediation steps from there are to push the changed code or config live and monitor for any issues, ready to roll back if anything breaks. Only when all the new systems are safely consuming the new vaulted credential appropriately can the team revoke the original. Getting this out of order turns a security fix into an incident.
GitGuardian’s service account credential rotation checklist covers these steps in detail.
Verify the fix and keep the evidence
Only close the ticket when the key is safely revoked, and the danger is removed. There needs to be an audit trail about what you fixed and how you proved that. You need verifiable confirmation that the old credential no longer authenticates. Optionally, and depending on the circumstances, you can show that the old secret was removed from all surfaces.
Any incidents closed while the credential remains valid deserve their own review queue. This common case happens when a team rotates a key in one system while the old key remains active and valid in another. This means a siloed team only accounted for their one occurrence in their tooling that lacks a unified view or relies on manual tracking.
The incident record also serves auditors and security leaders. It shows what was found, who acted, and how long remediation took.
One credential, start to finish with GitGuardian
At GitGuardian, we have helped thousands of developers and organizations streamline their remediation process.
To help visualize how we can help, imagine a Kubernetes application that calls an external service with an API key stored in a secrets manager. During troubleshooting in our imagined scenario, a developer copies the key into a local configuration file and commits it. This is a fairly common scenario we have seen play out many times.
GitGuardian scanning finds the secret as soon as it is committed. The platform generates a new open incident and alerts the assigned team. An automatic validity check confirms the key is still active, and the Secret Analyzer lists its permissions. A presence check confirms the secret is still in the codebase. All these checks can be rerun as remediation progresses.
For customers with full platform integrations, the GitGuardian Exploration Map shows a production workload depending on it, and fingerprint matching ties the committed value to the vaulted copy. The security team can bring that context to the owning developer and operations team.
Once a replacement key is issued, everyone can track the progress of the rotation and see when the PR that accounts for the deployment configuration is pulling from the vault. There is no guessing about whether revoking the original will affect anything critical. GitGuardian then rechecks validity and confirms the committed copy is gone.
The incident might also expose a pattern worth investigating across other teams. Has this same codebase seen similar incidents? Has the same user caused the same issue before? Are vaulted credentials ending up in unmanaged files on developer laptops on a regular basis? These all point to a wider issue that needs to be addressed to prevent further incidents and an increased remediation backlog.
From fixing to preventing
Remediation reduces risk one credential at a time. It also shows where exposures keep coming from.
The third and final article in this series covers prevention, starting on developer machines and in AI coding workflows. Teams that want to see this remediation workflow can take an interactive tour of the GitGuardian platform.
Take a Guided Tour of GitGuardian
FAQ
What is credential remediation?
Credential remediation is the work of removing the risk from a leaked or exposed credential. The goal is to replace and revoke the leaked key quickly, in a way that does not interrupt production or break pipeline builds, and then to confirm the old credential no longer authenticates.
Why does credential remediation take so long?
The team that finds an exposed credential rarely has the authority or the knowledge to fix it alone. A security engineer can see the credential is valid and dangerous, but usually cannot tell which services will fail when it is revoked. The developers, identity, platform, and endpoint teams each see only their own slice of the credential layer, so responders spend their time gathering context instead of fixing the leak.
How do you prioritize which leaked credentials to fix first?
Prioritize by impact, not validity alone. GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 found that validation-only prioritization misses 46% of critical secrets, because some secrets cannot be verified automatically. Access to sensitive data or core systems raises urgency, and a public leak raises it further. The risk score should explain which factors drove it and change as new context arrives.
What is the safe order for rotating a leaked secret?
Issue a replacement credential and store it in the vault. Replace every plaintext copy of the old secret with a call to the vault, across every known consumer. Push the changed code or configuration live and monitor for issues, ready to roll back. Revoke the original only when every system is consuming the new vaulted credential. Getting this out of order turns a security fix into an incident.
How do you verify that a leaked credential has been remediated?
Close the ticket only when you have verifiable confirmation that the old credential no longer authenticates. Keep an audit trail of what was fixed and how it was proved, including who acted and how long remediation took. Incidents closed while the credential is still valid deserve their own review, since a team may have rotated the key in one system while it stayed active in another.

articles.title: Lenovo's Legion Tower 5i is the creator PC I'd pick — now $1,440 off
articles.text:
The Lenovo Legion Tower 5i is the streaming and editing PC I'd pick — now $1,440 off at $2,230 for Black Friday
A liquid-cooled Intel and Nvidia tower for serious gamers, streamers, and creators
If you want a ready-built PC for streaming and content creation, as well as handling modern gaming, the Lenovo Legion Tower 5i Gen 10, at $2,230 (was $3,669) gets my vote this Black Friday.
The PC pairs an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F processor with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti (16GB GDDR7), 32GB of DDR5 memory, and a 1TB SSD. Lenovo says you can run Discord, Twitch and OBS alongside a game.
It also ships with Windows 11 Pro, a 240mm liquid cooler, an 850W power supply and a three-month Xbox PC Game Pass trial. Lenovo estimates delivery by Wednesday, December 2, with free delivery included.
A prebuilt desktop built around an RTX 5070 Ti with 16GB of GDDR7 memory, a 20-core Core Ultra 7 265F, 32GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 1TB SSD. Liquid cooling and an 850W power supply keep it running steadily, and the tool-less side panel makes upgrades easy.
Why we recommend it
What really stands out is the GPU. The RTX 5070 Ti is a high-end Nvidia Blackwell GPU, and with 16GB of GDDR7. That's paired with 32GB of DDR5-5600 and a 20-core Core Ultra 7 processor.
It's built to be upgraded, too. The transparent side panel comes off without tools, memory supports up to 128GB, and there's room for up to three SSDs, with one slot supporting Gen 5. The rear has HDMI 2.1 and three DisplayPort outputs, so multi-monitor setups are covered.
The liquid cooler is a nice touch at this price, and Lenovo's Legion Coldfront cooling aims to keep temperatures and noise in check. Lenovo is also offering extended returns through January 27 and a price match guarantee, which takes some of the risk out of a big purchase.
Things to know before you buy
The warranty is one year, mail-in, which is on the short side for a $2,000-plus system. The 1TB drive will fill up quickly with modern game installs, but the extra SSD slots make it easy to fix. And since this is a prebuilt, you're paying for convenience as well as parts.
Price Context
At $2,229.99, the Legion Tower 5i isn't the cheapest this configuration has been, but it's reasonable for what you get right now. Earlier this year, a near-identical Legion Tower 5i was about $550 cheaper than today's price and had twice the storage.
However, in fairness, graphics card prices have climbed, and most RTX 5070 Ti cards on Amazon now sit above $1,500 on their own, so $2,229.99 isn't unreasonable for a full system with 32GB of DDR5, a 20-core processor, a 240mm liquid cooler and an 850W power supply.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Legion Tower 5i if... you want a powerful, liquid-cooled gaming desktop ready to use, with strong 1440p performance and room to upgrade.
