articles.title: AI infrastructure economics takeaways from Fully Connected
articles.text:
Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event
AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.
As inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.
“What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante said. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”
During the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.)
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:
Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:
Insight #1: AI infrastructure economics hinge on productive capacity.
The commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.
“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”
Memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.
“You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”
For AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.
“We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:
Insight #2: Reducing operational risk protects AI infrastructure investments.
Protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.
“It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”
At Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production issues, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.
“If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti said during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very important metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”
For International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.
“This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:
Insight #3: Physical AI puts infrastructure investments to the test.
For organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.
“We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely quickly,” Ernst said during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:
Walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.
“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”
Here’s theCUBE’s full video discussion with John Mancuso and Adrien Gaidon:
Other highlights from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event include:
- Bartley Richardson, chief of AI at CrowdStrike Holdings Inc., and Jim Higgins, chief information security officer of CoreWeave, talk with theCUBE about machine-speed defense, infrastructure-level security and operational trust.
- Rob Bahr, senior engineer at BattleBots Inc., sits down with theCUBE to discuss AI simulation for robot combat design and the potential for AI-driven robot autonomy.
- Harsh Banwait, senior director of product at CoreWeave, and Hannah Coutand, director of product marketing, Vera CPU, at Nvidia, talk with theCUBE about CPU requirements, sandbox performance and infrastructure security.

articles.title: Google Russie fait saisir 1,9 milliard d'euros chez Google France
articles.text:
Un commissaire de justice s’est rendu ce mercredi 25 novembre au siège de Google France pour y signifier une saisie conservatoire de 1,9 milliard d’euros. Elle est réclamée par le liquidateur de Google Russie, qui veut récupérer une partie des recettes publicitaires encaissées par Google Ireland.
Le cabinet WJ Associés, qui défend Google Russie en France, nous a confirmé la démarche. Elle vise à faire appliquer ici une condamnation prononcée à Moscou, au sujet de recettes perçues entre 2018 et 2022.
De la marge rabotée en 2018 à la saisie parisienne
Depuis 2009, Google Russie vendait les espaces publicitaires de Google Ireland et gardait 20 % du chiffre d’affaires. En 2018, cette part tombe à 3 % pour les grands comptes et à 1,5 % pour les autres clients. Selon le cabinet, ni le coût des services de Google Ireland ni la répartition du travail ne justifiaient cette baisse. Les salariés russes assuraient le même niveau de prestation. Le chiffre d’affaires de la filiale progressait, mais ses bénéfices et sa trésorerie reculaient. Elle versait aussi chaque mois à l’avance l’essentiel des sommes encaissées, sans attendre l’échéance trimestrielle. Pour WJ Associés, Google Ireland aurait cherché à fragiliser sa filiale.
Google a suspendu ses ventes publicitaires en Russie en mars 2022. Google Russie a été déclarée en faillite en 2023 et a fermé son bureau de Moscou, où travaillaient 224 personnes. En octobre 2023, nous rapportions que la justice russe avait officialisé cette faillite, notamment à cause d’amendes supérieures aux liquidités de la filiale et au gel de ses comptes bancaires. Pour le cabinet, la baisse de 2018 y a aussi contribué.
Le liquidateur de Google Russie a saisi le tribunal de commerce de Moscou en octobre 2024. Le 3 mars 2026, le tribunal a annulé le contrat de 2018 et condamné Google Ireland à restituer 101,7 milliards de roubles (environ 1,12 milliard d’euros). La décision a été confirmée en appel le 16 juin, puis en cassation le 1er septembre. Google Ireland a saisi la Cour suprême de Russie en octobre.
Pour faire appliquer ce jugement en France, le liquidateur passe par l’exequatur. Cette procédure permet de rendre une décision étrangère applicable en France. Google Russie, qui a obtenu gain de cause à Moscou, demande au juge français d’autoriser l’exécution de la condamnation de Google Ireland. Le juge ne rejuge pas l’affaire. Il vérifie notamment que Google Ireland a pu défendre sa position devant les tribunaux russes. En attendant, la saisie conservatoire sert à préserver des avoirs sur lesquels les créanciers de Google Russie pourraient être payés, explique Me William Julié, l’avocat de Google Russie en France.

articles.title: CNPq reformula Plataforma Lattes com novo visual
articles.text:
CNPq reformula Plataforma Lattes com novo visual
Atualização permite localizar pesquisadores por identificadores acadêmicos e adiciona QR Code aos currículos. Base chegou a 10 milhões de perfis cadastrados.
O Conselho Nacional de Desenvolvimento Científico e Tecnológico (CNPq) lançou uma nova versão da Plataforma Lattes. A ferramenta de busca agora permite localizar pesquisadores não apenas por nome e CPF, mas também por identificadores como ORCID, ISSN e DOI.
Outra mudança está na apresentação dos currículos. Os perfis passam a contar com cartões de visita com QR Code, que facilitam o compartilhamento, além de recursos para visualizar relações acadêmicas e indicadores de produção.
A busca também ganhou filtros por modalidade de bolsa, tipo de produção acadêmica e data da última atualização do currículo. Já a página inicial agora reúne estatísticas sobre os perfis cadastrados, incluindo números de mestres, doutores e instituições.
As novidades foram anunciadas ontem (24/11) e estão sendo liberadas gradualmente para toda a base acadêmica. A plataforma reúne 10 milhões de currículos cadastrados, dos quais cerca de 2 milhões foram adicionados apenas em 2026, segundo o CNPq.
A atualização também inclui ajustes de visualização e integração com o VLibras, ferramenta que traduz conteúdos digitais para a Língua Brasileira de Sinais.
A versão anterior da plataforma continuará disponível temporariamente durante a transição. O CNPq afirma que os dados já cadastrados foram preservados.

articles.title: Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?
articles.text:
Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?
For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.
That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.
These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.
Model overkill
The popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.
“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”
“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.
DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he said.
The ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.
Three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.
In September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.
Cost concerns
Enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the big players.
“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.
Cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.
“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.
By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.
“The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”
Hidden expenses
The pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.
In a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders said managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.
“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” said Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.
Experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” said Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.
Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, said open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.
“If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she said. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.
They’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., said in an interview with the Financial Times.
Sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing issue for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.
“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.
Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.
- AT&T Corp. shifted 40% of its AI workloads to open models and plans to grow that share to 70%, according to The Information. By delegating tasks such as code summarization to cheaper engines and using a router to direct work to the most efficient model, the telecom giant cut AI operating costs by 56% with only a 2% decline in quality.
- Pinterest Inc. achieved over 90% cost savings on its AI operations by moving away from frontier models, said William Ready said on the company’s second fiscal quarter earnings call in August.
- Uber Technologies Inc., which unexpectedly burned through an entire year’s AI budget in the first four months of this year, has cut model requests by one-third and costs per session by over half since February, largely by shifting more workloads to open-weight models.
Advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.
An agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.
“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.
Open weight ≠ open source
Though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.
One is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” said Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”
Although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.
“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.
Baljević said two hidden liabilities are data distribution rights for public training datasets used upstream and the evaluation, stability and legal audit costs that shift directly to the enterprise. “When using open-weight models, you need to lean in on understanding data distribution rights, copyright, contractual restrictions and consent,” she said. “In most cases, this carries costs.”
Evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.
Baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.
More than tokens
Finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.
Organizations that plan to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.
Lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software company went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.
If a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.
“The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” said Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”
Self-hosting isn’t always cheaper
Using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.
Cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” said Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.
For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.
“On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” said Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”
Model-swapping fallacy
When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data shows that approach is usually a dead end.
Most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.
This interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.
“Every time a new model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” said Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.
When open-weight makes sense
Though the open-weight option is viable for any company, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as important as cost.
Compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.
Training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.
But deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” said TEKSystems’ Franco.
Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” said Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”
In contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.
“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” said David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.
“The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss said. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”
Performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency issues can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.
Executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.
Hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.
Are open-weight models for you?
Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.
Complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.
Google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.
Source: Google DeepMind
The corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.
Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” said TekSystems’ Franco.
Poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders said dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.
Feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.
Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.
Continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.
Because new models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can quickly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.
Rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.
“Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” said Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”
Lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.
ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he said. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”
Enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as important an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” said Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.
The shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.
At the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., said in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”

articles.title: “Bienvenue dans la Singularité” : pour Elon Musk, la superintelligence est là et l'humanité a franchi le point de non-retour
articles.text:
“Bienvenue dans la Singularité” : pour Elon Musk, la superintelligence est là et l'humanité a franchi le point de non-retour
Oui, encore
"Une superintelligence indiscutable est arrivée. Bienvenue dans la Singularité." Pour Elon Musk, l'humanité vient de basculer. Le déclencheur est une énigme mathématique vieille de 167 ans, qu'une IA aurait aidé à résoudre. Ce n'est que la quatrième annonce du genre depuis janvier, et l'IA en question appartient à un rival.
Dimanche 22 novembre, à 12h26 heure de Paris, Elon Musk a lâché sur X une phrase vertigineuse : "Une superintelligence indiscutable est arrivée. Bienvenue dans la Singularité."
Le patron de Tesla et de SpaceX répondait à l'ex-championne de poker et vulgarisatrice scientifique Liv Boeree. La veille au soir, celle-ci s'amusait de voir une question vieille de 170 ans peser sur la valorisation d'une entreprise d'IA à mille milliards de dollars. Le message de Musk frôle les 5 millions de vues.
Unequivocal super intelligence has arrived. 
Welcome to the Singularity.
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 22, 2026
Hypothèse de Riemann : 17 millions de lignes de code que personne n'a encore comprises
Formulée par Bernhard Riemann en 1859, la conjecture affirme que tous les zéros non triviaux de la fonction zêta se trouvent sur une même droite, dite critique. Ces zéros gouvernent la répartition des nombres premiers. La conjecture figure parmi les sept problèmes du millénaire de l'institut Clay, dotés chacun d'un million de dollars.
Le 20 novembre, Levent Alpöge, mathématicien chez Anthropic, a annoncé avoir trouvé une démonstration "en travaillant avec Claude". Dès le lendemain, la Lean FRO et la Mathlib Initiative, qui développent le langage de vérification Lean et sa bibliothèque mathématique, ont déclaré avoir "pleine confiance" dans le résultat, après l'avoir passé au crible de plusieurs vérificateurs indépendants.
Reste un sérieux bémol : la preuve se présente sous la forme de 17 millions de lignes de code, qu'aucun mathématicien n'a encore réellement comprises. Interrogé par la revue Nature, le théoricien des nombres Andrew Granville, de l'Université de Montréal, juge la note d'accompagnement d'Alpöge "confuse". Il soupçonne surtout un calendrier dicté par la Bourse : l'annonce a suivi de près un décrochage de la valorisation d'Anthropic, introduite en Bourse quelques jours plus tôt sur la base de 1 500 milliards de dollars. Alpöge récuse ce "point de vue cynique". Le chercheur Gary Marcus, critique notoire de l'IA, estime de son côté que la machine n'aurait pas abouti seule, sans des mois de pilotage humain.
Ces derniers mois, les IA ont enchaîné les coups d'éclat en mathématiques, depuis ce casse-tête qu'aucun humain n'avait déchiffré, bouclé en trois jours, jusqu'aux seize problèmes revendiqués par OpenAI sous les yeux du médaillé Fields Hugo Duminil-Copin. Des percées suffisamment sérieuses pour que Cédric Villani et 24 autres médaillés Fields se disent secoués.
Elon Musk, lui, ne s'embarrasse pas de nuances, et il ne réserve pas le mot aux mathématiques. Cinq minutes avant sa réponse à Liv Boeree, il saluait déjà la "singularité" à propos du FSD V15 de Tesla, censé gérer 25 fois mieux les situations critiques que la version précédente.
Some people thought we meant 25% improvement, no we mean 25 times!
Welcome to the singularity. Hope you’re enjoying your stay. https://t.co/QcLUuhY8Si
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 22, 2026
Qu'est-ce que la Singularité technologique, annoncée par Elon Musk ?
La Singularité désigne le moment où une IA deviendrait assez intelligente pour s'améliorer toute seule, sans aide humaine. Chaque version en concevrait une plus brillante, dans un emballement impossible à prévoir et à contrôler. L'idée remonte au statisticien I. J. Good, ancien compagnon d'Alan Turing à Bletchley Park, qui parlait dès 1965 d'"explosion d'intelligence". L'écrivain et mathématicien Vernor Vinge l'a popularisée en 1993 sous ce nom emprunté à la physique des trous noirs, où les lois connues cessent de s'appliquer. Le futurologue Ray Kurzweil la situait vers 2045.
Superintelligence : Elon Musk récidive, Yann LeCun le recadre
Le milliardaire n'en est pas à sa première annonce. En février 2025, il se disait déjà "à l'horizon des événements de la singularité". Le 4 janvier 2026, il répondait au fondateur de Midjourney, David Holz : "Nous sommes entrés dans la Singularité." Le 22 juillet, rebelote. Son meilleur ennemi Sam Altman, patron d'OpenAI, a lui aussi annoncé que l'IA avait franchi un point de non-retour.
Le patron de Tesla a l'habitude des prophéties : il annonçait cet été que l'argent n'aurait plus d'importance en 2036, et confiait avoir traversé une demi-douzaine de "psychoses IA" cette année. Ces envolées rythment une année vertigineuse pour l'IA, que je vous avais décortiquée dans un grand dossier dédié.
Sous le message de Musk, Yann LeCun, prix Turing 2018, a dégainé une réplique vue plus d'un million de fois : "Appris aujourd'hui : nous avons la superintelligence, mais toujours pas de conduite autonome de niveau 5. Une tâche que la plupart des jeunes de 17 ans maîtrisent en 20 heures de pratique." Et le chercheur de conclure : "Voilà une bien curieuse superintelligence."
TIL: We have superintelligence  but we still don't have level-5 autonomous driving. 
A task that most 17 year olds can learn in 20 hours of practice. 
And we have (you have) billions of hours of training data.
We don't have robots that can come close to doing what an 8 year…
— Yann LeCun (@ylecun) November 22, 2026
La pique fait mouche, du moins, sur Tesla. Déployé depuis le 21 novembre, le FSD V15 porte toujours la mention "Supervised" dans son nom et reste un système de niveau 2 : le conducteur doit garder les yeux sur la route en permanence. Mais la comparaison a ses limites : une preuve mathématique se joue dans un univers clos, aux règles parfaitement vérifiables, quand la conduite exige d'affronter un monde physique imprévisible. Reste que Musk a lui-même mêlé les deux sous le même mot, à cinq minutes d'intervalle.
Alors, superintelligence ? Pour l'heure, l'humanité dispose surtout d'une preuve validée par des machines, que des mathématiciens doivent encore déchiffrer. Quant à la Singularité, elle ne se reconnaîtra sans doute qu'avec le recul, bien après que Musk l'aura proclamée une énième fois.

articles.title: Falla crítica en VMware permite entrar sin contraseña al sistema que controla los servidores de empresas
articles.text:
Broadcom, la empresa propietaria de VMware, publicó parches para corregir una falla crítica en vCenter, el programa con el que muchas empresas administran sus servidores virtuales. El error permite que un atacante con acceso a la red entre al sistema sin credenciales.
La compañía le asignó 9,8 puntos sobre 10 en la escala de gravedad CVSS, la más alta de su categoría crítica. La firma de seguridad Rapid7, que analizó el aviso, explicó que el problema está en el servicio de directorio de vCenter, el componente que guarda las cuentas y los permisos de acceso.
Según Rapid7, quien alcance ese servicio por la red puede acceder al sistema sin autenticarse. Para el atacante, el resultado equivale a tener las llaves de la sala de control: vCenter gestiona los servidores y las máquinas virtuales de una organización.
Broadcom no ofrece una solución alternativa para esta falla: la única salida es instalar la actualización. Las preguntas frecuentes que la compañía publicó junto al aviso dicen que no hay soluciones provisionales para estas vulnerabilidades, y que los parches de vCenter no admiten el método de actualización rápida.
Una prueba de ataque ya es pública
Rapid7 señaló que existe una prueba de concepto pública, es decir, un código que demuestra cómo explotar el error. La firma afirmó que la validó y que logró saltarse la autenticación. Hasta la publicación de su análisis, el 25 de noviembre, no había reportes de ataques reales con esta falla.
La recomendación es actualizar con urgencia, fuera de los ciclos habituales de mantenimiento, los sistemas expuestos. Advirtió que los atacantes ya apuntan a vulnerabilidades en ese mismo servicio de directorio de VMware.
El antecedente es otra falla, CVE-2026-123890, que también afectaba al servicio de directorio de vCenter. Según Rapid7, esa vulnerabilidad se explotó en ataques reales. Broadcom aclaró que son errores distintos: aquella se alcanzaba mediante un protocolo de llamadas remotas y la nueva se alcanza a través de LDAP, un protocolo de consulta de directorios.
Qué versiones hay que instalar
El aviso de seguridad, identificado como VMSA-2026-0011, indica las versiones corregidas. Para VMware Cloud Foundation y vSphere Foundation 9.1 corresponde la versión 9.1.2, y para la rama 9.0, el parche 9.0.2.0300. Quienes usan vCenter 8.0 deben instalar la actualización 8.0 U3m.
Quien ya instaló vCenter 8.0 U3m para corregir la falla anterior, CVE-2026-123890, también quedó protegido contra esta y no necesita otra actualización.
Para los clientes con soporte extendido de vCenter 7.0, la tabla de Rapid7 indica que deben contactar a Broadcom. Las versiones corregidas también resuelven otras seis fallas de gravedad alta o media incluidas en el mismo aviso, entre ellas de CVE-2026-123904 a CVE-2026-123909.
El aviso agrupa además errores en ESX, el software que ejecuta las máquinas virtuales. Las preguntas frecuentes de Broadcom precisan que dos de ellos, CVE-2026-123910 y CVE-2026-123911, son los más graves de ese producto y permiten ejecutar código en el servidor con acceso a la red, sin entrar antes a una máquina virtual.
Rapid7 informó que sus clientes podrán detectar los sistemas vulnerables con una comprobación que prevé publicar en su actualización de contenido del 25 de noviembre.
Bases de datos sin protección dejaron a la vista 3.500 millones de credenciales
Investigadores de seguridad hallaron, en internet y sin clave de acceso, dos bases de datos que en conjunto sumaban 3.500 millones de registros: contraseñas, usuarios, números de identidad y documentos.
Una, con 2.000 millones de credenciales, fue detectada por Jeremiah Fowler, de Black Hills Information Security, y parece compuesta por datos robados mediante virus que copian lo que una persona usa para iniciar sesión. Incluía correos, cookies y claves de sesión en texto sin cifrar, además de unos 400.000 perfiles completos de víctimas.
La otra, hallada por Greg Pollock, de UpGuard, con 1.640 millones de documentos, parece orientada a ciudadanos de China y contenía 840 millones de números de identidad, 300 millones de teléfonos y registros de estudiantes y empresas, incluso de menores y personas fallecidas.
No se identificó a los responsables de ninguna de las dos bases.

articles.title: Après une crise historique sans précédent, Microsoft a déclenché le Code Rouge
articles.text:
La panne mondiale qui a affecté Microsoft durant 24 heures a laissé des traces. En réponse, le géant américain lance son initiative Code Rouge.
Souvenez-vous. Les 12 et 13 novembre derniers, Microsoft expérimentait une des pires pannes de son histoire, qui touchait à la fois Outlook et Microsoft 365. Une panne mondiale qui avait affecté autant les entreprises que les services publics ou bien les hôpitaux. Autant dire que le géant américain ne veut pas voir l'événement se répéter, et commence à s'organiser en conséquence.
Microsoft lance l'initiative « Code Rouge » après la panne de la mi-novembre
Microsoft vient de lancer sa nouvelle initiative dite « Code Rouge », selon une information de Reuters. Celle-ci a pour ambition de revoir totalement la stratégie de prévention et de gestion des pannes majeures chez Microsoft, après les événements de mi-novembre qui ont représenté un véritable échec.
« Le niveau "Code Rouge" signifie qu’il s’agit de la tâche la plus prioritaire pour notre équipe » a expliqué dans un mémo interne le président de Microsoft 365 Core, Jason Henderson. Il faut dire qu'il y a sûrement du travail à faire de ce côté. Car dans une autre note, la vice-présidente de Microsoft en charge de M365 Core et de Work IQ, Amanda Silver, explique que les équipes d'intervention ont dû échanger plus de 11 000 messages sur près de 11 conversations Teams afin de gérer la panne.
Les agents IA pourront à l'avenir aider à répondre plus vite à l'urgence d'une panne
Ils ont ainsi eu beaucoup de mal, du fait de la dispersion des systèmes de suivi internes, a avoir une version cohérente permettant de juger les hypothèses et les décisions à prendre. Pour rappel, il a finalement été découvert que c'était un bug passé inaperçu pendant plus de trois mois qui était l'origine de la panne mondiale.
Cinq axes de travail ont ainsi été dégagés par Amanda Silver, dans le cadre de ce « Code Rouge ». L'objectif est pouvoir résoudre les futures pannes qui pourraient arriver en moins d'une heure. Des agents IA devront par ailleurs être déployés dans ces situations pour aider à une analyse plus rapide des données de la part des ingénieurs. Suffisant pour ne pas voir les déboires se répéter ?
Source : Reuters

articles.title: Huawei convicted of money laundering, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and fraud by US jury — FBI says Chinese tech giant built its success on deception and theft
articles.text:
Huawei convicted of money laundering, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and fraud by US jury — FBI says Chinese tech giant built its success on deception and theft
The sentencing hearing will not happen until September 2027, though.
A jury has found Huawei guilty of bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of the U.S. sanctions against Iran, among others. According to Bloomberg, the verdict was the result of a nearly three-month trial in which a foreign company has been prosecuted by the U.S. Department of Justice. This is a rare occurrence, resulting in a conviction of 10 out of 12 counts, with the Chinese company getting cleared of conspiracy to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy.
“Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion, and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies, they are serious crimes,” James Barnacle, the Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI New York Field Office, which conducted the investigation on the tech firm, told the publication. “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”
Huawei has long been in the crosshairs of the U.S., with the company getting banned from the country in 2018 alongside other Chinese telecommunications hardware manufacturers. It has even sued the U.S. government, claiming that the equipment ban against the company is unconstitutional. Nevertheless, Washington proceeded with the move and built a case against the company as early as 2019. This has been hit by multiple delays, though, owing to the COVID-19 Pandemic, as well as Huawei’s multiple attempts to halt the investigation even before the case went to trial. There was even an allegation that two Chinese intelligence officers offered $61,000 in Bitcoin to a U.S. law enforcement official to get insider information about the case.
It was also in 2018 that the daughter of Huawei founder and company CFO Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Canada on suspicion of the firm’s attempt to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Iran. Washington even attempted to have her extradited to the U.S., but she was able to return to China in 2019 after admitting to the company’s illegal business in Iran. Aside from that, the U.S. Department of Justice provided other examples of Huawei’s violations, including the theft of T-Mobile’s robotic touch screen testing robot, with a Huawei employee stealing a part of the device from T-Mobile’s controlled lab, the copying of Cisco router source code, another Huawei employee photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment, and using confidential information gathered through an NDA from Quintel, a U.S. antenna manufacturer, which was subsequently included in Huawei’s patent application.
On the other hand, the company’s lead defense attorney, Brian Heberlig, focused on its acquittal on two of the charges. “It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig told Bloomberg. The racketeering conspiracy “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”
Sentencing hearing for the company is set for September 2027, although it’s still unclear what penalties the U.S. government is seeking. The Chinese Foreign Ministry, on the other hand, said, “The Chinese government firmly opposes the U.S. suppression and containment of Chinese companies and firmly supports Chinese companies in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests.”

articles.title: Nvidia might be about to cut GPU supply in a major way — which means Black Friday deals on graphics cards suddenly look even more tempting
articles.text:
Rumor suggests Nvidia will cut GPU supply by 20% to 30% over the next few months — so if you don’t buy soon, prices could get even scarier
A solid Black Friday deal could be a smart move
- A rumor claims Nvidia will reduce gaming GPU supply in China by 20% to 30% over the next quarter
- If true, this will likely be reflected in the global picture for Nvidia's consumer GPUs
- It comes on top of some big price hikes for GPUs already, and could mean an even more miserable start to 2027 for PC gamers
We don't need any more supply shocks in the desktop GPU world right now — but we're about to be dealt another blow by Nvidia, if a fresh rumor is correct.
VideoCardz reports that there's been more news from the Board Channels (a source of supply chain rumors over in China) which suggests that Nvidia is dropping its allocation of chips for consumer and gaming GPUs over the next quarter (November to January, or Nvidia's fiscal Q4).
We're told that graphics card makers over in China are going to be subject to a 20% to 30% reduction in supply for gaming GPUs over these next few months, with supply in Q3 already having been tight.
As a result, the (translated) Board Channels post notes that consumer GPU pricing is going to be volatile — although I assume the volatility will purely be a function of how big a price spike might occur.
While this rumor pertains specifically to China, that market doesn't exist in a bubble, and there's a good chance that Nvidia will have similar global priorities — at least to an extent.
Analysis: more GPU misery
This is obviously very disappointing news, although we must take it with some seasoning. It's only a rumor, of course, and as noted, one that applies to China. However, the trouble is that it's quite believable that Nvidia would increasingly focus on its AI GPUs at the cost of consumer products, and that this is going to apply on a worldwide basis to some extent.
GPU pricing is already in a bad way, with recent major increases taking their toll — especially with higher-end Nvidia graphics cards. If more pricing pain is in the cards, well, that could push many GeForce GPUs into truly frightening territory in terms of just how expensive they're getting.

articles.title: Como desligar o PS5 com segurança (com ou sem controle)
articles.text:
Como desligar o PS5 com segurança (com ou sem controle)
Desligar o PS5 com segurança evita a corrupção de saves e a reconstrução do banco de dados do sistema
Você pode desligar o PlayStation 5 de forma rápida pelo menu “Energia” utilizando o controle DualSense ou segurando o botão de energia diretamente no console. Independentemente da escolha, aguarde sempre a luz indicadora parar de piscar e apagar por completo antes de desconectar o cabo da tomada.
Seguir esse cuidado para desligar PS5 corretamente protege o SSD interno e garante que os processos em segundo plano sejam encerrados sem falhas. Cortes bruscos de energia podem corromper seus saves de jogos e até exigir a reconstrução do banco de dados do sistema.
A seguir, o Tecnoblog te mostra o passo a passo para desligar o PS5 com segurança.
Para desligar o PS5 pelo controle DualSense de forma segura, basta acessar o menu rápido do console em poucos segundos.
Dê um toque rápido no botão PS, aquele com o logotipo da marca localizado no centro do DualSense, para abrir o Centro de Controle do PS5 na parte inferior da tela.
Use os direcionais do controle para navegar até o ícone Energia, geralmente posicionado na extremidade direita do Centro de Controle, e confirme a seleção apertando o botão X.
Escolha a opção “Desligar PS5” para desligar o PlayStation 5 com segurança e aguarde até que a luz indicadora do console pare de piscar em branco antes de removê-lo da tomada.
Se o controle DualSense descarregou ou não está por perto, você pode desligar o PS5 corretamente diretamente pelo botão de energia do console. Então, faça os seguintes passos:
- Localize o botão de energia na parte frontal do PS5.
- Mantenha esse botão pressionado por cerca de três segundos até ouvir um bipe emitido pelo console.
- Solte o botão imediatamente após o bipe para não forçar um desligamento brusco.
- Aguarde a luz indicadora piscar em branco e apagar por completo antes de mover o console ou desconectá-lo da tomada.
Desligar o PS5 puxando o cabo da tomada com o console ligado corta a energia bruscamente, o que pode corromper arquivos salvos e danificar o armazenamento SSD interno. Na próxima vez que você ligar o aparelho, o sistema operacional precisará executar uma reconstrução do banco de dados para tentar reparar esses erros.
Para proteger o console, certifique-se sempre de que todos os processos em segundo plano tenham sido encerrados antes de desconectá-lo da rede elétrica. Observe a luz indicadora do gabinete e só retire o fio quando ela estiver completamente apagada, já que qualquer sinal luminoso indica a gravação de dados em andamento.
Sim, é possível desligar o PS5 pelo celular usando o app PS Remote Play, ferramenta que espelha a tela do console pela internet para controle à distância. Como o PlayStation App não traz um botão direto para essa tarefa, basta iniciar uma sessão de Uso Remoto, tocar no ícone do botão PS na interface virtual e selecionar “Desligar PS5” no menu Energia.
Para realizar a ação, o console precisa estar ligado ou em modo repouso com a conexão à internet e o acesso remoto previamente ativados nas configurações do sistema. Além disso, o celular deve estar logado na mesma conta PlayStation (PSN) e contar com uma rede Wi-Fi ou móvel estável para evitar falhas de conexão.
Sim, você desliga apenas o DualSense pressionando o botão PS por cerca de 10 a 12 segundos até que a barra de luz do controle apague por completo. Esse atalho encerra apenas o pareamento sem fio Bluetooth do acessório para economizar bateria, mantendo o PS5 ligado enquanto você assiste a filmes ou faz uma pausa.

articles.title: Formal verification startup Sequent raises $2.2M to prove code obeys its safety rules
articles.text:
Formal verification startup Sequent raises $2.2M to prove code obeys its safety rules
Formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today announced that it has raised $2.2 million in new funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.
Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.
Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.
Following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.
Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who said AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.
Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.
For now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.
For two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.
Along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor plans priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.
Frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”

articles.title: Un abonnement VPN moins cher qu'un café : profitez de l'offre Black Friday CyberGhost
articles.text:
Black Friday VPN : CyberGhost passe à 1,59 €/mois, une offre à ne pas rater
CyberGhost réduit le prix de son VPN jusqu’à 83 % pour le Black Friday. Une offre à 1,59 €/mois qui mérite toutefois un coup d’œil sur les conditions de renouvellement.
Un VPN complet pour protéger jusqu'à 7 appareils
CyberGhost profite du Black Friday pour proposer son VPN avec jusqu'à 83 % de réduction, soit un abonnement dès 1,59 €/mois. Le service donne accès à des serveurs dans plus de 100 pays, tout en protégeant la connexion et en masquant l'adresse IP. Mais avant de profiter de ce prix, mieux vaut jeter un œil au montant prévu après le renouvellement.
Dans un café, à l'hôtel ou en déplacement, CyberGhost ajoute une couche de protection aux connexions internet. Le service chiffre le trafic et masque l'adresse IP, ce qui permet de naviguer avec davantage de discrétion. Il annonce par ailleurs ne pas conserver les journaux retraçant l'activité en ligne.
Son réseau compte des serveurs dans plus de 100 pays. Cette couverture permet de choisir une localisation selon ses besoins, par exemple pour retrouver certains services depuis l'étranger ou accéder à des serveurs optimisés pour le streaming et le téléchargement P2P.
Pas besoin de passer du temps dans les réglages pour utiliser CyberGhost. L'application permet de sélectionner un serveur en quelques clics ou de s'en remettre à la fonction « Meilleur emplacement ».
L'abonnement autorise jusqu'à sept connexions simultanées. Plusieurs équipements peuvent donc être protégés avec un seul compte, sur les principaux systèmes d'exploitation et appareils compatibles.
CyberGhost propose aussi des extensions payantes, comme l'IP dédiée et la Security Suite pour Windows, qui ajoute notamment un antivirus et une protection contre les logiciels malveillants. Ces options viennent compléter l'abonnement VPN classique.
Le tarif de renouvellement à vérifier avant de souscrire
Le prix de 1,59 €/mois constitue l'argument principal de cette promotion, mais il ne faut pas s'arrêter à ce montant. La réduction concerne une période initiale d'abonnement. Une fois celle-ci terminée, le renouvellement s'effectue à un tarif différent.
Il est donc préférable de vérifier le montant total à régler dès la première commande, mais aussi le prix et la périodicité du renouvellement. Ces informations permettent d'évaluer le coût réel du service sur la durée et d'éviter une mauvaise surprise quelques mois ou années plus tard.
CyberGhost laisse aussi 45 jours pour se faire une idée du service. Si le VPN ne convient finalement pas, il est possible de demander un remboursement intégral pendant cette période.
Au final, CyberGhost a de bons arguments pour séduire pendant le Black Friday : un vaste réseau de serveurs, sept connexions simultanées et un prix de départ attractif. Il reste toutefois à regarder ce que coûtera l'abonnement après la période promotionnelle pour savoir si le bon plan en vaut toujours la peine.

articles.title: Elon Musk y Jensen Huang coinciden: “No te quitará el trabajo una IA, sino alguien que sabe usarla”
articles.text:
Elon Musk y Jensen Huang, director ejecutivo de Nvidia, coinciden en que la inteligencia artificial (IA) está impactando el mercado laboral a gran velocidad, pero no necesariamente significa que un programa reemplazará una labor humana.
Huang ha sostenido en varias intervenciones que el riesgo no proviene solo de una máquina, sino de la ventaja que obtendrá el humano sepa incorporarla a su trabajo: “No te quitará el trabajo una IA, sino alguien que sabe usarla”.
Musk, líder de Tesla y SpaceX, coincide con la postura de Huang pero le ha sumado un componente más alarmante. En una entrevista con The Economist, afirmó que la IA podría superar la suma de la inteligencia humana en alrededor de cinco años.
Para ambos empresarios, la discusión ya no se limita a qué tareas puede automatizar un programa, sino a cómo se reorganizarán las capacidades, los salarios y las empresas ante sistemas cada vez más autónomos.
Cómo evolucionará la inteligencia artificial en los próximos años
Musk sostuvo que, hacia 2031, la IA podría exceder la capacidad intelectual combinada de todas las personas. “No habrá nada que la IA no pueda hacer mejor que los humanos, salvo, quizá, ser humano”.
La predicción sitúa el debate laboral en un horizonte cercano. Si los sistemas pueden resolver problemas, producir conocimiento y ejecutar tareas complejas con más rapidez, la adaptación profesional dejaría de ser una cuestión reservada a especialistas. La diferencia estaría en la capacidad de cada trabajador para usar esas herramientas y complementar sus resultados.
Qué impacto trae la inteligencia artificial general
Huang afirmó en marzo de 2026, durante el podcast de Lex Fridman, que la humanidad ya alcanzó la inteligencia artificial general (AGI), un concepto que suele describir sistemas capaces de realizar una amplia variedad de tareas intelectuales. Su definición se aparta de una medida puramente académica y se enfoca en la utilidad económica de agentes autónomos.
Sin embargo, el ejecutivo marcó límites precisos. Dijo que podría haber “cien mil” agentes capaces de crear aplicaciones exitosas, de atraer a millones de usuarios e incluso de generar ingresos rápidamente. Pero descartó que esos sistemas puedan reproducir la trayectoria empresarial, industrial y tecnológica de una compañía como Nvidia.
“La probabilidad de que 100.000 de esos agentes creen Nvidia es del cero por ciento”, afirmó Huang. La frase resume su distinción entre producir una aplicación viral y construir una organización con investigación, infraestructura, manufactura, clientes y capacidad de sostenerse a largo plazo.
Para el director ejecutivo, la IA puede multiplicar la productividad individual y abrir espacio para nuevos negocios, pero no elimina la necesidad de criterio humano. La creación de compañías complejas exige coordinar grupos, tomar decisiones de inversión, identificar necesidades de mercado y enfrentar riesgos que no se reducen a generar código o contenido.
Cuáles empleos se potencian con la expansión de la IA
Huang señaló en el Foro Económico Mundial de Davos que el despliegue de centros de datos, fábricas de chips y redes informáticas está aumentando la demanda de oficios técnicos. Entre los perfiles figuran electricistas, fontaneros, obreros de la construcción, trabajadores del acero, técnicos de redes e instaladores de dispositivos.
El dirigente aseguró que los salarios de esas ocupaciones han subido casi al doble en algunos casos. Huang habló de remuneraciones de seis cifras para quienes construyen fábricas de semiconductores, computadoras e infraestructura de IA.
La mirada de Bill Gates introduce un contrapunto. En una entrevista con The Observer, el fundador de Microsoft advirtió que las empresas pueden optar por “contratar al robot, despedir al humano y no mirar atrás”.
Ante esa posibilidad, propuso estudiar un impuesto al uso de IA para financiar redes de protección y recapacitación laboral, sumado a reservar determinadas ocupaciones para personas.

articles.title: Cyberattaques : l’étude 2026 révèle la vulnérabilité des collectivités locales
articles.text:
Dans près de six communes de moins de 25 000 habitants sur dix, les élus et les agents disent ne pas être prêts à affronter une cyberattaque, contre 54 % en 2024. Et parmi les rares mairies qui se disent prêtes, une sur quatre seulement a prévu comment relancer ses services après une attaque.
En avril 2024, un pirate est entré dans le réseau de la mairie de Gravelines, dans le Nord. Un robot avait d'abord essayé des milliers d'identifiants sur l'accès à distance prévu pour le télétravail, jusqu'à trouver le bon, et le pirate a ensuite désactivé les antivirus pour installer le rançongiciel LockBit. Grâce à son service informatique de dix personnes, la ville de 12 000 habitants a évité le pire, mais l'attaque lui a coûté 50 000 euros, selon la Banque des Territoires. Dans près des trois quarts des communes de moins de 25 000 habitants, la mairie emploie moins de dix agents en tout, soit moins que le seul service informatique de Gravelines, selon un baromètre sur la cybersécurité des collectivités (Sondage OpinionWay pour Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr). Depuis 2024, davantage d'élus et d'agents mesurent le danger, mais ils ont rarement les moyens de préparer leur commune à une attaque.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Une mairie prête sur quatre seulement a prévu un plan de reprise
Sur les 2 830 élus et agents interrogés entre la fin août et la fin septembre, 13 % estiment leur commune suffisamment préparée. Parmi eux, 24 % disposent d'un plan de reprise ou de continuité d'activité, c'est-à-dire d'une procédure écrite pour faire tourner la mairie pendant l'attaque, puis relancer ses services. Les autres répondent non (44 %) ou l'ignorent (32 %).
Si vous habitez l'une de ces communes, et c'est le cas de deux Français sur trois, une attaque peut d'abord vous priver des services de votre mairie. Au cours des douze derniers mois, 9 % des communes interrogées ont subi au moins un incident de sécurité informatique, et 37 % des victimes ont dû interrompre leurs activités et leurs services. Et 19 % des répondants ignorent si leur commune a été attaquée. « Près d'1 collectivité sur 3 a déjà été victime ou ne le sait pas », résume Jérôme Notin, directeur général de Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr.
Les mairies attaquées savent mieux qu'en 2024 d'où venait le coup. Au total, 65 % d'entre elles connaissent au moins une cause de l'incident, soit dix points de plus. L'hameçonnage revient dans 38 % des cas, et une faille non corrigée dans 15 % des cas.
Les appareils personnels servent de plus en plus au travail de la mairie. C'est le cas dans 65 % des communes, contre 58 % en 2024, et il s'agit presque toujours d'un téléphone portable (93 %). Près d'une commune sur deux écrit en outre à ses habitants depuis une messagerie grand public, de type Gmail ou Orange, et non depuis une adresse au nom de la commune.
La plupart des communes consacrent moins de 1 000 euros par an à leur sécurité
L'enquête a eu lieu quelques mois après les municipales de mars 2026, et 71 % des répondants travaillent avec une équipe municipale nouvelle ou différente. Pour 29 % d'entre eux, les élus entament leur premier mandat. Ces équipes héritent de budgets très serrés. Deux communes sur trois dépensent moins de 5 000 euros par an pour toute leur informatique, photocopieur compris, et parmi les communes qui connaissent ce budget, 71 % consacrent moins de 1 000 euros à la sécurité.
Pour 44 % des répondants, la hausse des cyberattaques n'a pas pesé sur les décisions budgétaires de leur commune, contre 38 % qui disent l'inverse. Et parmi les communes qui connaissent leur budget informatique, seules 16 % prévoient d'augmenter leur budget de sécurité l'an prochain, contre 10 % en 2024.
Les répondants citent d'abord le manque de connaissances (46 %), devant le manque d'argent (42 %). Près de sept répondants sur dix ne savent pas dire si les offres de sécurité vendues sur le marché répondent aux besoins de leur commune. Dans 64 % des cas, la mairie se tourne vers son prestataire informatique, mais 83 % des élus et agents concernés ignorent s'il détient le label ExpertCyber, délivré par Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr aux prestataires spécialisés, ou un visa de sécurité de l'ANSSI.
Pour aider les communes rurales, Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr et l'Association des maires de France (AMF) publient un mémento, moins de trois mois après le piratage de l'AMF. Le pirate affirme avoir volé près de 114 000 entrées, avec les noms, les adresses e-mail et les fonctions de maires, de conseillers municipaux et d'agents, et l'association a confirmé l'attaque. Le mémento contient les mesures prioritaires à prendre et la marche à suivre en cas d'attaque, avec les services à contacter. Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr met aussi en avant le 17Cyber, le guichet en ligne d'aide aux victimes. Mais dans 11 % des communes, personne ne gère la sécurité informatique, et 7 % des répondants ne savent pas comment elle est organisée.

articles.title: España tiene gas para afrontar el invierno, pero la crisis de Ormuz le va a costar 6.000 millones de euros
articles.text:
El 28 de febrero, Teherán decidió bloquear en gran medida el tránsito energético por el estrecho de Ormuz y, desde entonces, el mundo no ha vuelto a ser el mismo. La escasez de crudo y gas, las subidas del precio de la energía que están asumiendo tanto hogares como industria y transporte, y la inflación disparada sobre el resto de la economía son algunas de las consecuencias más conocidas de una situación que solo ahora comienza a estabilizarse gradualmente.
Hasta ahora, no sabíamos bien cuánto nos estaba costando esta crisis, pero el consejero delegado de Enagás, Arturo Gonzalo Aizpiri, ha ofrecido una estimación del sobrecoste que estamos soportando en la factura energética.
6.000 millones de euros adicionales. Como recoge Europa Press, durante su participación en un desayuno informativo en Nueva Economía Fórum, Arturo Gonzalo Aizpiri, consejero delegado de Enagás, ha cifrado en 6.000 millones de euros la factura adicional que ha pagado España estos últimos meses, a causa del encarecimiento del gas natural. Además, tomando a Europa como conjunto, Gonzalo ha compartido que este sobrecoste derivado del incremento de los precios del gas asciende ya a más de 52.000 millones de euros.
El suministro no corre peligro. Sin embargo, y a pesar de lo llamativo de estas cifras, el ejecutivo aclaró que no hay motivos para estar intranquilos, ya que el abastecimiento energético está asegurado para esta campaña invernal, incluso, con el fin de las importaciones de gas ruso a Europa previsto para el próximo mes de enero.
De hecho, Cinco Días apunta a que este mismo mes de noviembre las infraestructuras nacionales recibirán cargamentos procedentes de hasta 30 buques metaneros para seguir asegurando el suministro de energía en nuestro país.
España tiene buenas infraestructuras, pero no es inmune. En sus palabras, Europa está preparada y «muy bien» en cuanto a la seguridad del suministro, gracias a haber hecho «las apuestas correctas» en las últimas décadas. Como demuestran esos buques metaneros, en 2026 seguimos recibiendo gas natural licuado (GNL) de 13 países distintos. Se trata de una diversificación que sirve de escudo frente a los vaivenes del mercado y que, en opinión de Gonzalo, nos dota con una flexibilidad y resiliencia «únicas» en el continente para responder de la mejor manera ante crisis geopolíticas como la de Irán o episodios extremos, como el apagón, las danas o los incendios.
No obstante, España sigue comprando el gas en un mercado internacional y, aunque reduce el riesgo al recibir GNL de varios países, esa diversificación no evita las subidas de precios.
Los precios siguen siendo un problema. Otra de las cuestiones que señaló el ejecutivo de Enagás durante esta jornada es que los precios anteriores al conflicto en Oriente Próximo, que estaban alrededor de los 30 euros/MWh, no volverán a registrarse «durante un tiempo considerable». En la actualidad, las cotizaciones se sitúan en torno a los 90 euros/MWh.
