articles.title: UAE's Sooner raises $20 million to expand home financing solutions
articles.text:
UAE's Sooner raises $20 million to expand home financing solutions
- UAE-based fintech startup Sooner has secured $20 million in seed funding, comprising $5 million in equity led by Nuwa Capital, with participation from 500 Global, Annex Investments, Plus VC, Serkal Group, Axeed Group, 21Ventures, Iliad Partners and angel investors, alongside a $15 million Shariah-compliant debt facility from Amwal Capital Partners.
- Founded in 2026 by Mohammed Aziz, Gabriel García Leyva and Vlad Cherevkov, Sooner operates a down payment support platform licensed by the Dubai Land Department, enabling first-time homebuyers to pay 10% instead of 20% upfront on eligible properties, with the remaining down payment spread over 60 equal Shariah-compliant monthly instalments.
- The funding will give Sooner the capacity to support AED 1 billion ($272 million) in home purchases in 2027. The company also plans to launch a Home Equity Line of Credit (HELOC) product next year, enabling existing homeowners to access financing against their property equity, alongside plans for regional and international expansion.
Press release:
Sooner, the UAE's first down payment support platform, has announced a $20 million seed round. First-time homebuyers in Dubai usually have to pay a 20% down payment plus 7 to 10% in closing fees in cash upfront. This changes with Sooner, which is licensed by the Dubai Land Department, with buyers having to put down 10% instead of 20% with the rest paid monthly over five years.
The round comprises $5 million in equity led by Nuwa Capital, with participation from 500 Global, Annex Investments, Plus VC, Serkal Group, Axeed Group, 21Ventures, Iliad Partners and angel investors, including operators from AWS, Lean Technologies and Sarwa, and a $15 million Shariah-compliant debt facility from Amwal Capital Partners, which gives Sooner the capacity to support $272 million of home purchases in 2027.
Most first-time homebuyers can afford the monthly mortgage payments but are held back by the availability of immediate cash. The down payment plus closing fees come to 27 to 30% of the price, about $230,000 (AED 850K) on an $800,000 (AED 3M) home, against roughly 6 to 10% in the United States and the United Kingdom.
Sooner's mission starts with helping renters become homeowners about two years sooner. Homebuyers pick from Sooner-compatible homes, where they pay 10% instead of 20% upfront and the remainder in 60 equal Shariah-compliant monthly instalments, while getting access to first-time homebuyer mortgages from all leading UAE banks with the lowest mortgage rate guarantee.
Sooner's founders come from leading fintech and proptech startups. Mohammed Aziz (CEO) exited his payments company Pluto to Tamara and was the first UAE-based founder to be backed by Y Combinator. Gabriel García Leyva launched rent now pay later at Keyper, and Vlad Cherevkov previously led products at Revolut and Deel.
"We built the product we wished we had," said Mohammed Aziz, CEO and co-founder of Sooner. "I went through this by buying our first family home, saving towards the down payment while also paying rent. My co-founder Gabriel and his wife went through the same as they bought the unit they rented. Every year a first-time buyer spends saving for a down payment, which is a year of rent paid towards someone else's mortgage. We are solving that problem and making sure that people in the UAE can realise their dream of home ownership sooner."
Since its launch in July 2026, Sooner has received about 9,000 applications, representing $4.5 billion in buying demand, and has already supported around $10 million of home purchases.
That mission evolves beyond the first home into helping the same customers build wealth through real estate. In 2027 Sooner will launch the UAE’s first Home Equity Line of Credit (HELOC) product, allowing existing homeowners to unlock value from their current properties to easily secure financing for a new home. This is modelled on America's largest HELOC platforms: publicly listed Figure and Aven, a $2.2 billion unicorn backed by Khosla Ventures, Founders Fund and General Catalyst.
"The UAE market has been historically undercredited and investor-focused. It’s now ripe for a shift to end-user homeowners," said Gabriel García Leyva, co-founder of Sooner. "We reduce the barrier to access and leverage technology to deliver instant mortgage and Sooner down payment pre-approvals, as well as enabling a buyer-focused home discovery and closing experience that helps our customers get keys in hand in as little as 2 weeks."
The timing follows a shift towards end-user buying in Dubai. Residential mortgage lending hit a record $5.9 billion in the third quarter of 2026 (Cavendish Maxwell), and Dubai's Real Estate Sector Strategy 2033 targets a home-ownership rate of 33%.
"Down payment support and home equity release are standard in developed housing markets and still largely missing in the Gulf," said Arnav Danthi, partner at Nuwa Capital. "Sooner is building that for UAE homebuyers, and Mohammed, Gabriel and Vlad are one of the strongest early-stage fintech teams we've seen in the region."
"The Dubai property story is shifting from investor speculation to resident ownership," said Sharif Eid, Head of Fixed Income at Amwal Capital Partners. "Sooner is at the heart of this shift and is built on two simple observations: the down payment is the biggest barrier to ownership, yet it measures savings, not affordability; and people who own their home are people who stay. Sooner paired those insights with the right structure and technology, and that is why we backed them."
The UAE alone is a $4.1 billion revenue opportunity for Sooner's products, and the platform plans to expand to structurally similar markets, regionally and internationally.
Salaried homebuyers can get verified in about two minutes at www.joinsooner.com to get access to the platform.

articles.title: BYD veut une nouvelle usine en France : et cette fois-ci c'est un site Mercedes qui les intéresse
articles.text:
Les constructeurs chinois font plus qu’importer en Europe pour certains : ils veulent s’y installer durablement. BYD est certainement le constructeur chinois qui est le mieux parti pour y parvenir. En plus d’une gamme qui tend à trouver son public, la marque de Shenzhen est sur le point de lancer son usine hongroise de production de véhicules électriques. Et BYD confirme déjà s’intéresser à une seconde usine, cette fois-ci en France, qui est un ancien site de production Mercedes.
Une usine BYD en Moselle ?
Après Bugatti et Stellantis, il y aurait prochainement un constructeur chinois installé en Alsace ? C’est en tout cas le scénario qui se dessine puisque BYD a confirmé s’intéresser à l’usine d’Hambach, en Moselle. Cette usine appartenait à Mercedes, qui l’exploitait jusqu’en 2024 pour la production de Smart, avant de céder l’appareil industriel à Ineos pour la production de son tout-terrain, le Grenadier, qui reprend la philosophie du Defender classique.
Mais désormais, c’est BYD qui souhaiterait acheter cette usine à la société du milliardaire britannique Sir Jim Ratcliffe. Ce positionnement serait stratégique, car il offrirait à BYD une implantation centrale en Europe, permettant d’exporter sa production facilement vers les autres pays de l’Union européenne. Tesla a fait un choix similaire en s’installant près de Berlin, même si son usine est davantage septentrionale que celle d’Hambach.
BYD semble avoir de grandes ambitions pour cette seconde usine en Europe. Le communiqué de presse du constructeur annonce que cette usine servira à produire des véhicules spécifiquement conçus pour les automobilistes européens. Un discours que tient déjà BYD avec la Dolphin G DM-i, qui est, selon la marque, sa première voiture pensée pour les besoins de l’Europe, avec cependant une production chinoise.
Des négociations déjà en cours
Comme l’explique le communiqué de presse, les négociations entre BYD et Ineos sont déjà en cours pour l’acquisition de l’usine. Il s’agirait de négociations exclusives.
Stella Li, vice-présidente exécutive de BYD, a déclaré : « Notre engagement envers l’Europe s’inscrit dans le long terme. Notre projet d’investissement à Hambach reflète notre confiance envers la France et notre ambition de poursuivre notre croissance en Europe. Nous souhaitons proposer aux consommateurs européens une offre de véhicules produits en France, tout en leur permettant de bénéficier, au plus près de chez eux, de nos technologies et de nos innovations en matière de mobilité électrique. »
Dans son communiqué, BYD ajoute que l’objectif est le maintien des emplois locaux et la création de nouvelles opportunités pour les salariés et les fournisseurs de la région. En cas de rachat par BYD, cette usine devrait alors produire principalement des véhicules électriques compacts, un marché très porteur en Europe. Cela permettrait à BYD d’éviter les taxes à l’importation en Europe sur les véhicules électriques produits en Chine et de satisfaire, en France, aux critères de l’éco-score permettant l’éligibilité au bonus écologique. Tout cela sans avoir à faire sortir de terre une nouvelle usine, un processus long et coûteux qui engendre des retards dans la mise en exploitation de l’usine BYD en Hongrie.

articles.title: Quantum Act : l'initiative à 50 milliards d'euros de Bruxelles pour rester dans la course technologique
articles.text:
L'Union européenne ne veut pas abandonner la guerre technologique. Et elle va mettre les fonds dans un secteur où l'on a encore de bonnes chances de réussir.
Il est assez habituel aujourd'hui de moquer l'Europe pour son côté à la traîne dans la grande guerre de l'IA que se mènent la Chine et les États-Unis, avec d'un côté comme de l'autre des modèles toujours plus puissants qui sont présentés. Mais le Vieux Continent a aussi des choses à dire dans d'autres technologies d'avenir, comme le quantique.
Un fonds d'investissement à 50 milliards d'euros pour soutenir le quantique européen
Oui, l'UE pourrait peser à l'avenir dans le secteur de la technologie. Et elle va s'en donner les moyens semble-t-il, comme pourrait l'indiquer cette présentation du Quantum Act par la Commission européenne.
Ce règlement veut pouvoir soutenir l'écosystème européen dans le domaine en réservant un certain nombre de marchés aux entreprises du Vieux Continent. Il veut aussi soutenir la recherche fondamentale, et faciliter le passage de la R&D à l'industrialisation. Enfin, un fonds souverain (Sovereign Tech Equity Fund) va voir le jour, fonds qui pourrait mobiliser à l'avenir jusqu'à 50 milliards d'euros, selon le Financial Times. L'UE espère pouvoir le faire naître d'ici à 2028.
Le quantique, un secteur dans lequel l'Europe tient la dragée haute à la Chine et les États-Unis
Il faut dire que l'on vit une situation contrastée dans ce domaine. Alors qu'un tiers environ des entreprises du quantique sont implantées dans l'Union européenne, et que 44% des brevets sont déposés chez nous, les sociétés souffent de sous-investissement en provenance du privé.
Les jeunes entreprises de l'Union européenne ont ainsi attiré 1,1 milliard d'euros d'invstissement privés, contre 7 milliards aux États-Unis. Au niveau investissement public, on est par contre dans une situation inverse, avec 8,6 milliards d'euros de fonds publics disponibles en 2025 en Europe contre 5,3 milliards aux États-Unis (et 13,6 milliards en Chine).
« Les technologies quantiques façonneront l'avenir de l’industrie, de la sécurité et de l'innovation, et elles auront un impact profond sur nos sociétés » a défendu la vice-présidente exécutive de la Commission chargée de la technologie, Henna Virkkunen. L'informatique quantique pourrait à l'avenir permettre de traiter beaucoup plus d'informations, et avec moins d'énergie. Elle pourrait aussi permettre de grandes avancées notamment dans les médicaments, les batteries, la cryptographie et les communications sécurisées.
Source : Reuters, Financial Times

articles.title: PhonePe resumes IPO process; targets listing in Feb-March at $12-15B valuation
articles.text:
PhonePe resumes IPO process; targets listing in Feb-March at $12-15B valuation
PhonePe had earlier deferred its public listing plans amid geopolitical uncertainties, weak macroeconomic conditions and heightened volatility in equity markets.
PhonePe has revived its initial public offering (IPO) plans and is targeting a stock market listing in February-March at a valuation of $12-15 billion (around Rs 1.2 lakh crore to Rs 1.5 lakh crore), merchant bankers familiar with the development said.
The digital payments major is likely to file its revised draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) very soon. The proposed IPO is expected to raise Rs 12,000-14,000 crore and will entirely be an offer-for-sale (OFS), they added.
PhonePe had earlier deferred its public listing plans amid geopolitical uncertainties, weak macroeconomic conditions and heightened volatility in equity markets.
The company has now resumed preparations for the IPO, following an improvement in the broader market environment, stronger equity market sentiment and a recovery in its business performance, merchant bankers familiar with the development said.
The proposed listing is expected to be a significant milestone for India's digital payments and fintech sector.
The macroeconomic environment has improved, with foreign institutional investors (FPIs) returning to Indian equities. November has emerged as the strongest month so far in terms of FPI inflows.
The company's business performance has also gained momentum. After witnessing muted growth last year, PhonePe has returned to revenue growth of around 40% year-on-year, excluding merchant discount rate (MDR) and digital incentives, they said.
It has also turned profit-after-tax (PAT) positive at the group level in the first half of the current financial year, without adjusting for employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) costs. Its lending distribution business has nearly doubled year-on-year, they added.

articles.title: Wann hört KI auf dich? Wenn bei ChatGPT und Claude der Zufall entscheidet
articles.text:
Widersprüchliche Anweisungen: Wenn bei ChatGPT und Claude der Zufall entscheidet
Du hast in den Custom Instructions festgelegt, dass die KI angibt, wie sicher sie sich ist – bei manchen Aufgaben übergeht sie die Vorgabe jedoch einfach. Grund kann die Reihenfolge sein, nach der deine Eingaben priorisiert werden. Diese Erfahrung hat Prompt Engineer Susanne Renate Schneider gemacht.
Bestimmte Vorgaben sind gesetzt
Ganz oben stehen dabei die Sicherheitsregeln der Anbieter wie OpenAI oder Anthropic. Kein Prompt hebelt sie aus, außer gezielte Jailbreaks. Das sind Versuche, durch bestimmte Eingaben Sicherheitsvorkehrungen zu umgehen.
Danach folgen im Job die Vorgaben deines Unternehmens, etwa bei Microsoft Copilot. Auch diese umgehst du nicht per Prompt. Nutzt du KI jedoch privat, fällt diese Ebene weg.
Chat überschreibt mitunter Custom Instructions
Erst im nächsten Schritt kommen laut Schneider deine Eingaben. Dabei hat sie selbst eine Hierarchie überrascht: Die Chat-Eingabe wiegt schwerer als deine Custom Instructions. Das sind die Eingaben, die du in den Grundeinstellungen deines Nutzeraccounts hinterlegst. Mit ihnen forderst du ein bestimmtes Verhalten der KI dir gegenüber an. Die Custom Instructions sind demzufolge laut Schneider eher eine Grundhaltung, die einen einzelnen Prompt überlagern kann.
Außerdem können sich Regeln widersprechen, etwa „Antworte kurz“ und „erkläre jeden Schritt ausführlich“. In solchen Fällen kannst du nicht darauf vertrauen, dass ChatGPT oder Claude dich auf diese Eingaben-Kollision hinweisen. Möglicherweise entscheidet der Zufall, welche Eingabe dabei befolgt wird.
Wie du damit umgehen kannst und welche Eingaben in den Custom Instructions recht zuverlässig funktionieren, hörst du in der verlinkten Folge von t3n MeisterPrompter. articles.title: Programar mensajes en WhatsApp hasta por dos semanas: cómo hacerlo en chats individuales y grupales
articles.text:
WhatsApp incorporó los mensajes programados, una función que permite redactar un aviso en cualquier momento y fijar su envío entre 10 minutos y 14 días después. La herramienta está disponible para conversaciones individuales y grupales, y acerca a la aplicación a opciones ya conocidas en plataformas de correo electrónico como Gmail y Outlook.
La novedad busca resolver situaciones cotidianas en las que el contenido está listo, pero el horario no es el adecuado. Puede servir para enviar un saludo de cumpleaños a la medianoche del país donde vive el destinatario, recordar una cita laboral o desear suerte antes de un examen sin tener que permanecer pendiente del reloj.
Cómo programar un mensaje dentro de WhatsApp
El proceso comienza en el chat individual o grupal elegido donde se escribe el texto y luego se debe mantener presionado el botón de enviar donde WhatsApp muestra una opción para seleccionar la fecha y hora de la entrega.
La aplicación permite programar el envío desde 10 minutos hasta un máximo de 14 días. Una vez confirmado el horario, el mensaje queda en espera dentro de la plataforma y será enviado de forma automática en el momento definido por quien lo creó.
Por su parte, el envío de una sola vista para videos e imágenes sigue manteniendo el mismo proceso.
Para qué tipo de conversaciones funciona la opción de programar
Los mensajes programados pueden utilizarse tanto en chats entre dos personas como en grupos. Esto amplía sus posibles usos: una persona puede preparar un saludo privado, mientras que administradores, familias o grupos de trabajo pueden dejar listos avisos para que lleguen cuando todos deban recibirlos.
En los grupos, la función evita depender de que alguien esté conectado a una hora determinada para compartir información. Un recordatorio sobre una reunión, una fecha límite o una actividad puede escribirse con anticipación y quedar previsto para el horario acordado, sin alterar el funcionamiento habitual de la conversación.
Qué contenidos se pueden dejar pendientes
La programación no se limita a los textos. La función admite mensajes de texto, fotos y videos, por lo que es posible preparar desde una felicitación acompañada por una imagen hasta un aviso audiovisual para familiares, compañeros o integrantes de una comunidad.
El contenido se verá como un mensaje corriente cuando llegue al destinatario. No aparecerá con una marca especial que indique que fue preparado antes ni requerirá una acción adicional de quien lo recibe. La diferencia queda del lado de la persona emisora, que organiza la entrega para una fecha posterior.
Dónde se consultan o borran los mensajes que aún no salieron
Quienes utilicen la herramienta podrán revisar los envíos pendientes antes de que se cumpla el horario elegido. Esta posibilidad permite controlar los mensajes ya previstos y modificar la decisión si las circunstancias cambian, por ejemplo, si una reunión se cancela o un saludo deja de ser pertinente.
Asimismo, es posible borrar un mensaje programado antes de su envío. La eliminación evita que el contenido llegue al chat seleccionado, siempre que se realice antes del momento fijado. La gestión de esos pendientes ofrece una alternativa para corregir errores o retirar información que ya no deba compartirse.
Qué pasa si el teléfono queda si batería
La entrega no depende de que el teléfono permanezca encendido, con batería o conectado a internet en la hora prevista. Según explicó WhatsApp, el mensaje aparecerá en el chat elegido aun si el dispositivo está apagado o se quedó sin carga cuando llega el momento programado.
La empresa señaló que estos envíos mantendrán el cifrado de extremo a extremo que aplica a las conversaciones personales. Esto implica que el contenido permanece protegido durante el proceso y que terceros, incluida la propia compañía, no pueden leerlo.
Con un límite de hasta dos semanas de anticipación, la función suma una herramienta de planificación a una aplicación utilizada para conversaciones personales, grupos familiares y coordinación laboral. La opción permitirá dejar listo un mensaje cuando surge la idea y entregarlo en el horario que resulte más conveniente para cada destinatario.

articles.title: Aunque suena a abuso, algunas cafeterías están cobrando 3 euros por estar una hora teletrabajando. Lo que dice la ley es más complicado
articles.text:
El portátil abierto, los auriculares puestos y un único café que lleva dos horas enfriándose, con el dibujito de la espuma disuelto por completo. Esta escena forma parte del paisaje de cualquier ciudad española y es, a partes iguales, el sueño del teletrabajador y la pesadilla del hostelero. Esta semana, El Español ha puesto cifras a la que parece ser la solución radical: 3 euros por hora y 22 euros por un bono diario.
¿Qué ha pasado exactamente?
La noticia proviene de un solo local: ‘Con·tempo’, recién abierto en la calle Montesa, en el barrio de Salamanca de Madrid, se presenta como un café de todo el día con espacio de trabajo flexible (All Day Café & Flexible Workspace) y la cuota ya mencionada: 3 euros por hora y silla. Sin membresía ni reserva previa.
También vende un Pase Diario de 22 euros que incluye 15 de consumo, así que el sitio en sí sale por apenas unos 7 (un cowork bastante rentable para freelances). La zona de trabajo ofrece puestos individuales, mesas compartidas, cabinas para llamadas y una sala para reuniones de hasta cuatro personas, tal y como indican en su nota de prensa. En la nota de prensa figura el resto de datos.
No es, por tanto, un bar que de repente te cronometra la tostada. Es un híbrido de café y coworking de zonas separadas. Su lema es "Less rush, more rhythm". Menos prisa pero con brío, lo que la separa del modelo Starbucks y la emparenta con el modelo de del Café Perfetto (o Coco Coffice, más bien), en plena Barceloneta, donde un café con leche cuesta 1,60 euros pero pasa a 2,50 si superas los 30 minutos y a 4 si pasas de una hora.
Fuera de España ya hay muchos modelos así: Anticafé en Francia (el que sobrevive en Estrasburgo, porque el de Lyon cerró) o el mítico Ziferblat, donde pagas por el tiempo, no por el café. Y también destacan los Bake Bros y Mama Shelter en Lisboa, que parten del modelo Desk Amigo: compartes mesa pero no café. En resumen, mucho brunch de bagel de salmón con queso crema y alcaparras, mucho diseño y conceptos heredados de la arqueología holandesa, pero pagas o te vas.
¿Te puede echar una cafetería por abrir el portátil?
Depende de lo que el local haya dejado por escrito. El derecho de admisión existe, pero no es un cheque en blanco. En la Comunidad de Madrid lo regula la Ley 17/1997 de Espectáculos Públicos, y cada comunidad tiene la suya.
El portal de consumo madrileño recuerda que el derecho sirve para frenar la violencia y las alteraciones del normal funcionamiento, nunca como excusa para la arbitrariedad o la discriminación en locales abiertos, por definición, a todo el público. Las condiciones tienen que estar a la vista en la entrada, eso siempre.
Sin embargo, entre juristas no hay unanimidad. El abogado Ignacio Palomar, de Servilegal, explicaba en Confilegal que una cafetería no alquila estancias, sino que vende consumiciones, así que puede ampararse en el derecho de admisión si tiene un protocolo claro y criterios objetivos. Su colega Laura Sierra replicaba en Consumidor Global que la norma no dice nada sobre usar dispositivos y solo prohíbe restringir el acceso de forma arbitraria o discriminatoria.
Quien sea expulsado por sacar el portátil podría reclamar ante Consumo o llamar a la policía. Lo que sí parece aceptado, como recogíamos en Genbeta, es la fórmula intermedia: limitar el portátil en horas punta, como ya hacen cafeterías de Valencia o Barcelona, y permitirlo cuando el local está vacío. El abogado Manuel Martínez Mercado lo avalaba en El Español siempre que no sea discriminatorio.
¿Y cobrar por el tiempo, es legal?
En principio, sí, si se avisa antes. El caso más sonado es el que citábamos más arriba, el Café Perfetto, en la Barceloneta, que se hizo viral en 2025 porque su café subía a 2,5 euros a los 30 minutos. Según VilaWeb, la Agència Catalana de Consum explicó que no existe una norma específica y que se aplica el código de consumo: es lícito tener precios distintos según dónde te sientes, siempre que se muestren de forma visible y clara.
Un análisis publicado entonces lo resumía así: no compras un café, contratas un servicio, y las condiciones deben conocerse de antemano. La OCU va en la misma línea: por el mismo refresco te pueden cobrar 2 euros o 10, siempre que el precio conste en la lista del establecimiento. Si la hostelería pierde mesas, este "tercer lugar" se convertirá en negocio con tarifa. La ley protege más contra la arbitrariedad que contra el cobro, pero mientras vayan de cara, legal sí es.

articles.title: 100 Go en 5G sans payer l’abonnement pendant deux mois chez NRJ Mobile
articles.text:
Black Friday : NRJ Mobile offre deux mois sur son forfait 100 Go en 5G
Black Friday NRJ Mobile : 100 Go en 5G à 0 € pendant deux mois, puis 9,99 €/mois sans engagement. Découvrez les 25 Go en Europe et les frais à prévoir.
Pour le Black Friday, NRJ Mobile offre les deux premiers mois de son forfait 100 Go en 5G. L’abonnement passe ensuite à 9,99 € par mois, sans engagement.
La formule comprend aussi 25 Go supplémentaires depuis l’Europe et les DOM, ainsi que les appels, SMS et MMS illimités dans les zones incluses.
L’opération est annoncée jusqu’au 30 novembre, avec une carte SIM à 1 € et la livraison offerte.
Deux mensualités en moins dès le départ
Changer de forfait peut attendre des semaines. Puis une promotion suffit à remettre le sujet sur la table. Celle de NRJ Mobile a un avantage facile à comprendre : 100 Go en 5G à 0 € par mois pendant deux mois, puis 9,99 € par mois. Les données et les communications incluses restent disponibles pendant la période offerte.
À tarif inchangé, ces deux mensualités représentent 19,98 € d’économie. Sur douze mois d’abonnement, dix sont payants, soit 99,90 €. Avec la SIM à 1 €, la dépense atteint 100,90 € la première année, hors options et hors-forfait.
100 Go pour quitter le Wi-Fi plus souvent
L’enveloppe française laisse de la place aux vidéos dans les transports, aux réseaux sociaux et à la musique écoutée en chemin. Pour quelqu’un qui surveille encore son compteur avant de lancer une vidéo, passer à 100 Go peut changer quelques habitudes. Le Wi-Fi du prochain café devient moins urgent.
La 5G est incluse, avec un smartphone compatible et dans une zone couverte. Le forfait utilise le réseau Bouygues Telecom. Les performances dépendent notamment de la réception et de l’affluence : le volume disponible ne garantit pas le même débit partout.
Une fois les 100 Go consommés en France métropolitaine, le débit est réduit. Le suivi de consommation, accessible en ligne avec les factures et les options, permet de repérer les usages les plus gourmands.
Une enveloppe distincte pour les séjours en Europe
Les 25 Go depuis l’Europe et les DOM s’ajoutent aux 100 Go français. Ils peuvent accompagner un week-end prolongé ou des vacances, pour consulter les cartes, réserver et partager des photos. La liste des destinations mérite d’être vérifiée avant le départ ; le forfait ne couvre pas automatiquement tous les voyages.
Les appels, SMS et MMS sont illimités en France métropolitaine et, depuis les zones Europe/DOM incluses, vers ces zones et la France métropolitaine. Au-delà des 25 Go à l’étranger, internet devient facturé.
Une offre sans engagement à saisir avant le 30 novembre
Cette promotion concerne l’ouverture d’une nouvelle ligne. La SIM coûte 1 €, avec livraison offerte. L’abonnement est sans engagement, mais des frais de résiliation de 5 € sont prévus : liberté de départ et absence de frais ne sont pas synonymes.
Le forfait intéresse surtout ceux qui cherchent une enveloppe confortable autour de 10 € par mois. Les deux mois gratuits donnent une raison supplémentaire de changer maintenant. Ensuite, c’est le tarif de 9,99 € et la couverture dans les lieux habituels qui feront durer l’intérêt.

articles.title: Kioxia to Showcase XL-FLASH Generation 3 Technology, the Next-Generation Low-Latency, High-Performance Flash Memory for AI
articles.text:
Wednesday, November 25th 2026
Kioxia to Showcase XL-FLASH Generation 3 Technology, the Next-Generation Low-Latency, High-Performance Flash Memory for AI
Kioxia Corporation, a world leader in memory solutions, today announced that it will showcase a prototype of its XL-FLASH generation 3 technology, the next generation of its low-latency, high-performance flash memory for AI applications, at KIOXIA Forum in Tokyo on November 26, 2026.
XL-FLASH features significantly lower read latency and higher write endurance than typical NAND flash memory and is being developed for use as a new memory tier that bridges the gap in performance, capacity and cost between storage and DRAM.XL-FLASH generation 3 flash memory leverages CMOS directly Bonded to Array (CBA) technology, a key feature of Kioxia's BiCS FLASH 3D flash memory, to deliver approximately 70% higher bit density than XL-FLASH generation 2 flash memory while maintaining high performance. It also achieves an average read latency of 3 microseconds—less than one-tenth of BiCS FLASH generation 8 TLC products. In addition, power efficiency for reads in 512-byte units has been improved by approximately 135% compared to XL-FLASH generation 2 flash memory. Samples for functional evaluation are scheduled to ship to select customers in March 2027.
The growth of data-intensive applications, including generative AI, has driven a rapid increase in demand for high-capacity memory in computing systems. However, keeping most data in DRAM presents challenges in terms of capacity, cost and power consumption. By leveraging the read latency and power efficiency of XL-FLASH, new system architectures can store data appropriately based on access frequency and performance requirements, complementing DRAM or replacing a portion of it with flash memory. This approach will expand memory capacity and reduce system total cost of ownership (TCO) in AI servers, data centers and other applications.
Kioxia will continue to leverage the speed, power efficiency and endurance of XL-FLASH while pursuing its use across a range of applications, including Super High IOPS SSDs and Compute Express Link (CXL)-enabled memory expansion modules. Through these efforts, Kioxia aims to create a new memory tier that bridges the gap between DRAM and conventional storage.

articles.title: Ladybird browser’s first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable
articles.text:
Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault.
After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it’s an installable package with automatic updating.
Ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google’s Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird’s rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. “The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork,” project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday’s announcement. “The browser around it is modest, but functional.”
A fourth engine
Nearly the entire modern web currently runs on three browser engines. There’s WebKit (Safari), Gecko (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, Blink (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that’s where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.
An independent implementation of web standards has value not just by providing additional competition in the market, but because it can’t help but reveal places where sites depend on Chromium behaviors rather than published specifications. The fact that Ladybird exists isn’t likely to shift the market tides any time soon, but every new browser engine increases the number of implementations that standards can be tested against, which can surface Chromium-specific assumptions and push the ecosystem toward the spec.
Some background
The Ladybird project was borne out of Kling’s SerenityOS project, an attempt to develop a new independent OS from scratch, before splitting off as a separate project. Kling formed the Ladybird Browser Initiative, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by sponsorships and donations. The project’s site highlights that there are no sponsored search engine deals supporting the project like many other popular browsers, and sponsoring entities have no say in the project roadmap.

articles.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
articles.text:
OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.
The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.
That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.
Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.
While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.
Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.
The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

articles.title: Rockstar parent Take-Two cracking down on fanmade GTA VI PC ports
articles.text:
Rockstar Games parent company Take-Two Interactive has shut down a fan-made PC port of Grand Theft Auto VI.
As reported by The Verge, a 15-year-old modder named “NotRexed” had been trying to use AI to bring an Xbox build of GTA VI to PC. However, his project, dubbed “Leonida,” has been removed from the web after he was hit with a DMCA takedown notice from Take-Two.
Per The Verge, the gaming giant has also targeted the main GitHub repository for Leonida and more than 2,900 forks of it on the basis of copyright infringement. Amid all of this, NotRexed took to X (Twitter) to say he’s giving up on porting efforts both due to Rockstar’s takedown notice and not wanting to have “middle-aged men yell and complain.”
Naturally, though, Leonida was just one of many AI-driven efforts to port GTA VI to PC, and Take-Two is no doubt working hard to crack down on all of them. Despite the game having not even been out for a week, modders have apparently been closing in on getting AI-powered PC ports fully up and running. It remains to be seen how well those will actually work over the course of playing such a massive and technically complex game, though.
It should be noted that Rockstar hasn’t yet confirmed a PC port of GTA VI. For its last two games, GTA V and Red Dead Redemption II, Rockstar ultimately released PC ports over a year later.
However, VentureBeat recently reported that Rockstar is planning a Q1 2027 release for a PC port of GTA VI. Former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij also speculated in an interview with RockPaperShotgun that Rockstar will likely expedite the launch of an official PC version in response to these AI-driven ports.
Image credit: Rockstar Games

articles.title: New CPU benchmark tool promises 40 years of compatibility, with support as far back as i386, Windows 95 — CrystalMark CPUix tested on NEC PC-98 21Bs, Pentium 100, and more
articles.text:
New CPU benchmark tool promises 40 years of compatibility, with support as far back as i386, Windows 95 — CrystalMark CPUix tested on NEC PC-98 21Bs, Pentium 100, and more
Want to directly compare your Duron 900, Pentium G3258, and Core i9-9990XE CPUs? CPUiX is scheduled for release on March 31, 2027.
There's a new CPU benchmark on the way designed to handle and contextualize 40 years of personal computer chip development. The upcoming CrystalMark CPUix "evaluates performance from i386 through the latest processors using a single standard across past and future CPU generations," says developer Noriyuki Miyazaki [machine translation]. In terms of hardware/software compatibility, the benchmarking tool will evaluate processors as old as the i386 running on OSes as out of date as Windows 95 and NT 3.51.
Miyazaki says that the upcoming CPUix app will support 16-color environments, which might help folks at the more ancient and creaky end of the PC retro hardware spectrum. Even this limited color UI will have a base maroon theme, as used in the announcement graphic.
The developer is also welcoming feature requests on social media. Don't ask for support for OSes earlier than Windows 95, though, as it has already been stated by Miyazaki that stretching compatibility to Windows 3.1 "is a bit much."
To aid in the development of CPUix, Miyazaki has recently acquired an NEC PC-98 21Bs. This lovely beige desktop arrived on the developer's desk on Sunday, but it has already been used to implement and verify CPUix's functionality on processors without an FPU. Other older systems have been purchased, including a Pentium 100, to ensure wide compatibility. More systems, old and new, are also going to be acquired for testing.
We don't have a lot of information on the inner workings of CPUix as yet. Aspects of the benchmark's test workloads, score weighting, and so on aren't shared on the official pages or social media postings we found. As CPUix comes from the developer of CrystalDiskMark, it looks like it could be a more ambitious version of the CrystalMark Retro 2.0.0 release, which we reported on last year. That also supported systems back to Windows 95/NT 3.51, and CPUs from the i386 era.
CPUix is still in development, and its release date is currently penciled in for March 31, 2027. It seems to have been revealed early, as Miyazaki celebrates the 28th anniversary of Crystal Dew World.

articles.title: Signal now blocks screenshots by default to keep AI agents from reading your chats
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Signal has begun blocking screenshots by default in its messaging app. The change is aimed at AI agents that can read a phone's screen and capture sensitive information in the process. Signal argues that agents built into the operating system can bypass the end-to-end encryption that is the app's main selling point.
The company's concern is where these agents operate. Signal says Google, Apple, and Microsoft are integrating autonomous agents "deep" into their device operating systems. An agent with that level of access does not need to break an app's encryption because it can see messages, pictures, and emails after the app decrypts them for display. Any safeguards built into an individual app can therefore be bypassed.
Udbhav Tiwari, Signal's head of strategy and global affairs, put the stakes in strong terms. "The ability for billions of devices to permanently spy on their users makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke," he told Politico, referring to the 2013 disclosures about mass US government surveillance.
He also raised a potential legal avenue for surveillance. Governments seeking access to private information could ask technology companies for data collected by their agents. That would eliminate the need to break encryption or install malware on a target's phone.
Apple, Google, and Microsoft declined to comment on Signal's claims. Signal wants operating system makers to give apps a way to opt out of AI data access and processing. Blocking screenshots is a temporary measure until such tools become available.
Privacy groups share the unease. Gus Hosein, executive director of Privacy International, pointed to what a phone holds. "Probably the most sensitive device in your entire life is your phone. If it gets nicked, the person stealing your phone is not going to have access to your whole life. We're undoing all those safeguards by inviting AI agents onto these devices," he said.
Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, a policy adviser at the European digital rights group EDRi, called for "serious limits" on what agents can access. She described a future in which "the companies controlling our operating systems can effectively decide how much privacy we are allowed to have, even when we deliberately choose services designed to protect it."
Operating-system-level agents have already launched in many countries. Their rollout has been slower in the European Union, where Apple has cited the bloc's digital competition rules as a key obstacle to introducing its newest AI assistant features. Meta is also advancing its own agent, Muse, which has launched in the United Kingdom.
The UK's Information Commissioner's Office warned last month that AI agent products "may amplify and accelerate risks" to consumers. It said this week that Meta committed to a "voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme" so regulators can keep watching the product. The office is also preparing new guidance on how privacy law applies to AI agents. Meta says Muse is "private, safe and secure by design" and that it has "engaged constructively" with regulators.
Beyond the most serious privacy risks, there are also concerns about what happens to data once an agent gains access to it. Critics worry that the information could be repurposed for AI training or targeted advertising.
Regulators are focusing on one particularly difficult aspect of this problem: data belonging to people who have never interacted with the agent. Third-party data includes messages and holiday pictures sent to a friend who has quietly allowed an AI agent to access their conversations. The sender may have no idea their information is being collected.
Ireland's Data Protection Commission, which oversees privacy matters involving Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and other major technology companies, has begun taking action. In the past month, it stepped in to stop X, owned by Elon Musk, from using third-party data collected by its Grok chatbot to train AI models.
Irish Data Protection Commissioner Niamh Sweeney said last week that it is "much more challenging" to inform third parties that their data is being processed or give them an opportunity to opt out when they have "no idea" their information could also be collected. Her point highlights a weakness in consent-based privacy protections: Users can choose a private messaging app and still have their information exposed through the device of the person on the other end of the conversation.

articles.title: AI Makes Formal Verification Practical
articles.text:
LONDON, U.K. — Math AI foundation model startup Harmonic is expanding into formal verification for software and hardware, starting with C, Verilog, and Rust.
Formal verification is a well-known technique for proving code is correct, and when extended to hardware description languages such as Verilog, for proving hardware designs are correct and will function exactly as the specification demands. Though it’s well known, formal verification is used in a relatively limited way today, and only by specialists, Harmonic CEO Tudor Achim told EE Times.
There are two main techniques used for formal verification today. Most existing schemes use model checkers, which run the code many times over to explore all the possible states to try to find a state for which the code doesn’t behave as intended. Model checkers are powerful, but as the complexity of hardware increases, they are increasingly compute-intensive.
The other method, theorem proving, creates a logical proof that the implementation of the code is mathematically equivalent to its specification. Until now, this required humans to write proofs, and was very difficult for complex hardware.
“Historically, theorem proving has been horrible compared to model checkers,” Achim said. “Because to write a theorem proving proof, you need to write a lot of language, and to write a model checking proof you just need to solve some very specific algorithmic math problems.”
Computers have historically been good at solving specific problems, such as those in model checking, but unsuitable for tackling unstructured problems such as writing proofs. AI has changed everything, Achim said.
“With AI, computers are now unbelievably good at writing unstructured things. So now theorem proving which had no promise for 50 years now has all the promise, because it’s very scalable, if you can write down the right proof,” he said.
Trained for math
An AI model trained for math, such as Harmonic’s Aristotle, can be applied to solve this type of proof. Aristotle has been trained using reinforcement learning over a period of two years, recently achieving gold-medal equivalent performance at the International Mathematical Olympiad.
Hardware and software are not handled differently by Aristotle; C or Verilog code is compiled via Harmonic’s proprietary compilers into a math problem, which is given to Aristotle to solve. Harmonic’s IP is in both turning the problem into math and solving that math, Achim said.
“It’s easy to vibe code a compiler that turns [code] into a math problem, but it’s hard to do one that’s actually correct across all the code on GitHub or can handle 30-million-gate designs,” he said. “There’s a lot of infrastructure [required] to actually do the proofs with this technology. You also need some models that are fast and cheap at doing it, because to write a proof of some code you probably need 10 to 100× as much code in the proof script as is in the original code.”
The actual theorem proving isn’t difficult, Achim said; in fact, it’s very simple compared to the hardest math problems.
“All it’s doing is what a smart developer would do — they have a mental model of what are the inputs to my function, what does my function do to it, and what’s the output,” he said. “You can think of it as really elaborate bookkeeping of the program state — there’s a lot more stuff you’re writing down for bookkeeping than in the code itself.”
This “elaborate bookkeeping” might be used to, for example, prove that there is no set of inputs to the chip that would result in deadlock. A natural-language statement gets turned into a mathematical theorem (written in Lean, a programming language invented for math), and the AI solves that theorem. The idea is to effectively build a model of what happens when the chip runs and prove for all possible inputs that a certain condition can’t happen. If it fails, the AI can produce a counterexample — perhaps a waveform for a particular set of conditions that results in deadlock.
This technique can be used to find bugs very deep in the design. AI chip company Tensordyne, a Harmonic customer, used Aristotle to find bugs more than 100,000 cycles deep, multiple orders of magnitude beyond what model checkers could have found, according to Achim.
How big a design can Aristotle handle?
“We’re at probably a million FLOPS and 20 million to 30 million gates right now, so still not quite full CPU scale,” Achim said. “Empirically, we have scaled the size of designs we can handle by 10x every two and a half months, and we see that continuing, so I think by the middle or end of next year, we’d ideally be at full CPU scale.”
In practice, Aristotle typically runs on blocks of the design, and theorems that have been proven for individual blocks can be reused to prove things about other blocks that depend on them, Achim said. This technique can be used to verify arbitrarily large designs.
The size limitation for single runs is the size of the proof scripts, which are orders of magnitude bigger than the original code, and the artifacts these scripts generate, which are even larger. Eventually, the infrastructure just isn’t big enough.
“Ultimately it becomes a data management question and a parallelization question,” Achim said.
There are also human factors that limit the size of designs that can be verified in a single run.
“As you approach larger designs, you start to run into limitations of the clarity of the specification the designer made — there might be assumptions baked in that are not clear,” Achim said. “A formal analysis is the most detailed analysis of a chip, and it forces you to have all your assumptions out in the open. Traditionally, teams have not been forced to do that.”
With AI, the ability to prove theorems is today outstripping humans’ ability to write specifications, especially as designs get more complex, Achim said.
AI-driven workflows
Formal verification has been used at the end of a workflow to ensure the design is correct before tape-out, but with the dawn of AI-driven workflows, Aristotle could be used during the design process as the specifications evolve with the design, testing that all the properties still hold for every revision, Achim said.
“What we see across the board is that people are rethinking what their flow looks like,” he said. “The old flow was very human-centric; you had well-integrated tools across the board, but people now want to develop at the speed of agents, and I don’t know that people are as wedded to their workflows as one might have thought a year ago.”
Many customers are using agents to assist with designs and write code, but verifying hardware (and software) has been a stubborn holdout for automation so far, Achim said. Automating formal verification could therefore be another step toward removing humans from the chip design process entirely.
Achim expects that easier, scalable formal verification will change the economics of chip design too, since it should make large chip designs approachable even for small teams. “Historically a lot of money in chip development has gone toward verification, 70% to 80% by some estimates,” he said. “Even if you’re spending that much, you’re still limited in what you can be sure is correct, so I think people stayed away from super complex and weird designs … but once you have formal verification and correctness, I think all bets are off.”

articles.title: Bosgame's Ryzen 9 P3 Pro is the best PC I've seen under £500
articles.text:
Bosgame's Ryzen 9 P3 Pro is the best PC you can buy under £500 this Black Friday, and Reatan's A8 is a close second
I found two mini PC deals under £500 that are definitely worth your time this Black Friday
If you've been holding out for a Black Friday desktop deal that doesn't cost a month's rent, these two are worth a look.
The Bosgame P3 Pro packs an AMD Ryzen 9 7940HS (eight cores, 16 threads, boosting to 5.2GHz), 16GB of DDR5 memory and a 1TB NVMe SSD into a mini PC small enough to sit behind your monitor. It's £486.45 (was £579) for Amazon Prime members, a saving of £92.55.
Alternatively, if the P3 Pro sells out, or you'd rather not rely on Prime, the Reatan A8 is a strong alternative at £499.99, down from £599.99 in Amazon's Black Friday Big Deal. That's 17% off, and the price isn't Prime-exclusive.
A compact mini PC with Radeon 780M graphics, Windows 11 Pro, triple-display output, and Wi-Fi 6E. Memory is upgradeable to 64GB and storage to 4TB.
This mini PC uses an AMD Ryzen 7 8745HS (eight cores, 16 threads, up to 4.9GHz) with the same Radeon 780M graphics, plus 16GB of DDR5 and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD. It holds a 4.4-out-of-5 rating from 123 reviews on Amazon.
Why we recommend the P3 pro
Mini PCs often trade power for size, but the P3 Pro leans on a laptop-class flagship chip. The 7940HS handles everyday work, multitasking, and light photo and video editing comfortably, and the 780M is one of the stronger integrated GPUs around. Expect smooth play in esports titles and moderate settings in newer games.
It's easy to live with as well. There's room to upgrade the RAM and storage later, so you can start at 16GB and grow into it. Windows 11 Pro is already installed, so you can plug in and go. It's eligible for free delivery, and you can return it for 30 days.
Some caveats. The listing says dual 1Gb Ethernet, so don't expect faster 2.5G networking. You get a one-year warranty, and the discounted price only applies if you're a Prime member.
The close second: Reatan A8
The A8 beats the P3 Pro on connectivity. You get dual 2.5GbE ports, support for up to four 4K displays (through USB4, USB-C, HDMI and DisplayPort), Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.2. There's also an OCuLink port, which lets you add an external graphics card later.
The dock, power supply and graphics card are sold separately. The hybrid metal-and-plastic case is designed to keep the wireless signal strong. Storage can be expanded to 4TB through a second NVMe slot.
The trade-offs are a slightly slower processor and only a single 16GB memory module in the listing. It also costs £13.54 more than the P3 Pro's Prime price. If you'd rather not pay for Prime, though, the A8 is £79 cheaper than the P3 Pro's standard price.
Price Context
The P3 Pro's list price is £579, so the Black Friday price is 16% below it. The Reatan A8's list price is £599.99, so its deal is 17% below that. Both deals are Black Friday offers and could change or end quickly, so check the price before you buy.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the BOSGAME P3 Pro if... you're a Prime member who wants the fastest processor for under £500, for work, study, and 1080p gaming.
✅ Buy the Reatan A8 if... you don't have Prime, want faster 2.5G networking, more display options, or an OCuLink port for an external graphics card later.

articles.title: “Cyberpunk 2 está cancelado” indicó su director debido a la calidad de GTA 6
articles.text:
“Cyberpunk 2 está cancelado, voy a barrer hojas otoñales en mi patio trasero”, escribió Igor Sarzyński, director de la secuela de CD Projekt RED, después de expresar su admiración por Grand Theft Auto 6. La frase fue una broma, pero resume la presión que el nuevo juego de Rockstar Games ha generado sobre otros proyectos de mundo abierto.
GTA 6 elevó las expectativas de una industria que ya destina años de trabajo y presupuestos elevados a los grandes videojuegos de acción. Para estudios como CD Projekt RED, el desafío no consiste solo en crear una ciudad amplia o una historia ambiciosa: deberán demostrar que sus sistemas, personajes y actividades sostienen esa escala sin repetir problemas de lanzamientos anteriores.
El director de Cyberpunk 2 destacó la escala de GTA 6
Sarzyński compartió su reacción en la red social BlueSky tras conocer el alcance de Grand Theft Auto 6. El responsable de Cyberpunk 2 definió el trabajo de Rockstar Games como un logro artístico y tecnológico por la densidad de su mundo, la coherencia de sus sistemas y la ambición de su producción.
El comentario sobre la cancelación de la secuela no fue un anuncio de CD Projekt RED. La publicación utilizó la ironía para describir el impacto que puede tener un lanzamiento de esta magnitud entre quienes desarrollan otros títulos de mundo abierto.
La comparación resulta inevitable porque ambos proyectos parten de expectativas altas. Cyberpunk 2077 llegó al mercado en 2020 como uno de los juegos más esperados de su generación, mientras que GTA 6 se convirtió en uno de los estrenos más seguidos tras un largo período de desarrollo.
La diferencia está en que Cyberpunk 2 deberá cargar con el antecedente de la primera entrega, que tuvo un estreno marcado por fallos técnicos, problemas de rendimiento y funciones ausentes en varias versiones. CD Projekt RED corrigió parte de esos inconvenientes con actualizaciones posteriores y con la expansión Phantom Liberty, aunque la recepción inicial dejó una referencia difícil de ignorar.
Por qué GTA 6 subió la exigencia de los futuros videojuegos
Grand Theft Auto 6 sitúa su historia en Leonida, un estado ficticio que incluye una nueva versión de Vice City, zonas rurales, carreteras, humedales y regiones costeras. El juego propone un entorno donde la actividad urbana, el clima, la fauna y las reacciones de los personajes buscan dar continuidad a la exploración.
La narrativa se centra en Lucía Caminos y Jason Duval, una pareja que avanza dentro del mundo criminal de Leonida. La decisión de construir el relato alrededor de dos protagonistas apunta a dar mayor unidad a la campaña, frente a la estructura de tres personajes que utilizó Grand Theft Auto V.
Rockstar también incorporó una mayor presencia de redes sociales ficticias dentro del juego. Los delitos, accidentes y situaciones ocurridas en las calles pueden aparecer en transmisiones o videos compartidos por habitantes de la ciudad. Ese tipo de sistemas amplía la sensación de que el entorno responde a las acciones del jugador.
El nivel técnico del título también condiciona a sus competidores. La iluminación, la física de los vehículos, la densidad de peatones y el comportamiento de los personajes secundarios forman parte de una expectativa cada vez más alta para las producciones de gran presupuesto.
Cyberpunk 2 tiene una identidad distinta a la de GTA
La secuela de CD Projekt RED no busca replicar por completo la fórmula de Rockstar. Cyberpunk 2077 es un juego de rol de acción ambientado en Night City, una metrópolis futurista donde las decisiones, los implantes tecnológicos y la construcción del personaje ocupan un lugar central.
Su mundo se organiza alrededor de misiones, diálogos, habilidades y rutas que pueden variar según las elecciones del jugador. GTA, en cambio, prioriza la sátira social, la conducción, el crimen y la interacción libre con una ciudad contemporánea.
Aun así, ambas franquicias comparten un reto: ofrecer un entorno capaz de sostener la curiosidad del jugador durante decenas de horas. No basta con ampliar el mapa; las actividades, la inteligencia de los personajes y las consecuencias de cada acción deben justificar la escala.
El estudio polaco ha reorganizado parte de su desarrollo para la secuela. Entre las medidas figura una mayor presencia de responsables creativos en su oficina de Boston, con el objetivo de reforzar el conocimiento del contexto cultural estadounidense que inspira su universo.
Cyberpunk 2 todavía se encuentra en desarrollo y no cuenta con una fecha de lanzamiento anunciada. La broma de Sarzyński no altera esos planes, pero muestra que el impacto de GTA 6 ya se extiende más allá de sus ventas: obliga a otros estudios a reconsiderar qué espera el público de un mundo abierto.

articles.title: Huawei found guilty of attempting to steal US trade secrets - but not guilty of conspiracy to obstruct justice or racketeeting
articles.text:
Huawei found guilty of attempting to steal US trade secrets - but not guilty of conspiracy to obstruct justice or racketeeting
US court finds Huawei guilty on some charges
- Huawei reportedly stole trade secrets from Cisco, T-Mobile and more
- It also used a company in Iran to commit bank fraud, case reports
- The company plans to "take all necessary legal actions" following verdict
Huawei has been found guilty by a US federal jury of conspiring to steal trade secrets, with prosecutors presenting evidence of IP misappropriation spanning over two decades.
Prosecutors accused Huawei of using these activities to accelerate its growth to become one of the world's largest telecoms equipment manufacturers, with IP involving source code, networking equipment designs, antenna technology and robotics.
Among the companies involved in the case was Cisco, whose router software was said to have been reproduced. Internal engineering notes were even said to have been referenced, but with 'Cisco' spelled backwards.
Huawei accused on more than one count
The company was also said to have obtained T-Mobile information about a robotic touchscreen testing system – Quintel, CNEX, Fujitsu and Motorola Systems were also impacted.
Besides theft of intellectual property, Huawei was also found guilty of committing bank fraud. The brand was said to have conducted operations in Iran through a company called Skycon, which it portrayed as an independent partner, even though it controlled the business.
The Department of Justice concluded that Huawei had committed the following crimes: "conspiracy to steal trade secrets; wire fraud conspiracy; wire fraud; bank fraud conspiracy; bank fraud; conspiracy to defraud the United States; conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA); IEEPA violations; and money laundering conspiracy."
Attorney General Blanche accused the Chinese firm of conducting decades of business in the US "on the basis of lies and theft."
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
"Huawei violated our laws, empowered our enemies, and harmed our national security,” Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Proctor added.
"[Huawei] confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years," the company said in a formal statement, noting that the five trade secret-related disputes had been resolved.
"We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests," the company added.
It noted the jury had also found Huawei not guilty of conspiracy to obstruct justice or conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act, or RICO.
“A jury in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York acquitted Huawei of the government’s RICO charge. Huawei welcomes this decision. It confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years," the company told TechRadar Pro in a statement.
We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit. The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades. No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation. We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.
Huawei operates in more than 170 countries and regions, holds over 165,000 active granted patents, and has invested more than US$270 billion in R&D cumulatively since 2007. Huawei's success is the result of nearly 40 years of continuous investment in R&D, an unwavering commitment to innovation and quality, dedicated employees, and a customer-centric culture. Huawei has always adhered to integrity in business, upheld business ethics, respected intellectual property, and remained committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations.
Huawei takes its compliance obligations seriously. We remain focused on serving our customers and partners and ensuring continuous and stable business operations. We stand firmly committed to long-term investment in R&D and technological innovation for sound operations and sustainable growth.”

articles.title: Amazon’s cumulative ecommerce exports from India reach $27B
articles.text:
Amazon’s cumulative ecommerce exports from India reach $27B
The milestone marks continued progress towards Amazon’s goal of enabling $80 billion in cumulative e-commerce exports from India by 2030, the company said.
Ecommerce major Amazon on Wednesday said it has reached $27 billion in cumulative ecommerce exports from India through its Amazon Global Selling programme, with the number of exporters on the platform rising 20% in a year to 2.4 lakh.
The milestone marks continued progress towards Amazon’s goal of enabling $80 billion in cumulative ecommerce exports from India by 2030, the company said in a statement.
Launched in 2015, the programme has registered over 2.4 lakh exporters, who have sold more than one billion 'Made-in-India' products to customers across Amazon's global marketplaces.
The increase in cumulative exports was $7 billion this year, the same as last year, when it rose from $13 billion at the end of 2024 to $20 billion in October 2025.
"India has the potential to become a global powerhouse for consumer exports, and e-commerce is helping turn that ambition into reality, creating opportunities for every Indian seller to become a global exporter. We see tremendous opportunity in sectors like textiles, where India's manufacturing strengths, craftsmanship and entrepreneurial talent can translate into globally recognised brands," said Srinidhi Kalvapudi, Head of Amazon Global Selling in India.
He said the India-UK trade pact would benefit sellers as lower tariffs take effect, adding that it was still early days and a meaningful assessment would take about a year.
On the upcoming Budget 2027-28, Kalvapudi said the government has begun recognising e-commerce exports as a separate category requiring a different approach.
"We're hoping that they're going to double down on it in the coming budget," he said.
Delhi, with over 36,000 exporters, tops the list of states and Union Territories on the Amazon Global Selling programme, followed by Rajasthan (over 32,500), Uttar Pradesh (over 29,000), Gujarat (over 28,000) and Maharashtra (over 23,500), according to the company.
Among smaller cities, exporters from Erode in Tamil Nadu crossed $121.5 million in sales between January 2025 and the third quarter of 2026.
Health and personal care (45%), grocery (44%), beauty (42%) and toys (35%) emerged as the top-performing categories, recording the highest compound annual growth rates (CAGR) over the last 10 years, the company said.
The programme gives Indian sellers access to 18 or more Amazon stores in countries, including the US, UK, Germany, Canada, UAE, France, Italy and Spain.

Black Friday : les prix des TV Oled et Mini-Led s'effondrent enfin, voici nos 6 modèles préférés dès 550 €
Un Mini-Led à moins de 600 €, un Oled polyvalent à prix plancher ou un téléviseur haut de gamme pour profiter pleinement de ses films et séries : voici notre sélection des meilleurs bons plans TV de ce Black Friday 2026, selon votre budget et vos envies.
Les promotions du Black Friday sont l’occasion de s’équiper d’un bon téléviseur à des prix très intéressants et les prix sont enfin en train de chuter après un début novembre assez mollasson il faut l’avouer. Encore faut-il choisir le modèle adapté à son salon, à ses usages, mais surtout à son budget ! Parmi les références passées dans notre laboratoire, nous avons retenu six TV Oled et Mini-Led, du modèle abordable pour le quotidien aux Oled les plus performants pour le cinéma.
LG C6 : un des meilleurs rapport qualité prix Oled
Le LG C6 reste l’un des choix les plus équilibrés de cette sélection. Il conserve les noirs parfaits et l’absence de blooming propres à l’Oled, avec une colorimétrie très juste et une luminosité qui progresse enfin sensiblement. Les joueurs sont également bien servis avec une dalle qui monte à 165 Hz sur PC, quatre ports HDMI 2.1 et une excellente réactivité.
Le C6 constitue donc une excellente option, d’autant que le 55 pouces tombe à 1200 €, son prix le plus bas jamais atteint depuis sa sortie. Le 65 pouces est quant à lui proposé à 1600 €.
LG 55C6
Samsung S92H : l’Oled à privilégier si les reflets vous gênent
Pour ceux qui regardent souvent la télévision en journée, le Samsung S92H a un argument de poids : son filtre antireflet. Avec une réflectance mesurée à environ 8 % dans notre laboratoire, il atténue beaucoup plus efficacement les reflets des fenêtres et des luminaires. Sa qualité d’image est par ailleurs très convaincante, avec une dalle Oled 165 Hz et quatre ports HDMI 2.1.
À 1300 € en 55 pouces, le supplément de 100 € face au C6 se justifie donc surtout par l’antireflet. En 65 pouces, les deux concurrents sont au même prix : 1600 €.
Samsung 55S92H
LG G6 : un Oled haut de gamme désormais bien plus accessible
Si vous pouvez augmenter votre budget, le LG G6 apporte un vrai supplément de luminosité face au C6. Sa dalle Tandem Oled atteint environ 2340 cd/m² sur une fenêtre de 10 %, et dépasse même les 3100 cd/m² sur les petites zones lumineuses. L’antireflet est également plus efficace que celui du C6, tandis que les quatre ports HDMI 2.1, la dalle 165 Hz et le faible retard à l’affichage en font un excellent compagnon pour jouer.
Le 55G6 est proposé à 1600 € et le 65G6 à 2000 €, là encore, leurs meilleurs prix depuis leur sortie.
Philips OLED951 : une belle image Oled avec de l’Ambilight en bonus
À 2000 € en 65 pouces, le Philips OLED951 constitue une alternative particulièrement intéressante au LG G6 pour les amateurs d’Ambilight. L’éclairage sur quatre côtés prolonge les couleurs de l’image sur le mur et reste un vrai élément de différenciation pour ceux qui apprécient cette ambiance lumineuse.
Le Philips ne mise pas uniquement sur cet équipement. Sa dalle Tandem Oled délivre un pic lumineux proche de 2700 cd/m², une colorimétrie très fidèle et des noirs impeccables. Il prend également en charge le Dolby Vision et le HDR10+, tout en proposant quatre ports HDMI 2.1 et une fréquence maximale de 165 Hz. Notre réserve concerne surtout Titan OS, moins complet et moins abouti que Google TV ou webOS. Un boîtier multimédia externe pourra contourner cette limite si nécessaire.
TCL C89L : du Mini-Led très lumineux à partir de 800 €
Pour profiter d’une image lumineuse sans atteindre les tarifs de l’Oled, le TCL C89L mérite clairement le détour. Son rétroéclairage Mini-Led lui permet de dépasser les 3000 cd/m² avec un contraste solide. Google TV, le bon système audio et les quatre ports HDMI 2.1 associés à une dalle 144 Hz complètent une fiche technique très convaincante.
L’Oled conserve l’avantage sur les angles de vision et l’absence de halos autour des objets lumineux, mais le TCL fait valoir un tarif nettement plus accessible. Le 55C89L est affiché à 800 € et le 65C89L en 65 pouces à 1200 €. Une bonne piste pour ceux qui veulent un plus grand écran. On le trouvera d’ailleurs à 1500 € en 75 pouces et 2000 € en 85 pouces.
TCL C69K : un Mini-Led à moins de 600 €
Enfin, les budgets plus serrés pourront se tourner vers le TCL C69K, proposé à 550 € en 55 pouces et 700 € en 65 pouces. Ce modèle de 2025 conserve plusieurs atouts appréciables : une bonne colorimétrie en SDR, Google TV, une dalle 144 Hz et un système audio Onkyo dont la spatialisation nous avait agréablement surpris. On l'a vu un peu moins cher dernièrement et il pourrait repasser sous la barre des 500 € dans la dernière ligne droite.
Il faut bien sûr accepter davantage de compromis que sur le C89L. Le pic lumineux est plus limité, les reflets sont présents et les halos lumineux restent visibles dans les scènes sombres. Pour regarder la télévision, profiter des plateformes de streaming et jouer sans trop dépenser, il demeure néanmoins une option intéressante à ce tarif.
