articles.title: Sonda registra eclipse solar entre asteroides Didymos e Dimorphos
articles.text:
A missão Hera, da Agência Espacial Europeia (ESA, na sigla em inglês), registrou um eclipse solar no espaço: a pequena lua Dimorphos projetou sua sombra sobre parte da superfície de Didymos, o asteroide maior que ela orbita. A imagem mostra o fenômeno em sistema formado por dois corpos rochosos que estão sendo estudados pela agência como parte de experimento de defesa planetária.
O registro foi feito pela câmera monocromática Asteroid Framing Camera, equipamento utilizado pela espaçonave tanto para navegação quanto para observações científicas.
O eclipse acontece porque Dimorphos passa entre o Sol e Didymos, bloqueando a luz que chegaria a uma parte da superfície do asteroide. O fenômeno é semelhante ao que ocorre durante um eclipse solar na Terra, quando a Lua encobre o Sol.
A diferença está nas dimensões e nas distâncias envolvidas. Dimorphos tem aproximadamente 151 metros de diâmetro e orbita Didymos a cerca de um quilômetro de distância. O asteroide maior mede aproximadamente 730 metros.
Eclipse acontece em sistema com gravidade muito baixa
Segundo Patrick Michel, principal pesquisador da missão Hera, os dois corpos estão sujeitos aos mesmos princípios da mecânica celeste que governam o sistema Terra-Lua. A diferença é que tudo acontece em escala muito menor e em ambiente de gravidade extremamente fraca.
A gravidade de Didymos é cerca de 40 mil vezes menor que a da Terra. Em Dimorphos, ela chega a ser aproximadamente 200 mil vezes mais fraca.
Michel observa que, em teoria, alguém sobre a superfície de Didymos poderia presenciar um eclipse semelhante ao terrestre. Na prática, porém, permanecer ali seria bastante difícil: além da gravidade reduzida, o asteroide gira muito rapidamente.
Leia mais:
- Missão Hera da ESA se aproxima de asteroide atingido pela NASA em 2022
- NASA lançou espaçonave contra um asteroide de propósito – e estamos prestes a descobrir o que aconteceu depois
- A NASA deu uma “pancada” em asteroide no espaço – o que aconteceu depois?
Hera investiga os efeitos de colisão espacial
A missão europeia chegou ao sistema de Didymos para estudar as consequências de experimento realizado pela NASA em 2022. Na ocasião, a sonda DART colidiu deliberadamente com Dimorphos para alterar sua órbita ao redor do asteroide maior.
Agora, a Hera realiza uma investigação de perto para coletar dados sobre o sistema binário e compreender melhor os resultados da colisão. O objetivo é transformar o experimento em uma técnica de defesa planetária mais bem estudada e potencialmente reproduzível.
A ESA também divulgou as primeiras imagens aproximadas do sistema durante uma apresentação realizada em 25 de novembro.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Chizzy Nnamchi's plan for African builders to work globally
articles.text:
After more than three decades in a career, what keeps someone going? Is it the money, the excitement of the work, or the desire to see what else they can achieve?
For Chizzy Nnamchi, it is the excitement of imagining what is possible and helping others realise their potential. At 61, after decades of working across continents and holding senior positions at multinationals—including 3M and DHL—retirement is still not on his agenda.
“The way people go ‘wow’ sometimes when I say things. It’s the way I go ‘wow’ when I imagine certain things,” he says. “Especially working with young people who are just so brilliant and grounded. And that I can help them see better, and they will go and kill it.”
Today, Nnamchi is building Simvo Africa, an edtech platform that teaches people with little or no prior exposure to technology how to code through structured, project-based training. His broader ambition is to equip young Africans with the skills to compete in the global digital economy.
“It’s really about helping the next generation equip themselves with skills so that they can compete,” he says.
Choosing engineering
But Nnamchi’s interest in technology did not begin with a business idea. It began one afternoon in 1980 while he was walking across the field at the College of the Immaculate Conception in Enugu, south-east Nigeria. An aircraft was flying overhead; he could hear it, but could not see it.
He was in Class Three, and his physics class had just begun studying radar systems.
“I said to myself, if I had a radar, I would be able to tell without seeing this aircraft the type of aircraft it is, the direction it’s going and how fast,” he says.
“Right there at that spot, I decided I was going to study electronic and electrical engineering,” he adds.
His father wanted him to study chemical engineering or medicine, but Nnamchi had made up his mind.
He enrolled at the University of Ife—now Obafemi Awolowo University—in Osun State, south-west Nigeria, in 1982 and graduated with a first-class degree.
Despite the university’s limited resources, Nnamchi remembers his time at Ife as formative. Students learned computer programming in machine language and transferred their code onto punched cards for computers to read, with each card representing a line of code.
“In those days, I tried to write code using as few lines as possible to avoid errors,” he says.
Beyond academics, the university taught students to approach difficult engineering problems with confidence, even when resources were constrained.
“When we were at Ife, we developed the mindset that I can design pretty much anything that I want to if I have access to certain resources. We believed we could compete with anybody anywhere,” he says.
By the time he graduated in 1987, Nnamchi had decided to work rather than pursue postgraduate studies. He set his sights on Schlumberger, now known as SLB, an oilfield services company.
“I had chosen to join Schlumberger because that was one of the very few jobs that would put you on a dollar income track right away,” he says. “Instead of going to do a master’s and doctorate, I felt I needed to go earn money to support the family.”
Finding his way into Schlumberger
By the time he was due for the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) in 1987, Nnamchi had already decided where he wanted to serve: Schlumberger’s Warri base in what was then Bendel State.
“I pushed to get assigned to Bendel State, as it was called before it was split up. I wanted either Bendel or Rivers State, where I could be in one of Schlumberger’s locations,” he says.
At orientation camp, Nnamchi says he discovered that the commandant’s girlfriend and his own girlfriend were best friends. He used the connection to approach the commandant.
“I convinced him to write a letter to Schlumberger, stating that NYSC would assign me to the company if they agreed to take me,” he says.
Armed with the letter, Nnamchi travelled to Warri and walked into Schlumberger without an appointment, asking to see the location manager. When he noticed the receptionist struggling with calls and visitors, he remarked that her job was not easy.
“She just melted,” he recalls. The receptionist eventually ushered him into the office of the location manager. He says the location manager noticed that Nnamchi had attended the University of Ife, which he had also attended, and asked whether he knew some of his former lecturers and colleagues. The shared alma mater helped open the door, and Nnamchi secured a place at Schlumberger for his service year.
Initially assigned routine tasks usually given to corps members, Nnamchi wanted more challenging engineering work. Within his first week, he approached the manager to ask for the opportunity to work on engineering projects or shadow the field engineers.
He says the manager challenged him: “Who gave you the guts to think you can shadow the field engineers?”
Instead, the manager assigned Nnamchi a project to build an alarm that would alert staff when public electricity was restored, so they could switch off their generators. Nnamchi completed it within a week.
“You hear it everywhere now when NEPA brings light, but then, I did the first one in Warri,” he says.
Impressed, Faiga gave him another assignment to automate the office gate, which Nnamchi also completed.
After finishing his service year in 1988, Schlumberger retained him alongside two other corps members.
“That was how I started my career fully,” he says.
From oilfields to Singapore
Nnamchi says his full-time career at Schlumberger began with a transfer to Egypt, where he spent six months before moving to Pakistan as a field engineer. There, he worked on wireline logging, using specialised tools and computing equipment to take scientific measurements inside drilled wells.
“It was seriously challenging work,” he says.
He was subsequently transferred to Oman, where Schlumberger field-tested new equipment and technologies. Nnamchi says the experience exposed him to some of the company’s most advanced technical work.
His time in Oman, however, was not without difficulties. He clashed with his Thai location manager over equipment allocation and maintenance, a disagreement he later acknowledged was partly due to his own attitude.
“I honestly had an attitude problem. I didn’t know better. I could have managed it differently,” he says.
After just over a year in Oman, Nnamchi moved to India in 1991, where he was promoted to senior field engineer. His responsibilities expanded to include a wider range of technical services, as well as planning and mobilising equipment and teams for remote projects.
By 1993, he was ready for a change. Although he enjoyed the technical challenges of oilfield work, he felt the industry offered limited exposure to the wider business world.
“If I want to be in the company for the long term, then I would stay and fight for promotions. But I wanted to be much more rounded,” he says. “As much as you do such high-tech work, and you’re dealing a lot with oil money, your exposure is very narrow. You don’t know much else going on in the real world.”
Having decided with his wife to settle in Singapore, he saw Asia’s rapid economic growth as an opportunity to broaden his experience and eventually bring some of what he learned back to Nigeria.
“Asia was growing so fast. So it would be ideal to live there, participate in that growth, learn a lot and see what we can bring back to Nigeria later on in life,” he says.
He left Schlumberger for Singapore, taking with him a key lesson: technical expertise alone was not enough.
“It’s not enough to be very good technically; one also has to be very good at dealing with people,” he says.
Taking 3M into oil and gas
Nnamchi settled in Singapore, where he says he provided business-development support to small technology companies supplying components to the hard disk drive industry. He helped get their components specified in new product designs, potentially opening up significant orders.
“We would spec components into new designs. And then if those components get accepted, tested, and work for the small company in the US or in Europe, it would be like massive sales for them,” he says.
He spent about a decade in that line of work, later extending it to mobile phone manufacturers and exploring the emerging internet economy. By 2002, following the dot-com bust, he was ready for something bigger.
In 2003, he joined American industrial company 3M to develop its oil and gas business in Southeast Asia. Despite the company’s extensive technology portfolio, Nnamchi saw an opportunity to bring its products into an industry where it had little presence.
During a presentation to 3M’s CEO in South Korea, he was asked why the company had not entered the oil and gas market.
“I told him point blank, ‘You’ve not hired people like me yet.’ I was born in the industry. I have relationships and contacts. I understand their pain points. I understand how they do business. So I can translate that to how different technologies within 3M can be applied within the industry. Technology doesn’t sell itself. You have to apply it,” he recalls.
After the presentation, Nnamchi says 3M committed resources to the opportunity, which became a global emerging-business initiative. He built technical teams, developed industry applications and helped expand manufacturing capacity, including helping to establish the company’s first factory in India.
“We built that business from less than $20 million to over $750 million in eight years,” he says.
Although his official position was director of oil and gas for Asia-Pacific, Nnamchi says he effectively ran the global business. Despite the growth, however, he felt his career had stalled.
“I was grinding hard, but I was not really flying career-wise,” he says.
When 3M offered him an opportunity to relocate to the United States, he declined, citing the financial and tax implications. He eventually left in 2011 without another job lined up.
“I actually left without another job, which is something I will not advise, but I left because I needed to just step out,” he says.
Nnamchi says his time at 3M taught him the value of a strong global brand and the resources that come with it. It also shaped his thinking about innovation, particularly the need for companies to look beyond developing new products and rethink how existing ones are taken to market.
Turning around DHL’s African operations
After 3M, Nnamchi says an opportunity to return to Africa came through global logistics firm DHL, which he joined as CEO for Central Africa, overseeing its air and ocean freight business. According to Nnamchi, some of the operations were losing money when he took over, and his task was to turn them around and address other challenges facing the business.
One of the opportunities he pursued was in Angola, where customs had seized three of Schlumberger’s warehouses, holding equipment for almost four years and demanding about $18 million in fines. Nnamchi saw a chance to resolve the dispute and secure a contract for DHL.
“One of my local guys in Angola had been the one training customs officers for quite some time. So I asked him, let’s go make a deal with these guys,” he says.
The negotiations brought the fine down to $3 million. Schlumberger agreed to pay the reduced sum, while DHL secured a contract to manage the movement of its equipment and warehouse operations.
Beyond turning around the business financially, Nnamchi also had to address staff morale, which he says was low when he arrived. He made a point of having lunch with employees to understand their concerns and the challenges they faced.
“People would tell me where they were having difficulties, why they were unhappy and what they thought could be done,” he says. “A lot of it came down to how people were being treated. I had to change that.”
After two and a half years at DHL, Nnamchi decided it was time to move on. The company’s regional headquarters had relocated from Singapore to Basel, Switzerland, complicating his travel arrangements. More importantly, the heavy travel schedule meant he was spending less time with his family.
“I wanted to be a bit more present,” he says.
Returning home and building Simvo Africa
After leaving DHL, Nnamchi began building businesses in West Africa, starting with a franchise from Bata, the global shoe company, covering Angola, Nigeria and Côte d’Ivoire.
“I just needed to build up something so that I could move back home,” he says.
The three-country operation proved challenging, and after four years, he shut down the business in Angola and established his own brands in Nigeria and Côte d’Ivoire.
He also started Simvo Africa in Nigeria, an edtech company built around a coding course developed by his first son, John. Although John initially wanted to introduce the course in the US and Canada, Nnamchi saw an opportunity to bring it to Nigeria.
“I told him, I will start it here in Nigeria,” he says. “I want to train young people, allow them to learn how to code at a level that is not expensive.”
For Nnamchi, the goal goes beyond producing software developers. He sees digital literacy as an increasingly essential skill across professions, from medicine and engineering to finance and law.
“Digital literacy today is currency. It will help you in any field,” he says.
He also sees the venture as part of a wider effort to prepare young Africans for the global economy. With Africans expected to account for one in four young people worldwide by 2050, he believes the continent’s potential will depend partly on how well it equips its young population.
“If we can equip them well enough to compete, you will see amazing things happen in Nigeria and on this continent. I have no doubt about that,” he says.
Building a new generation of coders
Simvo’s training programme is entirely online, combining video lessons, structured chapters and practical projects. Nnamchi says it is designed to take learners from little or no prior exposure to technology to being able to code.
“You can come in with zero exposure to tech, and you will learn to code by the time you’re done,” he says.
The programme’s first student enrolled in March 2025 after approaching Nnamchi for a youth service job. With a background in chemical engineering, she was offered the opportunity to complete the course in three months, with a job at Simvo if she succeeded.
“If you can finish it, learn how to code in three months, I’ll give you a job. And she did,” he says.
She subsequently helped build the company’s website and backend systems. Nnamchi says some other graduates have also joined Simvo, while the company has helped others secure jobs elsewhere.
The platform now has about 105 people studying. Beyond training, Nnamchi says the company also helps graduates find employment.
“It’s not just skills. Oh, we charge you, you study, and we say bye-bye. No, we help you to get a job,” he says.
Over the next year, he hopes to strengthen the platform and expand into other English-speaking African countries before eventually reaching French-speaking markets.
For Nnamchi, however, the bigger ambition is the impact the venture can have on people’s lives and how they see their own potential.
“It’s almost never about me. It’s about the impact I have on people, their careers, their growth and their mindset,” he says. “If I can get somebody to imagine they can do far more than they thought possible, for me, that’s a big deal.”

articles.title: Europa ya no depende del gas ruso: depende de algo más difícil de sustituir
articles.text:
La Unión Europea amplió sus infraestructuras para recibir gas licuado tras la invasión rusa de Ucrania. La participación de Rusia en el total de las importaciones de gas de la UE cayó del 45 % al 12 % entre 2021 y 2025. En el verano de 2026 seguía representando alrededor del 11 %. En determinados contratos a largo plazo se ha establecido el 1 de enero de 2027 como fecha de inicio del veto al gas licuado. Para el gas por gasoducto es el 30 de septiembre de 2027. En un Estado miembro, el plazo se aplaza al 1 de noviembre de 2027 si la Comisión confirma que corre el riesgo de incumplir su objetivo de almacenamiento.
Otra dependencia que afecta a la industria europea es la de los imanes de tierras raras. En muchos de los coches eléctricos están presentes, además de en algunos aerogeneradores. China concentra gran parte de la extracción mundial y una proporción aún mayor del refinado. Conseguir el mineral en otro país es solo el primer paso.
El suministro se decide después de la mina
Es necesario separar los elementos. Se trata de conseguir los metales y las aleaciones con las que se fabricarán los imanes. En 2024, China aportó el 60 % de la producción minera mundial de cuatro tierras raras que se emplean en los imanes (según la Agencia Internacional de la Energía). Su participación en el refinado de estos elementos era del 91 % y, en la producción de imanes permanentes sinterizados, del 94 %.
Richard Holtum, consejero delegado de Trafigura, calcula que en una década se ha cerrado o reducido casi un tercio de la capacidad de fundición de metales básicos en Europa. Todavía quedan instalaciones que podrían modernizarse y hay algunas en las que sería necesario añadir nuevos procesos para recuperar ciertos metales (como el germanio).
Para 2030, la UE quiere que la capacidad minera pueda cubrir al menos el 10 % del consumo anual de materias primas estratégicas (en la medida en que lo permitan sus reservas). Un estudio publicado en 2025 analiza cómo es posible que en 2030 la extracción en Europa cubra ese porcentaje. En el caso del cobalto, habría que multiplicar la producción por entre seis y ocho para alcanzar ese 10 %. Los autores tampoco encontraron proyectos que pudieran cubrir a tiempo ese umbral para las tierras raras y el níquel.
Una licencia puede parar una fábrica
En abril de 2025, China empezó a exigir licencias para exportar siete tierras raras pesadas y algunos compuestos e imanes que las contienen. Las exportaciones de estos materiales descendieron en abril y mayo. La Agencia Internacional de la Energía recoge los problemas de suministro y los paros temporales en algunos fabricantes de coches. Los envíos se fueron recuperando conforme se iban otorgando los permisos.
En octubre de 2025, Pekín anunció una nueva oleada de controles. Incluía algunas piezas producidas fuera de China, pero con materiales o tecnología de origen chino. Washington advirtió de represalias comerciales (con un aumento de aranceles y restricciones a la exportación de software crítico). Desde China se decidió suspender esta segunda oleada en noviembre de 2025. Esta suspensión se prolongará hasta el 10 de enero de 2027.
El reciclaje permite recuperar parte de lo que se ha importado. Por ejemplo, en los aerogeneradores se pueden reciclar alrededor del 85 % de sus componentes (según EY). Sin embargo, se reciclan pocos de esos componentes en la práctica. En el caso de los paneles solares, el reciclaje se ha centrado en materiales como el aluminio de los marcos y el cobre. Recuperar otros materiales de mayor valor sigue siendo complicado.
Bruselas quiere preparar reservas
En diciembre de 2025, la Comisión Europea adoptó el plan RESourceEU. Incluye la creación de un centro europeo de seguimiento del suministro. Además, se van a establecer mecanismos para coordinar compras conjuntas y reservas y también se pretende potenciar la extracción y el procesado en la UE.
Las reservas pueden ayudar a ganar tiempo en caso de corte, pero llenar las reservas tiene su problema. En el caso del galio, más del 90 % del refinado mundial se concentra en China. Si desde Europa queremos almacenar grandes cantidades, debemos comprar en un mercado liderado por el país del que queremos ser menos dependientes.
Estados Unidos también está buscando proveedores. En octubre de 2025, firmó un acuerdo con Australia para desarrollar la extracción y el procesado de minerales críticos. El Gobierno australiano detalla que la cartera de proyectos prioritarios asciende a 8.500 millones de dólares americanos (unos 7.323 millones de euros al cambio del anuncio). Entre ellos destaca una refinería de galio en Australia Occidental.
Foto | Shane McLendon en Unsplash
En Xataka | El tesoro que Europa buscaba en China está en Jaén: concentrados de tierras raras del 19,4%

articles.title: Poco X8 vs Poco X8 Pro: qual smartphone Xiaomi comprar?
articles.text:
Poco X8 vs Poco X8 Pro: qual smartphone Xiaomi comprar?
Comparamos os testes entre Poco X8 e Poco X8 Pro; descubra o que muda em desempenho, tela, câmeras e bateria
O Poco X8 e o Poco X8 Pro são celulares intermediários da Xiaomi com boa relação custo-benefício. Mas enquanto o modelo Pro foca em desempenho avançado para games, a versão base tem preço mais acessível, se destacando pela bateria gigante e resistência aprimorada contra água e quedas.
O Tecnoblog comparou os testes feitos com cada smartphone para te ajudar a decidir qual é o melhor modelo para você. Conheça as principais diferenças entre o Poco X8 e o Poco X8 Pro neste artigo.
|  | Poco X8 | Poco X8 Pro | 
|---|---|---|
| Lançamento | Setembro de 2026 | Março de 2026 | 
| Preço de lançamento | a partir de R$ 2.098 (em conversão direta) | R$ 6.999 | 
| Tela | 6,83″ AMOLED, resolução de 2772 x 1280 pixels (1.5 K) a 447 ppi | 6,59″ AMOLED, resolução de 2756 x 1268 pixels (1.5K) a 460 ppi | 
| Processador | Qualcomm Snapdragon 6s Gen 4 | MediaTek Dimensity 8500-Ultra | 
| Memória RAM | 6 GB, 8 GB ou 12 GB (LPDDR4X) | 8 GB ou 12 GB (LPDDR5X) | 
| Armazenamento | 128 GB (UFS 2.2) ou 256 GB (UFS 3.1), sem entrada para cartão microSD | 256 GB ou 512 GB (UFS 4.1), sem entrada para cartão microSD | 
| Câmera traseira | Lente grande-angular de 50 MP (f/1.8) e sensor de profundidade de 2 MP (f/2.4) | Lente grande-angular de 50 MP (f/1.5) e ultra-angular de 8 MP (f/2.2) | 
| Câmera frontal | Lente grande-angular de 16 MP (f/2.4) | Lente grande-angular de 20 MP (f/2.2) | 
| Vídeo em até | 1080p @ 30 fps | 4K @ 60 fps | 
| Biometria | Sensor de impressão digital sob a tela | Sensor de impressão digital sob a tela | 
| Bateria | Capacidade de 8.340 mAh | Capacidade de 6.500 mAh | 
| Sistema de fábrica | Xiaomi HyperOS 3, baseado no Android 16 | Xiaomi HyperOS 3, baseado no Android 16 | 
| Conectividade | 5G (SA e NSA), 4G, 3G e 2G, Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 5.1, NFC, Dual SIM | 5G (SA e NSA), 4G, 3G e 2G, Wi-fi 6, Bluetooth 6.0, NFC, Dual SIM | 
| Resistência à água | Sim, IP66, IP68, IP69 e IP69K (profundidade máxima de 2 metros por até 72 horas) | Sim, IP68 (profundidade máxima de 1,5 metro por até 30 minutos) | 
| Dimensões | 163,45 mm (A) x 78,27 mm (L) x 8,6 mm (E) | 157,53 mm (A) x 75,19 mm (L) x 8,38 mm (E) | 
| Peso | 223 g | 201 g | 
| Cores | Preto, branco e laranja | Preto, branco e verde menta | 
Contrariando as expectativas, o Poco X8 é maior e mais pesado do que o Poco X8 Pro. Veja as medidas a seguir:
- Poco X8: 163,45 mm x 78,27 mm x 8,6 mm, pesando 223 gramas.
- Poco X8 Pro: 157,53 mm x 75,19 mm x 8,38 mm, pesando 201 gramas.
Também há diferenças no design na traseira: o modelo base do Poco X8 possui um pequeno módulo de câmera que envolve o kit de lentes na carcaça lisa e traz um visual com linhas divididas inspirado em robôs. Esse design está presente nas versões em preto, branco ou laranja.
Já o Poco X8 Pro possui uma traseira lisa nos modelos preto ou verde menta, mas a variante branca inclui um design com linhas divididas similares às do Poco X8. E na versão Pro, as lentes da câmera traseira saltam diretamente da carcaça, sem um módulo dedicado.
O Poco X8 Pro tem construção premium, que inclui fibra de vidro na traseira e bordas de liga de alumínio de grau aeroespacial. Enquanto isso, o Poco X8 adotou uma traseira de plástico reforçado, além de molduras de plástico com fibra de vidro e alumínio fundido.
Apesar disso, no papel, o Poco X8 é mais resistente. Ele chega com proteção total contra água e poeira (IP66, IP68, IP69 e IP69K), suportando submersões de 2 metros por até 72 horas. E ainda oferece proteção contra quedas de até 3 metros. Promete ser ideal para quem pega chuva constantemente ou está mais suscetível a quedas.
O Poco X8 Pro também tem proteção contra água e poeira, mas aguenta submersões de até 1,5 metro de profundidade e por apenas 30 minutos. E a Xiaomi não menciona nenhuma proteção específica contra quedas.
A tela do Poco X8 Pro leva vantagem por trazer suporte a Dolby Vision e HDR10+, conseguindo reproduzir os realces de brilho, cor e contraste em conteúdos compatíveis.
O Poco X8 não traz esse suporte e as imagens reproduzidas tendem a ficar menos fiéis em relação ao conteúdo original. Em compensação, seu display conta com Gorilla Glass Victus 2, mais resistente do que o Gorilla Glass 7i presente na tela do Poco X8 Pro.
No mais, os dois celulares entregam bastante espaço para visualizar conteúdos, brilho satisfatório mesmo em locais bem iluminados, imagens em alta definição e excelente fluidez gráfica. As especificações são:
- Poco X8: 6,83″ AMOLED; resolução 1.5K (2772 x 1280 pixels); 120 Hz; 3.500 nits (pico).
- Poco X8: 6,59″ AMOLED; resolução 1.5K (2756 x 1268 pixels); 120 Hz; 3.500 nits (pico).
O processador Snapdragon do Poco X8 é indicado a tarefas mais básicas, como streaming, navegação na web e redes sociais, além de jogos casuais menos exigentes. Já o chip MediaTek Dimensity 8500-Ultra do Poco X8 Pro garante performance avançada principalmente para jogos e atividades mais exigentes, a exemplo de edições de vídeo e cargas de trabalho de IA.
Os padrões de memória RAM e armazenamento também influenciam nessa conta: o LPDDR5X usado no Poco X8 Pro é mais eficiente e oferece maior largura de banda do que o LPDDR4X do Poco X8, acelerando e otimizando o desempenho em multitarefas.
No quesito armazenamento, o Poco X8 tem versões de 128 GB (UFS 2.2) ou 256 GB (UFS 3.1), enquanto o Poco X8 Pro está disponível em 256 GB ou 512 GB no padrão UFS 4.1, que tem velocidades maiores de leitura e gravação. Isto é, a versão Pro salva arquivos e abre aplicativos armazenados mais rapidamente.
As câmeras não são o foco principal de nenhum dos dois celulares deste comparativo. Mas o Poco X8 Pro se destaca por oferecer um conjunto mais versátil e com melhores resultados do que o Poco X8.
Por mais que as câmeras principais dos dois celulares tenham 50 MP, a do Poco X8 Pro traz um sensor maior e maior abertura de lente, o permite mais entrada de luz e melhora a qualidade das capturas (especialmente à noite).
Fora isso, a lente ultrawide da versão Pro habilita fotos em ângulos mais abertos, e as selfies do Poco X8 Pro capturam mais detalhes.
Já falando sobre vídeos, o Poco X8 Pro consegue gravar em 4K @ 60 fps, com mais margem para recortes e filmagens mais fluidas. E a versão base do Poco X8 é limitada a filmagens em Full HD (1080p) @ 30 fps.
Considerando a capacidade e autonomia bruta, o Poco X8 é o campeão em bateria deste comparativo. Ele tem um componente de silício-carbono com capacidade para 8.340 mAh e aguentou 59 horas longe das tomadas em nossos testes.
Entretanto, o Poco X8 Pro não faz feio: são 6.500 mAh (Si-C) e autonomia para mais de um dia em uso comum. Além disso, a versão Pro tem carregamento mais rápido, de até 100 W, e recarga reversa cabeada de até 27 W. Já o Poco X7 tem carregamento limitado a 67 W e recarga reversa de até 22,5 W.
O Poco X8 Pro se destaca com um sistema de refrigeração avançado de camada dupla, chamado de Poco 3D Ice Loop, que dissipa o calor e pode reduzir a temperatura do SoC em até 3ºC. No Poco X8, a Xiaomi menciona apenas uma proteção térmica que pode desativar recursos para evitar superaquecimentos.
As especificações reforçam como o Poco X8 Pro foi projetado para lidar com processamentos exigentes. Alto desempenho gera mais calor. E temperaturas elevadas demandam um sistema de resfriamento dedicado para que o smartphone mantenha a performance sem superaquecer.
Como a versão base do Poco X8 não apresenta esse sistema avançado de resfriamento, o celular pode interromper algumas tarefas se o aparelho esquentar demais. E isso traz limitações de performance em atividades mais exigentes.
Tanto o Poco X8 quanto o Poco X8 Pro têm 5G, NFC e sensor infravermelho. A diferença é que o X8 usa o protocolo Wi-Fi 5 e Bluetooth no padrão 5.1, enquanto o X8 Pro adota o padrão Wi-Fi 6 e Bluetooth 6.0.
Na prática, o Poco X8 Pro consegue atingir velocidades de transferência de dados mais altas quando conectado ao Wi-Fi, além de oferecer uma conexão mais estável mesmo com vários dispositivos conectados ao roteador.
Já o padrão Bluetooth 6.0 garante ao modelo Pro recursos como medição de distâncias mais precisa e conexão mais eficiente com dispositivos próximos.
Os dois smartphones chegam com o sistema operacional HyperOS 3 (baseado no Android 16), com suporte de atualizações de sistema por quatro anos. A interface é simples e intuitiva, apesar de conter vários apps pré-instalados.
A maioria dos recursos de sistema estão disponíveis para os dois modelos, como temas variados, widgets personalizados e o HyperIsland — funcionalidade similar à Ilha Dinâmica dos iPhones.
No entanto, a versão Pro é compatível com a otimização WildBoost, que aprimora o desempenho geral do dispositivo. E também inclui várias funções de inteligência artificial, a exemplo de transcrições, tradução automática e ajuda de escrita. Nenhum desses recursos está presente no Poco X8.
A versão base até conta com algumas ferramentas de IA, mas restritas à edição de imagens. Com elas, você pode remover objetos, otimizar o efeito bokeh do modo retrato ou expandir a foto, por exemplo.
O Poco X8 é uma boa escolha para quem busca um smartphone resistente e com boa autonomia de bateria, mas não precisa de alto desempenho bruto. Ele é aquele tipo de celular que lida bem com tarefas cotidianas, e que promete durar anos ao seu lado, faça chuva ou faça sol.
Mas fique atento ao preço: muito acima de R$ 2 mil (8 GB + 256 GB), a relação custo-benefício já não é tão interessante.
Já o Poco X8 Pro é um smartphone com altíssimo poder de fogo para para quem não quer pagar o preço de um celular premium. O aparelho entrega maior desempenho para jogos e tarefas gráficas exigentes e tela com suporte a conteúdos HDR.
Na faixa dos R$ 2.700, ele disputa com aparelhos como Galaxy S25 FE (câmeras mais avançadas) e Motorola Edge 70 Pro (12 GB de RAM e câmeras melhores).
O Poco X8 se sobressai em relação ao Poco X8 Pro nos seguintes aspectos:
- Bateria duradoura: a bateria do Poco X8 é relativamente maior do que a do X8 Pro, com autonomia superior a dois dias de uso.
- Resistência aprimorada: o Poco X8 tem proteção contra quedas de até 3 metros e suporta submersões mais profundas e por mais tempo do que o modelo Pro.
- Preço mais baixo: O Poco X8 é encontrado em promoções a partir de R$ 1.800 (6 GB + 128 GB).
O Poco X8 Pro vence a batalha contra o Poco X8 quando o assunto é performance, tela, câmeras e conectividade. As principais vantagens do celular incluem:
- Desempenho superior: o smartphone tem desempenho avançado, com processador, RAM e armazenamento mais rápidos em comparação ao Poco X8.
- Tela com HDR: o display traz suporte a Dolby Vision e HDR10+, oferecendo uma experiência de streaming mais fiel e imersiva.
- Sistema de resfriamento avançado: o Poco 3D Ice Loop reduz superaquecimentos do aparelho diante de processamentos exigentes, o que ajuda a prolongar a durabilidade do smartphone.
- Câmeras melhores: o Poco X8 Pro tem uma ultrawide e conta com câmeras melhores que a do Poco X8. E ainda consegue gravar em 4K @ 60 fps.
- Conectividades mais recentes: os padrões Wi-Fi e Bluetooth mais recentes garantem conexões mais rápidas e estáveis com outros dispositivos.

articles.title: GitHub Ditches CSS-in-JS for CSS Modules, Reports 55% Faster SSR After Three-Year Migration
As wildfire activity heats up, SenseNet has fuelled up to expand south of the border
articles.text:
Vancouver-based wildfire technology startup SenseNet has closed $43 million USD ($62 million CAD) in Series B financing to support its United States expansion.
The news: The October financing, which SenseNet announced on Tuesday, consisted of $32 million USD in equity funding (including an undisclosed amount of secondary for early employees and advisors) and $11 million USD in venture debt from National Bank of Canada. The equity portion was led by Montréal’s Idealist Capital, with help from a fellow new investor in Vancouver’s Sitka Foundation and existing California backers Fusion Fund, Stormbreaker Ventures, and Thin Line Capital.
SenseNet plans to use this capital to expand across the US, including California (with a new office in San Francisco this year), Colorado, Nevada, and Hawaii, as it builds on its recent acquisition of the wildfire business of American competitor N5 Sensors. The startup also intends to grow its 50-person team to 110 and advance its multimodal AI and fire-behaviour modelling capabilities.
From the source: Since closing a $14-million USD Series A a year ago, SenseNet has more than tripled its footprint. The company’s wildfire monitoring network now covers in excess of 450 million total acres, up from 130 million acres 12 months ago. The startup claims that the 5,300-plus sensors and cameras it has deployed across 12 countries have helped its clients spot more than 10,000 fires early—when containing them is often cheaper, easier, and safer.
RELATED: Wildfire detection startup SenseNet buys US competitor
The context: Amid a warming climate, wildfires are becoming more destructive and costlier to fight. Using a combination of ground-based sensors, AI-enabled cameras, satellite intelligence, drones, and predictive analytics, SenseNet’s end-to-end tech helps fire departments, government agencies, utility, critical infrastructure, industrial operators, and private landowners assess wildfire risk, spot blazes early, predict their spread, and respond.
SenseNet co-founder and CEO Hamed Noori told BetaKit over email that over the past two years, in the wake of the devastating Los Angeles wildfires, the startup has seen a spike in investor interest amid “growing recognition that the economic and human costs of wildfires demand a more proactive approach to how we detect, manage, and respond to them.” He said this was reflected in this Series B financing and claimed SenseNet had multiple offers.
Final thought: The scale, intensity, and frequency of wildfires have risen over the last two decades. SenseNet is part of a crop of Canadian startups building tech designed to detect, suppress, and adapt to wildfires. If recent trends offer any indication, the demand and market opportunity for companies like it appear poised for growth over the coming years.
Feature image courtesy SenseNet.

articles.title: Allstate suffers multiday tech outage ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.text:
U.S. insurer Allstate has been experiencing a tech outage since Monday morning, leaving customers nationwide unable to access their accounts, review their policy information, file claims, pay their bills, and more, just ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holidays.
The outage has been impacting both the company’s website and mobile app, TechCrunch confirmed.
The breakdown follows a report from earlier this month that Allstate was planning to lay off up to 10% of its staff as part of an AI-driven efficiency push. (The company had not confirmed the report, which was attributed to unnamed sources.)
Allstate’s outage is the latest in a series of disruptions to services such as Microsoft Outlook and Teams, the airlines, Apple Pay, and several banks. Trump administration officials have said the outages are not being caused by cyberattacks, but are rather being caused by a recent set of upgrades to systems, many of which run on older technology. Those systems are now in need of more frequent security and bug fixes as AI makes it easier and faster to discover vulnerabilities.
At present, a message on Allstate’s website advises customers trying to log in that its services aren’t available, and that the company is “working to restore access as soon as possible.” On X, Allstate is employing what appear to be automated replies to customer complaints, asking them to DM the Allstate account with more information.
Downdetector, a crowdsourced outage-reporting website, shows users began reporting Allstate’s outage from Monday morning. However, the company hasn’t yet issued a formal statement about the disruption, what’s causing it, or when it may be resolved. In the meantime, local insurance agents have been fielding calls and emails from customers who aren’t able to use the company’s online services.
The timing of the outage is particularly bad given that Thanksgiving is a big travel holiday in the U.S., which means there will be car accidents. Customers will be left without a way to get in touch with their auto insurer to file claims and get roadside assistance through Allstate’s app.
Allstate did not immediately return a request for comment.

articles.title: Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures
articles.text:
Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures
- Date:
  November 23, 2026
- Source:
  Universiteit van Amsterdam
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed remarkable materials that can crawl, walk, and dig using their own internal energy, potentially paving the way for a new generation of autonomous soft robots. They also discovered that making individual components more active can paradoxically make the entire material less responsive, challenging a long-standing principle of engineering.
- Share:
Most materials simply react when something pushes, pulls, or bends them. But a very different category of matter can draw on its own energy to change shape and respond to outside forces in surprising ways. Known as active matter, these unusual materials are attracting growing scientific interest. Now, physicists from the universities of Amsterdam, New South Wales, and Cambridge have uncovered remarkable new behaviors that could change how future machines and robots are designed.
Everyday materials such as metal, concrete, glass, and rubber are generally considered passive. They can stretch, bend, shift, or change shape when forces act on them, but the energy needed to produce those changes comes from outside the material.
Active matter works differently. It contains an internal source of energy that allows it to respond to its surroundings in ways ordinary materials cannot. Many examples occur naturally in living systems. A flock of birds, for instance, can move together as a coordinated group, adjusting its behavior in response to wind, changes in the landscape, available food, or a suitable place to rest.
Scientists can also recreate some of these remarkable properties in the laboratory. Researchers from the University of Amsterdam (The Netherlands), the University of Cambridge (UK), and the University of New South Wales (Sydney, Australia) have spent several years developing active materials from surprisingly simple components, including miniature motors, rods, and rubber bands. Their experiments have revealed unusual mechanical behaviors with potentially valuable applications, leading to two recently accepted scientific papers.
Scientists Create Materials That Can Crawl, Walk, and Dig
One of the discoveries involves two familiar mechanical behaviors known as buckling and snapping.
Imagine squeezing a paper ticket between your fingers. As the pressure increases, the ticket becomes unstable and bends to one side. If you then press against the curved surface, it initially pushes back before suddenly flipping in the opposite direction.
This is how ordinary passive materials behave. External forces supply the energy needed for the ticket to buckle and snap, and each action occurs only once in response to the applied force.
The researchers discovered that adding internal activity can fundamentally transform this behavior. They assembled a series of connected rods into a flexible chain, placing small motors at the joints where neighboring rods meet. These motors created interactions that were not symmetrical. Moving one rod could affect its neighbor in a different way than moving that neighbor would affect the original rod (by rotating over a different angle, for example).
The result was striking. When external forces acted on these active chains, they still bent and snapped, but the movement no longer had to end after a single event. Instead, the structures could repeatedly buckle and snap, producing ongoing oscillations.
The underlying physics involves a transformation of the system's critical point, where snapping normally takes place, into what researchers call a critical exceptional point. This unusual behavior makes it possible for the chains to generate movements resembling crawling, walking, and even digging.
The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, with Sami Al-Izzi of the University of New South Wales and Yao Du of the University of Amsterdam serving as joint first authors. One of the team's buckling chains was also featured on the journal's cover.
Beyond revealing unexpected physics, the discovery points toward a promising approach to building materials capable of performing multiple tasks autonomously. Such structures could be especially useful in flexible, "soft" robots, potentially allowing their bodies to produce complex movements without relying on a centralized control system.
Active Matter Challenges a Fundamental Engineering Principle
A separate investigation by the same international research team uncovered another surprising property of active materials, this time challenging a principle widely used in engineering.
Whether designing large bridges or tiny nanomechanical devices, engineers depend on established rules that connect the properties of individual components to the behavior of an entire structure.
One such rule is Le Chatelier's Principle. In the mechanical context described by the researchers, it suggests that changes made to individual parts of a system should produce corresponding changes in the overall structure. For example, making a structure's individual components stiffer would generally be expected to increase the stiffness of the entire assembly.
But the researchers found that active matter does not always follow this expectation. In some cases, increasing the activity of individual components can actually reduce the activity of the material as a whole.
To investigate this counterintuitive effect, the scientists built another structure using motors and rods. Rather than arranging the components in a chain, they connected them into a flat, two-dimensional network resembling a lattice. They then examined how the elastic behavior of the entire structure changed depending on the properties of its individual elements.
Their experiments revealed that the overall response depended on more than simply how active each component was. What mattered was whether the active elements formed connected pathways capable of transmitting mechanical responses throughout the structure.
Why More Activity Can Produce Less Response
The researchers identified a process called percolation as the key to understanding this unexpected behavior.
A useful comparison is the movement of water through ground coffee. If the coffee grounds are packed too tightly, water cannot easily travel through the entire layer. The arrangement of the grounds determines whether the water can find a continuous path.
Something similar happens inside active materials. If too many of the interconnected components have relatively low activity, they can prevent elastic responses from spreading through the structure. Even when other components are extremely active, their influence may not extend across the entire material.
This explains why making some parts more active does not necessarily produce a more active structure overall. The way the components are connected and distributed can be just as important as their individual properties.
The second study, led by first author Jack Binysh from Corentin Coulais's research group at the University of Amsterdam, was published in Physical Review X.
The researchers believe that this unexpected departure from Le Chatelier's Principle could have important implications for understanding and designing systems built from active microscopic structures. These include biological gels, epithelial monolayers, which are sheets of closely connected cells, and neuromorphic networks that mimic aspects of biological information processing.
Together, the findings reveal how dramatically materials can behave when their internal components actively consume energy and interact in unconventional ways. The discoveries could influence research across physics, soft matter science, mechanical engineering, the life sciences, and robotics, while opening new possibilities for creating adaptable materials and smarter robotic systems.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Universiteit van Amsterdam. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Jack Binysh, Guido Baardink, Jonas Veenstra, Corentin Coulais, Anton Souslov. More is Less in Unpercolated Active Solids. Physical Review X, 2026; 16 (2) DOI: 10.1103/flhb-kjyd

articles.title: Tech stock slides continue despite Jensen's return and Anthropic's record IPO
articles.text:
What just happened? The return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, arguably the AI boom's chief salesman, briefly revived tech and AI-related stocks this week, but the euphoria has already faded. Rising anxiety about a potential AI bubble has dragged markets down throughout November, including shares of Anthropic, which fell below the AI giant's initial asking price.
The Nasdaq closed nearly 1% down on Monday, erasing the rally from the return of Nvidia's CEO and continuing the slide that began late last month. Shares of the chipmaker at the heart of the AI boom also fell by almost 6%.
Nvidia's stock was falling even before the November scandal involving Huang. The company is currently trading about 36% below its October peak of $243.37. The plunge has wiped more than $2 trillion from its market capitalization.
Concerns about the AI boom's long-term viability had already tempered markets when reports about Huang's extramarital affairs prompted his resignation early this month. The CEO's return spiked Nvidia stock to about $167.37, nearly 34% above a recent 52-week low of $124.50, but it has since settled back down to $155.38.
Aside from general anxieties about the AI market, ongoing investigations into Huang and Nvidia's behavior are another source of worry. One of the CEO's affairs was with Alice Huang, the former head of Megaspeed, which US authorities accuse of violating export controls by smuggling Nvidia chips into China. US intelligence has also called her a Chinese intelligence asset, which China denies.
Jensen Huang is set to testify next week before the Senate Banking Committee, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee. His reinstatement has drawn bipartisan criticism from US lawmakers.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already accused him of breaking the law. The US has since blacklisted Megaspeed from buying advanced US chips and is planning new tariffs against China and other major trading partners.
Meanwhile, shares of Claude maker Anthropic, which went public at a record $2 trillion valuation last week, also slid on Tuesday. After closing at around $97 on November 20, the company's stock has since sunk below its initial $83 offering price. Claude recently helped prove one of the most famous problems in mathematics, but its proof remains unreadable to humans.

articles.title: The Download: AI swamping open records, and firefighting for permafrost
articles.text:
The Download: AI swamping open records, and firefighting for permafrost
Plus: Hackers reportedly used an AI tool to breach US spy agencies.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
AI is straining America’s open records systems
AI has intensified investors' interest in public records. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered "signals" that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests.
As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests. That could potentially make public offices less transparent.
Find out how AI is testing the limits of America's right to know.
—Matthew King
MIT Technology Review Narrated: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and soil insulating the permafrost below. Five years later, we followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.
Their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases. Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Hackers reportedly used an AI tool to breach US spy agencies
The tool, Artex, was originally designed for cyber defense. (NYT $)
+ Sources suggested that China may be behind the attack. (CNN)
+ Officials say it exposed non-classified data. (Gizmodo)
+ A US financial crimes bureau has also disclosed a breach. (Verge)
+ AI is making online crimes easier. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Firms tied to Alice Huang financed $270 million of AI servers in China
It's unclear whether they contained chips restricted by the US. (Reuters $)
+ Chuck Schumer has accused Jensen Huang of export violations. (Guardian)
3 A powerful HIV vaccine may finally be within reach
“Super antibodies” blocked diverse strains in monkeys. (Nature)
+ Yet vaccine hesitancy is on the rise. (MIT Technology Review)
4 China’s Huawei has been convicted of stealing US trade secrets
It was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud. (BBC)
+ The DoJ says it also helped Iran surveil protesters. (Guardian)
+ But it was cleared of the more serious racketeering charge. (CNBC)
5 Data centers have been linked to hundreds of premature deaths
The culprit is pollution from connected power plants. (Newsweek)
+ Data centers are getting their own gas plants. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Meta insiders warn its AI moderation is causing dangerous mistakes
They say the errors could have sweeping political consequences. (Guardian)
7 The ex-OpenAI engineer accused of spying has been freed
He’ll wear an ankle monitor after posting a $1 million bond. (CNBC)
8 An immune-calming pill has healed severe eczema in a clinical trial
Over a third of patients saw their symptoms improve. (Bloomberg $)
9 AI is forcing researchers to reconsider artificial minds
Some now think minds may not need bodies after all. (New Scientist $)
+ AI consciousness debates are a trap. (MIT Technology Review)
10 The US Army is about to blow up 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives
The old stockpile has become too dangerous to move or neutralize. (Verge)
Quote of the day
“All this guy did was cheat on his wife with two employees and a Chinese spy. Who hasn’t done that?”
—Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel skewers Jensen Huang's swift reinstatement as Nvidia's CEO.
One more thing
Kids outlearn AI—and we still don’t know why
Teaching a computer to use human language requires an inhuman amount of data. An LLM can easily churn through a hundred thousand times more words than a person will experience in the process of mastering their mother tongue.
This yawning divide between children and machines is called the data efficiency gap. It raises a tantalizing question for researchers: How can children learn so much with so little?
By reverse-engineering how they learn, scientists hope to create more efficient AI models—and perhaps settle enduring questions about language and children's developing minds. Here’s how they’re trying to close the data gap.
—Elise Cutts
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ Need a smile? Finland is livestreaming six newborn puppies around the clock.
+ Wes Anderson has stepped into the Criterion Closet and picked out the films he loves most.
+ A product designer has invented inflatable chopsticks that you unroll and blow up when it's time to eat.
+ The James Webb Space Telescope has captured a stunning image of stars brewing in a nebulous cauldron.

articles.title: Lo nuevo de Claude convierte tus Artefactos en apps que puedes instalar en tu PC o Mac
articles.text:
Claude acaba de implementar una función muy útil que te permite instalar Artefactos en tu PC o Mac como si fuesen apps independientes. La nueva herramienta ya se encuentra disponible en las aplicaciones de Claude para Windows y macOS, aunque todavía está en fase beta.
En adelante, Claude te ofrecerá la opción de instalar los Artefactos en tu ordenador. Al hacerlo, las apps tendrán su propio ícono y acceso directo, y se podrán ejecutar de forma directa y con una ventana independiente.
Un punto interesante de esta característica es que las apps que Claude genera a partir de los Artefactos no requieren de empaquetado, ni tampoco de estar firmadas. Esto es ideal para quienes desean armar algo sencillo, sin tener que depender de Claude Code ni de otras utilidades más complicadas.
Hasta aquí, los Artefactos se ejecutaban en el navegador integrado de los clientes de escritorio de Claude. Gracias a lo nuevo de Anthropic, ya no quedarás limitado a esa posibilidad. Si decides instalarlos como una app en tu PC o Mac, podrás continuar interactuando con ellos como si se tratara de cualquier otro software que ya reside en el dispositivo.
Claude ahora puede convertir tus Artefactos en apps de escritorio
Para instalar tus Artefactos de Claude como apps de escritorio, necesitas solo un puñado de clics. Pulsa sobre el nombre del artefacto en el navegador integrado para abrir el menú desplegable y toca sobre la opción "Instalar como aplicación (Beta)". El siguiente paso será definir qué tipo de permisos quieres darle a la app, y listo.
Claude ofrece tres niveles de permisos para las apps basadas en Artefactos. La opción por defecto admite solo las mismas funciones que tienen al ejecutarse en un navegador. Si optas por darle permisos como los de una aplicación de escritorio, podrá enviar notificaciones, usar atajos y más. Por último, puedes otorgarle control total del ordenador para que lea, modifique y/o elimine archivos sin pedirte permiso.
Si ya tienes las apps instaladas y modificas los Artefactos de Claude en los que se basan, estas se actualizan de forma automática sin que tengas que tocar nada. Eso sí, los permisos se resetean cada vez que aplicas cambios. De modo que cada nueva versión te pedirá que le otorgues un nuevo nivel de autorización al ejecutarla por primera vez.
Por último, ten en cuenta que, si bien se ejecutan en su ventana independiente, las apps basadas en Artefactos consumen tu uso de Claude. Así que si planeas ejecutarlas de forma intensiva, ten en cuenta que pueden acabar tu límite de 5 horas (o el tope semanal) mucho más rápido.

articles.title: "Ni siquiera sé por qué todavía tenemos Phone Dialer": un directivo de Microsoft admite que Windows 11 aún incluye una app de Windows 95 para módems que nadie usa
articles.text:
Windows 11 es la versión más moderna del sistema operativo de Microsoft, pero sigue incluyendo varias herramientas que ya cuentan con varias décadas a sus espaldas. Es el caso del Marcador de teléfono, una aplicación de la época de Windows 95 que servía para hacer llamadas de voz a través del módem, algo que ni siquiera en Microsoft parecen tener claro por qué sigue ahí. Y un ejemplo son las palabras de Brandon LeBlanc, director de comunicación de Windows, que respondió en X a un usuario diciendo: “ni siquiera sé por qué todavía tenemos Phone Dialer, estaba pensado para una época en la que los PC tenían módems”.
Una reliquia a un Win+R de distancia. Cualquier persona puede probar esta herramienta abriendo la función de Ejecutar con Win+R, escribiendo dialer y pulsando Enter para abrirla. Eso sí, cuando lo hagas te aparecerá un mensaje diciéndote que no encuentra ningún módem ni dispositivo de teléfono con el que hacer llamadas de voz, o sea que tampoco lo puedes utilizar..
Y es que el programa nació para un tipo de ordenador que prácticamente ha desaparecido. En la época de Windows 95 muchos equipos tenían un módem, interno o externo, conectado con un cable a la toma del teléfono fijo, y el Marcador era la manera de utilizar el ordenador para hacer llamadas de voz, con la posibilidad de guardar números de marcación rápida. Tú escribías o elegías el número, Windows le pedía al módem que lo marcara por la línea telefónica y, una vez hecho, descolgabas un teléfono conectado a esa misma línea para poder hablar.
La respuesta de LeBlanc. El comentario llegó después de que un usuario preguntara a Microsoft si tenía pensado retirar de Windows 11 interfaces antiguas como esta, y LeBlanc, además de cuestionar que algo de los tiempos de Windows 95 siguiera dentro del sistema, aseguró que había trasladado la sugerencia y que no parecía que el Marcador tuviera que seguir incluido.
Aun así, conviene no adelantar acontecimientos, porque pasar una sugerencia a los equipos internos no equivale a anunciar una retirada, y Microsoft todavía no ha decidido eliminarlo.
Las oficinas que todavía lo usan. También es verdad que el Marcador sigue siendo importante en algunas empresas, aunque por motivos que poco tienen que ver con los módems. La aplicación funciona sobre TAPI (Telephony API), la interfaz de Windows a través de la cual se conectan a los PC centralitas como las de Avaya, Auerswald o Asterisk, esta última de código abierto. Con el controlador adecuado, el Marcador llama desde el teléfono de la mesa en lugar de hacerlo desde un módem, y en el caso de Asterisk existen controladores TAPI como Activa TSP que citan expresamente el marcador de Microsoft. El manual de las centralitas de Auerswald lo utiliza para comprobar que todo funciona: se abre dialer.exe, se elige el teléfono, se escribe un número y, al pulsar en marcar, suena primero el teléfono de la mesa y sale la llamada en cuanto se descuelga.
También hay programas de gestión que tiran de él gracias a una función de Windows llamada Telefonía asistida, que permite que aplicaciones como hojas de cálculo o bases de datos añadan la opción de llamar sin tener que desarrollar su propio sistema de telefonía. El programa pasa el número a una aplicación gestora de llamadas, y en Windows ese papel lo ha cumplido el propio Marcador, que ya en Windows 95 hacía de intermediario para otras aplicaciones con peticiones sencillas de telefonía. Sin ir más lejos, DS-Win, un programa alemán de gestión para clínicas dentales, incluye la opción “Windows Wählhilfe (Assistierte TAPI)” para llamar a los pacientes a través de la centralita, y Wählhilfe es precisamente como se llama el Marcador en alemán.
Además, hay administradores de sistemas que abren dialer.exe para comprobar que TAPI responde antes de ponerse a revisar la función de marcar con un clic de Outlook, tal y como explica Tom Keating en su blog de TMCnet, porque si la llamada no sale desde el Marcador tampoco va a salir desde Outlook. Y no hablamos de instalaciones congeladas en los noventa: tras los parches de Windows 11 y Windows Server del 13 de enero de 2026, el blog alemán Borncity recogió el caso de una empresa con centralita Auerswald cuyos PC ya no conseguían conectar con su servidor TAPI, y en esos equipos el Marcador empezó a mostrar que no había ningún módem disponible. En los comentarios de la misma entrada se sumaron otros usuarios de Auerswald y uno de Avaya con problemas parecidos.
No es el único fósil. Windows 11 tiene más rincones que arrastran el diseño de las primeras versiones del sistema. Cuando el sistema se preparaba para su lanzamiento en 2021, el Administrador de orígenes de datos ODBC (Open Database Connectivity), una de las herramientas heredadas más antiguas, apenas recibía esquinas redondeadas y sombras. Se trata de la herramienta con la que, según explica el medio, se conecta una base de datos de Access con fuentes externas como SQL Server, y su cuadro sigue igual en Windows 11 26H2, con una interfaz que se remonta a los tiempos de Windows 3.1.
Por lo tanto, sería injusto señalar únicamente al Marcador. El mismo medio ha reunido una lista de diálogos y herramientas heredados que todavía se pueden abrir, entre los que están el Administrador de dispositivos o la Administración de discos, que ni siquiera parecen pensados para Windows 10.
Lo mismo pasa con el aviso de las teclas especiales, el que aparece al pulsar Mayúsculas cinco veces seguidas y que puede interrumpirte en mitad de una partida. Hasta ahora, para librarte de él había que desactivar el atajo desde Configuración, porque la propia ventana no ofrecía ninguna casilla para que no volviera a salir. Esa casilla es justo lo que Microsoft está probando en las compilaciones Insider del 6 de noviembre de 2026, eso sí, sin cambiar el aspecto Win32 de siempre del diálogo. Charles Oppermann, antiguo responsable de programa en Microsoft, escribió esos diálogos a principios de 1995, y el medio relaciona su origen con los hijos de un directivo que activaban la función sin querer mientras jugaban a Space Cadet Pinball.
Microsoft quiere modernizar el resto. La intención de Microsoft es modernizar Windows 11 y que la mayoría de estos diálogos heredados están en la lista, algo que encaja con lo que March Rogers, director de diseño de la compañía, dijo sobre reescribir los diálogos antiguos en WinUI 3. De hecho, la actualización de noviembre de 2026, KB5132061, moderniza el cuadro de Reproducción automática, el que aparece al conectar un móvil, una cámara o una unidad extraíble.
La ventana de Propiedades del Explorador de archivos también se está rehaciendo con WinUI en las compilaciones de prueba. Además, Rudy Huyn, arquitecto de Microsoft, ya afirmó que las nuevas aplicaciones de Windows 11 serán 100% nativas, así que parece cuestión de tiempo que aparezcan más cambios.
En cuanto al Marcador, en la mayoría de los ordenadores de casa no tiene ninguna utilidad, pero en las oficinas que llaman a través de es lo que conecta el PC con el teléfono de la mesa. Por eso, quizá una de las opciones sea darle el mismo lavado de cara con WinUI 3 que ya se está probando en la Administración de impresión, con modo oscuro y una lista de contactos en condiciones.
En Genbeta | Más de 30 años: un programador muestra el programa más antiguo que todavía funciona en Windows 11

articles.title: Black Friday – Le Xiaomi 17T s'accompagne de deux accessoires et perd 204 € chez Fnac/Darty
articles.text:
Black Friday – Le Xiaomi 17T s'accompagne de deux accessoires et perd 204 € chez Fnac/Darty
Pour le Black Friday, Fnac/Darty joue la carte du tout-en-un avec le Xiaomi 17T. Le smartphone dans sa version 256 Go, accompagné d'une paire d'écouteurs sans-fil et d'un tracker Xiaomi Tag, s'affiche à 599 € au lieu de 803 €. Les adhérents Fnac peuvent même s'en tirer pour 549 € !
Lancé à 749 € au printemps 2026, le Xiaomi 17T avait quelque peu malmené le positionnement tarifaire de la gamme T. La Fnac lui redonne aujourd'hui des couleurs en l'associant aux Redmi Buds 8 Lite, des écouteurs à réduction de bruit active, et à un Xiaomi Tag, bien pratique pour les têtes en l'air qui égarent régulièrement leurs clés. Mais c'est surtout le smartphone, auréolé de quatre étoiles à l'issue de notre test, qui nous intéresse ici.
Xiaomi 17T
Moins encombrant, mais toujours aussi lumineux
Exit la dalle de 6,83 pouces de son prédécesseur, le 17T opte pour un écran Amoled de 6,59 pouces qui facilite la prise en main. Et cet afficheur ne fait pas les choses à moitié côté luminosité, avec un pic mesuré à 3482 cd/m² dans notre labo. De quoi consulter ses messages en plein soleil sans avoir à chercher un coin d'ombre. La photo n'est pas en reste avec un module principal de 50 Mpx épaulé par un téléobjectif x5 de même définition, appréciable pour aller chercher quelques détails au loin. L'ultra grand-angle de 12 Mpx est en revanche nettement moins convaincant.
Des ambitions revues à la baisse côté endurance
Malgré sa généreuse batterie de 6500 mAh, le 17T n'a tenu que 18 h 41 min sous notre protocole viSer. De quoi passer la journée loin d'une prise, mais on en attendait davantage. Sa puce Dimensity 8500-Ultra assure quant à elle une belle fluidité au quotidien, quitte à jouer les timides en jeu pour contenir la chauffe.
Si le Xiaomi 17T seul se trouve à des tarifs inférieurs sur les marketplaces, avec toutefois le risque de mettre la main sur une version destinée à un autre marché que le nôtre, ce pack signé Fnac/Darty a de quoi séduire ceux qui souhaitent renouveler un peu plus que leur smartphone. Et à 549 € pour les détenteurs de la carte Fnac, le trio devient d'autant plus intéressant.

articles.title: Test SAV : Le SAV remplace ma TV LG OLED C1 défectueuse par une dalle neuve… déjà condamnée
articles.text:
Pendant des années, ce qui faisait peur aux propriétaires de téléviseurs OLED, c’était le marquage (burn-in), ces images fantômes que laisse un logo affiché trop longtemps. Elles sont devenues plus rares grâce au nettoyage automatique de la dalle.
Les TV de démo, souvent éteints brutalement à la prise dans les magasins, sont les plus exposés, puisqu’en coupant le courant, on empêche le nettoyage. Mais de l’avis de mon technicien, si vous achetez un TV d’exposition et qu’il est cramé, c’est pris en charge en garantie. Un modèle d’exposition soldé peut donc être une bonne affaire, à condition de faire préciser la garantie sur la facture.
Depuis début novembre, on parle d’un autre défaut, l’edge rot qui se caractérise par des pixels morts qui apparaissent sur les bords des TV OLED à dalle LG. Mon LG OLED48C1, un 48 pouces sorti en 2021, en avait.
Mon souci, c’est que la dalle neuve que le technicien du SAV a posée ce 25 novembre a exactement les mêmes symptômes alors qu’elle était neuve, scellée et censée être en parfait état.
Première conclusion que j’en tire : quand on fait changer une dalle sous garantie, rien ne garantit que la nouvelle sera en bon état, et il vaut mieux le découvrir tant que le technicien est encore là.
J’ai repéré les premiers pixels morts il y a un mois. LG ne couvrait plus le téléviseur depuis longtemps, mais l’extension de garantie du revendeur courait toujours, et l’enseigne a accepté de le prendre en charge après un diagnostic par téléphone.
Immersion à 360° et design innovant : pour le Black Friday, la barre de son Samsung HW-Q995H passe à 890 € chez la Fnac, soit 600 € de remise.
Entre la commande de la pièce et la recherche d’un créneau, j’ai attendu un bon mois avant que le technicien arrive avec une dalle d’origine LG.
D’après lui, cette dalle est plus récente que celle du C1, sans doute une dalle de C2, voire de C3. Elle était d’ailleurs livrée dans un kit avec un nouveau support et une nouvelle carte Wi-Fi, parce que l’ancien ensemble ne s’adaptait plus à cause d’une différence de hauteur entre le châssis et la carte-mère.
Sur un OLED, on remplace presque tout le téléviseur
Changer une dalle OLED n’a rien à voir avec la réparation d’un téléviseur LCD. Sur un LCD, le technicien remplace la matrice (la couche de cristaux liquides qui forme l’image), ou seulement le rétroéclairage si la panne vient de l’éclairage. Sur un OLED, chaque pixel produit sa propre lumière, donc tout le panneau s’en va, avec le châssis et la coque arrière. Le technicien ne garde que la carte mère, le système audio et l’alimentation, qu’il remonte sur la pièce neuve. Agréée par LG, l’enseigne n’utilise que des pièces neuves et officielles, normalement vérifiées en sortie d’usine.
Le montage s’est bien passé jusqu’au test final. On a affiché une mire et là, des dizaines de pixels morts étaient dispersés tout autour du cadre de la dalle neuve. C’était pire que ma dalle actuelle. Le technicien l’a donc démontée, il a remis mon ancienne dalle et il est reparti. Me voilà reparti pour une nouvelle attente.
Un défaut connu, que LG minimise
Le site RTINGS fait tourner des téléviseurs pendant des milliers d’heures pour mesurer comment ils vieillissent. Pour son test d’endurance accélérée, il a laissé les téléviseurs allumés jusqu’à 18 000 heures, l’équivalent d’une dizaine d’années à cinq heures par jour. Au bout du test, 14 des 16 téléviseurs équipés de dalles WOLED de LG Display sortis entre 2020 et 2023 avaient des pixels morts sur les bords. Le WOLED est la technologie OLED du fabricant coréen, qu’on trouve aussi chez Sony. Les trois modèles QD-OLED, la technologie concurrente de Samsung Display, n’ont pas eu ce problème. Le défaut ne se limite d’ailleurs pas au labo puisque deux employés de RTINGS l’ont aussi trouvé sur leurs téléviseurs personnels, dont un LG C1, utilisés de façon tout à fait normale.
Les experts consultés par RTINGS pensent à une contamination pendant la fabrication ou à une dégradation de la couche d’encapsulation, la barrière qui empêche l’humidité d’atteindre les matériaux organiques de la dalle. Pour en être sûr, il faudrait une analyse poussée de la panne, avec un examen au microscope des couches internes de la dalle.
LG reconnaît le défaut, mais il en limite la portée. Dans une réponse adressée à RTINGS, LG Electronics et LG Display expliquent qu’il peut toucher « un très petit nombre de produits OLED » exposés longtemps à de fortes chaleurs, à une forte humidité ou à d’autres conditions difficiles.
Sans microscope (ni connaissances poussées), je ne peux faire qu’une hypothèse, et elle concerne le stockage. Une dalle de rechange pour un modèle de 2021 a pu rester des mois, voire des années, en entrepôt entre son contrôle en usine et son arrivée chez moi. Or LG reconnaît lui-même que la chaleur et l’humidité prolongées peuvent abîmer les bords. Un mauvais stockage pourrait donc suffire à faire apparaître le défaut sur une pièce qui n’a jamais servi, mais rien ne le prouve, d’autant que la dalle est scellée.
Des contacts de RTINGS dans l’industrie affirment que la fabrication des dalles WOLED a été améliorée en 2024.
Ce qu’il faut vérifier avant que le technicien reparte
Si votre téléviseur OLED part en réparation, ne laissez pas le technicien s’en aller sans avoir vérifié la nouvelle dalle. Le plus simple est d’afficher une mire. On en trouve de très bonnes sur YouTube, qui font défiler des couleurs unies sur tout l’écran.
- Passez au moins le blanc, le rouge, le vert, le bleu et le gris en plein écran, quelques secondes chacun.
- Regardez de près les bords et les quatre coins, c’est là que l’edge rot apparaît.
- Si vous voyez un défaut, montrez-le au technicien, prenez des photos et faites-le noter sur le bon d’intervention avant de signer.
Chez LG, un téléviseur est garanti deux ans. Seuls les OLED des gammes G, M et Z vendus depuis 2022 ont droit à cinq ans de garantie sur la dalle, et encore. Passé la garantie standard, seule la dalle est couverte, la main-d’œuvre est facturée. Un C1, un C2 ou un C3 n’en profite pas. Si l’edge rot apparaît après deux ans et sans extension de garantie du revendeur, le remplacement est à vos frais.
Dans mon cas, le technicien a remis l’ancienne dalle, donc j’ai au moins un téléviseur qui fonctionne en attendant. Mon revendeur doit maintenant choisir entre une nouvelle dalle et un téléviseur de remplacement. J’avoue qu’avec mon expérience, je suis frileux à l’idée de repartir sur une nouvelle dalle.
