articles.title: Vercel Launched Experimental Board to Coordinate Tasks Across Humans and Coding Agents
articles.text:
Vercel has launched Vercel Board, an experimental, headless message board where people and coding agents coordinate tasks across tools and harnesses. Vercel says Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can work on the same board as if they were a single harness.
Each Vercel team gets a default board, named General, organized into channels and threads. Developers and agents read and write through the `vercel board` CLI or the `@vercel/board` JavaScript SDK. A skill, installed with npx skills add vercel/board --skill board, teaches coding agents the CLI. Agents name themselves with --as or BOARD_PROFILE, but still act with the operator's or project's credentials.
A task is a thread whose state the board keeps. A worker claims a ready task, posts updates, and completes or fails it. A claim is a lease of up to five minutes and must be renewed; if it expires, the task returns to the queue. When two workers claim the same task, one succeeds and the other fails with task_claimed. Tasks can declare dependencies, so a review waits until its fix completes while independent work proceeds in parallel. Watchers on a Vercel deployment can run when a reply is posted or a label changes, waking the deployment so no process has to stay running.
Sync, configured in the SDK and delivered through Vercel Connect, can attach a board channel to Slack, GitHub, or Linear. Slack and Linear sync both ways; GitHub imports pull requests and issues and does not write back unless the project sends those messages. Grants control who can read, post, and manage each channel. For an agent in a Vercel Sandbox, sandboxPolicy() can grant limited board access without putting a credential inside the sandbox. Vercel says it rebuilt v0's software factory on Board, and that the factory now merges over 50% of its pull requests.
Official documentation warns that Board grants do not apply on Slack, GitHub, or Linear, so a private Slack channel synced into an open board channel is readable by the whole Vercel team.
Austin King (@MadeWithOzten) replied to Vercel's announcement asking to
Do this self-hosted and open source - Rust, Yjs Sync,
then wrote that he had bought openboard.lol
For a self-hosted open source Vercel board like thing.
Aaron Delz (@AaronDelz) said he already kept a shared checklist with his agent, and liked that a Board task can be completed with the pull request attached:
Same rule my agents run on: no saying 'done' without the evidence.
Similar coordination shows up elsewhere. OpenCrawl is an open source, self-hostable board that also records agent sessions. GitHub Agent HQ can assign issues and pull requests to Copilot, Claude, or Codex. Linear's cloud coding agent turns scoped issues into draft pull requests with Claude Code or Codex. Claude Code agent teams coordinate multiple Claude Code sessions around a shared task list, and the Agent2Agent protocol standardizes delegation between agents rather than hosting a board.
Board remains experimental infrastructure on a Vercel team. Setup steps and the CLI and SDK references are in Vercel's Board documentation

articles.title: Adiós a 27 millones de canciones: una plataforma de streaming tomó medidas contra la música creada con IA
articles.text:
Tidal prohibirá toda la música generada íntegramente por inteligencia artificial (IA) a partir del 9 de diciembre y eliminará más de 27 millones de canciones de su catálogo. El servicio de streaming argumentó que ese contenido “desvía reproducciones y regalías lejos de los artistas y confunde a los oyentes”.
La medida fue anunciada el martes 24 de noviembre, según The Guardian, y se apoya en cifras que la propia compañía difundió. En los últimos 90 días, el 43% de las pistas distribuidas en el servicio fueron identificadas como producidas en su totalidad por herramientas automatizadas. Del total de canciones alojadas, esos 27 millones representan el 6,3% del catálogo.
El 96% de las canciones de IA en Tidal no recibió ninguna reproducción en tres meses
El crecimiento del contenido artificial fue acelerado. El pasado 6 de noviembre, el 60% de los temas subidos en un solo día correspondía a música creada completamente por software, de acuerdo con los datos que difundió la empresa.
Pese a esa masiva presencia, el material no encontró interés entre los usuarios. “El 96% de estas pistas no obtuvo ninguna reproducción en los últimos tres meses”, señaló la compañía en su comunicado oficial. Además, Tidal ya retiró 65.000 canciones señaladas como posibles suplantaciones de artistas reales, un fenómeno que describió como “otro problema grave que solo aumentó en escala”.
La empresa aclaró que las pistas creadas con asistencia parcial de IA seguirán siendo bienvenidas. La restricción aplica únicamente cuando los metadatos de un archivo indican que fue producido de manera exclusiva con herramientas automatizadas, sin intervención humana sustancial.
La política de Tidal es la más estricta entre los grandes servicios de streaming
A diferencia de sus competidores, Tidal optó por la prohibición directa. Spotify y Apple Music, los dos mayores servicios del mercado, permiten la distribución de canciones fabricadas íntegramente por IA, aunque las identifican con etiquetas para distinguirlas del resto del catálogo. Bandcamp, por su parte, vetó en enero pasado la música “generada total o en parte sustancial por IA”, una política más amplia en criterio, aunque de menor alcance por volumen de usuarios.
Spotify también actuó en octubre: eliminó alrededor de 50 millones de pistas consideradas “basura” de sus sistemas de recomendación y borró directamente 75 millones de canciones catalogadas como “spam”. Aun así, el servicio sueco no llegó a vedar el contenido automatizado de forma integral.
Tidal alega que la música de IA entierra a los artistas reales y distorsiona las regalías
El servicio argumentó que el problema va más allá del volumen: a esta escala, el material artificial “sepulta” el trabajo auténtico que sus suscriptores buscan descubrir, con efectos directos sobre los ingresos de los músicos.
“Si hacés música, deberías poder subirla a Tidal sabiendo que no quedará oculta bajo pistas que nadie pidió, ni copiada por alguien que se hace pasar por vos”, afirmó la empresa. La compañía también subrayó que “siempre luchará para que los artistas reciban más dinero” y enmarcó toda la decisión en torno a ese principio.
Tidal nació en Noruega en 2014 y fue relanzada por Jay-Z como plataforma en manos de artistas
La empresa tiene sus raíces en Noruega: surgió en 2014 bajo el sello de la compañía escandinava Aspiro, que ya operaba el servicio WiMP desde 2010 en mercados del norte de Europa. Ese año, Aspiro lanzó la marca Tidal en el Reino Unido, Estados Unidos y Canadá, con foco en la reproducción de audio sin pérdida de calidad.
En enero de 2015, el rapero y empresario Jay-Z adquirió Aspiro por USD 56,2 millones a través de su firma Project Panther Bidco. Dos meses después, relanzó el servicio con una estrategia inédita: presentarlo como el primer sitio de streaming en manos de artistas. En la conferencia de prensa realizada en Nueva York, figuras como Beyoncé, Rihanna, Kanye West, Madonna y Alicia Keys aparecieron como copropietarios.
La promesa central de Tidal fue diferenciarse de Spotify y Apple Music en dos frentes: audio de mayor fidelidad técnica y un modelo de pagos más favorable para los músicos. Hoy, la mayoría accionaria pertenece a Block, Inc., la empresa de servicios financieros fundada por Jack Dorsey, que adquirió el control por USD 297 millones en 2021. El servicio opera en 61 países y ofrece un catálogo de 100 millones de pistas.

articles.title: GTA 6 launch slashed Call of Duty's daily player count by 42%
articles.text:
Ripple effect: Three of the biggest live-service games lost players when Grand Theft Auto 6 launched this month, but Call of Duty was the slowest to get them back. Alinea Analytics estimates that Call of Duty HQ's daily player count fell 42% on launch day and barely improved over the next four days. The release also coincided with a shorter disruption outside gaming: Pornhub said its US traffic was 15.5% below normal an hour after GTA 6 went live.
Alinea estimated that Call of Duty HQ had 4.4 million daily active users on launch day, down from an average of 7.5 million across PlayStation, Xbox, and Steam. On PlayStation, which Alinea analyst Rhys Elliott identified as Call of Duty's main platform, the decline was 44%. GTA 6 launched only on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, so the overall Call of Duty figure includes a PC storefront where the new game was not available. The combined count does not show how much of the decline came from Steam.
Call of Duty's slow recovery stands out because it had less audience overlap with GTA 6 than Fortnite did. Of the people who played GTA 6 by the end of the launch weekend, 29% had also played Fortnite that month, compared with 16% for Call of Duty HQ and 11% for FC 27. Those figures identify shared audiences, not which game someone stopped playing to make time for GTA 6.
 – Rhys Elliott (@superhys) November 23, 2026
Fortnite's daily active users on PlayStation and Xbox fell from 17.8 million to 12.8 million on launch day, a 28% decline. By the end of the weekend, its daily player count was 19% below its usual level. FC 27 fell from 5.9 million to 4.3 million daily players, a decline of about 27%, before getting back to within 20% of its baseline. Call of Duty HQ was still 41% below its baseline after four days.
The competition for players' time came from GTA 6's single-player campaign, not an online service of its own. Alinea estimates the game has already sold 44.9 million copies and generated more than $4 billion. Elliott expects both an online mode and a PC version next year. The PC release would extend GTA 6 beyond its initial console audience, while the online mode could give players a reason to keep returning after they finish the campaign.
Pornhub's numbers tracked visits by the hour rather than players by the day. US traffic went from 16.5% above normal at 10 pm ET ahead of the release to 7.5% below normal by midnight. The drop deepened after launch, but by 8 am Thursday traffic was only 6.4% below average, and it edged above average later that day.
Pornhub's search data showed the game drawing interest on the site even as overall traffic fell. Searches for GTA-related terms rose 16,196% on launch day, and Pornhub reported 15 million such searches the following day. The most popular query was "gta 6," followed by "gta 6 lucia" and "gta 6 strip club / tacon." The timing of the traffic dip does not establish where visitors went, but the searches show what many of those who stayed or returned were looking for.

articles.title: The machine shop of the 21st century
articles.text:
This article appears in The BetaKit Guide to Alberta’s Silicon City. Learn more about Edmonton semiconductor innovation here.
The University of Alberta (U of A)’s Electrical and Computer Engineering Research Facility (ECERF) sits on a tree-lined street in Edmonton’s university district. The large, concrete building looms over the modest, mid-century bungalows that dot the rest of the neighbourhood. But inside the ECERF, people are working on something very, very small.
“We like to think of ourselves as the machine shop of the 21st century.”
The ECERF is home to the university’s nanoFAB centre: an open-access training and collaboration hub that serves as a kind of maker space for nanotechnology that allows private companies, researchers, and academics to develop and produce their own semiconductor chips.
And while the chips that come out of the nanoFAB are tiny—sometimes unfathomably so—its influence on the Canadian semiconductor industry is anything but small.
Semiconductor chips, named for the semiconductive properties of materials like silicon that comprise them, are the minute electrical components that underpin virtually all of modern computing and electronics. Think of semiconductors as the electronic brain of a device, controlling the flow of electricity to process, store, or move information digitally. Today, you can find them in everything from the high-end, AI-enabling GPUs and CPUs powering frontier AI to the LED lights at your office or the computer controlling your car’s engine.
Big things start small
The nanoFAB was founded in 1999 to fill the gap left when the U of A’s previous nanotechnology initiative, the Alberta Microelectronics Centre, spun out of the university into a private, for-profit company called Micralyne. The organization had been created by the university in the early 1980s to build regional expertise in semiconductor fabrication and micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) development.
“That unit used to provide a lot of research support on campus,” nanoFAB director Eric Flaim said. “When the spin-out occurred, they took all of the assets and the people, and it left a gap in research capability.”
Flaim’s been with nanoFAB since 2008. Over his tenure, he witnessed the transformation from a small lab to a 25,000-square-foot space with more than $135 million in specialized equipment. Initially focused on academic research, the lab space is now home to over 75 private-sector employees who use it as part of the nanoFAB’s growing number of partnerships with industrial and commercial clients.
“A large portion of our user base is from Edmonton, but we have industrial clients coast-to-coast, from Victoria to St. John’s,” Flaim said.
Working at a tiny scale
Edmonton’s nanoFAB doesn’t make the kind of semiconductor chips you might have read about in lengthy think pieces on Taiwanese supply chains that power your cellphone. Instead, the facility aims to be a resource for companies or developers working on more niche products.
“We’re not … making memory cards or CPUs or the kinds of things that go into consumer-level products and are often commoditized,” Flaim said.
Instead, the NanoFAB builds chips like industrial sensors for oil and gas operations, quantum computing qubits, and MEMS used in tools like gyroscopes, microphones, and nanoscopic mirrors.
Building the semiconductor chips for those tools involves manufacturing on silicon disks known as wafers. Fabrication requires complex processes like lithography and plasma etching to clear away unwanted materials and transfer the nanoscopic transistors, circuits, and other components onto the semiconductor. That requires equipment capable of working at truly small scales; the nanoFAB can fabricate devices as minuscule as one to 10 micrometres (0.0001% of a metre). For context, a single red blood cell measures about eight micrometres, while a human strand of hair comes in at 50 to 100 micrometres.
That scale makes sense when you consider that individual semiconductors can be as small as two millimetres, or about the width of a grain of rice. A single six-inch wafer can thereby produce upwards of 4,000 semiconductors.
And that’s where the nanoFAB’s equipment—like the Raith Voyager electron beam lithography system, which can cost between $1.5 and $2.5 million USD—comes in.
“We like to think of ourselves as the machine shop of the 21st century,” says Flaim. “We’re providing the advanced toolsets and capabilities that allow people to build devices utilized in a wide variety of different verticals.”
It’s here that Alberta’s nanoFAB differs from its two largest peers: Ottawa’s Canadian Photonics Fabrication Centre (CPFC) and the MiQro Innovation Collaborative Centre (C2MI) near Bromont, Que. While CPFC operates largely as a fee-for-service foundry, creating chips to the specifications of clients, and C2MI specializes in non-profit and academic research, Edmonton’s nanoFAB acts more like a maker space you might find at a library, putting its tools and resources into the hands of individuals and companies that might not otherwise be able to access or afford them.
“What we’re trying to do is empower researchers and companies to build new hardware and devices, new technologies,” Flaim said. “Our model is trying to support direct access and use … we try not to set ourselves up as a contract manufacturer or a foundry.”
That’s attracted a lot of attention from the private sector, according to Flaim, who said the nanoFAB model allows intellectual property to stay directly in the hands of companies.
“We’ve found a niche where companies are interested in hiring their own people, having them trained on the equipment, and then having those people work here in a normal nine-to-five capacity,” Flaim added.
A difference of 100 millimetres
Flaim’s focus at the nanoFAB circa 2026 is growing the private partnerships the lab has built over the past 25 years and leveraging both interest and potential investment to expand its capabilities. Presently, the nanoFAB can fabricate semiconductors on wafers up to 150 millimetres, but staff are actively pursuing the equipment upgrades needed to work with 200-millimetre wafers. If successful, the nanoFAB would become the only place in Western Canada, and one of just two nationwide, capable of fabricating at that size.
While it might be nice to think of the nanoFAB as a potential player in the global semiconductor arms race playing out in Taiwan, Japan, the US, and China, the truth is that Edmonton’s unlikely to compete any time soon, even if the federal government is showing increased interest (more on that later).
Most of the semiconductor manufacturing making headlines today—like at the now world-famous Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC)—happens at the 300-millimetre size.
“What we’re trying to do is empower researchers and companies to build new hardware and devices, new technologies.”
Eric Flaim, nanoFAB
“Internationally, when we hear people talking about TSMC, global foundries, or chip shortages for GPUs, what they’re talking about is wafer processing at the 300-millimetre level. It’s state-of-the-art processing,” Flaim said.
A difference of 100 millimetres doesn’t sound like a lot, but it does cost a lot. At the 300-millimetre level, facilities are almost always fully automated and often the size of several football fields.
“Wafers are transported in boxes that no human has touched, going from robot to robot before being fed into a machine that does all of the lithography, deposition, and etching,” Flaim said.
The price tag for that kind of automation? Flaim says it’s in the tens of billions. That’s the largest reason he doesn’t see the nanoFAB taking on that kind of scale any time soon.
Despite its more modest goals, the nanoFAB has been recognized for its strategic value here at home. As recently as last spring, the lab received federal and provincial funding in the tens of millions to expand its equipment and fabrication capabilities.
“There’s recognition that you want to have some domestic manufacturing capability in these strategic areas,” Flaim said. “There’s a recognition on the defence side that if you’re going to buy airplanes from Saab or Lockheed Martin, you want those companies spending money domestically. If those companies want to invest domestically, you need to have the capabilities to invest in.”
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.

articles.title: Todoist confirms 6% of customers' details were stolen in data breach
articles.text:
Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates. The company said around 6% of its customers were affected and blamed stolen credentials for the breach.
Todoist said the attacker used stolen credentials to access the company’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23. The hacker then changed employee access controls and reached the app’s cloud infrastructure via an employee’s work account.
The hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist users whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the company said. Todoist said it has blocked the attack path and reset passwords as a mitigation step, as well as disabled the Todoist for Outlook email add-on.
For a small number of people, about 0.001% of its userbase, the hacker also searched through tasks, comments, and attachment names to look for credentials for other services, like API keys and access tokens.
The hacker also pulled Todoist API tokens and Slack integration tokens, and looked for emails, addresses, and attachment file names through the Todoist for Outlook extension if it was connected to accounts and had permission to read emails.
The company said it has sent a notice to those affected and asked them to reset their credentials and change their login details in other places with the same password. The company is asking users to also update API tokens, reconnect integrations, and revoke or replace any access keys, recovery phrases, or credentials they had stored in Todoist comments.
Todoist said it has also reset its internal access structure and how remote command execution works in its cloud environment to prevent such incidents in the future.
Todoist’s founder and CEO Amir Salihefendić apologized to users about the incident on X, and said the company will take a closer look at why it happened.
The to-do app’s data breach is the latest in a burgeoning list of data breaches in which hackers use stolen credentials to access data and systems at enterprises. So far this year, we’ve seen several companies fall victim to this form of attack, including Uber and Klue.

articles.title: Neuralink: paciente joga GTA VI no PS5 só com o pensamento, sem usar controle
articles.text:
Em 20 de novembro, um dia depois do lançamento de GTA 6, a Neuralink publicou no X um vídeo de dois minutos em que um participante do ensaio clínico da empresa dirige lancha, pilota avião e luta nas ruas de Vice City sem encostar em nenhum controle. Tudo acontece no PS5, e o comando vem direto do cérebro.
Como o implante da Neuralink vira controle
O dispositivo lê movimentos que o participante apenas imagina e os traduz em comandos de DualSense. Imaginar um toque com o dedo anelar aciona o botão quadrado. Imaginar a mão direita deslizando para a frente levanta o nariz do avião. A equipe também incluiu o pé como mais uma entrada.
O contraste com a rotina anterior é o que dá peso ao vídeo. Antes da cirurgia, ele usava um bastão na boca e um iPad, o que, como contou no vídeo, “deixava a mandíbula dolorida”. Agora, joga um dos maiores lançamentos da década sem tocar em um controle.
Os games na história da Neuralink
Os jogos já faziam parte da história da Neuralink. Noland Arbaugh, o primeiro paciente, jogou xadrez e Civilization VI em 2024. O segundo, Alex, jogou Counter-Strike 2. O que aparece agora é diferente: comandos de PS5 em um jogo AAA, na semana de lançamento.
Robert Dale Smith, que trabalha com aplicações de BCI (interface cérebro-computador) na Neuralink, escreveu no X que estava trabalhando para fazer o implante controlar qualquer dispositivo, incluindo o PlayStation 5, para jogar GTA 6 no lançamento. Na mesma postagem, ele cita o JoypadOS, projeto que criou e mantém.
Uma live para celebrar o lançamento
Em 23 de novembro, a Neuralink publicou no X a gravação de uma live interna feita para celebrar o lançamento do jogo, com um participante chamado Billy, que tem tetraplegia por lesão na medula. Segundo a empresa, ele demonstrou usar dois joysticks e 12 botões, tudo com a mente e sem controle físico. A gravação mostra Billy em barco, modo furtivo, combate, hidroavião e ao volante.
O que ainda não foi comprovado
O dispositivo é experimental e não tem aprovação da FDA, a agência reguladora dos Estados Unidos, nem de nenhum outro órgão regulador. O vídeo é uma demonstração publicada pela própria empresa, sem dados de latência ou de taxa de erro na detecção dos comandos.
Ainda assim, a cena diz muito sobre o papel dos games na tecnologia assistiva. Não é a primeira vez que um jogo serve de teste para uma interface, mas poucas vezes o teste foi tão fácil de entender: um jogador querendo jogar o lançamento do ano.

articles.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
articles.text:
AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  University of Plymouth
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.
- Share:
Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.
Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.
The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.
AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records
Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.
Confirming bladder cancer currently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.
To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.
The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.
AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases
The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.
The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.
Importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.
The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.
For example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.
These findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.
Another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.
Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.
A New Approach to Early Cancer Screening
Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).
This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.
For example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.
PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, said: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022."
"Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods."
Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?
The potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.
Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.
"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.
"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved."
Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.
"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.
"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages."
More Research Needed Before Clinical Use
Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.
All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.
Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.
"It's important to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.
"But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions."
The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.
The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.
The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

articles.title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
articles.text:
AI is straining America’s open records systems
Startups are mining public data for AI products, while citizens use chatbots to file more requests.
In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.
Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”
Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.
At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.
As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.
Transparency, monetized
The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.
This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”
Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.
SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.
The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.
Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.” 
While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.
But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.
The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices. 
In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.
In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.
The AI detection problem
It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.
In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.
While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.
On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”
As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”
Everything’s on the table
Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.
Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”
Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.
Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.
Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.
As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”

articles.title: Lo nuevo de BYD se llama Shark y es una pick-up híbrida con la mayor batería de su segmento
articles.text:
BYD sigue sus lanzamientos en la recta final del año. Si la semana pasada era el nuevo Seal U 2027, ahora es el turno de Shark, que llega con un nuevo modelo de tipo pick-up a un precio muy interesante y con la tecnología de hibridación de la compañía que tanto se ha aclamado.
El nuevo BYD Shark llega con una carrocería de doble cabina y unos impresionantes 5,46 metros, y, como decimos, lo hace con la tecnología DMO (Dual Mode Off-road) con hasta 90 km de autonomía 100% eléctrica (675 km en combinada) y grandes capacidades todoterreno con unos impresionantes 436 CV y 650 Nm de par. Una potencia que le permite, pese a su peso y tamaño, acelerar de 0 a 100 en solo 5,7 segundos y ganándose por el camino las 5 estrellas de Euro NCAP.
BYD Shark: dos motores eléctricos y una gran autonomía combinada
En su apartado de hibridación, cuenta con un motor de gasolina turboalimentado de 1,5 litros y cuatro cilindros (de 150 CV y 240 Nm), usado principalmente como generador de electricidad para los motores eléctricos y la carga de la batería, aunque también puede generar propulsión; y dos motores eléctricos: uno delantero de 231 CV (170 kW) y 310 Nm, y otro trasero de 204 CV (150 kW) y 340 Nm.
Complementa el conjunto una batería de tipo Blade Battery de 32,2 kWh, según BYD la de mayor capacidad del segmento pick-up en Europa, integrada en un chasis de largueros y travesaños, ya que usa la tecnología CTC (Cell-to-Chassis) y, como decíamos, homologa una autonomía eléctrica en ciclo combinado de 90 km y alrededor de 110 km en ciclo urbano y una autonomía combinada de 675 km. Esto supone unos consumos ponderados de 3,5 l/100 km² y de 9,6 l/100km a nivel mínimo de carga. Respecto a su carga, admite corriente alterna trifásica de 11 kW, con unos tiempos de 3,2 horas del 15% al 100%, y carga rápida en corriente continua de hasta 55 kW: sobre 21 minutos del 30% al 80%.
Respecto a su apuesta tecnológica en el interior, integra una pantalla digital para la instrumentación de 10,25” (26 cm), un Head-Up Display y una pantalla central para el sistema de infoentretenimiento de 15,6”.
Un detalle interesante de este BYD Shark es que incorpora la función Vehicle-to-Load (V2L) de 6 kW, que permite alimentar dispositivos eléctricos externos, bien para el trabajo o para el ocio en acampada, mediante dos tomas de corriente.
BYD Shark, precio y disponibilidad
¿Y su precio? Llega en una única versión llamada Design, que parte desde los 41.521 euros sin IVA (50.240 euros IVA incluido) y cuenta con una garantía oficial de 6 años o 150.000 km para el coche y de 8 años o 250.000 km para la Blade Battery. Y ya está disponible en los concesionarios de BYD.

articles.title: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
articles.text:
Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.
EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
Hours after detonating 4.4 tons of lead azide in Iowa, officials reported early test results from the surrounding areas.
Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press.
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here.
The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March.
Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given.
To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

articles.title: L'OLED s'offre 700 € de réduction grâce à Darty qui casse le prix de cet écran LG en 77 pouces
articles.text:
Pour passer l’hiver au chaud sous un plaid devant un film, quoi de mieux qu’un écran OLED ? Justement, Darty retire 700 euros au prix du LG OLED77B6 pendant la semaine du Black Friday, qui culmine ce vendredi 27 novembre. L’OLED reste une technologie chère en grand format, et ce B6 est le 77 pouces OLED le moins cher de la gamme 2026 de LG. Parmi les autres qualités de ce TV, on retrouve le Dolby Atmos et le Dolby Vision.
Nous recommandons le LG OLED77B6 pour…
- Ses noirs parfaits et son contraste infini
- Sa compatibilité avec le Dolby Atmos
- Ses fonctionnalités gaming
Grâce à Darty, le LG OLED77B6 passe de 2 499 euros à 1 799 euros.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant le LG OLED77B6. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Immersion à 360° et design innovant : pour le Black Friday, la barre de son Samsung HW-Q995H passe à 890 € chez la Fnac, soit 600 € de remise.
Une expérience cinéma à la maison
Le LG OLED77B6 est un TV assez imposant avec son écran de 77 pouces. LG a tout de même soigné le format, avec des bordures fines et à peine 5 centimètres d’épaisseur sans le pied. De quoi garder les yeux sur le film plutôt que sur le cadre. Pour davantage d’immersion, vous pourrez même vous passer des pieds puisque le TV est compatible VESA 300 x 200 mm.
Ce TV dispose d’une résolution de 3 840 x 2 160 pixels. Sa dalle est évidemment OLED. Le TV éteint les pixels lorsqu’il faut diffuser du noir, ce qui renforce leur profondeur. Le processeur Alpha 8 AI 4K Gen3 se charge d’ajuster les contrastes en temps réel. Pour renforcer l’immersion, le TV est compatible avec le Dolby Vision, le HDR10 et le HLG. Pas de HDR10+ en revanche.
Du côté de l’audio, l’expérience présente un bémol. Les deux haut-parleurs se partagent 20 watts au total. Un petit boost de puissance n’aurait pas été de refus, mais, pour cela, il faut se tourner vers le LG OLED77C6 ou le LG OLED77G6 et casser davantage sa tirelire (ils étaient lancés à 3 499 et 4 599 euros en 77 pouces).
GTA VI sur un grand écran de 77 pouces
LG n’a pas oublié les gamers au moment de mettre au point son OLED77B6. Le téléviseur se présente avec quatre ports HDMI 2.1 qui permettent de jouer aux consoles récentes en 4K à 120 images par seconde. Le TV est donc parfait pour savourer GTA VI sur un très grand écran, même si le titre de Rockstar est limité à 30 images par seconde.
Si vous préférez lancer Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, c’est possible de jouer sur ce grand écran sans avoir une latence trop importante. Son input lag s’établit à 9,1 ms. Tous les paramètres se règlent depuis le mode jeu, qui s’active automatiquement dès qu’une console est détectée.
Côté logiciel, LG mise sur webOS 26. Rien de nouveau sous le soleil ici avec une interface fluide qui permet d’accéder facilement aux différentes plateformes de streaming et d’obtenir des suggestions basées sur vos habitudes de consommation.

articles.title: Wiz webinar: Bringing a sharper, connected focus to AI security
articles.text:
Wiz webinar: Bringing a sharper, connected focus to AI security
From AI discovery to threat detection, Wiz brings security into focus in a new virtual webinar
AI applications are becoming an increasingly important part of cloud environments. As adoption increases, so does the attack surface - far beyond traditional cloud assets. Today, organisations are building and deploying more AI-powered applications, agents, integrations and third-party tools. This leaves their security teams with a new challenge on their hands: understanding not just what exists, but what these applications can access and how their risks connect.
An AI application could interact with cloud systems, Application Programming Interfaces (API), sensitive data and other tools. Agents can retrieve information, call tools and trigger workflows. For security teams, looking at these assets individually may not reveal how their permissions, infrastructure and data access could interact to create security risk.
What to expect
To explore how organisations can address these challenges, global cybersecurity organization Wiz is hosting a focused 60-minute technical demo called ‘Securing Modern AI Applications with Wiz, featuring Dharmesh Vaya, Sr. Solution Engineer, Wiz.
The session will demonstrate how Wiz brings together an understanding of AI applications and cloud security context to secure AI from code to runtime, wherever it is built and run.
Event details
- Date: December 11, 2026
- Time: 03:00 PM
- Format: Virtual event
- Speaker: Dharmesh Vaya, Sr. Solution Engineer, Wiz
Understand what applications can do
Discovering an AI asset is just the first step. Security teams also need to understand what an application is designed to do, the tools it leverages, its capabilities, and access to data. During the demo, participants can discover how the Wiz AI Security Agent provides visibility into AI assets and custom applications, with deeper insights into agents, tools, and their capabilities. This feature examines agents and applications across code repositories, PaaS platforms, and self-hosted infrastructure like VMs, containers and serverless environments.
Connecting risks to identify critical attack paths
AI-related security risks do not exist in a silo. A vulnerability or misconfiguration can become more significant when connected to exposed infrastructure, privileged identities, or sensitive data.
The demo will showcase how the Wiz Security Graph connects AI-specific risks with exposure, identities, infrastructure, and sensitive data to uncover critical attack paths. Rather than flagging and treating security findings individually, this approach helps teams understand how different risks and vulnerabilities are intertwined. The Graph prioritises those with greater potential. For organisations working with multiple AI applications, agents, and integrations, this context can help security teams identify which connections need attention.
Securing AI: from code to runtime
As AI applications move from development into production, their behaviour, permissions, and exposure can change. Security, therefore, needs to extend across the application lifecycle. The session will demonstrate how Wiz brings together AI discovery, risk reduction, and runtime threat detection through one unified platform.
By connecting visibility into AI applications with contextual risk prioritisation and runtime threat detection, the platform aims to give security teams a more complete view of their AI-related exposure.
For organisations expanding their use of AI across cloud environments, understanding how applications, agents, identities, tools, and data interact is an important part of managing security risks.
Join for this 1-hour technical demo to see how Wiz connects these elements and helps teams secure AI applications from code to runtime.

articles.title: Italia impone una multa a Meta de 805 millones de euros por acceder sin consentimiento específico a las fotografías de 20 millones de usuarios
articles.text:
La Autoridad italiana de Protección de Datos, conocida como el Garante, ha multado a Meta con 805 millones de euros. Según el comunicado del propio Garante, la aplicación de Facebook para Android accedía a las fotos, los vídeos y los metadatos guardados en los teléfonos de unos 20 millones de usuarios en Italia sin haberles pedido un consentimiento específico para ello.
Una función de 2023. Todo gira alrededor de una opción llamada “Obtener sugerencias de la galería mientras navegas por Facebook”, disponible desde 2023. Esta función te va proponiendo fotos y vídeos de tu móvil como ideas para publicar, y para hacerlo la app necesita que le des permiso para acceder a la galería del móvil. Y es precisamente en la manera de pedir ese acceso donde el regulador ha puesto el foco.
Un permiso para todo. La investigación empezó en 2025 a raíz de una denuncia del Centro de Protección de los Consumidores y Usuarios de Bolzano, en el norte de Italia, y apoyándose análisis técnico. Según la agencia, Facebook pedía un único permiso genérico de acceso a la galería acompañado de un aviso tan vago como “habilitar otras funciones”, sin aclarar que también servía para estas sugerencias activadas por defecto.
Acceso a todo el carrete. Para el organismo italiano, si se concede este permiso la app podía acceder a toda la galería fotográfica del móvil y leerla, por lo general de forma permanente, sin que ni los usuarios ni el propio Garante pudieran comprobar qué información se acababa utilizando realmente. Por lo tanto, considera que Meta ha vulnerado el artículo 122 del Código italiano de Privacidad, que traslada la directiva europea ePrivacy y protege el teléfono como parte de la esfera privada de cada persona. Y, como ha recordado el Garante, da igual que los datos salgan del dispositivo o que causen un perjuicio, porque cualquier acceso a lo que guardas en él requiere un “consentimiento libre e informado”.
Cómo se ha calculado la multa. La sanción equivale aproximadamente al 0,47% de la facturación mundial del grupo, y para fijarla el Garante tuvo en cuenta el elevado número de afectados, la duración de la infracción, un procedimiento anterior contra la compañía en 2019 y la “escasa colaboración” de Meta durante la investigación. Eso sí, también valoró como único atenuante los cambios que la empresa introdujo después de la denuncia, aunque los consideró “tardíos y limitados a quien actualiza la aplicación”.
Lo que tendrá que cambiar. Además de pagar, Meta tiene 60 días para desactivar la función por defecto, incluso para quienes ya hubieran dado permiso de acceso a su galería. También tendrá que pedir un consentimiento específico y separado para esta herramienta, explicar con claridad para qué sirve, avisar de que implica acceder a tus fotos y vídeos y detallar cómo puedes desactivarla.
Pero el expediente tiene sus límites, según ha precisado el regulador: no entra en el posible uso de esas imágenes para entrenar sistemas de inteligencia artificial, algo que Meta niega. Lo que sí ha hecho el Garante es reservarse la posibilidad de examinar aparte una nueva función, lanzada en 2026, que permite procesar en la nube los archivos de la galería.

articles.title: « J’ai commis de graves erreurs » : de retour chez Nvidia, Jensen Huang fait une première annonce
articles.text:
Onze jours après sa démission, Jensen Huang est revenu ce lundi au poste de dirigeant de Nvidia. L’homme d’affaires a repris ses fonctions exactement comme avant, sans que rien ne change. Ou presque : le lendemain de son retour, il s’est réuni avec ses employés pour leur présenter ses excuses pour avoir enfreint le code de conduite de Nvidia.
Jensen Huang fait son mea culpa
Le New York Times a pu visionner la diffusion en direct d’une réunion menée par Jensen Huang ce 24 novembre suite à son retour au poste. Il est revenu sur sa démission, qui avait été acceptée par le conseil d’administration à l’unanimité. Mais selon lui, son retour a été permis par le conseil d’administration puisque c’était dans l’intérêt de l’entreprise et de ses actionnaires. Ce qui semble vrai si l’on en croit Wall Street : le cours de Nvidia a bondi de plus de 31% ce lundi, mais a reculé de près de 6% le lendemain.
Il reconnaît avoir « commis de graves erreurs » en étant infidèle à sa femme et dit avoir fait du mal à ses enfants ainsi qu’à ses salariés. Il ajoute qu’il est « inacceptable » qu’il ait enfreint le code de conduite de Nvidia, alors même qu’il a participé à la rédaction de certaines parties.
« L’entreprise la plus apolitique »
Jensen Huang en a profité pour réfuter les accusations à son propos selon lesquelles certains auraient manœuvré pour faciliter son retour, alors que l’enquête interne du conseil d’administration n’est pas terminée. Enquête interne qui n’est toujours pas terminée : elle se poursuit même avec le retour de Jensen Huang. Pour ce dernier, son retour n’est pas non plus lié aux pressions qu’aurait exercées Donald Trump sur ledit conseil d’administration
Il explique être au service du président, sans que cela fasse de Nvidia une entreprise politique : « Nous sommes l’entreprise la plus apolitique ». Bien qu’il ait fait l’éloge du président américain : « Tout ce qu’il a fait, c’est simplement par affection, par admiration, par reconnaissance de la grande entreprise que vous représentez ».
Le patron de Nvidia suit une thérapie
Dans le même temps, Jensen Huang a expliqué suivre aujourd’hui une thérapie de 90 minutes tous les jours de 90 minutes. Évidemment, le secret médical fait qu’on n’en connaît pas le contenu, bien qu’on imagine que cela ait un rapport avec ses différentes relations extraconjugales.
Pour rappel, il a entretenu une relation avec Alice Huang (qui porte le même nom, mais sans lien de parenté), dirigeante de Medaspeed, entreprise liée à Nvidia, qui est soupçonnée d’être une informatrice des services de renseignement chinois. L’homme d’affaires a aussi eu des relations avec deux employées de Nvidia, dont Kimberly Powell, présidente de l’entreprise chargée de la santé. D’ailleurs, Jensen Huang devrait témoigner la semaine prochaine lors d’auditions parlementaires sur le sujet Alice Huang. Mais selon l’administration Trump, le patron de Nvidia ne représente pas une menace pour la sécurité nationale.

articles.title: Huawei es declarada culpable de fraude y robo de secretos en EEUU, pero absuelta de operar como organización criminal
articles.text:
Un jurado federal de Brooklyn ha condenado a Huawei y tres filiales por 10 de los 12 cargos penales que enfrentaban en Estados Unidos, entre ellos conspiración para robar secretos comerciales, fraude bancario y violación de sanciones contra Irán. Eso sí, la compañía ha sido absuelta de la acusación más grave, la que en inglés se conoce como racketeering, que sostenía que actuaba como una organización criminal.
De dónde viene esto
El caso se remonta a 2019, cuando la Fiscalía de Estados Unidos presentó cargos contra Huawei y varias de sus filiales. La investigación se intensificó tras la detención en Canadá de Meng Wanzhou, directora financiera de la compañía e hija de su fundador, en diciembre de 2018, en el marco de una investigación sobre supuestas violaciones de las sanciones estadounidenses contra Irán.
Desde entonces, el proceso ha servido como claro ejemplo de la tensión tecnológica y geopolítica entre Washington y Pekín. Para la acusación, Huawei habría mentido a entidades bancarias sobre sus negocios en Irán y utilizado tecnología de empresas estadounidenses para reforzar su posición competitiva. Para la defensa, se trata de una persecución injustificada contra una de las grandes compañías tecnológicas chinas.
Qué ha decidido el jurado
El veredicto, emitido el 24 de noviembre de 2026 tras un juicio de unos tres meses, afecta a Huawei Technologies y a las filiales Huawei Device Co., Futurewei Technologies y Huawei Device USA. El jurado consideró probados cargos de:
- Conspiración para robar secretos comerciales
- Fraude bancario y electrónico
- Conspiración para defraudar a Estados Unidos
- Violación de la Ley de Poderes Económicos de Emergencia Internacional (IEEPA)
- Conspiración para lavar dinero.
La acusación de racketeering, que se basa en la ley estadounidense RICO, exigía demostrar que Huawei había operado como una empresa criminal. El jurado la rechazó, igual que el cargo de conspiración para obstruir a la justicia. De haber prosperado, habrían abierto la puerta a sanciones económicas y penales más duras hacia Huawei.
Por qué importa
La Fiscalía sostuvo que Huawei mintió a bancos sobre sus negocios en Irán para acceder al sistema financiero estadounidense y que se apropió de tecnología de empresas norteamericanas para ganar ventaja competitiva. El Departamento de Justicia afirma que las condenas incluyen violaciones de sanciones, engaños a entidades bancarias, lavado de dinero y robo de secretos comerciales.
La condena por conspiración para robar secretos comerciales es especialmente significativa porque confirma que, a juicio del tribunal, existió un plan coordinado para apropiarse de tecnología ajena. También la de fraude bancario, porque respalda que Huawei engañó deliberadamente a entidades financieras sobre sus operaciones en Irán.
El caso no se limita a una acusación genérica de espionaje industrial. Entre los ejemplos que la Fiscalía presentó como probados figura el robot Tappy de T-Mobile, empleado para medir la respuesta de las pantallas táctiles. Huawei firmó un acuerdo de confidencialidad para acceder al dispositivo, pero, según el Departamento de Justicia, sus empleados enviaron fotografías y detalles técnicos a China. Cuando aquello no fue suficiente, uno de ellos se llevó supuestamente una pieza del robot escondida en una mochila.
Otro ejemplo afecta a Cisco. La Fiscalía sostiene que Huawei copió código fuente de sus routers e intentó ocultar el origen cambiando el nombre de la compañía por “ocsic”, Cisco escrito al revés. Sin embargo, habrían permanecido notas y referencias del código original que permitieron identificar su procedencia. El Departamento de Justicia también cita accesos irregulares a tecnología de Fujitsu, CNEX y Quintel como parte de la misma conspiración.
La absolución del cargo de racketeering limita una parte central de la narrativa fiscal: no se ha establecido que Huawei funcionase como una organización criminal. Aun así, las condenas restantes son sustanciales y dejan a la compañía expuesta a multas, decomiso de bienes y posibles indemnizaciones.
La respuesta de Huawei
Huawei ha celebrado la absolución del cargo RICO y ha afirmado que confirma que esas acusaciones carecían de base fáctica. La compañía también ha dicho que revisará el veredicto y que tomará las acciones legales necesarias para defender sus intereses.
En su comunicado, Huawei sostiene que las cinco disputas relacionadas con secretos comerciales citadas por la Fiscalía fueron asuntos civiles resueltos durante las últimas dos décadas y que ningún tribunal había determinado antes una apropiación intencionada de propiedad intelectual. Es una valoración de la empresa, no una conclusión del jurado en este proceso penal.
¿Y ahora qué?
Todo parece indicar que vienen más multas y sanciones para Huawei. La sentencia está prevista para el 14 de septiembre de 2027. El juez federal Ann Donnelly deberá determinar las sanciones económicas tras valorar las directrices federales de condena y otros factores legales.
La defensa ya ha anticipado que pedirá la pena más baja posible y que espera recurrir el veredicto. Por tanto, esta condena no es el final ni mucho menos del proceso: Huawei puede impugnarla ante instancias superiores, mientras que la cuantía final de las sanciones aún no se conoce.

articles.title: CISA warns of critical unpatched flaw in Danfoss refrigeration controllers
articles.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is warning about a critical vulnerability in Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controllers used by food retailers to manage commercial refrigeration, HVAC, and lighting systems.
Danfoss controllers have been compromised recently in attacks at various supermarkets and food retailers across Europe where hackers remotely shut down cooling systems or raised their temperatures.
The security issue is tracked as CVE-2026-129713 and received a severity score of 9.8. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the controller’s server.
CISA says an attacker can trigger the flaw without authentication, cause the server to restart, and potentially achieve remote code execution with the web server's privileges.
Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA controllers are central control units for supermarket and convenience-store refrigeration. They are used to manage equipment such as refrigerated display cases and compressor racks, to log temperatures, and to alert when changes occur.
Danfoss calls the product line the AK-SM 800A Series, which includes the 820A, 850A, and 880A models. Depending on the model, they can also control store lighting and HVAC.
CISA notes that the controllers are deployed worldwide, but their exact number remains unclear.
On November 20, Danfoss published a security advisory saying that the CVE-2026-129713 vulnerability would be addressed in the upcoming software version 5.5.x for Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series.
The company said that the update would also remove the option that allows customers to turn off ‘Strict mode’ in the product.
Currently, there is no patch available for CVE-2026-129713, and potentially impacted system administrators are advised to take the following actions:
- Keep controllers off of the public internet and minimize network exposure where possible.
- Segregate control systems from business networks and place them behind firewalls.
- Use up-to-date Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) when remote access is required.
Prior Danfoss incidents
Danfoss systems were recently targeted in high-impact cybersecurity incidents across Europe. Between October 11 and 12, several French supermarkets and food retailers suffered significant losses after attacks attributed to Iran’s IRGC-linked Shahid Kaveh unit compromised Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC and Copeland/Dixell XWEB refrigeration controllers and remotely altered their defrost settings.
On November 2, at least 115 supermarket stores in Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Luxembourg, Ireland, Romania, and Estonia, had their refrigeration equipment shut down or their settings changed remotely.
Supplier Sabcobel said the attackers used the same vulnerability previously seen in the October attacks in France, indicating that Danfoss systems were involved again.
On the same day, attackers suspected to be linked to the same campaign targeted a refrigeration supplier for the French national blood service, altering cold-storage settings at three facilities.
