articles.title: Nigerian cybersecurity startup Aeon extends pre-seed to $2 million
articles.text:
Aeon, a Nigerian cybersecurity startup building tools to help organisations protect their digital infrastructure, has extended its pre-seed round to $2 million to expand its engineering team and accelerate product development.
Launch Africa Ventures and Octerra Capital joined the extension, alongside existing investors including Terra Industries, the Nigerian defence-tech startup; Resilience17, the venture fund founded by Flutterwave co-founder and chief executive officer Olugbenga Agboola; and Kaleo, DFS Labs, Ajim Capital, and Seedstars.
The extension follows Aeon’s initial $1 million pre-seed round in September, led by Terra Industries. The investment established a commercial relationship between the two companies, which plan to develop a joint venture to pursue some of Terra’s corporate and government contracts together.
Samuel Ogbonyomi, Ben Eluan, and Alex Idowu began building Aeon in February 2026 through PipeOps, a cloud infrastructure management platform. Aeon has two products: Aeon Console, an AI-powered, web-based cybersecurity and compliance platform that helps organisations identify and remediate vulnerabilities across cloud infrastructure, and Aeon Edge, a network security device that sits within an organisation’s network, giving security teams visibility into connected devices and network activity.
“We need to build the infrastructure, technical expertise, and capabilities to defend the systems our economies depend on. We believe Africa should be actively building that future,” Ogbonyomi said in a statement.
According to Aeon, the new capital will finance the expansion of its engineering and cybersecurity teams, strengthen local technical expertise, and accelerate product development as the company plans to move its existing pilots toward commercial deployments.
The expansion comes as African organisations face a complex cybersecurity environment. According to INTERPOL’s African Cyberthreat Assessment 2026, artificial intelligence is now enabling approximately 55% of reported cybercrimes across the continent. The organisation also reported that financial losses from cybercrime more than doubled between 2024 and 2026, rising from $192 million to $484 million.
“As cybersecurity threats evolve and the complexities surrounding data sovereignty and protection intensify, AEON’s approach to integrating fragmented security operations is particularly compelling,” Ashim Egunjobi, Managing Partner at Octerra Capital, said in a statement. “For Octerra, AEON is a natural extension of our conviction and investments in the trust layer of the digital economy.”
AI as an accelerator of cyberattacks
As businesses and organisations adopt more digital systems, AI is making it easier for malicious actors to carry out activities that previously required technical expertise, lowering the barriers to cyberattacks. In a three-part documentary released by Aeon, the company’s leadership said AI makes it easier to run phishing campaigns and identify vulnerabilities, allowing attackers to operate at greater speed and scale.
Microsoft’s 2025 Digital Defence Report found that AI-generated phishing emails recorded a 54% click-through rate, compared with 12% for emails written by humans. The findings illustrate how AI can help attackers produce more convincing messages and increase the effectiveness of social engineering campaigns.
AI is also becoming a tool for cyber defence. The same capabilities that help attackers identify weaknesses can help security teams investigate incidents and correlate information across different systems. AI-assisted cybersecurity can reduce repetitive manual analysis and help security professionals respond more effectively.
“AI is fundamentally changing the threat landscape. The technical barriers that previously limited sophisticated cyberattacks are falling, and the speed and scale of these threats are increasing,” Ogbonyomi said.
However, African organisations still rely on multiple security tools that operate independently, leaving security teams to manually piece together information from different platforms to understand their exposure and decide what needs attention. Aeon’s documentary also highlights the cost of cybersecurity licences, integration requirements, and shortage of specialised talent as barriers to comprehensive protection.
Aeon is operating in a market with established global cybersecurity players, including Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, and Check Point, competing alongside African providers such as Kenya’s Serianu and Morocco’s Nucleon Security.
The startup is betting that a deeper understanding of local infrastructure and operating conditions can help it build products suited to African organisations. Its ambition, it noted, is to develop sovereign cyber defence infrastructure for Africa and the Global South.
“For two years we have looked for a team building cyber defence for Africa’s critical infrastructure from the ground up,” Uwem Uwemakpan, Head of Investments at Launch Africa Ventures, said in a statement. “As AI makes attacks cheaper to launch and harder to detect, banks, grid operators and telecoms across the continent need security built for their own systems and regulators. That is what Aeon is building.”

articles.title: Datenbanken mit 3,5 Milliarden Zugangsdaten offen im Netz gefunden: Was du jetzt tun solltest
articles.text:
Mit Daten von Infostealern: Datenbanken mit 3,5 Milliarden Zugangsdaten offen im Netz gefunden
Im Januar 2024 hatten Sicherheitsforscher:innen in einem als „Mother of all Breaches“ bezeichneten Datenleck rund 26 Milliarden Datensätze mit sensiblen Informationen entdeckt. Branchenbeobachter:innen zufolge soll es sich dabei aber größtenteils um schon bekannte Daten gehandelt haben.
Größte Sammlung von Zugangsdaten
Die „Mutter aller Sicherheitslücken“ setzte sich aus Daten von tausenden verschiedenen alten Lecks, Sicherheitslücken und Datenbanken zusammen. Jetzt will der Sicherheitsforscher Jeremiah Fowler die größte Sammlung von Zugangsdaten gefunden haben, die ihm je in einer einzelnen offenen Datenbank untergekommen sei.
Wie Wired berichtet, enthält die von dem Sicherheitsforscher der Firma Black Hills Information Security entdeckte ungesicherte Datenbank rund zwei Milliarden personenbezogene Daten wie Benutzerdaten und Passwörter. Die Daten stammen demnach zum Teil aus Aktivitäten von Cyberkriminellen.
Von Infostealern entwendete Daten
Außerdem sollen sich Fowler zufolge auch von sogenannten Infostealern gestohlene Daten in der geleakten Datenbank befunden haben. Bei Infostealern handelt es sich um Schadsoftware, die sämtliche auf einem infizierten Gerät eingegebenen Anmeldedaten ausspähen kann.
Neben E-Mail-Adressen und Passwörtern finden sich entsprechend auch Cookies und Sitzungstoken in der Datensammlung. Damit könnten Angreifer:innen laufende Sitzungen übernehmen, ohne auf Passwörter oder Zwei-Faktor-Authentifizierung angewiesen zu sein. Nutzer:innen sollten entsprechend nicht nur Passwörter ändern, sondern sich auch auf allen Geräten abmelden, um aktive Sitzungen zu beenden. Zudem sollten Betroffene ihre Geräte auf Schadsoftware prüfen.
„Digitale Leben“ der Opfer kapern
Für den Sicherheitsforscher am Erschreckendsten seien aber 400.000 Dokumente gewesen, in denen gezielt Informationen zu einzelnen Opfern wie Anmeldedaten, Cookies oder Browserdaten zusammengetragen worden seien. Diese Daten könnten ein detailliertes Profil einer Person und ihres digitalen Lebens ergeben, heißt es bei Wired. „Wer all das hat, hat diese Person in der Hand“, erklärte Fowler.
Wem die Datenbank gehörte, konnte der Sicherheitsforscher nicht feststellen. Nach einem Hinweis an den Hostinganbieter sei diese aber aus dem Internet entfernt worden. Unklar ist, wie lange sie zuvor online gewesen ist und wer noch Zugriff darauf gehabt hat.
Datenbank mit sensiblen Daten aus China
Ähnliches gilt für eine zweite öffentlich zugängliche Datenbank, die Greg Pollock, Forschungsleiter beim Sicherheitsunternehmen Upguard, entdeckt hat. In dieser finden sich mehr als 1,5 Milliarden Zugangsdaten von überwiegend chinesischen Privatpersonen und Unternehmen. Einer Stichprobe Pollocks zufolge waren auch Daten mit Angaben zu Kindern und Verstorbenen darunter.
Ob die in den beiden Datenbanken gefundenen Datensätze noch aktuell sind und wie viele Informationen doppelt oder schon bekannt waren, müssen weitere Auswertungen zeigen. Wer wissen will, ob die eigenen Anmeldedaten schon im Netz kursieren, kann das etwa auf dem Portal „Have I Been Pwned“ überprüfen.

articles.title: Learning Out Loud (Under Near-Existential Pressure)
articles.text:
Transcript
Laura Savino: Several friends and colleagues have come to me to tell me recently that they are pregnant with their first child, and have taken comfort from a really odd bit of perspective that I've given them, because I have two lovely kids, two very much wanted and uneventful pregnancies. I hated being pregnant. Every so often, I look around a crowd of people, and I'm like, everyone here is the result of a pregnancy, and it creeps me out. It's beautiful. It's a miracle of life. It is also not my jam. The thing that made me willing to do it at all and that gave me great comfort along the way was actually the myth of the frog. This frog is swimming around in water that starts at a comfortable temperature, but is slowly heated through to a boil, and if you do it gradually enough, the frog won't really notice that its environment is no longer like anything it's ever experienced before, and the frog is eventually cooked.
This odd myth gave me a lifeline of hope, because if that frog can adapt to extreme, unprecedented conditions, so can I. Because the difficult parts usually come on gradually, day by day. If having a child started with the eighth-month pregnancy discomfort, very few of us would do it. It would be banned as inhumane torture if we could instantly make people eight months pregnant.
Some of you are like, "It's 9:00 in the morning. We're at a software conference. Can we please not talk about spontaneous advanced gestation? It is a repulsive idea." When we see a person eight months pregnant who got there gradually, the way we all luckily do, we just think, how nice. It's not repulsive at all, it's beautiful. On the Bleeding Edge
I experienced a massive at-the-time transition in Cocoa, in the Apple development community that did this well. See, it was possible for a long time to go into Apple development with a great deal of hubris. You were an Apple developer. You knew all the tricks and tips. You'd hand-molded a lock and knit release cycles. Back of the cabinet here means, sure, no one's going to see this part of the code, but we're still going to make it just so because we take pride in our work. For a minute there, you could be confident that your deep UI kit and Objective-C knowledge meant that big companies would pay you and a team of three or four devs and a crack designer, absolute truckloads of cash to write them an app because everyone needed apps and no one knew how to write them except us. It was a really good time to be an Apple developer.
Then Apple dropped Swift, brand new language. You're welcome, everyone. Soon all our new APIs will be in this brand-new language that you have to use. We were willing to give up our semicolons. No one likes those, but they ripped away our square brackets too. This was one of those watershed community moments. One perspective I really liked at the time was, we're knocked back to being beginners again, and we like it. We're on even footing. We're learning together. Isn't this exciting? The change electrified us in good and bad ways. On the good side, I distinctly remember watching people who'd shipped indie software on CDs, people who were intimately familiar with why NSString is prefixed that way because they used to code in NEXTSTEP. These developers dived headfirst into the new language. I was sitting around with The Omni Group folks, like OmniFocus, OmniGraffle, these are Apple ecosystem legends, with our laptops out in the hotel lobbies of San Francisco, just trying to figure out, what can I do with this new language? On the less good side.
Swift was announced in June, and on my production app, we had an intern who waited several weeks till late July, before Xcode, our IDE was even out of beta, the intern added Swift to the project just for fun. The tool chain support was abysmal. I couldn't exactly embrace the beginner's mind when I was trying to ship a feature and couldn't even type because my IDE kept lagging out with this message. It was frustrating and not at all production ready because the tool chain was literally in beta. On the whole, with the benefit of rose-colored nostalgia, it was good. Most super senior principal developers, these pinnacles of technical excellence, were having to relearn how to get the eighth element out of a string, like just rookie stuff. The behaviors that got rewarded were the ones where people learned in public. The people who learned the most were the ones who asked the most questions, who'd notice when they didn't understand something and say, this is something I don't understand.
How interesting? They'd post forum questions and ask each other how things worked. They would post early code samples where they did not look like geniuses who knew all the answers, but just enthusiastic rookies who wanted to learn. You know how much people love correcting people on the internet, so anyone who posted something inaccurate got told about it real quick. How do you be ok with that, though? How do you psychologically handle going from the expert hot commodity to a total noob and keep up decent spirits while you do it?
First and Second Order Denial
My friends, has anyone considered the old standby straight-up denial? I don't think any of us are in first-order denial about AI where we refuse to accept that it exists or is changing things, but for myself, I am absolutely deep in second-order denial where you acknowledge the basic facts of the thing, but you deny the implications of those facts. Sure, the technology is here, but I am not ready to face its implications. I usually try to add a lot of details when I'm giving a talk, but here, I am going to kindly draw a veil and let the camera discreetly pan away because you do not need me to share my particular doomsday flavors. Besides, it weakens the denial. Denial can also stem from a fear that you or those you love lack the skills or resources to handle the consequences of a change. That's real.
Apparently, denial can have protective effects, though. This one study, "The role of denial in recovery from coronary heart disease," found that people who were in deep denial actually had better short-term outcomes than the ones who were actually facing reality. If you had deeper denial, you'd spend less time in intensive care and have fewer heart-related symptoms while you were in hospital. This rings true for me. Even if I've decided a thing is important to me, even when it's well-aligned with my values, if I face the full implications of how hard it's going to be, I will probably not do it. I might say, I don't have to exercise at the gym. I'm just going to put my shoes on and show up and we'll just see what happens. Denial can work to get us to start down a hard road and give us hope long enough to adapt to this ever-changing water.
Protective denial, it's incredibly common. We're also all going to die someday, but memento mori has somehow fallen out of fashion. If you want to sit in second-order denial with me for a little longer, that's ok. For a little longer, because the heart patients with serious denial had worse outcomes long-term. They didn't follow their medical advice, because why would they? They were fine. They got re-hospitalized more. Denial is not sustainable. If a little self-misdirection is what it takes to follow your values to stay in the room and not make a down payment on a yacht, go ahead, indulge. Let me suggest another indulgence, brain candy. When I was trying to improve my Spanish, I read the Twilight books, and I'm guessing most of you haven't read them or won't admit to having read them, because they're cloying vampire, werewolf, romance novels written for pre-teens. My Spanish became tan brillante como el pelo de Eduardo a la luz del sol, because brain candy, in the domain you're trying to learn, is just like the little carrot thrown down the path to convince the recalcitrant, what, I'm supposed to be good at this part of you, to at least look over and start to think about how to maybe head down this otherwise daunting path.
Sometimes you truly need to lower the stakes mentally just so you can push through. Get out of that intense, life-threatening pressure. Solve an actual problem that only you have. Make some tool, make some toy, make a flatulence app with your 8-year-old, something real, but where no one will evaluate you on the outcome because evaluation changes us. We don't learn so we can achieve the task we care about, we learn to pass the test assigned to us. This is bad even if you're an excellent test taker.
Building Fluency
I took a break from my French major one summer to spend eight weeks in an intensive Japanese language study in northern Japan, where they promised to teach us the equivalent of two university semesters of Japanese. I was very good at French at that point. I had just breezed through a pair of graduate seminars and my placement test in the Japanese program put me in the very lowest level class. I'd only taken two basic Japanese classes by this point, but I just still felt like, "Hello, don't you know who I am? I'm good at languages. Why am I in the beginner's class with these people who can barely put a sentence together?" Granted, I couldn't say, do you know who I am, in Japanese, which is maybe a sign that their class placement was somewhat valid, but I had a demonstrated skill in a fundamentally different but still related area.
Some of us are feeling this way about computing right now. I'm good at computers. I am a senior professional programmer. I once learned Python in an afternoon. If this new computing skill is hard for me, either is something is wrong with the system or something is wrong with me. Don't you know who I am? For me in Japan, my identity was so caught up in being good at languages that I worked hard to avoid ever making a mistake, not just on coursework, but asking the bus driver for a transfer ticket. I wanted my Japanese to be perfect. I actually learned the most about learning that summer on a weekend excursion, just me and a classmate, where we stayed at a family-run Buddhist temple out in the countryside. I won't go into the expectation thrashing experience of preparing myself for a solemn weekend of meditation and instead watching sumo wrestling on TV with a priest and his family, but the larger foundation-shattering surprise was the way my classmate spoke to our Japanese hosts and that she would just say things.
She'd trip over words. She'd mess up her verb endings. My grammar wasn't great, but I could recognize a bunch of mistakes even if I couldn't correct them. I was so deep in this prove to everyone that I'm good at this mentality that if I didn't know how to say something properly, I'd keep quiet so I didn't embarrass myself. Amy, though, just talked. They're like laughing, conversing. The priest gets another beer. What stuck with me long after I forgot all the extra kanji I learned that summer, is that interacting imperfectly builds fluency. You get early feedback before unwanted behaviors are calcified. Find your version of a Zen retreat where you can just play with the tools with no expectations of evaluation. You'll develop facility and fluency that much faster.
Another way to fail when something's not a test. Many years ago, as I was just learning to code, like mapping out how to do red-black trees on a whiteboard level, I went out with some friends and some friends of friends to rent a karaoke room. One of these friends of friends turned out to be an engineering manager at Microsoft, which is a hazard of where I live in Seattle. I remember the fear and dread and shame that I felt when I was unable to successfully navigate the karaoke interface via any of the in-room remote controls. See, I saw this as my chance to prove my technical prowess and maybe get hired on at Microsoft. Why would the engineering manager consider my resume if I couldn't even modify the output settings of a retro karaoke system? I don't remember what any of us saying, but I do remember holding that remote in my hand and thinking that I was never going to get a job in tech.
Now we're all looking back at 15 years ago me and inwardly shouting, everybody knows these systems are hard. Just try, don't give up, it's fine. We have so much compassion. What is your tool today that you're like, I still don't have this thing working. What are they all going to think of me? I better hide it and fake it and just play it cool. If you have that mental block, lower the stakes, make a tool, make a toy, something unspeakably inane that is tailored to exactly your interests. It can lower the activation energy required to take that next step towards learning.
Another way I make daunting things feel more approachable is thinking of them as a practice round. Picture this, every Sunday morning, I'm at a former aircraft hangar that's been turned into an indoor kids' sports hell hole arena. There are five football fields, a dozen simultaneous kid classes, there's adult workout classes, there's birthday rooms, plus an enormous bouncy house situation. I promise you whatever you're picturing, there are more bouncy houses. There's screaming and there's tears and there's kids running and begging for snacks, and I'm paying to be here. I went to great effort to dig the 4-year-old's soccer uniform out of his dirty laundry hamper and convince him to leave the house and convince him to leave the car. My reward for that is sitting on an uncomfortable bench drinking truly some of the worst coffee in Seattle. I want to paint for you this picture of aggressively, brightly colored despair, because what you need to appreciate is that it was a big deal for me to change perspectives.
Because I realize that if you see this not as a whole collection of circumstances designed to maximize my suffering, but hundreds of families who each separately fought through the chaos that is having a child on a chilly, damp weekend morning and got them to leave the house. If we could see in a little heads-up display what people overcame to get through that door, we would be walking around high-fiving and pouring each other pints. Nobody mentions all these hurdles. They just act like, yes, kids are wearing their kits here on time, relatively few boogers, as if they didn't execute a dozen fancy maneuvers to get there. If I don't tell someone that I struggled to get my kid there dressed, I won't hear their advice. Yes, my kid sleeps in her football kit. Sunday mornings have become my time to bask in the glory that not only have all of us made it through a gauntlet, but we've also successfully identified flaws in our own getting-out-of-the-house systems.
We're basically red teaming our own lives. How did you do at getting out of the house without yelling and tears? C-minus. How will you do at learning from what went wrong? Are you committed to bringing better snacks next time? The point isn't how well you executed the thing today, but how well you've internalized and applied the changes for next time. Put the snacks in the car right now, and today counts as a success.
Generating Energy to Learn
When I was deciding whether to take this job I had at Photoshop, I called up a friend for advice, because I had two offers for very different jobs, one that I was sure I would be good at, that they would be lucky to have me, and the other was a stretch. This advice was perfect when I was choosing my destiny, and learning modern C++ was supposed to be my last big career challenge. Now, very few of us have a choice about whether to invest a ton of energy in learning this new thing.
I have to somehow generate energy for learning or hit burnout real hard. I feel like maybe external energy building works for salespeople. Like I could just shout, are you ready? Let's get pumped. Everyone would be like, yes, let's go. We're engineers who got to where we are by taking skepticism to an art form. How many people have looked at some shiny new tech, said, no, and then just watched it crumble off into the sunset? No amount of like, rah, rah, do it, is going to convince us in all of the do it, learn, go. It's like being told by a scowling Simon Cowell to do a heartfelt interpretive dance. You're not at your best. How do we, the hopeful skeptics who do believe in a better future, in spite of it all, how do we generate energy to learn? Let's actually start by not spiraling, perhaps, by not leaking happiness.
One way I patch the leak is comparing current me to past me, because I'm obviously better than I was 10 years ago, aren't you? Think of you 10 years ago, and the glimmers of what you most value now that we're just starting to show. We were all goobers then compared to us now. Yet, we are all deeply discounting how much wiser we will be in the next 10 years, because we've got it figured out now. This is an actual studied phenomenon with a whole name, the end of history illusion. More specifically, we see the present as the moment where we have finally become the person we'll be for the rest of our lives.
More published sources. Just this year, Dr. Maya Shankar published a really timely book called "The Other Side of Change." I feel like she gets us as software people today, because she was well on the path to becoming a professional violinist when she had a career-ending injury, at which point she went into the field of psychology. She eventually became the behavioral sciences advisor to the UN. She did all right. I am clinging to her perspectives like a lifeline. She adds to this end of history idea, not about years, but any large change, when we imagine what it will be like to navigate an unexpected change and its aftermath, we tend to assume that we'll be the same person from beginning to end. Research shows that we greatly underestimate how much we'll change in the future, even though we fully acknowledge that we've changed considerably in the past.
Am I just going to keep reading you quotes? Yes, I am. Because these are literally professional studiers of brains, and they said this better than I can. You can think of this as the audiobook interlude. "The unique stresses and demands of being thrust into a new reality can uncover unexpected insights about ourselves and the world around us. These insights, coupled with the experience of the change itself, can transform us in extraordinary ways." I hear that, and I externally nod. Like, yes, maybe I'll grow on the other side of whatever this unprecedented time is. Also, a small part of me throws an absolute foot-stomping fit. I do not want to. I've barely got it together with the current state of things, and now you're coming at me with, think of all the personal growth you'll get. Like, no, I'm sorry. How many people are actively fantasizing about goat-herding careers right now?
There is some comfort in knowing that the person who will undergo the full experience will be different from the person we are in this very moment. We will become new people on the other side of change in ways we are capable of shaping. I still don't want to. I don't. I remind myself to take a breath, or six, because, see, the frog is facing physical challenges and doesn't have biohacking tools there in its pot. Our challenges are all in our minds, for better or worse. As my favorite book series says, my head is where 90-plus percent of my problems are. We believe in neuroplasticity. We can change and grow our minds from the inside out. I promise this is related, but did you know in the competitive equine sports world, all horses have the same official birthday? In the Northern Hemisphere, they all turn one year older on January 1st.
That means that if your horse was born on New Year's Eve, for juvenile racing purposes, they'll be considered 2 years old when they turn 366 days. You can see how a 700-day-old 2-year-old race horse would have an advantage. Breeders often arrange for foals to be born as close to January 2nd as they can. Football in the States has the same effect, actually, where a statistically improbable number of professional footballers are born in the first quartile of the year. Few parents plan their kids' births around the football season for some reason. There's something to be said for always being a little ahead of your peer group. You literally win more. If the kids on your football team look up to you because they're barely 6 while you're nearly 7, and coaches look to you to lead the team's comeback when they're behind 3-0, you develop leadership skills and confidence from a very early age.
I am on the other side. I came to technology late, so I got used to seeking coding advice from literal teenagers from day one of my first professional programming job. Since then, every team I'm on, I've been in the middle quartile in terms of raw technical Leet code acumen. Before anyone starts DMing me about imposter syndrome and telling me to believe in myself, I'm going to stop you, because I'm on the Photoshop engineering team, and I'm solidly in the middle of the pack. It's like being in the bottom third of Man City players, like, I'm one of the worst world-class athletes. Like, it's fine. I'm no slouch. I just keep moving up to better and better leagues. Because I started out behind and have stayed in the middle, I've never developed an ego around being the fastest prototyper or the most effective algorithm tuner. I have learned how to learn.
The Growth Mindset, and Learning in Public
There's this famous study on which learning tasks people will take if given the option to improve their skills. One task is advertised as majorly effective, the other as so-so. It turns out the researchers could easily influence which participants chose which task. See, in the ineffective task, people could try and fail privately, and the highly effective one involved practicing in front of the group so everyone saw your mistakes. Clearly different paths with different risks and outcomes, and you all might have a sense of which group you would tend towards. How would a researcher influence you to pick one over the other? They gave people reading material about the malleability of the particular skill, debating in this case. One group read that debate is mostly an innate skill, the other that anyone can do it. It just takes training. It takes practice. The people who were in the inborn skill group, they did not participate in the activity that would help them improve, because then everybody would see that they lacked the skill.
The trainable skill group people were like, ok, let's go. Who cares if other people see that I can't do this yet? Showing people you're ignorant of something today can and should be super low stakes. It goes along with believing in neuroplasticity. This study is out of Carol Dweck's research about growth mindset, which had a whole Silicon Valley trend moment. I think it's not as trendy now, but the research is still solid. People who believe that their traits and abilities can significantly change are more likely to engage in behaviors that improve them. One problem that I ran into face first, like a very clean plate glass door one, is that when you start paying attention to whether you have a growth mindset and realize that without the researcher's priming that you would definitely be in the group that's like, better make sure no one finds out I'm a terrible debater.
It throws you extra, because you, by definition, don't really believe that you can change how fixed your mindset is. These research scientists, I have to believe them because they approach this problem with rigor and with science at Stanford. They say quite plainly that cherished traits can be developed. I want to be better at believing in change and in neuroplasticity, so I'm working on it.
Part of my identity has become someone who learns out loud, and I've modeled learning out loud in public. The first time a principal engineer on the Photoshop team wanted to show me how to use a new AI tool to bolt a tricky feature onto our existing architecture, I recorded our screen share session and posted it for the rest of the team because seeing a tool used in a real-world context is always more instructive than the demo-worthy vacuum. Especially because, like all my comrades who brought their kids to weekend morning soccer practices, we each come to AI and use AI in completely different ways. My favorite take on this is from Dr. Cat Hicks. She is a research psychologist studying software teams and gets riled up in a very data-driven way when people talk about things like measuring team effectiveness. She emphasizes that none of us are having the same experience.
"When you have a highly adaptive, dialogical tool," which means the user is in dialogue with the tool, "where the user is shaping the context and wielding progressive disclosure to probe very different parts of its capabilities, different people will continue to get very different answers. Until we get real about the personalized, adaptive nature of this." People are each running their own individual experiments with new tools, and if we don't tell each other what our own tool uses look like, no one will know that you can put your kid to bed already wearing their football kit. This is not the time to experiment alone until your output seems to resemble other people's. Plus, even if I just complain about a tool, I usually get some really good alternative suggestions. Even though we've all transcended onto this higher plane of mental abstractions, there is still value in showing your actual footwork. Where did your tool fall over? Why did you keep using it anyway?
I actually literally do this in a surprising social context. Otherwise, awkward dance floors. Specifically at weddings or oddly corporate events that have decided to have a dance floor. Basically, collections of people of very mixed abilities who don't know each other super well and yet are celebrating something important together. I pride myself on understanding the assignment to look like I am enjoying myself in a way that invites other people in. I am very specifically not dancing like no one's watching. I am dancing like there's no downside to looking like a goon. I actually want people to see me and think, what a goon? That actually looks fun. Then I, as an enthusiastically mediocre dancer, will also have more fun because more people will be dancing. I also do this in socio-professional groups. I run a biweekly hallway track meeting for Photoshop developers where we just get together and talk off the record about our most recent formal meeting.
Sometimes there's a lull in the conversation. I'll just jump in with an inane comment, sometimes a spicy question, just to let people know we aren't here trying to impress each other. I'll set the bar and then open the door and get out of the way because I love hearing experienced people hash things out. Being mediocre in public can invite people out with you. It brings out other intermediate-level folks. It brings out some shy experts because you've made it obvious that the bar for participation is one that they can easily clear. Now you're in a group of people sharing information and refining ideas before they've fully calcified, and you make each other better. Don't wait to be an expert to join a conversation about your tools. A caveat, when I tell people my advice to be joyfully imperfect in public, I usually mean it a little bit glibly.
Like in the sense of, but obviously not things that are core to your central identity. That would be terrible. No, like I can take up watercolors and show people that I'm an amusingly bad artist, or take up Chinese and let people laugh. When your skill at something is core to your identity, being mediocre in public is like doing a penance for a sin that you didn't even really get to enjoy committing. What I'm trying to do with every fiber of my being is to push this other skill, this meta skill of learning and adapting to change even deeper into my identity and recognizing that this squeaky, uncomfortable like, no, I'm terrible at this. It's like the lactic acid buildup the day after a workout. Is it comfortable? No, it sucks. It is the concrete feeling of getting better.

Another aspect of bringing people with you. A few months ago, I used an AI agent to help me plan out decluttering my basement. Cursor came back with a useful plan and some excellent advice, which included, do not start with the miscellaneous bins. They will just exhaust you. Better to focus on low-decision weight, high-impact tasks. You all sighed with relief along there with me. Like, "Low-decision weight, high-impact? Yes, this plan will work. It's going to feel so good and productive." It did. I got the tower out. I got rid of expired food and old toiletries. I made so many easy decisions, and I wrapped up the day feeling tired but satisfied and a good day's work. Then I go to work the next day, and the AI agents are like, "Good, you're back. I saved all these high-decision weight tasks for you. You're welcome." It turns out I'm not the only one who's had this, hold up, I feel like I'm doing more work now. We're working harder. Birgitta mentioned this too.
We are tired. Please keep in mind that when you're telling people how great this tool is, it is not zero cost. It is free as in puppy. You can't just drop it on people's doorsteps. If you're walking around insisting that everyone adopts one, you've got to provide material support. One specific practice, Photoshop's strongest AI tooling advocates host weekly office hours. We're constantly re-explaining to each other how to export the right environment variables this week. The support is critical because you're asking people to work harder. If you're patient when you're asking someone if they've sourced their, Oh My Zsh config recently, they're more likely to keep trying your next, "You'll like this one, I promise." They're more likely to try that idea.
Fear of Lack of Skills
I know that some of you are very worried that some of us aren't fully embracing how different our jobs will be in five years. I actually said that to troll you a little because I know it's an order of magnitude faster. Remember that a source of denial can be a lack of certainty that we have the skills to deal with the change. The more you remind your teams and your colleagues that they have done hard things before, that they can learn and grow, that neuroplasticity is real, the more they can loosen their hold on denial. The more we all believe that we do have the skills to face it, the more likely we are to engage in real protective behaviors. My favorite researcher, Cat Hicks, again, if our teams have a culture of learning, we report more productivity. This next part is me, non-professional scientist, extrapolating, but I think if you have a choice between a team with one expert tool user and a team who believes that they can learn and has faith in the organizational support behind it, choose the team that identifies as learners, the team that thinks they can't use the tool yet.
Why, and How Are We Here?
Why are we here? This is a question whose spiritual pay grade is much higher than mine. I'm going to narrow it to something that I'm actually qualified to speak to, how did we get here? First, approximately one lifetime ago, a lot of people suffered through a lot of months of pregnancy. Some number of years ago, we went from not knowing technology to being paid to be good at it. Some number of weeks ago, we all decided it was a good use of three solid days of our time to sit at a tech conference, and then every single person got it together and left their home. If we had heads-up displays showing each of our logistical contortions we used to get here, we would be high-fiving and pouring each other pints all day. We all decided that, yes, it's worth it to take that skeptically optimistic next step to learn a new thing from a stranger rather than chatting up friends in the hall.
We've been through a lot to get here, and it's all been in the mad hope of finding that next good thing. We got here, and here and now is oddly harder than anything our industry has encountered, and even this is just a practice round for the next. The beginner's mindset that you're dusting off, the resilience that you did not want to have to shore up, and the communities that you're building now, this is not the last time you'll be calling on them. We're all just brains in training for the next swell, so if you usually avoid things that make you feel like a December-born horse, take a minute to practice being new at things. Start with watercolors if you want, but also today you could go to a talk whose topic intimidates you. If a popular or mandated tool is giving you blisters, you can say so.
Talk to your peers to commiserate, to your juniors so they know it's not just them, to your management if you've got some political capital burning a hole in your Slack drafts. This is what leadership looks like in this world where everyone's a beginner. It looks like being unafraid to say, don't you know who I am? Yes, I'm someone who learns out loud.

articles.title: JetBrains’ latest Mellum coding model uses 45% fewer tokens. It got there by not thinking.
articles.text:
JetBrains’ latest Mellum coding model uses 45% fewer tokens. It got there by not thinking.
JetBrains has launched a new variant of its open source coding model, one designed to tackle quick code edits, tool calls and all the smaller tasks that AI coding agents perform in the course of solving bigger problems.
Mellum2.1 Instruct, as it’s called, is the latest installment in JetBrains’ in-house coding model lineup. The original Mellum, which debuted back in 2024, was a proprietary model built specifically for low-latency code completion in JetBrains’ IDEs.
Then in June this year, JetBrains introduced Mellum2, a more versatile, 12-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model released under an Apache 2.0 license in both reasoning (Thinking) and non-reasoning (Instruct) variants. While Mellum2 was trained to handle individual coding tasks and tool calls, the next iteration would focus more specifically on how agents operate across entire code repositories.
That came last month with Mellum2.1 Thinking, which retained the same underlying architecture as Mellum2, but with an additional stage of reinforcement learning (RL) in which the model learned to navigate repositories, use shell and file tools, and make changes that would pass hidden tests.
With Mellum2.1 Instruct, JetBrains is now extending that same repository-level training to its non-reasoning model, which generates answers without an explicit chain-of-thought. As with its Thinking sibling, the company used Nvidia’s open source NeMo RL and NeMo Megatron-Bridge libraries to train the model using infrastructure capable of running 10,000 sandboxes concurrently.
The result is a leaner coding model fine-tuned for speed and token efficiency, capable of handling many of the same agentic tasks as its Thinking counterpart, with about half the token consumption, according to JetBrains’ testing.
The cost of overthinking
In a blog post published on Wednesday, Gleb Ingman, who works on the Mellum model team at JetBrains, notes that Mellum2.1 Instruct was built specifically for “sub-agents, tool loops, and chat.”
In real terms, this means that while Mellum2.1 Thinking is better suited to investigative tasks such as diagnosing why a unit test is failing, much of a coding agent’s day-to-day work involves more straightforward operations, such as modifying a few lines of code or retrieving information from a codebase. It’s these kinds of tasks that Mellum2.1 Instruct is geared toward, either operating independently or handling assignments delegated to it by a more powerful model.
“Every extra thinking token adds to the time you’re waiting.”
“In these cases, reasoning adds time and computing resources without adding quality,” Ingman writes. “This is especially true when the model runs locally — every extra thinking token adds to the time you’re waiting.”
Indeed, in the wake of the Thinking release, Ingman says that JetBrains fielded numerous requests from developers running models locally for a less verbose alternative capable of handling “moderately hard tasks.”
In its own benchmarking, JetBrains pits Mellum2.1 Instruct against the previous Mellum2 Instruct model, as well as Alibaba’s Qwen3.5 9B and Google’s Gemma 4 E4B, with reasoning disabled in both competing models. The six benchmarks cover agentic coding, multilingual code generation, tool use, instruction following and mathematical problem-solving.
Mellum2.1 Instruct doubled its predecessor’s score on SWE-bench Verified, which measures a model’s ability to resolve real-world software issues, jumping from 20.2% to 40.4%. It also outperformed all three models on the MultiPL-E code generation benchmark and broadly matched Qwen3.5 9B on ToolHop, which evaluates multi-step tool use.
Qwen3.5 9B, it’s worth noting, still came out ahead on SWE-bench Verified, scoring 49.8%. However, JetBrains points to Mellum’s MoE architecture, which activates just 2.5 billion of its 12 billion parameters for each token. According to the company’s earlier testing, this enables Mellum2.1 to generate tokens around 1.4 times as fast as Qwen3.5 9B for individual requests and 1.8 times as fast under load.
Perhaps more pertinent to this particular release, though, is how Mellum2.1 Instruct compares with its Thinking sibling in terms of token generation. In JetBrains’ agentic coding tests, the new model generated an average of 5,600 tokens per task, compared with 10,100 for Thinking — a reduction of 45%.
When tokens associated with tool calls were excluded, that reduction rose to 73%.
There are trade-offs, of course. While the two variants perform almost equally well on SWE-bench Verified, the gap widens on benchmarks that draw on competitive programming and mathematics competitions.
“On hard algorithmic and math problems, such as those in LiveCodeBench and AIME, thinking is crucial, and so Mellum2.1 Thinking remains the better choice,” Ingman writes.
“On hard algorithmic and math problems…. thinking is crucial, and so Mellum2.1 Thinking remains the better choice.”
Mellum2.1 Instruct is available on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license, including a GGUF version for running the model locally on hardware with limited memory. JetBrains is also releasing a multi-token prediction (MTP) head alongside the model, which predicts multiple tokens ahead to accelerate generation by up to 1.8 times, according to the company.
A model for the multi-agent era
Mellum2.1 Instruct arrives as JetBrains increasingly focuses its core developer tools on agent orchestration. In September, the company introduced a revamped version of Air, its development environment for working with multiple coding agents. JetBrains has also been expanding the capabilities of Junie, the coding agent it launched last year, with a renewed emphasis on local execution.
As developers delegate more work to agents, and those agents in turn delegate tasks to other agents, there is clear scope for using different models according to the complexity of the job at hand.
As developers delegate more work to agents, and those agents in turn delegate tasks to other agents, there is clear scope for using different models according to the complexity of the job at hand. A more token-efficient model such as Mellum2.1 Instruct, therefore, could help keep inference costs and latency in check across such a system.
Whether JetBrains intends to deploy Mellum2.1 Instruct in its own agentic products, such as Air or Junie, remains unclear.

articles.title: Perdió el cargo de CEO de Nvidia, pero el regreso de Jensen Huang podría dejarles USD 18 millones a sus hijos
articles.text:
El regreso de Jensen Huang a la conducción de Nvidia podría asegurar una herencia millonaria para los hijos de Colette Kress, quien dejó el liderazgo interino tras apenas 11 días para reasumir su puesto como directora financiera del gigante tecnológico en Estados Unidos.
Una investigación de Barron’s sobre registros de la Comisión de Bolsa y Valores reveló que el histórico repunte de la compañía en Wall Street rescata una compleja maniobra patrimonial: según las proyecciones del medio, los dos hijos adultos de la ejecutiva ahora tienen al alcance un paquete cercano a las 120.000 acciones, valuadas en más de USD 18 millones.
El director ejecutivo de Nvidia, Jensen Huang, es recibido entre aplausos por numerosos empleados en el atrio central de las instalaciones de la empresa.
Ese monto no constituye una cifra garantizada, sino un cálculo preliminar que elaboró la publicación financiera a partir de las fluctuaciones del mercado. El beneficio familiar depende de dos instrumentos que Kress y su esposo, David Kress, exejecutivo de Microsoft, establecieron en diciembre de 2024 mediante 1,47 millones de acciones que sumaban entonces USD 200 millones.
El derrumbe previo de la cotización amenazaba con liquidar por completo las ganancias de sus herederos, pero el cambio en la cúpula corporativa revirtió ese destino de manera radical.
Por qué el regreso de Jensen Huang a Nvidia beneficia la herencia de los hijos de Colette Kress
La crisis en la conducción estalló a mediados de noviembre de 2026, cuando la dimisión de Jensen Huang aceleró el declive bursátil de Nvidia. Tras alcanzar un récord de USD 239 a principios de octubre, los títulos se hundieron un 41% hasta registrar un cierre de USD 125,53 el viernes previo a su retorno, según datos del equipo de mercado de Dow Jones que citó Barron’s.
La renuncia ocurrió tras salir a la luz un vínculo sentimental del fundador con una presunta espía de China y con al menos una subordinada. Aunque la junta directiva colocó de inmediato a Colette Kress al frente de la empresa, presiones del gobierno federal precipitaron la vuelta del histórico directivo el lunes 23 de noviembre.
La reacción del mercado batió marcas: la compañía sumó cerca de USD 1 billón de capitalización en una única sesión bursátil en Estados Unidos. Ese salto histórico llevó la cotización a unos USD 155 por papel al cierre del martes 24 de noviembre.
Para los planes patrimoniales de Kress, ese rebote representa un salvavidas. Las estimaciones que publicó el medio indican que, si la cotización se estancaba en el piso del viernes anterior, los fondos debían entregar cada acción remanente a Kress para cumplir con los pagos obligatorios, un desenlace que dejaba a sus hijos sin un solo dólar.
La recuperación del valor devolvió a los fondos un margen de ganancia libre de impuestos para sus beneficiarios.
Cómo funcionan los fideicomisos GRAT que usan los ejecutivos de Nvidia para transferir acciones
La estrategia de la directora financiera recurre a los fideicomisos GRAT (fideicomiso de anualidad retenida por el otorgante), una herramienta que eligen las familias más ricas en Estados Unidos para traspasar fortunas intergeneracionales sin consumir la exención federal de impuestos sobre donaciones y sucesiones, cuyo límite alcanza los USD 15 millones por persona en 2026.
Quien crea el fondo deposita activos con alto potencial de crecimiento por un plazo fijo —habitualmente dos o cuatro años— y cobra anualidades equivalentes al capital inicial más una tasa de interés que estipulan las leyes fiscales.
Todo el crecimiento de las acciones que supere esa tasa mínima fijada por el fisco pasa directamente a los descendientes con una ventaja central: pagan cero impuestos sobre esa ganancia. Por el contrario, si los títulos sufren un desplome y el mercado no revierte la caída antes de la fecha límite, la estructura fracasa.
En ese escenario, los títulos vuelven al aportante para saldar los pagos pautados y los beneficiarios se quedan con las manos vacías, lo que anula la transferencia patrimonial que planificó la familia.
Cuál es el riesgo real que aún enfrentan los fideicomisos de Nvidia creados en 2026
El alivio que trajo la reincorporación de Jensen Huang no disipa todos los riesgos para los Kress. A principios de 2026, la ejecutiva financió otros dos instrumentos similares mediante un lote de 2,3 millones de acciones, según detalló la publicación financiera con base en las presentaciones regulatorias. En esa fecha, los papeles de la tecnológica cotizaban a USD 185, una marca todavía distante de los precios actuales en los tableros bursátiles.
El desenlace de esta segunda tanda de fondos dependerá del comportamiento de Nvidia en Wall Street. Si la cotización de los títulos no remonta por encima de aquel valor inicial antes del vencimiento de sus plazos, estos fideicomisos experimentarán la misma anulación que casi destruye los acuerdos de 2024.
De esta manera, el traspaso definitivo de la fortuna familiar continúa atado al pulso del gigante de los semiconductores.

articles.title: Motorola Signature (256 GB) fica mais barato com cupom da Black Week
articles.text:
Motorola Signature (256 GB) fica mais barato com cupom da Black Week
Motorola Signature com tela de 165 Hz, câmeras de 50 MP e chipset premium recebe ótimo desconto ao combinar cupom e pagamento via Pix
O Motorola Signature (256 GB) entrou em oferta por R$ 4.199 no Pix com o cupom MENOSPRATECH no Mercado Livre. O primeiro smartphone ultra-premium da Motorola com tela AMOLED e câmeras de 50 MP, lançado por R$ 5.999, atinge o menor preço já visto pelo Achados do TB nesta promoção de Black Week 2026.
Esta oferta é o menor preço que já encontramos para o Motorola Signature 5G 256 GB. Nas outras 1 ofertas publicadas desde novembro de 2026, o melhor foi R$ 4.498,20 (Magalu, 6/11/2026).
O Motorola Signature se destaca pela tela Extreme AMOLED de 6,8 polegadas, igual ao recente Signature 27, reproduzindo imagens na resolução Super 1.5K e taxa de atualização de 165 Hz. Além dos recursos Dolby Vision e HDR10+, o painel atua com brilho máximo de até 6.200 nits.
A câmera tripla traseira é composta por sensores de 50 MP, que fazem fotos com zoom híbrido de até 100x e registram vídeos em até 8K. A câmera frontal também adota um sensor de 50 MP, entregando selfies detalhadas com recurso de Foco Automático.
Com foco em alto desempenho, o Motorola Signature é equipado com o chip Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 e 12 GB de RAM. Os 256 GB de armazenamento interno oferecem um espaço equilibrado para mídias, aplicativos e outros arquivos.
A bateria de silício-carbono de 5.200 mAh do smartphone da Motorola tem autonomia de até 39 horas de uso moderado. O modelo ainda possui carregamento rápido de até 90 W, indo de 0 a 50% em apenas 15 minutos.
O dispositivo é fabricado com estrutura de alumínio e acabamento traseiro em silicone imitando sarja ou linho. Os certificados IP68/IP69 de resistência à poeira e à água e militar MIL-STD-810H garantem ampla proteção contra mergulhos, quedas e condições extremas.
Na parte de conexões, o Motorola Signatura (R$ 4.199 no Pix com o cupom MENOSPRATECH) tem 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, Ultra WideBand (UWB) e NFC. O modelo sai da caixa com o Android 16 e, segundo a marca, receberá ao menos 7 grandes atualizações do sistema operacional.
A Black Friday 2026 acontece no próximo dia 27 de novembro, mas diversas lojas estão antecipando promoções e cupons de desconto desde o início do mês. Então, siga o Achados do TB para não perder nenhuma oferta.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Des claviers gaming magnétiques dès 46,99 € : The G-Lab élargit son offre
articles.text:
Faut-il forcément investir une somme astronomique pour s’offrir un clavier gaming de qualité ? La marque française The G-Lab est la preuve concrète que performances, technologies de pointe et prix accessibles ne sont pas incompatibles.
Un clavier gaming sur trois vendu en France est un The G-Lab ! Oui, un sur trois, rien que ça ! Une belle réussite pour cette marque française qui, en seulement dix ans, a su se faire une place de choix sur un marché pourtant dominé par les géants du gaming.
Et visiblement, cette équipe de passionnés n’a pas l’intention de s’arrêter en si bon chemin. Avec sa nouvelle gamme Elite et ses switches magnétiques, elle s’invite désormais sur le terrain du gaming compétitif, bien décidée à imposer sa vision : celle de produits performants, proposés à des prix raisonnables.
En dix ans, les règles du jeu ont bien changé
Au milieu des années 2010, choisir un clavier gaming reposait sur des critères simples : un design agressif, quelques touches programmables, un rétroéclairage bien visible et, surtout, une offre de switches mécaniques plutôt basique.
Du clavier gaming classique au périphérique de précision
En 2026, cette vision paraît presque désuète.
Le clavier gaming est devenu un périphérique de précision, capable de s’adapter aux préférences, aux habitudes et au style de jeu de chacun. Il ne s’agit plus seulement de choisir une sensation de frappe, mais aussi de déterminer à quelle profondeur une touche doit s’activer, avec quelle sensibilité et dans quelles conditions elle peut être réinitialisée pour enregistrer une nouvelle commande.
De nouvelles fonctionnalités se sont ainsi imposées dans les discussions entre joueurs, jusqu’à devenir des arguments de différenciation majeurs pour les fabricants.
Parmi elles figurent le Rapid Trigger et les points d’activation ajustables, tandis que la démocratisation des switches hot-swappable a ouvert de nouvelles possibilités de personnalisation. Mais l’essor des claviers magnétiques à effet Hall constitue sans doute l’une des évolutions les plus marquantes de ces dernières années.
Les switches magnétiques ouvrent de nouvelles possibilités
En mesurant en continu la position des touches grâce à des capteurs magnétiques, ces claviers permettent de dépasser les limites des points d’activation fixes des switches mécaniques traditionnels. Les joueurs peuvent définir avec précision la profondeur à laquelle chaque touche s’active, parfois au dixième de millimètre près.
The G-Lab a accompagné ces nombreux changements en faisant évoluer son offre. Mais avec sa nouvelle gamme Elite, la marque franchit une étape en investissant le segment majeur des claviers magnétiques.
Quel est le meilleur clavier gaming en 2026 ?
En une phrase : tout dépend de votre façon de jouer !
Un énervé de la gâchette, obnubilé par les FPS, n’aura pas forcément les mêmes attentes qu’un joueur de RPG, qu’un passionné de jeux de stratégie ou qu’une personne qui utilise son clavier aussi bien pour travailler que pour jouer. Et c’est d’ailleurs sur cette diversité des profils que The G-Lab fait la différence.
Pour découvrir le gaming : le Keyz Caesium EX en promo à 19,80 €
En quête d’un premier clavier gaming ? Inutile de casser sa tirelire pour s’équiper. Le Keyz Caesium EX représente un choix cohérent pour les joueurs occasionnels, les premières configurations ou ceux qui recherchent simplement un clavier polyvalent sans multiplier les fonctionnalités dont ils n’auront pas nécessairement l’utilité.
Son format compact libère de la place sur votre setup et notamment pour la souris, histoire de ne plus se retrouver bloqué par le pavé numérique; ce qui arrive constamment avec un clavier classique.
Il dispose aussi d’une technologie anti-ghosting pour appuyer sur plusieurs touches simultanément sans subir de conflits. Ajoutez à cela une molette de réglage du volume, un rétroéclairage sympa et un budget ultra abordable et vous avez le clavier parfait pour débuter !
Pour goûter au clavier mécanique : le Keyz Rubidium en promo à 43 €
Un clavier gaming mécanique pour un budget raisonnable ? Le The G-Lab Keyz Rubidium, proposé à 43 € pendant le Black Friday, constitue une option intéressante pour les joueurs qui recherchent davantage de réactivité, de précision et de confort.
Il est équipé de véritables switches mécaniques Outemu Red, qui assurent une frappe réactive, un choix pertinent notamment pour les jeux rapides comme les FPS. Et pour ceux qui ont tendance à multiplier les commandes, l’anti-ghosting intégral avec N-Key Rollover est aussi de la partie. Ainsi, même lorsque plusieurs touches sont pressées simultanément, chaque commande est bien prise en compte.
Ajoutez à cela un repose-poignets magnétique amovible, et vous pouvez prolonger les sessions gaming.
Pour jongler entre travail et gaming : le Keyz Elite 300 Mécanique à 89,90 €
Qui a dit qu’il fallait choisir entre un clavier pour travailler et un autre pour jouer ? Avec le Keyz Elite 300 Mécanique, The G-Lab fait de la polyvalence une force.
C’est d’ailleurs avec la gamme Keyz Elite que la marque a franchi un cap : son succès a marqué un véritable tournant pour The G-Lab, qui s’est ainsi fait une place sur le segment premium en adoptant des choix de conception longtemps réservés à des claviers bien plus onéreux.
Son format compact 75 % libère de la place sur le bureau tout en conservant les principales touches utiles au quotidien. Un compromis intéressant lorsqu’on souhaite gagner de l’espace sans passer à un clavier ultracompact.
Ses switches mécaniques linéaires KTT Wine Red, pré-lubrifiés en usine, offrent une frappe fluide dès le déballage, et ils sont hot-swappables, ce qui permet de les remplacer sans soudure pour changer de sensations. Ils reposent sur une structure gasket à cinq couches qui amortit chaque appui et atténue les résonances, pour une frappe plus douce et plus feutrée, tandis que les touches en PBT double injection résistent mieux à l’usure et conservent des inscriptions qui ne s’effacent pas avec le temps.
Enfin, sa triple connectivité (USB, Bluetooth et sans-fil 2,4 GHz) permet de passer d’un usage à l’autre et de jongler entre plusieurs appareils sans multiplier les claviers sur son bureau.
Pour les amateurs de FPS : le Keyz Elite 300 HE Magnétique à 94,95 €
Avec le Keyz Elite 300 HE Magnétique, on entre dans une autre catégorie. Celle des claviers conçus pour les joueurs qui souhaitent personnaliser très finement la réactivité de leurs touches.
Ce modèle dispose de switches magnétiques à effet Hall, ce qui permet, comme on l’explique plus haut, d’ajuster le point d’activation des touches selon ses préférences.
Il intègre également la technologie Rapid Trigger et sa fréquence d’interrogation peut atteindre 8 000 Hz, ce qui aide à réduire la latence avec l’ordinateur, même si l’avantage réel dépend également du jeu et de la configuration utilisée.
Comme sa version mécanique, il profite du savoir-faire qui a fait le succès de la gamme Elite : une structure gasket à cinq couches qui réduit les vibrations et rend la frappe plus douce et plus stable, des touches en PBT double injection et des switches hot-swappables.
Il y ajoute une molette multimédia pour régler le volume sans quitter la partie, et un châssis d’environ un kilo qui reste fermement en place sur le bureau, même lors des phases de jeu les plus intenses. Face au Titanium HE, c’est cette construction plus aboutie, son format 75 % plus complet et sa molette dédiée qui justifient l’écart de prix.
Pour découvrir le magnétique à petit budget : le Keyz Titanium HE à 46,99 €
Enfin, avec le Keyz Titanium HE, The G-Lab propose la porte d’entrée la plus accessible vers les switches magnétiques. À 46,99 €, il réunit l’essentiel de ce qui fait l’intérêt de cette technologie dans un format compact 65 %, qui dégage davantage d’espace pour les mouvements de souris, un détail qui peut avoir son importance pour les amateurs de FPS.
Ses switches magnétiques à effet Hall, pré-lubrifiés et hot-swappables, offrent un point d’activation réglable de 0,1 à 3,4 mm, et il intègre lui aussi le Rapid Trigger ainsi qu’une fréquence d’interrogation pouvant atteindre 8 000 Hz, le tout surmonté de touches en PBT double injection.
Ce qu’il laisse à l’Elite 300 HE, c’est surtout la structure gasket, la molette multimédia et un format un peu plus complet. Pour résumer, le Titanium HE donne la priorité à la réactivité et à l’optimisation de l’espace, et constitue une excellente façon de découvrir le magnétique sans se ruiner.
FAQ : les questions fréquentes avant d’acheter
Quel est le meilleur clavier gaming en 2026 ?
Tout dépend de votre utilisation : pour les FPS,un clavier magnétique doté du Rapid Trigger et de points d’activation ajustables peut offrir un véritable intérêt. Pour les joueurs occasionnels ou ceux qui alternent entre travail et gaming, un bon clavier mécanique, voire à membrane, peut largement suffire.
Quel clavier gaming offre le meilleur rapport qualité-prix ?
Pour une quarantaine d’euros, le The G-Lab Keyz Rubidium constitue une option intéressante grâce à ses switches mécaniques Outemu Red, son anti-ghosting intégral et son repose-poignets amovible.
Quel clavier choisir pour les FPS ?
Pour les amateurs de FPS comme Valorant, Counter-Strike 2 ou Call of Duty, un clavier magnétique à effet Hall constitue un choix idéal. Dans la gamme The G-Lab, le Keyz Elite 300 HE Magnétique coche toutes les cases : switches magnétiques, Rapid Trigger et fréquence qui grimpe à 8 000 Hz.
Mécanique ou magnétique : lequel choisir ?
Le mécanique est excellent pour la polyvalence et les sensations de frappe. Le magnétique offre davantage de réglages pour les déplacements rapides et les usages compétitifs.
Quel clavier magnétique pas cher acheter ?
Le Keyz Titanium HE est un choix naturel, il embarque des switches à effet Hall avec un point d’activation personnalisable, le tout dans un format 65 % très agréable.
Quel clavier pour jouer et travailler ?

articles.title: US Treasury’s FinCEN Disconnects Systems Following Cyber Incident
articles.text:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the US Treasury Department’s financial intelligence unit, has disconnected some of its systems while investigating a cyber incident.
“FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline,” the agency said in a notice on the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) E-Filing System website.
The website is operational, but some FinCEN services may be temporarily unavailable, and the agency has extended the deadlines for qualifying filers affected by the disruption.
“FinCEN is granting temporary, limited exceptive relief in response to a service disruption that is hindering filers’ ability to adhere to reporting obligations,” the agency said in a November 24 order (PDF).
The agency has not shared further details on the nature of the incident and made no mention of a potential data breach, but said it was working to return all systems to normal.
It is unclear who was behind the attack and if any data was accessed or stolen. SecurityWeek has emailed FinCEN for additional information and will update this article if the agency responds.
FinCEN disclosed the incident amid a wave of cyberattacks and outages impacting US government agencies, including the CIA, which had an unclassified system breached.
The Department of Defense’s National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence were also affected by the open source intelligence system breach, The New York Times reported on Tuesday.
Last week, the National Security Agency temporarily took offline an internal network used to communicate classified information, and the FBI is looking into an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database.
