articles.title: Q&A: Why nanotech research is booming in Alberta
articles.text:
This article appears in The BetaKit Guide to Alberta’s Silicon City. Learn more about Edmonton semiconductor innovation here.
Nanotechnology first became a hot commodity in the early aughts. Heralded as the next revolution, it was common to see pop-culture visions of a future where nanobots would scour our bloodstreams for cancer cells and skyscrapers would self-assemble. The tech attracted billions in federal and VC dollars, with both US Presidents Bill Clinton and George Bush making hefty investments in the field.
Nanotech’s high profile has dissipated since then, but the technology hasn’t. Today, nanotech is more prevalent than ever, underpinning everything from the semiconductor chips powering AI to vaccines and even sunscreen.
The sector also continues to garner interest from government, business, and academia. To find out what that renewed interest means for the future of nanotech, and Canada’s place as a potential leader, BetaKit sat down with Dr. Andrew Myles, the director of research and development at the Quantum and Nanotechnology Research Centre (NANO) in Edmonton.
The following interview has been edited for both clarity and length. 
Many people might not really know what nanotechnology means. Can you define it for our readers?
Nanotechnology is any technology that exploits features on the nano scale; between one and 100 nanometres is usually the common definition. The way I like to explain it is: one nanometer compared to one millimetre is the same as one millimetre compared to one kilometre. So that gives you an idea of perspective.
Once you get down to these small particles, you have unique features, like an extremely high surface area of any material that is reduced to a nanoparticle, and you can exploit that kind of feature in any technology that would benefit from high surface area. It’s very applicable to biology and medicine because our bodies have DNA, proteins, and all of these enzymes that have little nooks and crannies in them at the nano scale. So for the medical side, for solar cells, for batteries, these types of technologies can all benefit from nanotechnology.
What’s the coolest thing being researched at NANO right now?
One thing that really motivates us here now is remote environmental sensing. We work a lot in the North and with Indigenous communities doing environmental sensing research and looking at detecting toxins in water, for instance, but also networking that information. So we have different sensors networking through and collecting that data and looking at those advances of not only the technology but also that digital technology component.
Seeing the technology and what it can do for these communities, I think that’s probably one of the most exciting things we’ve seen in the last little while.
What’s one thing you think people should know about nanotech today?
Nanotech can be applied across industry sectors and is often incorporated in more conventional applications than you may imagine. When you talk about nanotechnology being in things like tennis rackets or lubricants or bandages, people are kind of surprised. But it’s already deployed to a large extent, and there are a lot of benefits already. So it’s not as out of reach as some people may think. It’s a fantastic area to explore because it has a lot of interesting science still going on, but a lot of excellent applications already in place.
Biomedicine is extremely active in this space. I would remind you of the COVID-19 vaccine that was based on lipid nanoparticle technology developed in Canada. This is the beginning. Now this is being explored for all kinds of different biomedicines.
Why do you think Alberta has become an institutional home for nanotech and R&D in Canada? What makes the province so appealing to the industry?
It’s a combination of a couple of things. One is that Alberta’s always had this entrepreneurial, get-‘er-done spirit. I would also say that our universities are fantastic. There are a lot of universities in Alberta; they’re all strong; they all interact; there’s connections and engagement; people graduating with high-tech degrees, getting jobs, and bringing that expertise into companies.
What does Canada need to do to become a leader in nanotech, or to maintain its edge?
We like to look at demonstrating technologies to industry and really trying to move industry and our academic base closer together. I think you’re seeing that across the country in many universities. Places like the University of Alberta’s NanoFAB have many companies every single day, side by side with people at the university working on actual new products. It’s extremely exciting.
I feel like Canada’s move towards really funding and sponsoring technology development and science is very promising. Now it’s up to us as scientists to make sure that we deliver that value to our industries.
If Canada becomes a leader in nanotechnology, how does that benefit the country?
I think it’s all part of moving to a knowledge-based economy and having high-tech as a major pillar. It bolsters all of our industries. The concept of nanotechnology applied across sectors can be beneficial all over the place. It also just gets more conventional, maybe risk-averse companies to sort of step out and look at some options for how they could improve.
And, certainly, global competitiveness is a driver. But it also just strengthens industry locally. It strengthens our position, our major sectors. If we have more of these technologies introduced into our major resource sectors, it strengthens them and bolsters them even more than we already do.
What do you think the future of nanotech looks like, both here in Alberta and more broadly?
I see a lot of more conventional industries adopting nanotechnologies, and in the future you’re going to start seeing nano elements within lots of different technologies. Also, more specifically, connected sensing. So being connected through the Internet of Things and the use of AI to get real-time, remote, and complex data analyzed for us through sensing systems. I mentioned nanomedicine earlier, and with the success of lipid nanoparticle technology, I do expect to see more of that in the future as well.
Feature image courtesy Andrew Myles.

articles.title: Teen helps find girl kidnapped over a year ago after meeting her in Among Us
articles.text:
What just happened? People who try to monitor or restrict communications often don't realize that online video games are also technically chat networks. This oversight usually emerges in discussions about online child safety, but in one recent case, an online friendship led to the rescue of a teenager who had been missing for more than 500 days.
A 39-year-old Oregon man is currently in jail awaiting trial on allegations that he kidnapped and sexually assaulted a teen who was reported missing last year. Police recovered the girl from the man's residence days after she began chatting with a Colorado teen and his mother in the online game Among Us.
While chatting with 16-year-old Landon Tresp in late October, Jenny (an alias), 17, admitted she had run away from home after years of abuse but was now being held against her will in an unknown location in Oregon. She had met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media last May. He told her he was disabled and offered her money for help getting to Oregon.
However, after Harmel picked up Jenny in Utah, he threw away her phone, kept her in the basement of his Oregon home, and forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed while keeping a knife (pictured) under his pillow. Jenny said he became aggressive and abusive and forced her to remove her braces with pliers so she couldn't be identified. She also said she had tried to escape before.
Harmel gave Jenny a phone that couldn't make calls but could access Wi-Fi, which is how she was able to play Among Us. After striking up a friendship with Tresp in the game in mid-October, more than a year after her disappearance, she eventually moved their conversations to Discord, revealed she was being held against her will, and shared links to news stories about her disappearance. She knew what town she was in, but not her exact location.
When Tresp told his mother, 41-year-old Khristina, on Halloween, she immediately jumped into action. The pair later told the BBC that Khristina asked Jenny over video chat to retrieve any documents in the house that might contain her captor's full name. The mom then searched tax and property records and matched photos of Harmel's property from Zillow with Jenny's description.
After contacting Jenny's mother on social media, Khristina received a call from the FBI almost immediately. On November 1, when Harmel next left the residence, Khristina used a video call to guide Jenny out of the building while receiving minute-by-minute updates from police.
Jenny later received medical treatment and remains in daily contact with the Tresps.

articles.title: Nem elétrica, nem a combustão: essa moto é solar
articles.text:
Uma scooter elétrica equipada com painéis solares promete reduzir a necessidade de recargas na tomada. Batizado de Lightfoot, o veículo de dois lugares aproveita a luz do Sol para alimentar sua bateria e pode recuperar até 29 quilômetros de autonomia por dia em condições ideais.
O modelo foi desenvolvido pelo inventor Saul Griffith e tem painéis fotovoltaicos instalados nas laterais, próximos ao assento. Segundo a fabricante, o sistema consegue acrescentar cerca de 4,8 quilômetros de alcance por hora de exposição solar. Em regiões menos ensolaradas, porém, esse rendimento pode cair pela metade.
A bateria tem capacidade de 1,5 kWh e também pode ser recarregada em uma tomada convencional. Nesse caso, o processo leva aproximadamente quatro horas.
O conjunto elétrico conta com dois motores de mil watts cada. Durante um teste realizado em São Francisco (EUA), o veículo conseguiu subir ladeiras com facilidade e atingiu cerca de 32 km/h. A scooter também possui frenagem regenerativa, que recupera parte da energia durante as desacelerações.
Scooter solar tem espaço para bagagem e custa R$ 24 mil
- O Lightfoot tem linhas inspiradas na Vespa, mas se diferencia pelo conjunto de painéis solares que ocupa boa parte das laterais;
- O veículo oferece espaço para transportar bolsas e outros objetos, além de carregador integrado;
- A experiência de condução foi comparada à de uma bicicleta pelo jornalista Michael J. Coren, do The Washington Post, responsável pelo teste;
- Ele percorreu diferentes regiões de São Francisco sem demonstrar preocupação com a autonomia. Por outro lado, apontou alguns problemas de acabamento, como encaixes irregulares, dificuldade para alcançar o descanso lateral e uma tela digital considerada lenta;
- O conforto também recebeu ressalvas. O banco estreito e comprido funcionou bem em trajetos curtos, mas começou a incomodar depois de aproximadamente 11 quilômetros;
- O preço é outro obstáculo: o Lightfoot custa US$ 4.495 (cerca de R$ 24 mil). Por enquanto, a comercialização está concentrada na América do Norte, começando pela Califórnia (EUA).
Leia mais:
- Honda apresenta bicicleta elétrica de montanha com motor de 750 W
- Homem transforma bicicleta elétrica em pequeno carro para fugir da chuva
- Caloi relança Mobylette elétrica no Brasil com 60 km de autonomia
Economia com energia pode ser limitada
Apesar da proposta de recarga solar, o principal atrativo do Lightfoot não parece ser a economia na conta de luz. Segundo a reportagem, uma recarga completa na tomada custa menos de US$ 0,50 (cerca de R$ 2,70), com base nas tarifas residenciais médias dos Estados Unidos.
Considerando que a energia solar substitua duas recargas completas por semana, a economia anual seria de aproximadamente US$ 50 (cerca de R$ 270).
A proposta pode fazer mais sentido pela conveniência: o veículo consegue recuperar energia enquanto fica estacionado ao ar livre, reduzindo a frequência com que precisa ser conectado à tomada. Isso também pode beneficiar pessoas que não têm acesso fácil a pontos de recarga próximos de casa.
O desenvolvedor Saul Griffith ainda enxerga potencial para o Lightfoot em frotas de veículos utilizadas em ilhas, resorts e universidades. Nesses locais, a recarga solar poderia reduzir os custos de operação, especialmente em regiões onde a infraestrutura elétrica é limitada.
A empresa pretende ampliar a distribuição internacional e tem como objetivo alcançar vendas globais de dez mil unidades por ano.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
articles.text:
Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store.
The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.
According to a Wednesday report by Fortune, citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.
One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.
Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter.
Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported.
Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

articles.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
articles.text:
AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  York University
- Summary:
  AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.
For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.
But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."
A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI
The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.
If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.
"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.
The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.
Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.
AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story
The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.
AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.
This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.
"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.
The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.
Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.
That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.
"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.
Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior
The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.
If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.
"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.
Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.
The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.
Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain
Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.
By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.
"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."
A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.
To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.
Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.
The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.
Story Source:
Materials provided by York University. Original written by Sandra McLean. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sabine Muzellec, Kohitij Kar. Reverse predictivity for bidirectional comparison of neural networks and biological brains. Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026; 8 (3): 474 DOI: 10.1038/s42256-026-01204-0

articles.title: Así conecta ‘Blade Runner 2099’ con las películas, según sus protagonistas: «Los replicantes están en el poder»
articles.text:
Acaba de estrenarse en Amazon Prime Video su nuevo gran proyecto, Blade Runner 2099. Se trata de una serie de ciencia ficción que se ambienta en la legendaria franquicia creada por Ridley Scott hace casi 45 años. Esta vez, la saga da el salto al streaming con una historia de ocho episodios que promete seguir indagando en su complejo y fascinante universo.
Cincuenta años después de los sucesos de Blade Runner 2049, Los Ángeles ha renacido, aunque no a manos de la humanidad. Cora, una fugitiva que intenta dejar de huir de una vez por todas, adopta una última identidad: la de Blade Runner. Obligada a asociarse con Olwen, una replicante a la que le quedan pocos días de vida, da caza a un fugitivo que oculta una verdad capaz de hacer colapsar su frágil ciudad.
De cara al estreno de Blade Runner 2099, en Hipertextual hemos podido atender a la conferencia de prensa de sus dos protagonistas, Michelle Yeoh (Todo a la vez en todas partes) y Hunter Schafer (Euphoria). Y en ella nos han contado cómo será el mundo que los fans se encuentren en la serie. Porque, después de tantos años, ahora son los replicantes los que tienen el control y los humanos lo que deben esconderse.
Los replicantes de Blade Runner 2099
"Creo que al final de Blade Runner 2049 se empieza a vislumbrar el germen de una revolución o algo que se ha estado gestando. Y han pasado muchas cosas desde entonces. Los replicantes están en el poder y, no solo eso, sino que han mantenido el sistema al estilo de Blade Runner y, de hecho, lo han invertido por completo. Ahora son los humanos a quienes se persigue", explica Schafer.
"Mantienen a los humanos a raya. Cuando ganas una guerra, ¿cómo te aseguras de mantenerte en el poder?", se une Yeoh a su compañera de reparto. "Me encantan las preguntas que plantean esta serie e incluso las dos primeras películas: ¿qué es ser humano? ¿Qué es la humanidad? ¿Nacemos con humanidad o es algo que hemos aprendido con el tiempo y la experiencia de la vida?", se plantea a su vez.
"Los replicantes no nacieron con emociones. De hecho, no tenían alma. Fueron creados de carne y hueso a nuestra imagen y semejanza, pero más fuertes para poder hacer cosas que nosotros no haríamos o que físicamente no podríamos hacer", prosigue la veterana actriz.
"Pero cuando se les da tiempo y recuerdos... ¿les estamos dando esperanza? Porque lo que hacen los replicantes en 2099 también da esperanza a los humanos. Si eres bueno, si haces esto, podrías ir a un lugar mejor. Y eso es mentira, porque cuando Cora descubre que no hay nada ahí fuera, siente una gran sensación de traición. Esto es todo lo que tienes", sugiere, dejando entrever algunos detalles de por dónde discurre la trama y el componente filosófico de Blade Runner 2099.
Dos personajes muy distintos
Las dos protagonistas de Blade Runner 2099 son Cora, una joven humana que debe hacerse pasar por replicante y Olwen, una androide a la que el tiempo se le acaba. Se trata de dos mujeres totalmente antagónicas que se encuentran en un mundo en el que deben aliarse. Pero, en el fondo, ambas luchan sus propias guerras. "Cora es un personaje que, en cierto modo, ha perdido su identidad. ¿Cómo se interpreta a alguien que no sabe quién es?", revela Schafer sobre su papel.
"Y, además de eso, ¿cómo interpretas a alguien que no sabe quién es y que se hace pasar por otra persona durante gran parte de la serie? Sabía que iba a ser un gran reto y me daba miedo, lo cual es en parte por lo que quería hacerlo. Era una cuestión de encontrarlo y volver a ello constantemente", añade. "Cada vez que se volvía abrumador o me daba un poco de vértigo, tenía que recordar que ella simplemente actúa en modo de supervivencia y lo único que quiere es sobrevivir y mantener con vida a su hermano y a ella misma", cuenta sobre su personaje.
"Por mi parte, cuando conoces a Olwen por primera vez, te das cuenta de que es una replicante muy segura de sí misma. Es, como dirían, la replicante más dura que hay", menciona Yeoh acerca de su personaje de Blade Runner 2099. "No permite que la fecha de caducidad defina todo lo que ha hecho como Olwen, la Blade Runner, ni lo que ha conseguido. De hecho, ella misma lo dice: «He dado a luz a estrellas». Ya sabes, «he hecho todo lo que quería ver y hacer». Pero esa es la Olwen que quiere que los demás perciban", sugiere después.
"Se supone que no debes sentir empatía, que no debes tener este tipo de deseos porque eres una replicante. Así que hay que mantener eso dentro, mostrar control. Pero luego hay momentos... ¿Por qué estaría ella, en sus últimos días, tan decidida a completar una misión? Hay secretos. Secretos que no puede permitir que otros replicantes, otros humanos, vean, porque eso sería mostrar un lado terriblemente vulnerable de sí misma. Eso no solo la hundiría a ella, sino a todo el ecosistema. Todo el lugar es muy frágil en este momento porque los humanos quieren recuperar lo que hay allí y los replicantes quieren continuar, quizá ser más y evolucionar", concluye.
Blade Runner 2099 ya está disponible en Amazon Prime Video.

articles.title: 1Password breach leaked customer names and emails, but not passwords
articles.text:
1Password says a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident. It’s unclear how many users are affected.
1Password breach leaked customer names and emails, but not passwords
1Password says the security breach didn’t compromise its vaults, but didn’t mention how many customers were affected.
The password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers.
It also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to users to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess.
The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a new detection system for similar attacks. It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The company says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that users should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.

articles.title: Seagate's Black Friday HDD deals are some of the cheapest desktop drives
articles.text:
Black Friday discounts on Seagate's Expansion Desktop Hard Drive make it one of the cheapest of its kind, with discounts of up to 22% on higher storage capacities
Unbeatable prices for reliable, high-capacity external storage
Seagate's Expansion Desktop Hard Drive is a great pick for buyers who need a lot of storage for a cost-effective price. Backed by one of the biggest names in storage, this one comes with a two-year manufacturer's guarantee and Seagate's Rescue Data Recovery Services, plus a fresh new design compared with earlier models.
Now, Amazon has dropped the price of the 8TB hard drive to £217 (was £272) for Black Friday, with other discounts on the 4TB model, which is £145 (was £158), and the 20TB HDD, now priced at £522 (was £666).
The drive promises 120MB/s read speeds via a handy USB-C connection, but it's slightly more limited by its Micro-B USB connection on the hard drive's end, so it's ideal for home users who need capacity, not speed.

articles.title: Winbond Widens Edge AI Reach, Certifies NOR Flash
articles.text:
Winbond Electronics is betting that a little less customization will put its 3D-stacked memory architecture into a lot more designs, while expanding its 16-nm DRAM portfolio and adding security certification to NOR flash offerings.
The company’s new CUBE-Lite is a semi-custom memory offering derived from its Customized Ultra Bandwidth Elements (CUBE) platform, which debuted a few years ago. It aims to give edge AI designs CUBE’s bandwidth with lower non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs than a fully customized CUBE design.
“It’s still customized, but it’s more of a ‘standardized’ customized, if that’s not too much of a contradiction,” Brian Watson, marketing manager for Winbond’s customized memory solutions, said in a briefing with EE Times.
CUBE works best for workloads with low-to-medium density requirements but high bandwidth requirements, he said. Rather than replicate high-bandwidth memory’s combination of capacity and bandwidth, Winbond is targeting smaller working sets that still require rapid data movement. “It’s not trying to mimic HBM in terms of both density and bandwidth, but just the bandwidth.”
Watson offered on-device language translation in a wearable as a hypothetical example. The audio-processing working set might be relatively small, but responsiveness requires bandwidth. These types of devices are cost sensitive, he added. “You might not be able to amortize the NRE cost of a fully custom 3D-stacked memory architecture across the number of devices that you’re selling in the unit price of the device.”
CUBE-Lite delivers up to 8 GB/s of memory bandwidth at approximately 70 mW, and Winbond’s engineering data shows the simplified interface can reduce SoC controller power consumption by more than 10× compared with an LPDDR4X implementation.
A full CUBE design is tailored to each customer’s bandwidth, density, power, and SoC requirements. CUBE-Lite instead offers a menu of density and I/O options—Watson used 128, 256, and 512 I/Os as hypothetical examples. “It wouldn’t be fully customized, right, because you would have to select among the available options,” he said. CUBE-Lite also requires the customer to provide a memory controller.
Filling DRAM density gaps
Winbond is also expanding its 16-nm DRAM portfolio with 8-Gb LPDDR4 devices with an x16 interface, 16-Gb LPDDR4 with an x32 interface, and 16-Gb DDR4. The additions fill density gaps and give customers more options across product tiers.
The 16-Gb devices double per-device capacity compared with 8-Gb parts, potentially reducing component counts and board space. DDR4 targets include switches and server peripherals, while LPDDR4 applications include automotive systems, drones, and surveillance equipment. The new 16-Gb products are scheduled for availability by year-end 2026, with mass production planned for the second quarter of 2027.
Securing NOR flash with CRA
Separately, Winbond introduced a Cyber Resilience Act Conformance and Integration Kit for its TrustME W77Q Secure Flash family. The package combines hardware security, software, integration guidance, testing resources, and documentation to support manufacturers’ product-level compliance work.
In a briefing with EE Times, Nir Tasher, VP of technology for Winbond’s secure memory products, said many equipment suppliers lack the security expertise needed to translate regulatory requirements into implementations. Supplying silicon and a data sheet alone does not address that gap, he said.
The W77Q’s SESIP Level 2 certification can help manufacturers document component security, but it does not establish CRA conformity for the finished product, Tasher said.
Instead, the kit maps CRA requirements to Secure Flash features. It also includes sample code, a test suite to verify integration, and the written collateral needed for conformance documentation. “This is like a secret sauce,” Tasher said. “You add that to your system, and you are 90% of the way there.”
Those resources, together with documentation, allow customers to move through conformance work more efficiently, he said.
W77Q has achieved SESIP Level 2 certification, though Winbond notes that this alone doesn’t establish a finished product’s conformity with the CRA. Tasher said other regions, including the U.S. and Japan, could follow the EU’s regulatory approach.
Winbond to absorb Infineon memory business
The trio of product updates follows Winbond’s September agreement to acquire Infineon Technologies’ NOR Flash and F-RAM business in an all-cash transaction valued at $1.12 billion.
Winbond will operate the business as a standalone entity headquartered in Silicon Valley. Infineon will retain its SRAM, HYPERRAM, nvSRAM, and SONOS-based radiation-hardened memory products. Subject to regulatory approvals, the companies are targeting closing in the second half of 2027.
Neither Winbond nor Infineon was willing to discuss the transaction beyond the news release.

articles.title: Réseau Localiser, précision UWB : l'AirTag 2e génération est en promotion pour le Black Friday
articles.text:
Depuis sa première génération, l’AirTag s’est imposé comme la référence des traqueurs Bluetooth pour les utilisateurs d’iPhone. Cette deuxième mouture affine la formule sans la révolutionner : même format discret, même intégration transparente dans l’application Localiser, mais avec une puce U2 qui améliore la précision de localisation UWB, le son plus fort pour retrouver l’objet à l’oreille, et une meilleure résistance à l’eau. Face à lui, des alternatives existent, le Xiaomi Smart Tag peut se connecter à la fois à Apple Localiser et au réseau Find My Device de Google, ce qui lui vaut d’être régulièrement comparé à l’AirTag, mais aucune n’égale la fluidité du réseau Localiser d’Apple, fort de centaines de millions d’appareils. Pour le Black Friday, Joybuy le propose à 79,99 euros avec le code promo BFKOL10.
Les atouts de l’Apple AirTag 2e génération
- Réseau Apple Localiser, le plus dense du marché pour la localisation
- Puce U2 : précision UWB pour guider jusqu’à l’objet perdu
- Résistance à l’eau et à la poussière IP67
Sur Joybuy, l’AirTag 2e génération est affiché à 79,99 euros en appliquant le code promo BFKOL10 au moment du paiement.
Un format minimaliste qui s’intègre partout
L’AirTag 2e génération reprend le même boîtier rond et plat que son prédécesseur. Il tient dans la paume, pèse une vingtaine de grammes et se glisse dans une poche ou dans une housse accrochée à un sac. Apple n’a pas intégré de trou pour porte-clés, il faut acheter un accessoire séparé pour l’accrocher à un trousseau. C’est un point que Xiaomi a réglé sur son Smart Tag, qui livre un œillet d’emblée.
La résistance à l’eau et à la poussière est certifiée IP67 : une immersion jusqu’à un mètre pendant trente minutes. L’alimentation repose sur une pile CR2032, remplaçable sans outil, pour une autonomie annoncée d’environ un an. Pas de charge sans fil, pas de batterie intégrée rechargeable : il faut penser à changer la pile.
La précision UWB qui change vraiment quelque chose
Là où un Bluetooth classique vous dit « l’objet est dans cette pièce », l’AirTag 2e génération avec sa puce U2 vous guide directement jusqu’à lui, centimètre par centimètre, via la fonction Précision de recherche. L’iPhone affiche une flèche directionnelle et une distance en temps réel. C’est l’une des rares fonctions qui rend le traqueur réellement utile dans un appartement. Le son du haut-parleur intégré a aussi été renforcé par rapport à la première génération, ce qui facilite la localisation à l’oreille quand l’objet est enfoui sous une pile de vêtements. Le réseau Localiser, alimenté par des centaines de millions d’iPhone, iPad et Mac dans le monde, fait le reste : même à l’étranger, les chances de retrouver un bagage perdu sont nettement supérieures à celles qu’offrent les solutions concurrentes.

articles.title: I Played GTA 6 at "60 FPS"
articles.text:
One of the biggest issues with Grand Theft Auto 6 is that it runs at just 30 FPS on consoles. We recently explored why this is the case from some angles that aren't often discussed, and as a PC gamer used to playing games at frame rates above 60 FPS, I've found it a bit difficult to adjust to the game's relatively low frame rate. But over the weekend, I started seeing discussions online about a bizarre configuration that can be used to make GTA 6 run at 60 FPS, so to speak. Naturally, I was intrigued.
This configuration involves taking the 30 FPS GTA 6 output from a console like the PlayStation 5, routing it into a capture card connected to a separate PC, and then running 2x frame generation on that video input signal to produce a 60 FPS output. There are several applications that can be used to do this, but the one I've seen discussed most frequently is called Veyra.
Why this sounds like a terrible idea
When I first heard about this configuration, I thought it would be absolutely horrendous. And that's for a few reasons.
First, 30 to 60 FPS frame generation has generally been quite bad in my experience on PC. A game running at a low render rate tends to produce tons of visual artifacts when using frame generation, as the gap between frames is large, leaving the algorithm with more interpolation work to do. The shorter the gap between frames, the better frame generation tends to work, which is why I typically recommend a minimum render rate of 60 FPS.
Second, this type of frame generation doesn't have access to game data such as motion vectors or UI flags, so it's applying frame generation to the entire image every single time with little to no context. This makes the technique most similar to driver-based frame generation on PC, which delivers worse visual quality than frame generation integrated into games and is a feature I don't usually recommend.
Game data genuinely helps improve frame generation quality, especially when it comes to menus and UI elements, which will always be subject to interpolation with driver-based or video-based frame generation.
And third, one of the key reasons why 30 FPS sucks to play is the high levels of input lag relative to gaming at higher render rates. When you apply frame generation to a 30 FPS output, you increase latency due to the way frames are buffered, as well as the processing time of the frame generation algorithm itself. With this weird capture card method, you're adding even more latency on top of all that due to the time it takes for the capture card to process and display the incoming signal.
All of this makes the GTA 6 capture card method sound pretty bad: the potential for worse visual quality with tons of frame generation artifacts, and much higher input latency on top of what is already high latency from running at 30 FPS.
And yet, at least based on what I was seeing on social media, this technique was getting rave reviews, with some gamers saying it made GTA 6 "playable" for them. So I had to try it out.
Before getting into the setup process, it's worth touching on my personal experience playing GTA 6 at 30 FPS on the base PlayStation 5 as a predominantly PC gamer. I found it a bit harder than I expected to acclimatize to GTA 6 running at 30 FPS, with the biggest issue for me being the motion and display blur associated with running at a low frame rate...
With the default settings on a 4K OLED monitor, I found the game quite blurry during any sort of motion, an issue we discussed in our previous GTA 6 analysis.
Some of this was due to motion blur, which can be turned off or even increased in the settings. I found that turning off motion blur helped alleviate some of the blurriness, leaving me with display blur. But this also made the game choppier due to the low frame rate, and on an OLED monitor, you get another issue: judder.
As OLEDs have extremely fast response times, they're able to display each frame almost instantly. During panning motions, you get this juddering effect where objects quickly update their position and are then blurred somewhat by display persistence. On slower LCD monitors, this effect is reduced as response times are longer, effectively blurring away the judder to some degree.
I've seen some people suggest that turning up motion blur when using an OLED is better for reducing judder. In GTA 6, I found this made the game even blurrier and a bit nauseating due to the sheer amount of blur.
However, input latency wasn't a huge issue for me, mostly because GTA 6 is a fairly slow-paced game, with a lot of deliberate, slow, lifelike animations and a game engine that has never been optimized for fast inputs (looking at you, Red Dead Redemption 2).
It's obviously not as good as running PC games at a higher frame rate, but from an input latency perspective, I found the game playable. And when you engage with the world at a slower pace, avoiding huge camera pans or whips all the time, walking around, even driving at the speed limit, you don't end up seeing heaps of display blur all the time. The input latency is manageable enough, so in that sense, it is playable.
How to play GTA 6 at 60 FPS using Veyra
The good news for anyone wanting to try this 60 FPS conversion trick is that Veyra is a free and open-source application, so at least on the software side, there is no cost. You do, however, need a capture card connected to a reasonably capable PC.
When launching Veyra, select Capture Card. From here, you'll get a list of settings specific to capturing the game. Typically, you'll want to match the resolution to your monitor's resolution, in my case 4K, and then select either 30 or 60 FPS, depending on what your capture card supports. The most crucial setting is the pixel format: this should be set to NV12 if you plan on gaming in SDR, or P010 if you plan on gaming in HDR.
I own several different capture cards, including USB and PCIe models, and found that some combinations of resolution, frame rate, and pixel format aren't available simultaneously.
For example, on my Elgato 4K X over USB, capturing at 4K 60 FPS using P010 wasn't possible for whatever reason. I could only use NV12 at that resolution and frame rate, or drop down to 4K 30 FPS with P010. However, on an AVerMedia GC573 over PCIe, I could get everything working at the same time.
After selecting the pixel format, scroll down to the audio settings. Enable audio monitoring if you want the audio to route through your PC to whatever audio device you have connected.
Then, in the final section for format and picture, set the input color to HDR PQ if you want to use HDR. Otherwise, Auto is fine. I also used Auto for the other settings, although there is a minimum latency option that reduces buffering at the potential expense of dropped frames.
At this point, the capture card is configured, so you can hit Connect and Start. You should see the input from your console in the window, provided it's connected correctly to the HDMI IN port on the capture card. You don't need anything connected to the OUT port, as the output is routed through your graphics card to whatever display is connected to your PC.
However, at least on the PlayStation 5, you do need to disable HDCP in the console's settings. Head to Settings > System > HDMI > Enable HDCP and make sure this toggle is off.
It's also a good idea at this point to confirm everything is working as intended on the console side. Go to Screen and Video > Video Output and check the current video output signal. This should match the configuration you've selected in Veyra, and you'll want to confirm HDR is active if that's what you've set. If something doesn't look right, you may need to adjust either the console or Veyra settings.
The final major step is to enable frame generation. Using the tabs on the right, go to Frame Gen, enable the feature, and then under Frame Generation Method, choose NVIDIA VFG if you have an Nvidia GPU. I found VFG to work significantly better than the DLSS Frame Generation option, which produces way more artifacts. AMD GPU users should choose AMD FRC, though you can experiment with FSR FG as well.
I also chose to increase VFG quality to High, up from the default of Medium, and to enable strict frame pacing.
At the bottom of the settings, in the optical flow section, it's essential that you enable Remove duplicate frames and set it to 60 to 30 mode if you've configured the capture card to run at 60 FPS. As GTA 6 runs at just 30 FPS, there will be duplicate frames in a 60 FPS capture signal. You don't want those to be part of the frame generation process, otherwise it will look weird and run badly. I also enabled low latency mode but left the other settings at their defaults.
The last option you might want to consider is adjusting the audio delay if video and audio latency are mismatched. Veyra automatically applies some audio delay when enabling features like frame generation, but you can tweak this further in the settings.
Then, just click the full-screen button, and you're playing GTA 6 at "60 FPS" through a capture card and PC-based frame generation.
Further optimizations can be made in the GTA 6 settings themselves. I'd recommend turning off motion blur and setting both look and aim acceleration to the maximum. This makes inputs feel quicker and removes the game's motion blur from each frame, feeding the interpolation algorithm the cleanest image possible.
The surprisingly good 60 FPS experience
But is all this any good? Is GTA 6 actually more enjoyable to play through this weird system?
You might need some context for what I'm about to say. I don't like frame generation at low frame rates. I've tested frame generation extensively and consistently found 30 to 60 FPS to be a bad experience. I don't like that frame generation increases latency, I don't think it works particularly well without game integrations, and I'm highly sensitive to artifacts like flickering, boiling, and frame generation-related blending problems.
I typically only use it in some games to increase visual smoothness, especially when already rendering at a high frame rate in excess of 60 FPS. Despite all of this, despite my dislike of low frame rate frame generation on PC... I actually think this capture card method works.
I genuinely thought it would be terrible when I heard about it. I thought I would try it out and hate it, and maybe I'd even get a chance to poke fun at how bad it looks or works. But that's just not the case.
I can't quite believe how much I like the way this system enhances the GTA 6 experience. I'm actually a bit blown away.
For a better representation of image quality comparisons, check out the HUB video below:
What sealed it for me was running both options at the same time and switching between them. On my monitor, I had my PC connected over DisplayPort, running GTA 6 through Veyra at 60 FPS. On the HDMI input, I had the native game presentation at 30 FPS, using the passthrough output from the capture card.
I far preferred playing the game through Veyra at 60 FPS rather than natively at 30 FPS. In fact, every time I went back to the 30 FPS option, I was a bit stunned at how choppy and blurry it looked. When using this system, you do need to temper your expectations, though. This does not make GTA 6 play like a normal 60 FPS game on PC. There are artifacts, and there is an input delay problem that you simply don't get with proper, native 60 FPS gaming.
However, given there is currently no option to play GTA 6 at anything other than 30 FPS, I see this as more of an enhanced 30 FPS experience. Specifically, it makes the game significantly less blurry and less juddery on an OLED monitor, which makes it more enjoyable in my opinion.
In our previous analysis of the issues with 30 FPS gaming, we explained how low frame rates increase display persistence blur on sample-and-hold displays, by far the most common display type today. This makes 30 FPS look extremely blurry during any sort of motion.
Going up to 60 FPS is a significant improvement in clarity. It's not crystal clear or anything, but it doesn't immediately look like a blurry mess under the slightest camera movement. Provided you're delivering 60 frames per second to the monitor that actually look somewhat decent and have good clarity themselves, running at 60 FPS is a huge boost to motion clarity. There are additional benefits to smoothness, as there are simply more frames being presented to you, reducing choppiness.
What impressed me the most about using Veyra in this way is that the quality of frame interpolation is surprisingly good. It's not flawless, but it's generally free of obvious artifacts in a way that I haven't experienced before with 30 to 60 FPS video interpolation.
I've played around five hours of GTA 6 using this method and haven't experienced any huge, game-breaking artifacts or massive full-screen blur or warbling issues, as is common with other techniques. It's much better than TV-based frame smoothing, for example, which doesn't do a great job of preserving clarity and tends to blend frames together in a horrible, smeared way.
Part of this appears to be down to how Nvidia VFG works, especially on the High setting. Veyra reports that this frame generation system takes around 10ms to perform interpolation, which is much longer than you'd typically see from DLSS Frame Generation in a game. In Veyra, using DLSS Frame Generation instead of VFG drops the processing time to under 3ms. Essentially, VFG takes over three times as long to compute, and it's specifically tuned for video input.
So with Veyra producing decent frame interpolation, you get a genuine reduction in display persistence blur from running at 60 FPS, which makes the entire game look clearer in motion. This significantly improves one of the biggest issues with GTA 6 at 30 FPS, and it's this benefit that keeps me using Veyra for my GTA 6 gaming.
Of course, there are issues. Frame interpolation is not perfect, so there are going to be artifacts at times. I found VFG on the High setting tended to do a decent job of keeping the UI intact without obvious warbling or flickering artifacts, and even in menus or on the map, it held up well enough.
For a better representation of image quality comparisons, check out the HUB video below:
But there are limits. Occasionally, the frame generation system will produce artifacts on UI elements, such as the tracking markers on screen or when text animates in or out of the frame. It can also struggle with some types of movement, such as when complicated patterns or textures move or transform significantly between frames.
In a PC game, these artifacts would probably be a deal-breaker. You'd be better off lowering settings to get the game running above 60 FPS. This would reduce display blur in the same way as frame generation, but it would do so without interpolation artifacts and with even better motion quality. But with GTA 6, there's no "lowering the settings" option. So it's a question of whether the high levels of blur at 30 FPS or some artifacts from frame generation at 60 FPS make for a better experience. To me, 60 FPS with artifacts wins out whenever I try both options.
In-game artifacts are a bit worse when using Veyra's NVIDIA VFG option set to Medium. I found this mode struggled more with the UI and tended to produce warbling around text where VFG High would not. Medium is about twice as fast at generating frames and may be required on PCs with fewer resources.
I also found that the overall quality of each frame, even the real frames, is reduced slightly through the capture card method compared to sending the game natively to the display. There's a very faint line pattern that I'm noticing through Veyra. This might just be down to how the capture card actually captures each frame, I'm not entirely sure, but it's very slight and, again, not a deal-breaker compared to running at 30 FPS with increased blur.
Another factor worth considering when discussing frame generation artifacts is that GTA 6 already has quite a few visual artifacts of its own, especially when playing on the base PS5.
The upscaling method is awful in my opinion. It does a terrible job of reconstructing fine detail, it's quite blurry, and there are lots of sizzling and ghosting issues visible throughout the game. There is also a lot of noise due to the use of ray-traced lighting. The ray count in this game must be quite low, and the denoising solution doesn't appear to be particularly high quality, so many surfaces exhibit grain, pixelation, boiling, and so on in motion.
The overall visual fidelity is very impressive despite these artifacts and flaws, especially considering the relatively slow console hardware it's running on, so I fully understand why there are issues. It's not a PC game, and we can't expect a PC-like experience where these issues could be addressed with faster hardware.
But the good news is that, given there are already quite a few artifacts in the game, the frame generation artifacts introduced by Veyra don't stand out nearly as much as they otherwise might in a game with a cleaner, more artifact-free image. I find the sizzling due to upscaling much more noticeable during general gameplay than interpolation artifacts. And that sizzling is present no matter what. It's part of the native 30 FPS experience.
The cost of 60 FPS: Input latency
What about latency? This is the other major part of the equation, as running the game through a capture card and then applying frame generation will obviously increase latency. I tested this, and at least on my setup, the overall latency increase was around 35ms. This is made up of around 25ms of capture latency and around 10ms of frame generation latency.
Note that this is measured to the first point of change on screen, which in the case of frame generation will be an interpolated frame. Measuring latency with frame generation is always a bit different, so keep in mind there's another 17ms to account for if we're measuring real-frame-to-real-frame latency at 60 FPS.
At face value, this sounds like a noticeable latency increase. And it would be absolutely disastrous for PC gaming, where at decent frame rates in single-player titles, you typically see somewhere between 30 and 40ms of latency. Using a capture card and running frame generation would therefore roughly double the latency of a typical PC game, making it a pretty stupid solution that would feel awful.
The funny thing about GTA 6, though, is that this game has extremely high input latency to begin with.
On my monitor, running the game natively over HDMI without Veyra at all, I recorded approximately 160ms of input lag for most actions I attempted. This means the normal 30 FPS experience is pretty sluggish to begin with. I found getting used to the shooting mechanics quite difficult as a result, but once you get used to it, it's playable.
On top of this, GTA 6 is just a slow game in general. Actions are accompanied by lifelike animations that take time, there's lots of slower-paced gameplay, and it isn't really a game where you feel like you have instant control over the characters.
With Veyra frame generation added on top, latency in my configuration was around 190 to 200ms. That's a lot of lag, but relative to the 160ms baseline, the increase isn't that bad. We're already in the "really bad input lag" zone, so adding another 30-40ms isn't necessarily a deal-breaker. It amounts to roughly a 20-25% increase, which is not trivial, but it's not a doubling of latency like you'd see if the game was running with just 30-40ms of native latency.
I can tell that frame generation is adding a bit of latency when playing GTA 6, but it's not a deal-breaker for me because the game already has high latency. I was already having to adapt to the high-latency experience at 30 FPS, so it's much the same thing at 60 FPS with Veyra. After a while, I didn't really notice the difference, though it took some time to dial in the faster skills in the game, like driving and shooting.
As with everything else we've discussed, this comes down to a trade-off. Is GTA 6 a better experience at 30 FPS with heavy display blur and 160ms of latency, or is it better at 60 FPS with less display blur, somewhat more artifacts, and up to 200ms of latency?
To me, the reduction in blur from playing at 60 FPS is more than enough to offset the increases in artifacts and latency, so I prefer playing GTA 6 using the Veyra frame generation method. This is not going to be a low-latency, artifact-free experience no matter which path I choose, so I'm basically willing to concede some latency in a quest to fix display blur. Other gamers who are more latency-sensitive will disagree, and the Veyra method will be an even worse experience for them.
Is it worth the trouble?
Would I recommend gamers use Veyra to play Grand Theft Auto 6? As I've said, I prefer playing the game this way, and when switching back and forth between native 30 FPS and 60 FPS via Veyra, I consistently prefer the latter. However, I don't expect that will apply to everyone, especially those who prioritize latency above everything else.
If you don't mind the display blur and lack of visual smoothness but are concerned about the latency side of things, you should probably stay away from Veyra.
If you happen to own a capture card already and a PC that's capable of running Veyra (which should be most gaming PCs), I think it's worth giving it a try just to see which option you prefer. It's also easy to set up a quick comparison for yourself, with one display input connected to your PC running Veyra, and another connected to the HDMI passthrough from the console. That way, you can switch back and forth and decide for yourself which way you want to play.
If you don't own a capture card, I'm on the fence as to whether I'd recommend investing in one specifically to play GTA 6 this way. A high-quality PCIe capture card capable of 4K with HDR will set you back over $150, which is an investment compared to simply waiting for the game to come to PC. And there's no guarantee you'll even like playing through Veyra.
With that said, there are USB capture cards and models that are only capable of 1080p that are much cheaper, provided you don't need the game running at the highest resolution.
If you do want to buy a higher-end capture card, I'd recommend one from AVerMedia. I've tried a number of capture cards from different brands, and AVerMedia's have been by far the most reliable in my experience. I've used the GC573 for all my Veyra testing here and regularly use a GC553G2 for capturing footage for Hardware Unboxed videos. Unfortunately, my experience with Elgato cards hasn't been nearly as positive.
Ultimately, Veyra isn't a substitute for running GTA 6 at a native 60 FPS, and I still stand by my usual recommendations when it comes to frame generation on PC. But in this particular scenario, where there is no option to increase the game's render rate, the trade-offs make surprisingly good sense. I went into this experiment expecting to find yet another example of why frame generation at 30 FPS is a terrible idea. Instead, I ended up finding my preferred way to play GTA 6, at least until the PC version arrives.

articles.title: Google Messages pourrait adopter une des meilleures fonctions d’iMessage
articles.text:
Après avoir changé sa manière de répondre aux messages, Google Messages s’attaque aux conversations. Suivre plusieurs sujets en même temps dans une conversation n’est pas toujours évident. En effet, Google Messages se contente aujourd’hui d’accrocher un aperçu du message initial au-dessus de chaque réponse. Si cette méthode est suffisante pour une réponse isolée, elle devient vite brouillonne pour une longue discussion. Mais en fouillant dans le code de la dernière version de l’application, on remarque un nouveau fil de discussion plus structuré, aussi bien dans les conversations privées que dans les messages RCS.
Suivre plus facilement les fils de discussions sur Google Messages
Sur l’interface de test qu’ont réussi à débloquer nos confrères d’Android Authority, on peut observer que les conversations sont mieux organisées, et donc tout de suite plus lisibles, grâce à des connecteurs graphiques très précis. Une ligne verticale sur la gauche relie désormais le message de départ à sa réponse. Dès qu’une conversation s’allonge ou compte au moins deux réponses, cette même ligne intègre une boucle pour marquer visuellement le fil de discussion actif. Cela fonctionne aussi bien pour les messages texte que pour les émojis ou les photos.
Source : Android Authority
Avec cette mise en page, les membres d’une conversation à plusieurs pourraient donc basculer d’un sujet à un autre sans mélanger les réponses. On note également que tout l’historique d’un sous-échange reste attaché à son point d’origine, ce qui permet de remonter le fil si nécessaire.
Lire une conversation sans distraction
Si de nouveaux messages sans rapport viennent s’intercaler dans une discussion, l’application affiche un compteur sous le message initial. En appuyant dessus, une fenêtre dédiée s’ouvre et floute l’arrière-plan de la conversation générale. Cela permet d’isoler les messages rattachés au fil de discussion que vous avez choisis et ainsi de rattraper une conversation que vous avez manquée sans devoir tout faire défiler.
Source : Android Authority
Pour répondre dans ce « sous-espace », une zone de saisie dédiée « Répondre dans le fil » s’affiche au bas de l’écran. Pour sortir de ce mode, il faut simplement toucher la zone floutée ou appuyer sur la croix située en haut à gauche. La fonctionnalité n’est toujours pas déployée sur Google Messages, mais semble malgré tout bien avancée. Reste maintenant à voir quand Google se décidera à la déployer.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: More Pentests Without More Pentesters: Where AI Safely Helps
articles.text:
Demand for penetration testing keeps rising, be it due to DORA threat-led testing, NIS2, or customer security questionnaires. However, supply often cannot keep up.
Experienced testers are scarce, take months to hire and train, and every one of them spends part of each engagement on work that is not testing. For a company that sells hours, that unbillable part is the margin.
This article shows how to measure it, which parts AI can take over, and how to do that without sending client vulnerabilities to someone else's servers.
Step 1: Measure where an engagement's hours go
Most companies track billable testing time and lack a number for the rest. If you tag the last ten engagements by phase, the picture usually changes:
| Phase | What to count | Share of hours | 
|---|---|---|
| Scoping and kickoff | Calls, scope documents, access setup | 8% | 
| Testing | Recon, exploitation, validation | 50% | 
| Documentation | Writing findings, screenshots, formatting | 22% | 
| Review | Senior QA, rework, client comments | 8% | 
| Delivery and retest | Report handover, status questions, retest | 12% | 
Two ratios matter: documentation plus review as a share of testing time, and calendar days from last testing day to report delivery. The first sums up to the hidden cost, but only the second is what clients feel.
Step 2: Decide what AI should and should not do
The tasks that suit a language model are the ones where the tester already knows the answer and needs it written down:
- Drafting finding text from tester notes, using your own vulnerability library as the template, so tone and structure stay yours.
- Normalizing and de-duplicating scanner output from Burp, Nessus, Nuclei and similar tools into one set of draft findings.
- Consistency review: missing remediation, severity that does not match the CVSS vector, the same issue worded three ways.
- Executive summary drafts, built from the validated findings and then edited.
It will be helpful to decide beforehand in what capacity to keep humans on severity decisions, exploit validation and anything the client will rely on as a statement of fact.
A model that confidently describes and is set to run an exploit chain that nobody verified can be is worse than no help.
Run More Pentests With the Same Team, Using AI That Stays In-House
PentestPad covers the whole engagement, from scoping and scanner imports to findings, client delivery and retests.
Its AI can run against a self-hosted LLM inside your own network.
Book a Demo
Step 3: A reference workflow
- Import scanner output and tester notes into one project as draft findings.
- Pull in matching entries from your reusable vulnerability library.
- Let the model rewrite each draft in your house style. The tester edits and approves.
- Attach evidence to the finding at the time of capture.
- Senior reviewer works through comments on the report itself, not email.
- Export the branded report (DOCX or PDF) or deliver it through a client portal.
- Track remediation and retest status on the same findings.
If an AI agent is part of the process, give it a defined interface rather than a free hand. A typed tool interface (for example MCP) lets an agent create findings or fetch a project while permissions, audit and the data boundary stay in the platform.
Three numbers can be tracked:
- Documentation-plus-review hours as a percentage of testing hours.
- Days from last testing day to delivery.
- Rework rounds per report.
If the first two fall and the third does not rise, the change is working.
Doing this in practice
One way to do this in practice is by using PentestPad.
It’s is a pentest reporting and project-management platform designed around this workflow: 20+ imports (Burp Suite, Nessus, Qualys, Nuclei, OpenVAS, CSV, JSON), reusable vulnerability templates, a CVSS calculator, custom branded DOCX/PDF/XLSX reports, a white-label client portal, an AI writing assistant that can run against your own self-hosted LLM, an MCP server for agents, and a choice of EU cloud or full self-hosting.
| Area | Detail | 
| Deployment | Managed EU cloud, or fully self-hosted including air-gapped, on every plan | 
| AI | Hosted, or pointed at a self-hosted LLM in your own network | 
| Agent tooling | MCP server, plus a CLI agent for macOS, Linux and Windows | 
| Compliance | EU-based entity, GDPR, ISO 27001 certified | 
| Export | DOCX, PDF, XLSX and API | 
| Integrations | Two-way Jira sync, imports from Burp Suite, Nessus, Qualys, Nuclei, OpenVAS, CSV and JSON, REST API, MCP | 
Built for agents as well as people
PentestPad is built to be driven by software as well as by a person at a keyboard, and the model doing the driving can sit inside your own network.
The writing assistant works from what a tester already has. Hand it scanner output, a Burp finding, a screenshot or a log file, attach the evidence, and it returns a structured finding written to the instructions your organization has defined, so the draft arrives in your format rather than a generic one.
PentestPad is the knowledge base, a local model does the reasoning, and a terminal harness is wired to both.
Access to the context of the tested environment greatly helps PentestPad outperform other generic automated vulnerability detection tools.
The rest of the platform at a glance
A short tour of what else is in PentestPad, for readers who want the full picture:
- Reporting. Findings are added directly from terminal to the PentestPad platform. Custom branded templates, DOCX, PDF and XLSX export, encrypted PDFs with a password you set, and a built-in CVSS calculator.
- Proposal management with project scoping.
- Jira sync. A two-way Jira sync, so a finding becomes a ticket with its reproduction steps and priority, and when a developer marks it done the finding moves to ready for retest, and back to open if the retest fails.
- Findings. Reusable vulnerability templates, with evidence attached to each finding when you capture it.
- Interoperability. CSV and JSON exports, and the 20-plus imports from tools such as Burp Suite, Nessus, Qualys, Nuclei and OpenVAS.
- Project management. Engagements, findings and retests in one place, which the company says cuts project-management overhead by around 60%.
- Client portal. White-labelled with your logo, colours and domain, and a 2FA screen. Clients see only their own findings.
