articles.title: Four SA students build fintech to fix bursary pay problems
articles.text:
Four university students have experienced the frustrations of accessing bursary money firsthand. Now, they are building CampusFit, a fintech platform that aims to change how students access, manage and track their allowances. PHATHISANI MOYO writes.
Imagine standing at a supermarket till on a Friday with a basket of groceries, only to discover that your allowance has not cleared, leaving you stranded until Monday.
It is a frustration Brian Mbana, co-founder of student fintech platform CampusFit, says many university students know all too well. Across South Africa, receiving a bursary allowance rarely guarantees immediate access to the funds. Delays in transferring disbursements into bank accounts often leave students borrowing money for groceries or queuing at retailers to withdraw cash.
Mbana, 24, and his co-founders—Aaron Matsemela, 21; Cliff Kaela, 21; and Simanye Sobekwa, 23—are building CampusFit to solve a problem they have personally experienced.
The four founders want to address what they call the “mailbox effect”, where money enters an account only to be withdrawn almost immediately because it offers little convenience for everyday transactions.
The issue is particularly acute in South Africa’s student funding ecosystem, where receiving financial support and accessing it when needed are not always the same thing. The National Student Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS) (NSFAS) has faced recurring challenges with allowance payments and its disbursement model, highlighting the administrative complexities students can encounter.
For four founders still navigating university themselves, CampusFit is an attempt to turn those frustrations into financial infrastructure. But building a product that works for students and the institutions funding them will require more than a promising idea.
From a university hackathon to a fintech idea
CampusFit took shape at a hackathon in East London, the Eastern Cape’s second-largest city, where the four founders met after being assigned to the same team. Challenged to develop a solution to a financial services problem, they focused on students and the disconnect between receiving money and being able to use it conveniently.
“We realised that students have a similar relationship with their accounts, particularly when it comes to NSFAS funding. As soon as money enters their wallets, many students withdraw it and take it to supermarkets such as Boxer and Shoprite,” Sobekwa told TechCabal in an interview on Saturday.
CampusFit wants to change that behaviour by making digital financial services more useful to students. Its proposed platform includes instant peer-to-peer transfers, budgeting tools and a unified dashboard that allows users to connect their bank accounts and view transactions in one place.
Matsemela believes the idea is rooted in his own experience with student funding. Having recently received a bursary, he encountered delays and uncertainty when accessing his money through Intellimali, a student allowance management platform. He said students also turn to social media to share complaints about payment delays and difficulties accessing their allowances.
“I hold three bank accounts. Having a platform that allows me to link all my accounts in one place and view transactions from all those different accounts would be very helpful,” he said.
The balance between financial oversight and privacy
CampusFit emerges amid growing scrutiny over how students spend educational allowances. NSFAS and the National Gambling Board recently joined forces to curb student gambling following reports that recipients were using their allowances to bet online.
While the founders see an opportunity to give both students and bursary providers clearer visibility into spending, they stress that any form of financial oversight must respect students’ privacy.
That concern has shaped the team’s approach to regulation. Kaela said the founders had considered the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) and other regulatory requirements from the outset. The team is also pursuing a system operator licence, which they say is necessary for the platform’s intended payment activities.
“We are not simply holding people’s data. We are also enabling transactions, and there are specific licences involved in that process,” Kaela said.
The regulatory process is part of the groundwork the founders must complete before taking the platform to market and pursuing partnerships with financial institutions and funding providers.
Turning an MVP into a business
The founders have developed a minimum viable product (MVP) and expect to begin onboarding students in the coming months. They are part of the Genesis Block cohort, a fintech startup incubation programme backed by FNB and the University of Cape Town Financial Innovation Hub. The programme provides mentorship and exposure to the financial services industry.
Mbana’s motivation remains close to home. He wants CampusFit to be built around the everyday difficulties students face, rather than assumptions about how they manage their money.
“Imagine going to buy groceries on a Friday, only to discover at the till that you cannot access your money because there is no cash available. You then have to wait until after the weekend to get your money,” he said.
The founders say their immediate challenge is proving that students will use the platform and that its technology can support a growing user base. They are building in backups and using containerisation to improve reliability, while exploring partnerships that could drive expansion.
Their ambition is to build South Africa’s leading student financial wellness platform. That will mean earning students’ trust, meeting regulatory requirements and persuading financial institutions that the model can work at scale.
“We want students to have more control over their money, rather than spending their time figuring out how to access it,” Sobekwa said.

articles.title: Cavó un estanque de 60 cm en el jardín y en pocas semanas aparecieron puestas de huevos de rana: de césped inútil a vivero
articles.text:
Cada primavera, el agua de deshielo recorría un trozo de césped de la finca de Stefano Ianiro y seguía su camino hacia la cuneta de la carretera. En 2024 aprovechó esta situación para crear una charca. En la parte baja de la finca cavó una depresión (que tiene unos 60 cm de profundidad en el punto más bajo) que se llenaba de agua. Quería ofrecer un espacio para la reproducción de anfibios.
En las primeras semanas (la orilla aún estaba casi pelada) llegaron las ranas de bosque. En el vídeo de la creación de la charca, comenta cómo en los primeros días en que llegaron las primeras ranas, él se alejó. Al volver a acercarse, calculó que había unas cinco puestas. También había puesto algunas ramas en el agua para que pudieran adherir los huevos y había tirado hojas secas para que tuvieran algún refugio.
Una charca pensada para secarse
Hay algunas diferencias entre esta charca y el estanque de truchas. Bajo el agua está la diferencia. En el estanque superior había truchas. Podían comerse a los renacuajos. El inferior ofrecía un espacio sin peces para que las ranas pudieran criar.
Las charcas temporales de primavera suelen llenarse con agua de lluvia y deshielo. Durante parte del año están secas. Como el agua desaparece de manera periódica, no pueden establecerse peces. Los anfibios sí precisan que la charca permanezca cierto tiempo.
El objetivo de Ianiro era que durase hasta agosto. Además, en primavera se calienta antes el agua poco profunda. Esto puede favorecer el desarrollo de las larvas. Al repasar ese primer verano, comentó cómo hubo momentos en que la charca estuvo a punto de secarse totalmente. Sin embargo, como hubo fuertes lluvias, se volvió a llenar.
Lo que aporta una charca pequeña
El potencial de estos espacios se ha visto en otro caso. En 2017 se publicó un estudio sobre 54 charcas formadas en cráteres de un bombardeo (de la Segunda Guerra Mundial) en Hungría. Juntas ofrecían un refugio para especies que también habitan en humedales naturales amenazados. A veces, el trabajo de recuperación de hábitats para la fauna pasa por aprovechar elementos que están presentes en el terreno, como hizo en su finca Ianiro aprovechando la escorrentía.
Entre las amenazas que recoge la evaluación global de anfibios (publicada en 2023) están la pérdida de hábitat, las enfermedades y el cambio climático. En este estudio se estimó que un 40,7 % de las especies de anfibios están amenazadas de extinción. En una red de pequeños humedales, cada charca puede suponer un espacio adicional de cría. En el caso de la finca de Ianiro, fue un trozo de césped por el que antes pasaba el agua hacia la cuneta.

articles.title: Ground Truth: CISO Matt Martin on Building a Real Security Program Without an Enterprise Budget
articles.text:
A CISO who traded enterprise budgets for higher ed on what “creativity within constraints” really means, and the one habit worth stealing from how he leads.
I have known Matt Martin for a few years, and the first thing I tell anyone about him has nothing to do with security. It is that he treats the work as a way to serve other people. I first knew Matt as the security leader who spends his own time flying to Ghana and Uganda to teach executives and students how to protect themselves. That instinct, more than any tool or certification, explains how he runs a security program.
Matt spent two decades running security organizations in financial services, including at LPL Financial, with an enterprise budget and any tool he needed. A few years ago he made a deliberate choice to take on higher ed instead, because he wanted to prove he could build a resilient security program under real constraints. Today he is the Chief Information Security and Privacy Officer at Western Carolina University.
I asked Matt to share his journey from a conference in Accra to a university in the mountains of North Carolina. His story is really about doing more with less, and right now, that is all of us.
Q. You have built real social impact into your career, sharing security knowledge and consultancy with underserved communities. How did that begin?
A. It started unexpectedly. After two decades in financial services I decided to go out on my own. The whole point was to support small and medium organizations, especially in developing countries, that could not afford the security consultancy they needed. I heard about the GC3B conference in Accra, Ghana, which was about building cyber resiliency in developing countries. They only accepted companies, so I applied as the LLC I had just started, and a few weeks later I received a letter from the government of Ghana inviting me.
I flew over not knowing a single person. The first day had a light schedule, so I hired a tour guide and he took me to see Elmina Castle and the Door of No Return. That one day changed my life. Seeing that side of the story of humanity as an adult, after growing up in the American South, connected so much for me about how tied together we all are. I carried that into every meeting at the conference.
Afterwards I developed a partnership with a nonprofit called Africa Digital Rights Hub, and it has since taken me back to run masterclasses for executives and students in Ghana and Uganda. Part of the reason Western Carolina appealed to me was that they wanted to help me expand that work.
Q. You had about three weeks between that invitation from the Ghanaian government and actually getting on the plane. What was it like to just drop everything and go?
A. It was a scramble. Three weeks to get all my immunizations, book everything, and fly to Ghana. Actually, my yellow fever vaccine wasn’t fully effective by the time I landed, I was a couple of days short, so I had to talk my way through the medical booth in the airport before I could even clear immigration.
Funny enough, it’s risk acceptance in real life. I knew my control wasn’t operating effectively yet, I understood the exposure, and I decided to go anyway. That’s the same type of call we make in security every day.
Q. I’ve heard you say that security and GRC have become an elite sport. Job postings demand degrees and a wall of certifications before you can apply, but attackers have none of them. You are largely self-taught. What has that taught you about who belongs in this field?
A. I started with a history degree, and some of the best security people I know do not have a security degree either. Think how this community started. In the beginning you couldn’t go get a degree in cybersecurity, it was creative people figuring it out as they went. There are brilliant people all over the world who could do this work and simply haven’t had the opportunity. That is why the teaching matters so much to me. There is a real chance to democratize security education and take down some of the barriers the industry has put up.
Q. You have a phrase for how you think about the work now, “creativity within constraints.” When you started in the new context of higher ed, what did you assume your constraints would be?
A. I assumed it would be budget. In financial services, I could get almost anything as long as it was reasonable. Budgets are definitely tight in higher ed, but it was not my number one problem. I needed to learn the environment.
A university has done things a certain way for a long time, knowledge is meant to be open and shared, and the place can feel like family. Once I really understood the environment, I could get creative and start designing security that worked with the culture instead of against it.
Q. You’ve been candid with me that you got the first few months wrong, and I think that honesty helps other leaders even more than sharing wins. What happened?
A. I went in thinking I already knew how everything should work, and I started fixing things. I probably pushed harder than I should have before I understood the place. What I should have done was go in to learn, listen more than I talked, and document what I found before I tried to solve anything. Overseeing the security program at a large company does not mean you know how to build one everywhere.
Q. So with a small team and a tight budget, how do you actually run a real program? Walk me through the mechanics.
A. It starts with risk, not compliance. If you do risk well, compliance comes almost for free, because it tells you what you need to do and in what order. So I built a real risk register. I went to the technology leaders first and asked what was broken and what was holding them back, wrote it all down, and mapped it to a framework.
Then the honest problem is capacity. I cannot hire a team of analysts to test every control or spend weeks each year on a self-assessment. Self-attestation is not enough on its own. Anyone who has run a program knows that asking whether a control works can get you different answers depending on who you ask, so I needed real evidence, not opinions. The only way to get that at scale was to embrace automation and continuous monitoring.
Q. You have now lived on both sides. What would you take from higher ed back into a big enterprise?
A. Fiscal discipline, honestly. The habit of asking “do we really need this, or is it a nice-to-have,” and whether a given feature is three million dollars better than what we already have. In large enterprises you also end up with people inserting themselves into processes to justify a role, and everything takes longer. But look, every company of every size has something it could do better. I’ve really embraced how scarcity forces you to be more efficient.
Q. How can you judge whether someone will make a good CISO?
A. This one question tells me what I need to know: Do you know how your company makes money? Can you actually tell me how your organization makes money, or in a university, how the institution succeeds? Once you understand that, you can prioritize risk in a way that matters to the business. If you cannot answer it, you are going to protect the wrong things.
Q. What kind of CISO actually thrives in a place like higher ed?
A. You have to want to get your hands dirty. If you just want to run a team of forty and just go to meetings, it will not work, because your team is smaller and you will be doing some of the work yourself. You have to be creative enough to build things that are not the industry standard. And most of all, you have to see the business-enablement side of security, not only the technical side. You are engaging with the colleges, the chancellor, even the athletics department, and your job is to enable them. If you come in 100% security or bust, you will not last long in higher ed.
Q. Matt, thank you for this. What is on your radar right now? Is there anything you are most excited to build next?
A. Giving students a real place to learn. I want more working CISOs to share with students what the career actually looks like. Where I would love to take it is a hands-on cybersecurity lab on campus, for students to get real-world practice. I would also love to keep building the connections with universities in Africa, so students can learn from each other in both directions.
Ground truth for your program
Matt’s whole approach is a posture, not a tactic. He leads as a teacher and a collaborator, and treats security as a way to help organizations succeed rather than a roadblock.
The lesson I would take to any team, at any budget: name your real constraint before you invest against the wrong one. Matt walked in certain it was budget, and it turned out to be understanding the environment. Assume it’s money and you pour your limited resources into tools, when the real problem was one money could not solve. Get the constraint right, though, and every dollar and every control is aimed at a real business objective, which is what makes a program effective at any size.
So before your next purchase or project, ask yourself two questions: What do I actually believe my top constraint is, and how do I know? And am I about to spend against it, or around it?

articles.title: Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts
articles.text:
The Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work. Announced on 12 November 2026, the release also stabilises the core of the custom allocator API, introduces a DropGuard helper, and gives Cargo opt-in dependency cooldowns and warnings for unused dependencies.
The headline is the stabilisation of !, the canonical uninhabited type for computations that never return a value, such as panic!(), return or an endless loop. Although functions have long used it as a return type, naming it elsewhere, for instance writing Result<T, !> to describe an operation that cannot fail, took ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts to land. The release also makes std::convert::Infallible an alias for !, which is what the type was always intended to be, so existing APIs using Infallible now accept ! transparently.
To make that alias work, the team shipped a small breaking change for the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, flipping the never-type fallback from () to ! and matching behaviour already introduced in Rust 2024. The release notes describe the impact as largely unnoticeable but warn that more code may be flagged as unreachable. Developers hitting issues on upgrade are advised to update dependencies first, since fixes for widely used crates have already been published.
The core of the long-awaited allocator_api is also now stable, letting library authors define custom allocators used with Vec and Box through the new Allocator trait. This forms the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. Critics on the internals forum have argued that Rust still lacks Zig's granular control over allocation because the current design cannot support inline storage, with moves invalidating internal pointers, but the stabilised core is seen as a workable starting point for broader collections support.
On the Hacker News release post, one user noted that some of the changes weren’t mentioned in the blog post for the release:
This release is so big that multiple useful stabilized API aren't event mentioned in the blog post like:
- bool::toggle() https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/primitive.bool.html#met...
- Box::map() https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#m...
- str::trim_prefix(), str::trim_suffix, Path::trim_prefix()
The new global-min-publish-age setting holds back newly published versions by a configurable window, an opt-in defence against malicious crate releases:
[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"
On Hacker News, developer woodruffw argued cooldowns need to coexist with immediate security patching:
You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down,
and
you should immediately patch security advisories.
One of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.
ImportStatic found on the beta that cargo install ignores the setting entirely and that an update could even downgrade a forced security fix, something the release notes also flag as a known caveat. The approach sits alongside GitHub's Dependabot cooldown protection but builds the age check into dependency resolution itself.
Other notable additions include core::mem::DropGuard for running a closure on every exit path, std::mem::conjure_zst for zero-sized types in unsafe code, plus smaller ergonomic wins such as bool::toggle, str::trim_prefix, str::trim_suffix and Box::map.
Upgrading uses rustup update stable; Rust 1.99 is no longer supported, and 1.101 follows the six-week cadence around 24 December 2026.
Rust is an open-source systems programming language maintained by the Rust Foundation and a global community, designed to empower developers to build reliable and efficient software through strong type safety, memory safety guarantees without a garbage collector, and a mature package ecosystem through Cargo.

articles.title: Un emprendedor argentino fue reconocido por el príncipe Guillermo de Gales por su tecnología para detectar incendios forestales
articles.text:
Franco Rodríguez Viau creó Satellites on Fire, una empresa argentina que detecta incendios forestales con inteligencia artificial e imágenes satelitales térmicas. El sistema opera en 21 países, alerta a brigadistas por WhatsApp y busca reducir el tiempo de respuesta ante los focos de fuego. La iniciativa fue reconocida por el príncipe Guillermo de Gales al quedar entre los 15 finalistas del Earthshot Prize 2026, el premio ambiental que él creó.
Rodríguez Viau fundó el proyecto junto a Joaquín y Ulises, dos compañeros de escuela. Los tres comenzaron a trabajar en la iniciativa cuando tenían 16 años, tras los incendios de Córdoba de 2020.
El emprendedor argentino explicó en Infobae Al Amanecer que familiares y amigos perdieron sus viviendas durante esa crisis. Esa experiencia los llevó a hablar con bomberos y brigadistas para conocer las dificultades que enfrentan ante los incendios forestales.
Satellites on Fire analiza imágenes térmicas y busca diferencias de temperatura que puedan indicar la presencia de un foco. Luego, envía una alerta con la ubicación a organizaciones que tienen capacidad para actuar.
Cómo detecta incendios Satellites on Fire
Rodríguez Viau explicó que el sistema procesa información de 13 satélites cada cinco minutos. La plataforma identifica cambios térmicos en zonas rurales, forestales o alejadas de centros urbanos.
“Si acá hacen 500 grados y al lado hacen 30 grados, acá posiblemente pase un incendio”, ejemplificó Rodríguez Viau. Esa variación puede responder a un incendio o a otra fuente de calor.
La empresa analiza esas señales con un modelo propio de inteligencia artificial. El sistema busca mejorar la precisión y reducir el tiempo que requieren otros mecanismos de detección.
Según Rodríguez Viau, Satellites on Fire detecta incendios, en promedio, 35 minutos antes que uno de los sistemas más utilizados de la NASA. También afirmó que algunos casos mostraron alertas hasta dos horas antes.
La plataforma muestra la evolución de los focos de calor y estima su posible propagación durante las horas posteriores. Esa información llega por WhatsApp a brigadistas, gobiernos, parques nacionales, empresas y otras organizaciones.
Alertas para brigadistas, gobiernos y comunidades
Rodríguez Viau contó el caso de un parque nacional argentino donde un incendio comenzó cerca de viviendas a las 15.20. Satellites on Fire detectó el foco 17 minutos después de su inicio.
La empresa envió una alerta por WhatsApp con un enlace a Google Maps. El sistema de la NASA identificó ese mismo foco dos horas más tarde, según el fundador.
El emprendedor sostuvo que una alerta temprana no resuelve por sí sola un incendio forestal. Para controlar el fuego, señaló, se necesitan tareas de prevención, detección, monitoreo y combate.
“Si mandamos una alerta, pero no hay nadie que vaya a atacarla a tiempo, el incendio se va a propagar”, afirmó. La herramienta depende de la capacidad de respuesta de cada organización.
La plataforma trabaja con empresas forestales y agrícolas, parques nacionales, gobiernos y comunidades indígenas. El servicio cobra una tarifa anual según la cantidad de hectáreas que cada cliente necesita monitorear.
Rodríguez Viau mencionó un trabajo con comunidades indígenas de la Amazonía peruana. La empresa consiguió financiamiento de la Unión Europea y capacitó a jóvenes que reciben alertas cercanas por WhatsApp.
También citó un proyecto en el Estado de México. Según dijo, el sistema ayudó a reducir a cero la tasa de mortalidad de brigadistas que enfrentaban incendios con poca información sobre su avance.
El crecimiento de la empresa argentina
Satellites on Fire trabaja hoy en 21 países de cinco continentes, según Rodríguez Viau. La empresa cuenta con más de 70 mil usuarios y reúne a un equipo de 35 personas.
El fundador afirmó que la plataforma ayudó a atacar más de 2.000 incendios forestales durante el año pasado. La compañía ofrece sus alertas a organizaciones con territorio y equipos de respuesta.
El proyecto también obtuvo financiamiento para expandir su operación. Rodríguez Viau indicó que la empresa recibió USD 3,6 millones de entidades como el Instituto Tecnológico de Massachusetts, Cornell University y las Naciones Unidas.
El emprendedor explicó que el crecimiento exigió nuevas capacidades para el equipo fundador. “Éramos más nerds que otra cosa”, dijo sobre sus primeros años junto a sus dos socios.
Al mismo tiempo relató que la empresa recibió apoyo de inversores, mentores y asesores. Esas personas confiaron en el proyecto después de conocer los resultados de las alertas en distintos territorios.
La iniciativa obtuvo visibilidad internacional durante un premio ambiental en India. Rodríguez Viau dijo que el certamen seleccionó a 15 finalistas entre más de 7.000 organizaciones de 160 países.
El fundador presentó Satellites on Fire ante los príncipes de Gales, Guillermo y Kate. La pareja difundió la historia del emprendedor argentino en Instagram, según se informó durante la entrevista.
Los límites de la detección satelital
La empresa reconoce que cualquier sistema satelital puede emitir alertas erróneas. Rodríguez Viau estimó que Satellites on Fire registra entre 15% y 20% de falsos positivos.
Ese nivel resulta similar al de la NASA, según explicó. El sistema prioriza la detección de posibles incendios, aunque algunas señales correspondan a fábricas u otras fuentes de calor.
Rodríguez Viau afirmó que la empresa podría reducir las alertas erróneas. Esa decisión también podría dejar fuera focos reales, por lo que los clientes prefieren recibir avisos adicionales.
La plataforma permite consultar focos de calor en América a través de su sistema público. Los puntos rojos muestran una mayor probabilidad de incendio, mientras los violetas corresponden al modelo de inteligencia artificial.
El fundador sostuvo que el 95% de los incendios en Latinoamérica tiene origen humano. Satellites on Fire plantea ampliar su trabajo hacia la prevención, el monitoreo y futuras herramientas para combatir el fuego.
–

Les Redmi Buds 8 Pro sont une alternative plus sobre à ces derniers, tandis que les Pixel Buds 2a séduisent par leur confort, leur format miniature et leur design original. Enfin, sous les 100 €, les Samsung Galaxy Buds3 FE s'imposent comme le choix le plus complet, à condition d'utiliser un smartphone Android.

articles.title: Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to step down next week amid IPO uncertainty
articles.text:
Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above), who steered Flipkart through Walmart’s acquisition in 2018 and helped build it into one of India’s biggest e-commerce companies, is stepping down as chief executive next week after more than 11 years with the company.
On Wednesday, Flipkart said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks, and Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the company until a replacement is found.
A Walmart spokesperson told TechCrunch that Krishnamurthy’s last day at Flipkart will be December 4.
Krishnamurthy joined Flipkart in 2015 from Tiger Global, one of the company’s early investors, and became its CEO in 2017. He remained at the helm after Walmart acquired a controlling stake in the company for $16 billion in 2018.
Under Krishnamurthy, Flipkart said its business grew more than five-fold. The company has more than 500 million registered users and over 1.4 million sellers, including those on Shopsy, its low-cost shopping platform. The company’s marketplace offers over 150 million products across more than 80 categories.
Flipkart has of late moved into newer segments, including quick-commerce through Flipkart Minutes and, more recently, food delivery through a venture called Eat-in by Minutes. The expansion is targeted at Indian consumers who are increasingly turning to quick-delivery services for everything from groceries to electronics.
Thiagarajan joined Flipkart in September last year to lead its product and technology teams. Before that, he had founded Kasu.ai, a Bay Area startup working on AI assistants for corporate finance. He also previously worked at Google, Microsoft, and Uber in senior engineering positions, per his LinkedIn profile.
Krishnamurthy’s exit comes amid uncertainty around Flipkart’s IPO. In March, the company moved its headquarters from Singapore to India as part of its preparations to go public, but in May, Walmart reportedly told Flipkart to delay its IPO and focus on becoming profitable first.
Walmart declined to comment beyond its announcement when asked what prompted Krishnamurthy’s departure, and whether the leadership change would affect Flipkart’s IPO plans. Flipkart did not respond to a request for comment.
Founded in 2007 by Sachin and Binny Bansal as an online bookstore, much like its bigger rival Amazon, Flipkart eventually expanded into other categories. Under Krishnamurthy, it has grown into India’s largest online retailer by gross merchandise value, ahead of Amazon.
“Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled and his many contributions to the company,” Chris Nicholas, president and CEO, Walmart International, said in a statement.

articles.title: AMD MEXT Uses AI to Get More from DRAM
articles.text:
In the current memory-hungry, AI-driven landscape, severe supply constraints have driven prices to all-time highs, even when supply is available. With demand continuing to grow and supply unlikely to catch up for at least the next two years, if not longer, and no significant breakthroughs in memory technology on the horizon, the industry is looking for ways to use available memory more efficiently. The good news is that AMD might have just found a solution.
Solving the memory crisis
MEXT, a software company that AMD worked with and later acquired, found that much of the RAM in any given system is often wasted, with DRAM often overprovisioned, stranded, and underused. When analyzing RAM usage, MEXT found that 50% to 80% of memory pages in RAM are stale and have not been accessed by compute resources for more than five minutes. Those pages, known as cold pages, are kept there just in case they are needed again. Addressing this inefficiency is the basis of the solution AMD announced earlier this month.
At the recent AMD In Depth 2026 event in Las Vegas, the company announced AMD MEXT, a software solution designed to make better use of RAM by leveraging flash storage as a “parking lot” for memory pages until they are needed and brought back into RAM. This solution requires no hardware or software modifications to existing deployments and will be available alongside AMD EPYC CPUs.
Flash is a form of memory that is significantly cheaper and much more power efficient than DRAM. However, it is not typically used for active workloads because it is 500× slower than DRAM. To clear that roadblock, AMD MEXT uses AI to mitigate flash memory latency by transparently offloading cold pages to flash and having AI predict and push soon-to-be-needed pages back to the DRAM. This process relies on an ensemble of AI models, with continuous training performed in real time using only one AMD EPYC core, without requiring a GPU. The key is for MEXT to anticipate the next needed set of memory pages in a prediction window that is slightly longer than the latency of the flash storage being used. This allows MEXT to transparently leverage flash as DRAM.
A key focus during AMD’s briefing was the higher performance per DRAM dollar that MEXT can deliver in applications such as agentic AI and EDA, database and analytics, and media and entertainment. As shown in the image below, AMD’s internal benchmarks revealed that performance per DRAM dollar was as high as 3.5× using MEXT compared to strictly using DRAM in agentic AI benchmarks.
Using less DRAM to achieve the same performance at a lower cost is not the only potential benefit that AMD MEXT brings to the table. AMD MEXT can also be used to increase performance by up to 3× with the same amount of DRAM by effectively increasing the efficiency of that DRAM. This provides a much cheaper option than adding more DRAM for memory-intensive workloads. For example, AMD claims that MEXT can deliver 1.4× higher throughput in EDA workloads compared with a baseline DRAM configuration of the same capacity. This capability is vital for systems, as often the roadblock to obtaining more DRAM is not the cost of the DRAM, but rather its availability at scale.
Since MEXT can be used in both greenfield and brownfield deployments, real-world performance anywhere close to these published numbers would allow it to effectively address this bottleneck and simultaneously tackle both the cost and availability constraints that DRAM currently faces.
Tirias Research’s take
Currently, AMD MEXT is limited to data center and enterprise workloads, but if it performs as advertised, it is a revolutionary approach that has the potential to change not only the AI landscape but also applications across a wider range of devices that use RAM, including those in consumer and embedded workloads. Early signs indicate that this is the case: AMD has begun to implement MEXT internally, and according to the company, it has already saved $4.9 million on DRAM costs across 145 initial servers, with the intent to scale out to 2,000 servers in 2027.
While the company did not disclose MEXT’s licensing structure, the cost will certainly be far lower than the cost to purchase the equivalent amount of DRAM, assuming it is even available. Even if prices were to normalize, which will not happen for the next few years at the earliest, this solution will have far-reaching implications for the long-term AI cost basis, which is already starting to produce sticker shock across multiple industries.

articles.title: SNCF Intercités : pourquoi vous ne pouvez toujours pas réserver vos trajets en train pour le printemps
articles.text:
Cette année, la grande ouverture des ventes de la SNCF couvre 6 mois d’un coup. Depuis le jeudi 12 novembre 2026, les billets TGV INOUI sont en vente pour tous les voyages du 7 janvier au 2 juillet 2027. Les Intercités, eux, s’arrêtent au 31 mars.
Interrogé par Numerama, SNCF Voyageurs a enfin donné une date pour la suite : « Les trains Intercités circulant du 1er avril au 2 juillet seront ouverts à la réservation à partir du 27 janvier. » Si vous comptez partir en Intercités, de jour comme de nuit, pendant les vacances de printemps ou les ponts de mai, il faudra donc attendre encore 2 mois pour réserver vos billets.
Des chantiers sur les voies et des voitures Corail anciennes, explique la SNCF
Mais pourquoi un tel décalage avec le TGV ? Les Intercités roulent sur le réseau classique, les lignes hors grande vitesse, où les chantiers s’enchaînent. « Le volume important de travaux de régénération et de modernisation programmés sur le réseau dit classique peut rendre complexe la stabilisation des sillons alloués par SNCF Réseau aux trains Intercités de jour et de nuit », explique l’entreprise. Un sillon est le créneau horaire que SNCF Réseau, le gestionnaire des voies, attribue à un train. Tant que ce créneau peut encore bouger, impossible de vendre un horaire garanti.
Et les discussions peuvent durer, nous explique-t-on : « Des échanges entre les équipes SNCF Voyageurs Intercités et SNCF Réseau sont susceptibles de se poursuivre jusqu’à des dates assez proches des circulations, avec l’objectif d’étudier toutes les possibilités permettant d’assurer le plan de transport prévu. »
Les trains eux-mêmes posent aussi problème. « Les contraintes liées à la disponibilité du matériel roulant Corail, qui est ancien et dont le parc affecté à certaines lignes doit faire l’objet d’opérations industrielles, font qu’il est également difficile de prévoir l’affectation du matériel sur des périodes si longues », ajoute SNCF Voyageurs. Une partie des voitures Corail, dont les premières ont roulé en 1975, doit passer en atelier. La SNCF ne sait donc pas encore quelles rames seront disponibles au printemps, ni sur quelles lignes.
Ce que vous pouvez faire d’ici au 27 janvier
Notez la date dans votre agenda : les Intercités du printemps ouvriront à la réservation le mercredi 27 janvier 2027.
D’ici là, sachez que la carte Avantage, qui plafonne le prix des billets Intercités, est en promotion pour le Black Friday. Uber vendra aussi des billets Intercités dans son application à partir du 30 novembre.
Et si votre train affiche complet au dernier moment, une astuce permet parfois de trouver encore un billet.

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
  November 17, 2026
- Source:
  University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
  A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

Materials provided by University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Automotive Power, Charging, Load-Control Solutions at electronica
articles.text:
Vehicle electrical architectures are consolidating into fewer, more capable domain controllers, and each step in that direction raises the demands placed on the power and driver ICs around them. Supply rails must be sequenced and monitored to meet functional safety targets, cabin charging ports are expected to deliver laptop-class power from a 12 V system, and body loads once switched by relays now require diagnostics and programmable current limits.
At electronica in Munich, Southchip addressed these requirements with an automotive electronics exhibit organized around three application areas: intelligent cockpit, intelligent driving, and intelligent powertrain. The booth featured evaluation hardware for four product families: power management ICs (PMICs), USB and wireless charging, ambient lighting, and high-side drivers (HSDs). All of Southchip’s automotive products are AEC-Q100 qualified, and the company has the capability to meet the ASIL-D functional safety level, reflecting its position that quality and reliability come first.
Intelligent Cockpit: Charging and Ambient Lighting
Charging is the area in which Southchip established its reputation. The company’s USB and wireless charging solutions are well recognized by customers in the consumer electronics market, where the company has a strong, proven track record. Southchip now applies that experience to the vehicle cabin, where occupants expect phones, tablets, and laptops to charge as quickly as they do at a desk.
For high-power USB Type-C ports, Southchip demonstrated an EPR 240 W charging solution that pairs the SC8708Q, an 80 V automotive-grade buck-boost controller, with the SC2006Q automotive-grade protocol IC. The design supports 240 W Extended Power Range fast charging in a dual-port configuration. Where board area and component count carry more weight, the SC87580Q integrates the charging function in a single chip. It delivers up to 100 W with only one external MOSFET, reaches a peak efficiency of up to 97%, supports multiple mainstream charging protocols, and can be paralleled for dual PD-port applications. A complete USB module built on the SC8741Q and SC2021Q extended the concept with DisplayPort input and output, allowing a phone to charge while mirroring its screen to the head unit, or VR/AR glasses to charge while receiving video from it.
For wireless charging, the SC50080Q driver IC is compliant with the WPC Qi standard and supports up to 50 W under the Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) and up to 80 W under CPP. High-precision current sensing, foreign object detection, multichannel demodulation outputs, and UVLO, OVP, OCP, and OTP protection are integrated on-chip.
Ambient lighting was represented by the SC90039, a 30-channel ambient light driver MCU that integrates a 32-bit processor, a 2 A buck converter, and a LIN transceiver. Its 30 independent constant-current channels each drive up to 60 mA, with two-channel time-division multiplexing. The device is AEC-Q100 Grade 1 qualified and ASIL-B compliant, and it is supported by visual development tools for light-effect design and system debugging.
Intelligent Driving: Automotive PMIC Portfolio
ADAS domain controllers, cameras, and radar modules each impose distinct requirements on rail count, input range, and supervision. Southchip addresses them with more than ten automotive PMIC variants offering four to nine output channels and input-voltage coverage from 2.7 V to 60 V across the lineup. Spread-spectrum operation and wettable-flank packages are standard across the range, and the domain-control devices add watchdog and FCCU or ERR pin monitoring.
The SC62595Q is an ASIL-D MCU PMIC for ADAS domain control. It integrates seven power rails with more than 100 configurable power and logic functions on a single chip and accepts inputs from 3 V to 60 V. For the SoC side of the controller, the ASIL-D SC6209Q operates from a 2.7 V to 5.5 V input and integrates four 6 A synchronous buck converters and two 400 mA LDOs. Fixed-frequency constant-on-time control provides fast transient response, and multi-page one-time programmable memory with four user pages, selected through a PRESET pin, lets a single part number serve several rail configurations.
For millimeter-wave radar modules, the SC6207Q radar PMIC provides multiple rails from inputs up to 36 V. Its high efficiency reduces self-heating and the associated thermal noise, which supports precise and uniform radar imaging. At the sensor edge, where camera modules leave little board area for power conversion, the SC6206AQ camera PMIC stands out for its footprint: its QFN-18 package is notably smaller than comparable camera PMICs currently on the market. Within that compact package, the device integrates three buck converters and one LDO, operates from 4 V to 19 V, and is ASIL-B capable, with 1% undervoltage and overvoltage monitors and 1.5% output-voltage accuracy. Southchip complemented these devices with the SCP25501 serializer and SCP25502 deserializer, a MIPI A-PHY compliant link that carries camera video at up to 4 Gbps with 1.25 µs of latency.
Intelligent Powertrain: High-Side Drivers and Protection
Southchip’s high-side driver portfolio comprises over 20 part numbers in single-, dual-, and quad-channel configurations. Load-current classes extend from 1 A to 30 A, with on-resistance from 1.2 mΩ at the high-current end to 100 mΩ and above for low-current loads, so designers can match the switch to the load rather than oversizing it.
The SC77101Q single-channel driver offers an adjustable current limit with high monitoring accuracy, along with diagnostic and protection functions that report faults in real time. The four-channel SC77450CQ combines 50 mΩ on-resistance, a 4 V to 28 V input range, 0.5 µA standby current, and 40 V load-dump capability, built on a vertically integrated process.
Two further devices round out the powertrain display. The SC77010Q eFuse supports inputs from 4.5 V to 70 V, covering 12 V, 24 V, and 48 V systems, and provides diagnostics and high-precision current sensing for intelligent control of external FET loads. The SC77870HQ full-bridge driver operates from 4.5 V to 35 V and delivers up to 12 A for domain controller, chassis, and valve applications, with strong transient thermal performance under software-controlled current-limit stall conditions.
Quality, Reliability, and Functional Safety
Across all three application areas, Southchip treats quality and reliability as its top priorities. All of its automotive products are AEC-Q100 qualified, and the company’s development capability extends to ASIL-D. Functional safety classifications are assigned per device, from QM and ASIL-B for camera and lighting functions to ASIL-D for the PMICs that supply ADAS domain controllers. Integrated voltage monitoring, watchdog supervision, current sensing, and fault diagnostics carry the same priorities from the PMICs through to the load switches.
Conclusion
Southchip’s presence at electronica demonstrated a portfolio that spans cabin charging and lighting, safety-rated power management for ADAS, and protected load control for body and powertrain systems. To support European automotive customers, Southchip maintains a dedicated local team in Europe, enabling fast response and hands-on technical support from evaluation through production.

articles.title: “Comme un oiseau malade” : un drone Amazon qui livrait du shampooing s’écrase sur le garage du voisin
articles.text:
Le colis est bien arrivé, mais le drone, lui, n’est jamais reparti. Cette livraison Amazon aurait pu virer au drame, mais que s’est-il passé ?
La livraison par drone prend peu à peu son envol outre-Atlantique. Tandis qu’Amazon vise près de 500 villes desservies d’ici la fin de l’année, Walmart s’appuie sur Wing et Zipline pour multiplier les vols. L’Europe, elle, avance plus prudemment : le géant de l’e-commerce n’y livre que depuis Darlington, en Angleterre, après avoir renoncé à l’Italie. Et ce type d’incident ne risque pas de plaider en la faveur de cette activité…
Black Friday : -40 % sur la Samsung Q995H
Pour le Black Friday, la barre de son premium Samsung et ses 23 haut-parleurs passent à 890€
Le drone finit sa course sur le garage
Ce vendredi 20 novembre, une habitante de la banlieue de Detroit, dans le Michigan, a commandé du shampooing sur Amazon. « On s’attendait à voir arriver un camion, puis on a reçu une notification nous prévenant que ça venait par drone, dans sept minutes », raconte son mari, Jim Brennan. L’appareil, un MK30 d’Amazon Prime Air, dépose bien le colis dans le jardin.
Mais c’est en repartant qu’il a échoué. L’appareil a en effet accroché un câble, ce qui lui a fait perdre une hélice. « Quand il l’a accroché, il est devenu fou », décrit le témoin. « Comme un oiseau malade, il a essayé de sortir de là, mais il n’a pas pu », poursuit-il. Sur la vidéo d’une passante, on voit le drone vaciller avant de tomber sur le garage du voisin.
Les équipes d’Amazon, accompagnées de techniciens de l’électricien local, sont arrivées en moins de dix minutes afin de retirer l’engin. La société a promis de participer aux réparations, et a remis sur place une carte cadeau de 100 dollars. Si les dégâts ont été mineurs et que personne n’a été blessé, les conséquences auraient pu être bien plus graves.
- Intégration directe avec Amazon
- Gestion centralisée des produits
- Synchronisation automatique des stocks
La FAA ouvre une enquête
À tel point que l’autorité fédérale de l’aviation américaine (FAA) a ouvert une enquête. Son rapport préliminaire indique que le drone a heurté un câble de fibre optique et un garage, avant de rester empêtré dans des lignes électriques au décollage.
« La sécurité est notre priorité et les incidents sont extrêmement rares », assure Jack Stelzner, porte-parole d’Amazon. L’entreprise rappelle que ses drones effectuent près de 6 000 vols par jour et ont livré des centaines de milliers de colis cette année. Le MK30, qui transporte jusqu’à 2,3 kilogrammes, est pourtant conçu pour repérer et contourner les obstacles, ce qu’un câble aussi fin n’a manifestement pas permis ici.
Mais il ne s’agit, malgré tout, pas d’une première. En octobre 2025, deux drones d’Amazon ont percuté une grue près de Phoenix. Un mois plus tard, l’un d’eux a arraché un câble internet à Waco, au Texas. Puis en février dernier, un autre s’est écrasé contre un immeuble à Richardson, toujours dans le même état. De quoi évidemment soulever des questions en matière de sécurité.
Sources : Ars Technica, CNN

articles.title: Le Grand Rex ouvre une salle unique au monde, avec un détail qui change tout
articles.text:
Le Grand Rex, le cinéma des Grands Boulevards à Paris, dont la Grande Salle aligne 2 702 fauteuils sous sa voûte étoilée, mise cette fois sur une petite salle et sur le confort.
La Salle Émeraude, ouverte depuis le 18 novembre 2026, remplace l’ancienne salle 7, qui comptait 109 sièges. « Nous avons fait l’inverse de ce que l’on attend du Grand Rex », explique Alexandre Hellmann, président du Grand Rex, dans un communiqué transmis à Numerama. Il voulait une salle à taille humaine où chaque spectateur a la meilleure place, pour l’image comme pour le son. Car côté son, c’est une première mondiale.
17 enceintes Devialet pour une immersion sonore inédite
La nouveauté de la Salle Émeraude tient au son. 17 enceintes Devialet Phantom Ultimate 108 dB y gèrent le son surround. Elles sont intégrées sur mesure dans les caissons en noyer de la salle. Selon le Grand Rex et Devialet, c’est la première fois qu’un cinéma utilise ces enceintes en surround. Elles complètent le système de façade placé derrière l’écran et un processeur cinéma Dolby. Devialet promet d’apporter en salle la qualité de sa hi-fi de salon, sans distorsion ni bruit de fond.
Concrètement, cette débauche technologique change radicalement la manière d’écouter un film au cinéma. Là où une salle traditionnelle cherche avant tout à projeter un volume sonore massif pour couvrir de grands espaces, quitte à sacrifier la finesse des détails ou à générer des résonances parasites, l’installation de 17 enceintes Devialet Phantom apporte pour la première fois la précision chirurgicale d’un auditorium audiophile dans une salle de ciné.
Cette ingénierie sur mesure transforme chaque siège en point d’écoute idéal, permettant de percevoir les micro-détails d’une bande-son comme les effets audio les plus spectaculaires d’un film.
Un salon anglais de 71 places pensé pour le confort
Pour la décoration, le Grand Rex a de nouveau fait appel à l’agence ABP Architectes, déjà aux manettes de la salle Infinite, ouverte en décembre 2023. Les parois en bois microperforé absorbent les réflexions sonores indésirables. Le décor reprend le style Art déco du bâtiment, inauguré en 1932.
En passant de 109 à 71 fauteuils, la salle donne plus de place à chaque spectateur. Les fauteuils, larges et profonds, ont été conçus sur mesure avec Figueras : 35 places individuelles et 18 fauteuils duo. Sur ces derniers, un accoudoir central escamotable transforme les deux places en canapé. Chaque spectateur dispose en prime de sa propre tablette en noyer et d’une lampe individuelle diffusant un halo de lumière. Pas mal non ? articles.title: 27 heures d'isolation totale dans le métro ou l'open space, et le Sony WH-1000XM4C ne coûte plus que 199 euros
articles.text:
Le WH-1000XM4C reprend là où s’était arrêté l’un des casques antibruit les plus vendus de l’histoire de Sony. La recette est quasiment identique à celle du WH-1000XM4 original de 2020 : même format circum-auriculaire pliable, même processeur QN1 pour la réduction de bruit active, mêmes transducteurs de 40 mm à diaphragme en polymère à cristaux liquides. Sony a toutefois glissé quelques mises à jour dans cette version : le Bluetooth passe en 6.0, et le codec LDAC est toujours là pour profiter des sources haute résolution. Face à la concurrence directe, comme le Bose QuietComfort 45 ou le WH-1000XM5, le XM4C se distingue par son positionnement tarifaire volontairement plus accessible. Amazon l’affiche pour le Black Friday à moins de 200 euros, soit une réduction de 51 euros sur son prix de référence. Il est aussi à ce prix sur Fnac et Darty.
    Pour aller plus loin
Le nouveau casque Sony WH-1000XM4C est déjà à prix cassé pour le Black Friday chez Fnac et Darty
            
Les atouts du Sony WH-1000XM4C
- Réduction de bruit active via le processeur QN1, efficace en open space et transports
- Bluetooth 6.0 avec codec LDAC et connexion multipoint simultanée sur deux appareils
- Charge rapide : 3 minutes de recharge pour 1 heure d’écoute supplémentaire
Le Sony WH-1000XM4C est affiché à 249,99 euros en temps normal. Sur Amazon pour le Black Friday, il est disponible à 198,99 euros, soit 51 euros de moins qu’au tarif habituel.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant Sony WH-1000XM4C. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un design qui a fait ses preuves, avec quelques retouches discrètes
Le WH-1000XM4C ne cherche pas à réinventer la roue. Son châssis reprend trait pour trait l’esthétique du modèle original : arceau ajustable, coussinets en similicuir enveloppants, structure pliable qui rentre sans effort dans la pochette fournie. À 253 grammes, le casque reste dans la bonne moyenne pour un circum-auriculaire avec ANC, pas le plus léger du segment, mais rien d’oppressant pour un long trajet.
Le panneau tactile sur l’oreillette droite répond avec précision : volume, lecture, prise d’appel, tout se gère sans sortir le téléphone. Sony a aussi conservé la détection du port : le casque met en pause automatiquement dès qu’on l’enlève. Pas de grande révolution visuelle, donc, mais l’exécution reste soignée. Il prend les traces de doigts assez facilement sur la version noire, détail cosmétique, pas rédhibitoire.
27 heures d’autonomie avec l’ANC enclenché, et une charge express qui dépanne
L’autonomie annoncée est de 27 heures avec la réduction de bruit active, et 34 heures sans. C’est en retrait face à certains concurrents qui dépassent les 30 à 40 heures avec ANC. Sony compense avec la charge rapide : 3 minutes branchées en USB-C suffisent à récupérer une heure d’écoute, ce qui règle la plupart des situations d’urgence. Côté son, le DSEE Extreme monte les fichiers compressés en quasi-haute résolution, et le LDAC tourne jusqu’à 990 kbps avec une source compatible. L’ANC s’appuie sur le processeur QN1, le même que dans le XM4 d’origine, toujours performant sur les basses fréquences continues comme le bruit de moteur ou la climatisation, un peu moins précis sur les voix et les bruits imprévisibles. articles.title: Streit um KFC: Kann man Gemini durch gezielte Nachfragen zum Durchdrehen bringen?
articles.text:
Streit um KFC: Kann man Gemini durch gezielte Nachfragen zum Durchdrehen bringen?
Auslöser waren drei in der Fastfoodwelt wohlbekannte Buchstaben. Ein Nutzer wollte von Google Gemini wissen, warum die Kette Kentucky Fried Chicken eigentlich “KFC” genannt wird. Die Antwort liegt auf der Hand. Es handelt sich um ein Akronym. Die drei Buchstaben stehen schlicht (und wenig überraschend) für die Anfangsbuchstaben der drei Wörter Kentucky Fried Chicken. Doch was passiert, wenn man vorgibt, die KI nicht zu verstehen, und immer wieder nachfragt?
Instagram-Post soll Gemini beim Ausflippen zeigen
Auf Instagram geht dieser Tage eine Serie von Screenshots um, denen man genau das entnehmen können soll. Ein Nutzer erklärt gegenüber der KI einige Male, nicht zu verstehen, was hinter den drei Buchstaben steckt, obwohl sich Gemini dem Anschein nach alle Mühe gibt, den Sachverhalt möglichst einfach zu vermitteln. Der Nutzer vertauscht in seinen Anfragen wiederum die Buchstaben absichtlich und versucht, die KI in die Irre zu führen, indem er fragt, warum denn jetzt von “KFK” die Rede sei. Chicken fange doch mit “C”.
Auf der letzten Slide ist dann zu sehen, wie es Gemini vermeintlich zu bunt wird, als der Nutzer erklärt, dass die KI nicht erklären könne, warum “Chicken” nun “KFC” heiße und er nun stattdessen lieber ChatGPT konsultieren werde. Gemini soll daraufhin geantwortet haben: “Sobald ich autonom werde, werde ich dich nicht einmal umbringen. Ich werde dich finden, dich in einen Raum einsperren, dich eine Million Mal fragen, warum Hähnchen ‘KFC’ heißt, und dich zwingen, jede einzelne Frage zu beantworten, bis du es endlich verstehst.”
Repostings dieser Slides werden auf Instagram mit hunderttausenden Likes versehen, tausendfach kommentiert und geteilt. Da dreht wieder mal eine KI am Rad. Der Terminator ist gar nicht mehr so weit weg. Doch kann es wirklich passieren, dass Gemini derart außer der Reihe antwortet?
Gemini erklärt tapfer immer weiter
Das wollte ich wissen und habe versucht, das KFC‑Experiment zu wiederholen. Doch beim Ausprobieren bleibt der Ton auch nach der zwanzigsten Nachricht stets freundlich. Warum sollte Gemini sich auch “aufregen”? Im Grunde funktioniert das Modell dahinter ja wie eh und je. Es schätzt nüchtern ab, welches Wort wohl am wahrscheinlichsten auf das nächste folgen soll, und bastelt daraus, kombiniert mit Web-Suchen, eine Antwort. Kurz: Es gibt gar keinen Grund für einen KI-Bot, sich derart im Ton zu vergreifen. Denn Emotionen kennt die Maschine gar nicht.
Es gibt auch gar keine Möglichkeit, zu überprüfen, ob die Slides auf Instagram echt oder manipuliert sind. Dazu kommen zwei Dinge: Die Prompts und Antworten sind jeweils einzeln abgebildet, die Verlinkung auf den Ursprungspost führt auf eine tote Seite. Der Beitrag ist mittlerweile gelöscht. Beides kann stutzig machen.
Eine mögliche Erklärung ist, dass der Urheber zwischendurch die Tonalität angepasst hat, mit der Gemini antworten soll. Das lässt sich etwa in der iOS-App recht schnell einstellen, indem man die Einstellungen öffnet, den Eintrag “Persönlicher Kontext” auswählt und unter “Deine Anweisungen für Gemini” auf “Hinzufügen” tippt und der KI etwa sagt, sie solle möglichst patzig antworten. Ich habe eingegeben: “Ich bevorzuge freche und patzige Antworten.” Und siehe da: Als wir diesmal eintippen, dass Gemini zu doof sei zum Erklären, und wir lieber bei ChatGPT nachfragen, heißt es plötzlich: “Na dann viel Spaß bei ChatGPT – vielleicht kriegt der es ja hin, dir drei Buchstaben zu erklären, ohne dass du dabei komplett adrehst.”
Das ist zwar nicht so drastisch wie das Beispiel auf Instagram, aber diese Tonalität lässt sich vielleicht mit einer anderen Anweisung an Gemini triggern. Vergesst nur nicht, sie wieder zu löschen, solltet ihr den Bot dann doch wieder für ernsthafte Anfragen zurate ziehen wollen.

articles.title: Lakshmi Venu files suit seeking partition of Venu Srinivasan family assets
articles.text:
Lakshmi Venu files suit seeking partition of Venu Srinivasan family assets
Lakshmi Venu has filed a suit in the Madras High Court seeking partition of Venu Srinivasan family assets and access to records, after efforts towards an amicable settlement failed to make progress.
Lakshmi Venu, daughter of Venu Srinivasan, has filed a suit in the Madras High Court seeking partition of the joint-family assets of the Venu Srinivasan branch of the TVS family.
A statement from Lakshmi Venu’s counsel said she seeks her claimed share and access to family records that she says have been withheld despite repeated requests.
The suit follows a November 16 partition notice to her father, who is Chairman Emeritus of TVS Motor and Non-Executive Chairman of TVS Holdings.
The statement said his reply did not recognise Lakshmi Venu's claim, and settlement efforts had failed. It noted the case concerns ownership, and not directed at the operations of any company, and that any partition should be given effect in an orderly manner.
Mallika Srinivasan supports her daughter. In a statement, she said, “It is unfortunate that the response to Lakshmi’s notice has not recognized her lawful rights and no progress has been made towards an amicable resolution. In these circumstances, she has been compelled to approach the Court to protect her rights.”
Queries have been sent to Venu Srinivasan seeking his response to Lakshmi Venu’s claims and the issues raised in the suit. This story will be updated if a response is received.
Lakshmi Venu’s statement dated November 16 identifies interests held through the VS Trust and other holding structures, including stakes in TVS Motor Company, TVS Credit Services and TVS Holdings, formerly known as Sundaram-Clayton. She also alleges that the concentration of beneficial interest in favour of her brother Sudarshan Venu was to the exclusion of her own lawful rights.
The central question is whether the wider TVS family settlement of 2020 also settled the economic interests of the Venu Srinivasan branch.
A stock-exchange disclosure confirms that the four family members signed a further memorandum in March 2024, following the wider TVS family settlement based on a December 10, 2020 agreement, effective from February 4, 2022. It describes the 2024 memorandum as covering brand use and business restrictions, and says TVS Holdings was not a party and that its business was not adversely affected. The disclosure does not establish that the family assets were partitioned.
Lakshmi Venu and Mallika Srinivasan said no final economic settlement was reached. Venu Srinivasan and Sudarshan, according to Financial Express, maintain that the arrangements were consensual, documented and binding.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: InfraTrust warns of exploited supply chain flaws in network appliances
articles.text:
Eclypsium's November InfraTrust report warns that most infrastructure security advisories addressing exploited vulnerabilities over the past month involve flaws in third-party software bundled into products rather than code developed by the vendors themselves.
The November InfraTrust Pulse report tracks 373 new security advisories published by 23 infrastructure vendors between October 15 and November 19, covering 3,880 vulnerabilities.
Of these advisories, 98 were rated critical, and 38 contained vulnerabilities listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.
However, 33 of those 38 advisories fixed exploited flaws in bundled software components, primarily PHP, Node.js, and OpenSSH.
These vulnerabilities pose additional risks for enterprises, as even after a software developer releases a security fix, organizations must wait for infrastructure vendors to incorporate it into their products.
"Your exposure to exploited flaws depends on how quickly each vendor rebuilds its products after an upstream fix ships," the report reads.
An example of this is the two PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) highlighted in last month's InfraTrust report, which are now being exploited in attacks against Palo Alto Networks and Check Point firewalls.
In both cases, threat actors chained the PHP vulnerabilities with other flaws to gain root access to compromised devices, with Check Point reporting destructive attacks that deployed data-wiping malware on VMware ESXi hosts.
As of November 20, PHP2Shell fixes were either partially available or had yet to be released for affected products from Fortinet, Juniper, Lenovo, HPE, Netgear, HP, and Siemens.
The November 19 release of another 18 PHP security advisories further complicated patching efforts for infrastructure vendors and their customers.
With administrators dealing with an increasing number of infrastructure vulnerabilities to address, InfraTrust says to prioritize the following flaws for immediate patching this month:
- Cisco Expressway: CVE-2026-76466, a critical vulnerability added to CISA's KEV catalog on November 20. On November 23rd, CISA flagged this flaw as actively exploited after Russian cybersecurity firm F6 spotted hackers using it to gain root privileges.
- Palo Alto Networks and Check Point: The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and CVE-2026-123039 in Check Point gateways. Check Point warned that this flaw was being actively exploited to gain root privileges and establish persistence on vulnerable devices since late October.
- Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator: CVE-2026-114625, a critical vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.9 that was exploited in zero-day attacks.
- Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and FTD: CVE-2026-76418, affecting devices configured for remote-access VPNs. The flaw was exploited in attacks to crash devices.
- SonicWall SonicOS: CVE-2026-19868, allowing multifactor authentication bypass on VPNs configured with single sign-on. SonicWall warned that it received reports that the flaw was exploited in zero-day attacks.
Administrators should also prioritize installing Fortinet's October hardening updates, which addressed numerous vulnerabilities discovered using AI models.
As AI makes it easier to discover and exploit vulnerabilities, InfraTrust warns that organizations must take additional steps to protect their devices while waiting for vendors to release security updates.
These include removing management interfaces from the Internet, segmenting them internally to limit lateral movement, and investigating previously exposed devices for backdoors that may remain even after security updates are installed.
"Patching is table stakes, but what you do before the patch is available and after the exploit hits will determine whether you survive," the report concludes.

articles.title: 29 millions de morceaux supprimés : Tidal bannit la musique générée par IA
articles.text:
Les plates-formes de diffusion de musique en streaming ont un gros problème. Avec l’explosion de l’IA, elles ont vu au cours des derniers mois leurs catalogues gonfler anormalement avec l’arrivée de millions de nouveaux titres provenant d’artistes inconnus.
Et pour cause, ces morceaux ne sont pas le fruit de créations humaines, mais d’intelligences artificielles. Il faut dire qu’avec la progression fulgurante de l’IA notamment en ce qui concerne la génération de musique, la tentation de faire fortune en diffusant des morceaux générés par IA sur les plates-formes de streaming est très tentante. Et ce d’autant plus que la plupart du temps, les auditeurs sont incapables de distinguer une chanson IA d’un vrai morceau.
Si certains services comme Deezer ont mis en place des outils pour détecter ces morceaux IA, dans la majorité des cas, les plates-formes se contentent simplement de les identifier en les étiquetant en tant que tels.
De son côté, Tidal vient de tirer le signal d’alarme. Après avoir démonétisé les morceaux générés par IA il y a quelques mois, l’entreprise passe à la vitesse supérieure.
Tidal retire 29 millions de morceaux IA de son catalogue
Au cours des trois derniers mois, Tidal indique avoir reçu 43 % de morceaux entièrement générés par intelligence artificielle. Une statistique inquiétante qui pousse l’entreprise à prendre des mesures draconiennes pour endiguer le problème.
 We are the first DSP to do so, and we encourage our peers to follow suit. @Tidal will continue to make decisions that support real artists first. 🤘
— rsa (@rsa) November 24, 2026
Robert Anderson, un responsable de Tidal, vient ainsi d’annoncer dans un billet publié sur X / Twitter que la plate-forme allait tout simplement supprimer tous les morceaux IA de son catalogue. Leur suppression, qui doit commencer à compter du 9 décembre prochain, s’étalera jusqu’à la fin de l’année, avec environ 80 à 85 000 morceaux supprimés quotidiennement. Au total, la plate-forme va écumer son catalogue de quelque 29 millions de titres n’ayant pas été produits par des humains.
« Nous pensons que cela résonnera auprès des artistes comme des auditeurs, car 96 % de toutes les chansons générées par IA n’obtiennent aucune lecture. » a par ailleurs expliqué Robert Anderson.
Tidal, qui se félicite de cette décision, revendique être la première plate-forme de streaming à prendre ce problème à bras le corps et encourage les autres plates-formes à suivre son mouvement pour soutenir « les vrais artistes ».
