articles.title: Uber empezó a probar robotaxis sin nadie al volante en la Bahía de San Francisco
articles.text:
Uber, la empresa de transporte Nuro, que desarrolla el software de conducción autónoma, y el fabricante de autos eléctricos Lucid comenzaron a probar en calles públicas de la Bahía de San Francisco robotaxis sin ningún operador de seguridad a bordo.
Las pruebas se realizan en cuatro ciudades del sur de la bahía: Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos y Sunnyvale. Según las compañías, se extenderán a otras ciudades de la región el próximo año. Los empleados de Uber empezarán pronto a viajar en los autos sin conductor.
La flota usada en esta etapa supera los 100 vehículos Lucid Gravity, un SUV eléctrico, con mejoras de hardware y software respecto de los que circulaban con un operador al volante, según informó The Verge. Cada auto lleva cámaras, sensores láser (lidar) y radares, además de un aro luminoso en el techo.
El aro muestra las iniciales del pasajero y el estado de la recogida, para que cada persona identifique su auto. El sistema de conducción es el Nuro Driver, de nivel 4: puede manejar solo en las zonas y condiciones para las que fue diseñado.
El lanzamiento comercial se atrasó
La salida al público prevista para fines de 2026 pasó a el primer trimestre de 2027. Andrew Chapin, director de operaciones de Nuro, dijo a Axios que la empresa necesitaba afinar el producto y completar los permisos finales. “Un pequeño corrimiento a la derecha no es algo sustancial”, afirmó.
Houston, en Texas, será el segundo mercado comercial. El servicio llegará allí más tarde en 2027. Uber y Nuro ya prueban autos en esa ciudad, pero con un operador humano al volante, según reportaron algunos medios norteamericanos.
El paso a la conducción sin supervisión se apoya en un marco de seguridad de Nuro que combina pruebas en la calle, simulaciones a gran escala y ensayos en un circuito cerrado en Las Vegas. Allí los autos recorrieron sin nadie a bordo situaciones como el cruce de peatones y las infracciones de prioridad de paso.
Nuro es una de las seis empresas autorizadas en California para probar autos sin conductor en la vía pública, según The Next Web. La compañía obtuvo este año ese permiso, además de otro que permite llevar pasajeros con un operador de seguridad a bordo.
Uber apuesta por varios socios a la vez
Uber se comprometió a comprar al menos 35.000 vehículos Lucid equipados con el sistema de Nuro en los próximos años. La empresa comprometió unos USD 500 millones en cada una de las dos compañías, y espera tener al menos 2.000 vehículos totalmente autónomos en su plataforma a fines de 2027.
Uber tiene acuerdos con más de 30 empresas de autos autónomos en el mundo, informó Axios. Entre ellas figuran Zoox y Motional, que podrían competir con Nuro dentro de la misma aplicación. “La pregunta es si Nuro surge como el hijo favorito”, dijo a Axios Grayson Brulte, fundador de la consultora The Road to Autonomy.
Uber busca competir con Waymo, la filial de Alphabet que ya opera robotaxis y cuyos viajes están disponibles en la aplicación de Uber en Austin y Atlanta, aunque el acuerdo de exclusividad entre ambas finalizará a comienzos de 2028.
Lyft también incorporó estos vehículos a su plataforma en septiembre. Tesla, por su parte, opera una red propia de robotaxis. En el Área de la Bahía de San Francisco, Uber, Nuro y Lucid competirán con Waymo y Zoox y prevén habilitar el servicio para pasajeros en la aplicación de Uber durante el primer trimestre de 2027, tras una fase inicial de viajes para empleados.
El inicio de estas pruebas sin operador a bordo coloca a Uber, Nuro y Lucid ante una fase decisiva: deberán demostrar que la tecnología puede funcionar de forma segura, obtener las autorizaciones necesarias y ganarse la confianza de los pasajeros. El despliegue previsto para 2027 también intensificará la competencia con Waymo, Zoox, Tesla y otros operadores, en un mercado donde la autonomía ya no se mide solo por la capacidad del vehículo para circular, sino por la posibilidad de convertir esa capacidad en un servicio disponible, regulado y sostenible.

articles.title: SpaceX recebe autorização para lançar um milhão de satélites de IA
articles.text:
A SpaceX recebeu autorização da Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos (FCC, na sigla em inglês) para implantar constelação de até um milhão de satélites que funcionarão como data centers em órbita. Batizado de Starmind, o projeto pretende levar capacidade de processamento de inteligência artificial (IA) para o espaço, aproveitando a energia solar para alimentar os equipamentos.
A decisão foi anunciada nesta quarta-feira (25) pelo presidente da FCC, Brendan Carr. Segundo a agência, a iniciativa busca atender à crescente demanda por capacidade computacional necessária para desenvolver e operar sistemas de IA.
A empresa de Elon Musk havia solicitado a autorização no início de 2026. A proposta prevê o uso de módulos de processamento orbital capazes de lidar com grandes volumes de dados e transmitir os resultados de volta à Terra.
A aprovação, porém, não significa que a SpaceX poderá colocar toda a constelação em funcionamento imediatamente. A licença estabelece etapas para a implantação: a empresa deverá iniciar os lançamentos até novembro de 2033, colocar pelo menos 100 mil satélites em órbita até novembro de 2035 e alcançar 50% do total autorizado até novembro de 2038.
Como funcionarão os data centers espaciais da SpaceX?
- A ideia da SpaceX é transferir parte da infraestrutura necessária para o processamento de IA para fora da Terra. Em vez de depender exclusivamente de grandes instalações terrestres, a empresa pretende distribuir módulos computacionais em uma rede de satélites interconectados;
- Um dos principais argumentos apresentados pela companhia à FCC é a possibilidade de aproveitar a energia solar disponível em órbita, com menor necessidade de manutenção e custos operacionais. A empresa também argumenta que a infraestrutura espacial poderia reduzir o impacto ambiental associado aos data centers convencionais;
- Os equipamentos utilizarão conexões ópticas de alta capacidade para trocar informações entre si e se comunicar com a constelação Starlink. A FCC também autorizou o uso de radiofrequências como alternativa para comunicações de emergência, telemetria, rastreamento e controle dos satélites;
- De acordo com a documentação apresentada pela agência, os equipamentos poderão operar em diferentes órbitas, entre 500 e dois mil quilômetros de altitude.
Leia mais:
- Anthropic e SpaceX impuseram regras incomuns e irritaram bancos no IPO
- SpaceX é processada nos EUA por imagens sexuais geradas pelo Grok
- Tesla e SpaceX negociam fusão de US$ 3,5 trilhões até o fim do ano
SpaceX quer aproveitar foguete Starship para colocar satélites em órbita
A dimensão do projeto depende de outro empreendimento de Musk: o foguete Starship, desenvolvido pela própria SpaceX.
O veículo reutilizável de próxima geração é considerado fundamental para reduzir os custos de transporte e permitir a implantação de uma constelação dessa magnitude.
Afinal, a escala planejada é extraordinária. Segundo a Reuters, existem atualmente cerca de 17 mil satélites em órbita da Terra. A Starlink, rede de internet da própria SpaceX, possui pouco mais de 11 mil unidades em operação no espaço.
Ainda não está claro se a companhia realmente pretende utilizar todas as um milhão de autorizações concedidas. Operadoras de satélites frequentemente solicitam permissões para quantidades superiores às que efetivamente planejam lançar, garantindo maior flexibilidade para desenvolver seus projetos.
A proposta também enfrenta questionamentos de concorrentes. A divisão de satélites da Amazon, por exemplo, criticou a dimensão do empreendimento e levantou dúvidas sobre a capacidade da SpaceX de colocar tantos equipamentos em órbita. A empresa chegou a argumentar que a implantação poderia levar séculos.
Projeto faz parte da estratégia de IA de Elon Musk
A iniciativa Starmind ganhou importância na estratégia de negócios de Musk e também apareceu em sua apresentação a investidores antes da abertura de capital da SpaceX, em junho de 2026.
A companhia pretende ampliar sua atuação no setor de IA, indo além dos foguetes e dos serviços de conectividade oferecidos pela Starlink.
A movimentação acontece em meio à expansão dos investimentos em infraestrutura de IA. Grandes empresas de tecnologia precisam de cada vez mais capacidade computacional para treinar e executar modelos, o que aumenta a demanda por energia e instalações especializadas.
Com a autorização da FCC, a SpaceX passa a ter caminho regulatório para desenvolver uma infraestrutura de processamento fora do planeta. A agência também informou que continua avaliando propostas de outras empresas interessadas em construir data centers espaciais.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
articles.text:
Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
- Date:
  November 11, 2026
- Source:
  ETH Zurich
- Summary:
  Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
- Share:
A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.
Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.
By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.
The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.
Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers
The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.
Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.
The major difference lies in how that information is stored.
"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.
Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.
Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better
One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.
In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.
Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.
However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.
Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.
Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.
New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests
The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.
The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.
To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.
"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.
Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.
A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers
One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.
However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.
Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.
Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

articles.title: Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
articles.text:
Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations.
Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
The Ear Note buds look similar to Nothing’s previous earbuds, but now their case doubles as an AI-connected note taker for conversations.
Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.”
As previously reported by Bloomberg, the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to Bloomberg.
The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month, will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro. Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps.

articles.title: Quand les héros de GTA 6 deviennent de vrais mannequins sur les réseaux sociaux
articles.text:
Oubliez les braquages sanglants et les courses-poursuites avec la police de GTA 6 le temps d’une séance d’essayage. Comme on peut le voir partout sur les réseaux sociaux, une partie de la communauté s’est découvert une véritable passion pour le stylisme virtuel.
Si Rockstar Games n’offre pas la possibilité de sculpter le visage de ses deux protagonistes de zéro, la garde-robe, les coupes de cheveux, le maquillage et les accessoires offrent une liberté suffisamment vaste pour façonner des silhouettes radicalement opposées. Sans oublier la possibilité de faire de la musculation pour leur forger un corps d’athlète, les séances de maquillage ou encore les salons de tatouage.
Des looks dignes d’une campagne de parfum ou d’un festival dans GTA 6
D’un joueur à l’autre sur GTA 6, le duo criminel change complètement de visage et reflète directement la personnalité de celui qui tient la manette. Certains préfèrent habiller Jason et Lucia comme des festivaliers, tandis que d’autres leur composent des tenues minimalistes ou de méchants de films.
Les créations les plus virales poussent le chic encore plus loin. Certains clichés donnent l’impression d’avoir été extraits d’une publicité pour un parfum de luxe, tandis que d’autres s’amusent avec les époques en métamorphosant Lucia tantôt en star du R&B des années 1990, tantôt en icône pop-punk du début des années 2000. Cette souplesse esthétique permet de réinventer l’aura des personnages, et c’est une excellente chose. Histoire de vraiment s’approprier le duo.
Dans l’État fictif de Leonida, on trouve toute une ribambelle de boutiques de vêtements, de la friperie avec des pièces abordables à des enseignes de luxe où l’on peut acheter des robes ou des costumes pour plusieurs milliers de dollars. Soit de quoi se créer une garde-robe immense pour toutes les occasions, en fonction de ses moyens.
Un mode photo redoutable derrière ce phénomène viral
Si ces tenues font autant réagir, c’est aussi parce que Rockstar a doté son jeu GTA 6 d’un outil de capture redoutable. Le mode photo intégré permet notamment de placer des éclairages dynamiques dignes d’un véritable studio professionnel, sublimant les textures des tissus, les reflets sur la peau et les jeux d’ombres dans les ruelles de Leonida.
En combinant cette direction artistique ultra-soignée avec des options vestimentaires particulièrement riches, GTA 6 s’offre ainsi un terrain d’expression créatif inattendu, à mi-chemin entre le simulateur de vie et le studio de photographie. Une preuve supplémentaire que l’expérience imaginée par Rockstar dépasse largement le cadre du simple jeu d’action en monde ouvert.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
  November 7, 2026
- Source:
  University of Regensburg
- Summary:
  Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: Art of play in the age of AI
articles.text:
Art of play in the age of AI
Now that code ships faster than ever, you have more time to spend on projects just for the fun of it. Here’s what we can learn through that process as developers.
As kids, we spent hours tinkering and building and just messing with things. As an adult, I could watch my own young kiddos figure out how certain shapes and movement work all day. Through that play, we improved our problem-solving and language skills, and it’s probably not a stretch to say it was good for our early engineering skills.
In this era of development now, we’re starting to get a taste of that again. We’re experimenting more, and taking in more changes, because it’s all new!
For the last four years at GitHub Universe, we’ve had hackable conference badges. What started as a simple e-ink display for your name and job title morphed into a labor of love for Martin Woodward, VP of Developer Relations. This year, the badge evolved into a device with a color screen, rechargeable battery, accelerometer sensors, and touch-sensitive gaming controls.
The tinkering we’ve seen with the badges has been amazing.
Hacking the GitHub Universe Badge with these 3 apps that I made!! #GitHubUniverse https://t.co/Qy5wYPqXf5
— Connie Xu (@conniecodes) October 28, 2026
you can play octo drive on your @github universe badge! repo - https://t.co/DrYkhjvMVt https://t.co/S6jVwxPdEY
— Rishab Kumar (@rishabincloud) October 27, 2026
Coding needs room for play
According to the Octoverse report, 40% of pull requests were started by agents by September. That’s a big jump from the 17% we saw in March, which was already a pretty high number.
With that kind of pace of change, it’s easy to feel unsteady thinking about our coding skills that we’ve been honing as an industry for decades. At the same time, one might argue that the tools and changes in front of us offer more room for experimentation and creativity!
AI can turn our ideas into working code faster than ever before. We can build things just because we’re curious to see if it’ll work, without the burden of figuring out every single step before getting started. The learning is moving to different parts of the building timeline.
As Martin said in our GitHub Podcast episode, “Give yourself permission to play, call it learning,” but with the caveat that you should time-box it so that you don’t spend too much time perfecting it. Know when to stop, ship, and share.
You don’t need a big idea to start
What’s really exciting is how the scope of projects have changed. With AI tooling, we don’t have to build with everyone in mind every time (not that we necessarily did before, but it was definitely a default mindset for the industry). We can build things way more often for our exact use cases. It could “just work on my machine” and be feature-complete!
At the GitHub Universe closing keynote, Martin wanted to teach himself machine learning, so he built himself a pedometer onto his conference badge. He used Copilot to collect movement data from the badge’s accelerometer, trained a simple machine-learning model in his browser, and deployed it to the badge. Then he walked around to test whether it could tell the difference between walking, standing still, and fidgeting.
Imagine just a year or two ago wanting to dabble with machine learning. You totally could have! But for the average developer, that’s a daunting task. The barrier to entry for so many tougher concepts has gotten lower, and that means more people can experiment and have fun with any device they can think of, from a conference badge to a smart picture frame to a home TV.
AI with oversight
AI is top of mind all the time right now, but you are a part of the story, too.
In order to scale with AI, we need human judgement. We can see the AI tells in writing (“that’s the real unlock!”), in imagery (the fonts, man), or in code (commenting code blocks that have never been commented before). We need to keep the feedback loop, to be able to inspect, debug, and test what the agent produced, and to make whatever we’re building our own.
Be kind, keep maintainers in mind
It’s really fun to share your experiments with the world, but contributing to existing open source projects take a bit more consideration than that. Both our podcast episode and the keynote addressed this. We’re seeing maintainers get absolutely hammered with AI-powered contributions to their repositories, which adds a lot to the maintenance burden.
Efforts need to be made by all of us, like the one shared here, to help ease burdens for maintainers.
As Martin explained in the keynote, “Open source is the freedom to inspect, to remix, and to share without asking for permission. But it’s not the freedom to impose your will on others.”
Forking a repository gives you room to explore your own ideas, and there’s a really fun, exciting power in that. But before you impose those ideas on others and send them to the main repository, make sure you:
- Read the contribution guidelines
- Check existing issues
- Understand what the project needs
Respecting that work helps keep open source manageable (and even enjoyable) for the people looking after it.
Now it’s your turn
We answered the perennial question on our badge, “But can it run Doom?” Why yes, yes it does. Give it a go on our virtual badge, and try tinkering on it yourself.
Then get your hands on your own badge. We made some extra badges just for you. Order yours today, then tell us what you’ll be building. Plus, use code FREESHIPBLOG26 for free standard shipping through December 1, 2026.

articles.title: Norton baisse ses tarifs pour les fêtes avec des protections dès 24,99 euros
articles.text:
Achats du Black Friday : Norton réduit ses prix avec cinq appareils protégés pour 39,99 euros
Achats du Black Friday : Norton propose ses protections dès 24,99 € la première année. Comparez les offres pour 1, 3, 5 ou 10 appareils et les tarifs de renouvellement.
Les cadeaux se cherchent sur ordinateur, se comparent sur téléphone et finissent parfois dans le panier depuis une tablette.
Pour les fêtes, Norton propose ses abonnements dès 24,99 € la première année, et Norton 360 Deluxe couvre cinq appareils pour 39,99 €.
Avec Advanced à 44,99 €, cinq appareils supplémentaires coûtent seulement 5 € de plus.
Norton 360 Deluxe à 39,99 euros pour équiper le foyer
Un ordinateur pour commander les cadeaux. Un smartphone pour suivre les livraisons. Et, au milieu, des comptes clients dont les mots de passe méritent mieux qu'une variation du même prénom. À l'approche du Black Friday, une suite de sécurité trouve son intérêt dans ces petits usages qui s'accumulent.
Norton 360 Deluxe passe à 39,99 € la première année, contre un tarif de renouvellement affiché de 109,99 €/an. La réduction annoncée atteint 63 %, soit 70 € d'écart sur la première année. Le paiement est annuel : les 3,33 €/mois affichés correspondent à un équivalent, pas à une mensualité.
À ce prix, l'abonnement couvre cinq PC, Mac, smartphones ou tablettes, avec une protection contre les escroqueries, un VPN, le Dark Web Monitoring et le contrôle parental. Pour un couple équipé de deux ordinateurs et de deux téléphones, une place reste disponible pour une tablette. L'offre prend alors tout son sens.
Des protections utiles entre la commande et la livraison
Un faux suivi de colis, une boutique imitée, une pièce jointe reçue sans l’avoir demandée : les achats en ligne ne se limitent pas au moment du paiement. Les protections contre les escroqueries et les logiciels malveillants visent ces risques, avec des fonctions qui diffèrent selon l'appareil utilisé. Sur iPhone, il ne s'agit notamment pas d'une analyse antivirus du système comparable à celle d'un PC.
Le VPN, inclus dès Norton 360 Standard, chiffre la connexion entre l’appareil et son serveur. Il peut être utile sur un Wi-Fi public pendant une recherche de cadeau. Il ne garantit toutefois pas qu'un commerçant livrera sa commande : une boutique frauduleuse reste frauduleuse derrière un VPN.
Avec Deluxe, le Dark Web Monitoring ajoute une alerte lorsque des informations personnelles surveillées sont détectées sur le dark web. Cela permet de réagir, notamment en changeant un mot de passe compromis. Un gestionnaire de mots de passe peut faciliter l’utilisation d’identifiants différents pour chaque compte. Le contrôle parental peut aussi intéresser les familles, mais il ne s'installe pas sur le Mac d'un enfant et ses fonctions varient entre Windows, Android et iOS.

articles.title: La menace s’étend : le système OSINT de la CIA piraté, probablement par le même outil IA que la Commission européenne
articles.text:
ARTEX, voici le nom qui revient sans cesse dans les cyberattaques visant les institutions occidentales ces dernières semaines.
Le 24 novembre 2026, le New York Times a révélé, en s’appuyant sur une source proche du dossier, que des attaquants non identifiés avaient compromis un système d’OSINT de la CIA. L’intrusion aurait aussi touché le Bureau du directeur du renseignement national (ODNI) et la National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. Selon cette même source, les pirates se sont appuyés sur ARTEX, un logiciel open source qui confie à des agents d’IA les différentes étapes d’une intrusion informatique.
Ce nom avait déjà fait surface à Bruxelles. Le 19 novembre, Politico révélait qu’ARTEX avait servi dans la cyberattaque qui a paralysé pendant plus de dix jours les services internes de la Commission européenne.
Ce que l’on sait de l’intrusion à la CIA
Les informations disponibles sur le piratage des agences américaines restent minces. La CIA a refusé de commenter, et l’ODNI s’est contenté d’assurer à CNN qu’il n’y avait eu « aucune perturbation des capacités critiques ni des systèmes classifiés ».
Reste que l’outil visé rassemble des contenus publics ou achetés auprès de fournisseurs privés, comme des publications sur les réseaux sociaux, des images satellites ou des bases de données commerciales, qui peuvent devenir sensibles une fois croisés.
L’affaire tombe au milieu d’une série noire pour les institutions fédérales américaines. Quelques heures après les révélations sur la CIA, le FinCEN, la cellule de renseignement financier du Trésor américain, a annoncé enquêter sur un accès non autorisé à une partie de ses systèmes, sans que rien ne relie pour l’instant cet incident à ARTEX. Quelques jours plus tôt, le NCIC, le fichier national de la police fédérale géré par le FBI, avait déjà été la cible d’un piratage, selon BleepingComputer.
Qui se cache derrière l’attaque ?
Encore faut-il rappeler qu’un même outil ne fait pourtant pas un même attaquant. ARTEX a été publié sur GitHub en juillet 2026 par un développeur chinois connu sous le pseudonyme Autumn-27. Conçu pour aider les équipes de sécurité à tester leurs propres systèmes, l’outil a très vite été détourné. Son auteur a supprimé le dépôt début octobre, après la découverte de traces d’ARTEX dans des attaques contre de grandes banques sud-coréennes, mais de nombreuses copies circulent toujours.
Début novembre, le CERT-EU, le centre de cybersécurité des institutions européennes, aurait ainsi repéré l’usage d’ARTEX par des « hackers internationaux » contre la Commission, selon Politico, sans que Bruxelles désigne de responsable.
Dans son alerte du 13 novembre, le FBI indiquait que plus de 1 600 consoles ARTEX étaient exposées sur Internet début novembre.

articles.title: How to choose the next safe step in application modernization
articles.text:
How to choose the next safe step in application modernization
Learn how to assess a legacy application, choose a bounded modernization step, and reuse the method with a GitHub Copilot agent skill.
A request to modernize an application often starts with a technology question: Which framework should replace the old one? Before you choose, find out what still works. Then collect evidence that can act as a regression net for that behavior and show where modernization is necessary.
I used an evidence-first method on four public applications, from a small Node.js game to a large Java enterprise resource planning (ERP) application. Each needed a different treatment, but the way I collected evidence, chose the next experiment, and decided on possible proof points was repeatable.
This post walks through that process so you can apply it to one application of your own. It also shows how to encode the procedure in a GitHub Copilot agent skill while keeping architectural judgment with the people responsible for the system.
Build evidence before choosing a target
The label on an application rarely tells you enough. “Java microservices” doesn’t tell you which Java Development Kit (JDK) runs in production, where that version is pinned, whether the tests execute, or which interfaces other systems depend on. “Legacy monolith” doesn’t tell you whether the business core is broken or whether one retired platform dependency prevents the application from starting.
Before you recommend a change, build a small evidence inventory:
- Manifests, lockfiles, entry points, and deployable components
- Verified commands for installing, building, testing, packaging, and running
- Runtime pins in containers, CI workflows, deployment files, and developer tooling
- External contracts such as APIs, database behavior, file formats, and user workflows
- End-of-life frameworks and dependencies, with evidence that the application still uses them
Record uncertainty while you work. I use three simple labels: documented, inferred, and unverified. If two files disagree about the Java version, resolve the contradiction. If you can’t determine whether a CI check blocks merges, say so. Record the unknown rather than treating a guess as a finding.
That inventory gives you something concrete to review with the people who own the application before you propose changes.
Choose the least disruptive treatment that works
Once you understand the application, make the decision per component. A single system can contain code that should stay, dependencies that should be swapped, and one subsystem that genuinely needs a rewrite.
First, check whether a capability is still needed. Remove it only after verifying that it is unused or superseded and confirming that decision with its owner. Removal is a separate decision, and it’s not necessarily the most disruptive one.
For a capability you still need, start with the option that changes the least:
- Keep it. Supported code that still fits the job doesn’t need a modernization story.
- Upgrade it. Move to a supported major version and fix the breaking changes.
- Swap it. Replace an abandoned dependency while preserving the existing design.
- Wrap it. Stabilize a useful interface and replace the internals in increments.
- Rewrite it. Use this when no responsible upgrade path exists or the architecture cannot meet the requirement.
This is a decision order, not a universal ranking of effort or risk. Ask what evidence justifies choosing a more disruptive option. “The code is old” is not enough. A known vulnerability with no patched release for the pinned version, a dependency that fails on the required runtime, or a measured reliability target the current design cannot meet can justify escalation.
Decide what proof is possible
The next question is whether the component can run well enough to produce evidence, even if the legacy CI pipeline is not green.
Run a time-boxed feasibility check. Try to install dependencies, build on an available toolchain, start the component, and execute at least one meaningful test. Stop when the time box expires. The result sends you down one of two paths.
Capture behavior, then upgrade. Use this path when the old application can still run at an acceptable cost. Record its externally visible behavior, fix the test harness where practical, and use those checks to verify the upgrade.
Build a small modern slice first. Use this path when the old component cannot run until you have already changed it. Move the thinnest useful workflow to supported technology, prove it, and expand from there. Requiring a complete legacy test suite in this situation is circular. Restoring the test suite is part of the modernization.
I use the following safety levels, adapted from the doc-and-modernize skill, to describe the strongest regression protection available:
| Level | Strongest honest protection | 
|---|---|
| L0 | No usable regression net; treat the old code and available documentation as the specification. | 
| L1 | Small reversible changes, old and new paths in parallel, smoke checks, and domain review. | 
| L2 | Captured inputs and outputs, snapshots, or other behavioral comparisons. | 
| L3 | Automated checks cover part of the system, with the remaining gaps named. | 
| L4 | An automated CI gate combines lint, unit, behavioral, and end-to-end checks for the agreed scope. | 
State what you can prove and what risk remains. Even an L4 gate cannot establish that every possible behavior is correct. APIs, database effects, files, rendered output, and business workflows often make durable comparison points because those behaviors can survive a framework or language change.
PiggyMetrics: capture behavior, then upgrade
PiggyMetrics was the clearest example of an application that looked worse than it was. The project used Java 8, Spring Boot 2.0.3, Spring Cloud Finchley, Zuul, Hystrix, and the old spring-security-oauth2 library.
It would have been easy to call the application unworkable and start drawing a new architecture. The feasibility check told a different story.
The recorded feasibility results show these two probes against the legacy checkout with JDK 8:
| Command | Recorded result | What it established | 
|---|---|---|
| mvn -pl config -am compile | Exit code 0 | The selected config module and required reactor dependencies compiled. | 
| mvn -pl account-service -am test | 14 tests ran: five passed and nine errored | Some service logic passed; embedded MongoDB initialization blocked the other tests. | 
These are historical results, not commands expected to reproduce those failures on the modernized checkout. The nine errors traced through Failed to load ApplicationContext to an embedded MongoDB download returning HTTP 403. The pinned binary also targeted i386, which would not run on the Apple Silicon host.
The probes did not establish that the whole application ran or that its integration behavior was correct. They did give me a narrower next step: replace the test dependency and rerun the affected tests before changing the production stack.
That result saved me from making a very tidy, very expensive mistake. I had already started thinking about which parts of the architecture I might replace. One broken test dependency did not justify redesigning the application, and five passing tests established behavior I could check for unintended changes during modernization.
The modernization plan turned that evidence into a capture-then-upgrade sequence:
- Replace the embedded database dependency with Testcontainers and establish a green baseline on the existing stack.
- Put that baseline in GitHub Actions before changing the production runtime.
- Move from Java 8 to Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.3.
- Replace obsolete components behind their existing interfaces: Zuul with Spring Cloud Gateway, Hystrix with Resilience4j, and the retired OAuth stack with Spring Authorization Server and JSON Web Token (JWT) resource servers.
- Carry the baseline forward and add contract checks around the parts whose behavior changed.
The first acceptance gate was a passing baseline on the old stack, not merely the successful installation of a replacement dependency. Running checks in CI and enforcing them as merge requirements were also separate steps in the plan.
The result summary records the Java and Spring upgrades while retaining the microservice decomposition that the application exists to demonstrate. Eureka and Cloud Config stayed; the two monitoring modules used by the retired Hystrix and Turbine stack were removed. The in-scope build went from nine modules to seven.
Those versions describe the experiment, not a recommendation to select the same versions today. Choose targets against your current support requirements. The useful lesson is how the repository evidence narrowed the change.
The method changes with the system
The same process produced different answers on two smaller applications. Their pinned reports describe these choices:
| Application | What stayed | What changed | Strategy | 
|---|---|---|---|
| BrowserQuest | Canvas renderer, pathfinding, world model, protocol, and game-loop model | Node 0.4.7 to Node 22, two obsolete WebSocket stacks to ws, plus tests and GitHub Actions | Upgrade and swap | 
| DOOM | Renderer, 35 Hz simulation model, and WAD game-data format | X11 video and OSS audio replaced with SDL2; platform code adapted for modern 64-bit systems | Preserve the core and replace the platform | 
The comparison needs one important qualification: DOOM’s checks froze outputs from the modernized engine itself. They protected against later regressions; they did not independently prove parity with a period-correct legacy binary. Naming that limit is part of choosing an honest safety level.
Scaling the method without pretending the product is finished
I then applied the method to ADempiere, a large Java suite covering ERP, customer relationship management, manufacturing, supply chain, accounting, and point of sale.
The scale changed the controls, but not the method. The work established a reproducible build, moved the runtime to JDK 21, preserved SOAP web-service contracts while replacing XFire with CXF and Jakarta, captured legacy web behavior, and introduced a modern web path for selected users. The first modern business partner write was compared with a result frozen from the legacy application.
The fixed measurement report covers 30 merged modernization pull requests and 102,587.72 reconstructed Copilot credits through the first accepted portable demo. The credit total is not a dollar cost. More important, the report says exactly what the result was not: it was not a claim that every ADempiere screen or production deployment had been modernized.
I stopped because the proof-of-concept question had been answered. The result demonstrated a build on the selected runtime, old and new paths running together, and a real business write checked against the legacy result. Completing the rest would have required a product funding decision, not another technical proof. Stopping at that boundary was part of the method.
Turn the method into an agent skill
After repeating this work, I didn’t want the evidence checklist and decision rules to live only in my notes. I encoded them in the public doc-and-modernize agent skill.
Agent skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot can load when a task is relevant. A project skill can live with one repository:
.github/skills/doc-and-modernize/
├── SKILL.md
├── references/
└── scripts/
Only SKILL.md is required; the resource folders shown here are optional. The file needs YAML frontmatter with a name and a description explaining what the skill does and when to use it, followed by the instructions. The creation guide includes the full format.
Paraphrased from the commit-pinned skill source, its decision fork is:
- If the old component can run at an acceptable cost, capture its behavior before upgrading.
- If it cannot run without changes, build and verify a small modern slice first, then expand it.
The full skill adds the feasibility check, testability milestone, safety levels, phase gates, and evidence requirements.
The useful distinction is procedure versus policy. A shared skill can require repository evidence, bounded experiments, explicit safety levels, and runnable exit criteria. Your organization still needs to supply the parts only it knows:
- Approved runtimes, frameworks, and hosting services
- Application criticality and acceptable residual risk
- Security, compliance, and change-control requirements
- Which legacy or production results may be used as the expected answer
- Who can approve the architecture and declare a production change complete
The skill should make those decisions visible. It shouldn’t make them for you.
Start with one bounded application
Choose an application with an identified owner, known business value, and one workflow you can observe. Run the documentation workflow first. Review the architecture, commands, runtime surfaces, and unknowns with the people who own the system.
Then approve one experiment, not a portfolio rewrite.
Inspect the skill and its supporting files before adding it to a project. GitHub CLI’s gh skill commands are in public preview; check the current installation guidance when you’re ready to use them.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
  November 4, 2026
- Source:
  Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
  Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

Materials provided by Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo. Original written by José Tadeu Arantes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
